en: Bhairava, free from all affliction, was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa,
surrounded by Caṇḍa, Nandi, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, Vṛṣabha, and Bhṛṅgin.
The Great Lord was being praised by Kumāra, Indra, Yama, Āditya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, and was attended by the Gaṇas and the Mothers.
To the God who is the agent of creation and destruction, the cause of dissolution and maintenance, the bestower of grace, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him; SvaT_1.3.
Seeing Bhairava joyful, the Goddess spoke these words:
The Śrīdevī said:
"O Supreme Lord, that which you have told me regarding the *Svacchanda*," SvT 1.4.
The great tantra of the four seats, which extends for a hundred crores, is spread out with infinite divisions and brings about the arising of the fourfold fruit.
O Śaṃkara, human beings who possess little vigor and prowess, short lifespans, meager wealth, and weak resolve are unable [to achieve this].
For that purpose, please graciously explain its compendium, which expands upon the meaning of this concise scripture and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Maheśvara, what kind of guru and practitioner should one know?
What kind of person bestows fear and fearlessness, and what kind of ground is suitable for a disciple?
He [taught] the mantras in brief, as well as the time in brief;
the sacrifice, the oblation, the consecration, and the colored powders.
The five products of the cow, the sacrificial pap, the tooth-stick, the mandala,
initiation, the paths, consecrations, the pledges, and the means of accomplishment.
"Tell me likewise, O Maheśvara, how they achieve success by resorting to the Kali month.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, that you have thus urged me!"
For the sake of favoring mortals, I shall now tell you:
first of all, one should examine an Ācārya who possesses auspicious characteristics.
Born in the noble land, adorned with all his limbs,
he was a knower of the prescriptions of the Śiva scriptures and was proficient in both knowledge and the objects of knowledge.
He was devoted to divine rites, tranquil, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows;
he was endowed with courage and vigor, and possessed of compassion and courtesy.
Having obtained such a Guru— one who is renunciant, free from hypocrisy, and cultivated in the scriptures of Śiva— perfection and liberation are not far off.
He is prone to anger, fickle, mean-spirited, devoid of compassion and courtesy,
squint-eyed, protruding teeth, one-eyed, most wicked, and ignorant of the scriptures.
One who is excessively tall or short, emaciated or obese, afflicted by consumption,
a mere logician, possessed of hypocrisy, and devoid of truthfulness and purity.
One who is devoted to other scriptures does not bestow the fruit of liberation;
[the disciple], however, should be compassionate, steadfast, and free from hypocrisy and deceit.
Devoted to the gods, the fire, and the guru, he is devoted to the scriptures, firm in his vows,
intent on serving the guru, and endowed with perfectly tranquil senses.
Such indeed should be the disciple; he alone here is a vessel for grace.
One who is possessed by illusion, deceitful, cruel, devoid of truth, and fond of quarreling [is not].
One who is lustful, full of greed, devoid of devotion to Śiva,
and a reviler of the Guru and the scriptures, does not partake in liberation even if he has been initiated.
One should know that there is distress in one who is prone to anger, and that fortunes are fickle in one who is fickle;
moreover, O fair-faced one, a base preceptor destroys the accomplishment of the mantra.

Through one devoid of compassion comes misfortune; through one lacking skill, oppression by bandits; through one with squinting eyes, disease shall arise; and one with protruding teeth is a creator of strife.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one who is one-eyed causes enmity, and one who is bald brings about the destruction of wealth;
for one devoid of the scriptures, there shall be no success in initiation and other rites.
A long [tongue] should be known as a sign of fear of kings; a short one, the destruction of sons;
a thin one, a bringer of decline; and a thick one, a cause of calamities.
For one possessed by Kṣaya, death occurs; for a logician, there is execution or imprisonment;
and the hypocrite should be known as a producer of sin, O fair-faced one. (SvaT 1.26)
O Goddess, the mantras of one who is devoid of truth and the like do not succeed;
all of them are inauspicious, both in this world and in the next.
The ground, white, red, yellow, and black, purified by the boat-rite,
free from thorns, endowed with auspicious marks, and the accomplisher of all desired aims.
It was endowed with fragrant scents, adorned with heaps of flowers,
thick with the aroma of excellent incense, and beautified by a canopy above.
The teacher, having become pure, anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood, well-perfumed, serene in soul, and equipped with chalk and water; SvaT 1.30.
Facing either east or north, with a single-pointed mind and in a state of meditative composure,
one should spread out the *mātṛkā* there in its proper sequence from *a* to *kṣa*.
The beginning [of the alphabet], divided into sixteen parts, is indeed directly remembered as Bhairava;
likewise, the *ka*-group, the *ca*-group, the *ṭa*-group, and the letters *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*.
Endowed with the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra), Bhairavī is indeed known as the source (yoni);
one should worship the god Mātṛkābhairava with the letter-group *a*.
Bhairavī is to be worshipped with the *kā* group [of consonants]; one should worship her with the groups of Mothers (*mātṛvarga*).
Within the *a*-group is Mahālakṣmī, and within the *ka*-group is Kamalodbhavā.
In the *ca*-group is Maheśānī; in the *ṭa*-group is Kumārikā;
in the *ta*-group is Nārāyaṇī; and in the *pa*-group is Vārāhī.
Aindrī resides in the *ya*-group, while Cāmuṇḍā belongs to the *śa*-group;
these are the seven great Mothers (Mahāmātṛs) established throughout the seven worlds.
"One obtains all desires; thus Bhairava spoke to the Goddess. At the end, one should extract the mantras according to their sequential application."
The thirteenth [letter] joined with the Bindu is the supreme seat of Ananta;
by means of this, one should unite everything situated between the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
One should conceive of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśāna, and Śavānta;
one should fashion their form by means of the syllable *haṃsa* itself, distinguished by the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Above that, one should visualize the complete deity Svacchanda, who possesses a majestic crescent moon and has a luster like snow.
One should first utter the syllable OṂ, immediately followed by "aghorebhyaḥ";
having written "tha ghorebhyaḥ," one should then write the rest.
And from all those who are most terrible and even more terrible than the terrible, one should utter "Śarva" from all sides;
and from all [others], the other word "Namaste Rudra" should be uttered.
Having written [the mantra] from the forms (rūpa) and ending with the salutation, this king of mantras known as Aghora is praised by the gods. (SvaT 1.43)
O Goddess, when recited even once, it destroys all sins accumulated by those wandering through thousands of millions of births.
O Goddess, by remembering [this], one destroys darkness just as at the rising of the sun;
[the letters] beginning with *ya* and ending with *va* are joined together in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
The faces of Bhairava, joined with the Bindu at their crowns,
are to be applied in the manner of Brahmā, from the head down to the feet.

Furthermore, one should fashion faces looking upwards, eastward, southward, northward, and westward; having fashioned them, one should perform the ritual placement according to the division of the *kalās*.
And likewise the east, the south, the north, and the west;
the letter *kṣa*, whose form is that of Īśvara, is joined with the zenith above.
In this way, one should apply the fourfold face to the faces themselves;
as for that which is the fifth face, one should designate it by the syllable *kṣa*.
One should place [the mantras] in the heart, the neck, the shoulders, the back, the navel, the abdomen, the back, and the chest, respectively, with the Aghora mantra.
Likewise in the secret place and the anus, as well as in the thighs and the knees,
in the shanks and the buttocks, in the waist and on both sides.
And one should likewise place [the mantras] upon the left side of the body in due order:
the two feet, the two hands, the nose, the head, and then the two arms.
O Goddess, one should arrange all of this in due order by means of the *sadya* [mantra];
I shall now declare their names correctly and in proper sequence.
Tārā, Sutārā, Taraṇī, Tārayantī, and Sutāraṇī—
these five digits of Īśāna follow the stainless state (nirañjanapada).
Cessation, foundation, knowledge, and likewise peace—
these four are proclaimed as the powers (kalās) of the Person.
Delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age—these eight, O fair-complexioned lady, are indeed the powers (kalās) of Aghora. (SvaT 1.56)
Raja, Rakṣā, Rati, Pālyā, Kāmyā, Tṛṣṇā, Mati, Kriyā,
Ṛddhi, Māyā, Rātri, Bhrāmiṇī, and likewise Mohanī.
These are indeed the thirteen digits (kalās) of Manonmanī within Vāmadeva:
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Sudhā, and Sthiti.
Thus, the eight kalās of Sadyojāta have been fully proclaimed;
furthermore, O Goddess, the practitioner [should apply them] upon all the limbs in due order.
One should arrange the nine principles and the three principles with the *dhruva* mantra;
having further assigned the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*), hear their mantras, O Dear One.
Having written "Aghorebhyaḥ," one should write "Tha Ghorebhyaḥ" as the second,
and one should arrange the third as "Ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ."
O Śarva, one should arrange the fourth [syllable] for all [beings] from every side;
and the fifth, according to the rule, as "namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ."
O beautiful lady, one should first utter the syllable *oṃ*, and immediately thereafter the syllable *juṃ*; thus one should fashion the three eyes of the Vidyā-body.
One should know the auxiliary limbs of the Vidyā; learn from me their names as well:
Sarvātmā, Brahmaśiras, Jvālinī, and likewise Piṅgala.
The Pāśupata, which is difficult to pierce, and likewise that which is of the nature of light;
as well as Action, Knowledge, and Will—learn from me their mantras.
The letter at the end of *ha* (kṣa), joined with the fourth vowel (ī) and adorned with the bindu,
is declared to be the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which illuminates all creation.
The third letter after Śa, joined with the sixth vowel and provided with a bindu, is indeed known as Jñānaśakti; she is auspicious and the generator of awakening.
The letter *kṣa* joined with two vowels and intensified by the third and fifth [vowels] is declared to be the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) of Bhairava, whose nature is immeasurable.
The one called Haṃsa, conjoined with the Bindu, differentiated by the sixth vowel,
ending with the New Moon, the Nāda, and the Śakti, is known as the Niṣkala Svacchanda.
By the mere utterance of this [mantra], those who are burdened by all sins become like pure crystal and go to the state free from affliction.
One should fashion the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, Eyes, and Weapon mantras by using the six long vowels to differentiate the various classes of consonants.
The syllable Oṃ is their illuminator; at the end of these, one should arrange the birth [mantras]:
Namaḥ, Svāhā, Vauṣaṭ, Huṃ, Vaṣaṭ, and Phaṭ, in their proper sequence.
This Bhairavarāja is the accomplisher of all desires and goals;
it consists of "hara," "ī," and the letter "a," joined with the vowels beginning with "ṅ."
The letter *ya* joined with *e*, followed by the letter *ṣa* and modified by the letter *la*;
then the letter *la* joined with three vowels, and *haṃsa* conjoined with the *bindu*.
Endowed with the sixth vowel and terminated by the syllable *phaṭ*,
she is renowned as Aghoreśvarī, who moves within the lap of Svacchanda.
She is endowed with the limbs of Bhairava and joined with five faces;
[the mantra consists of] the letter *ya*, ending with *ha* and beginning with *ya*, ending with *ra*, beginning with *ra*, and joined with the sixth vowel.
Through the union of the bindu and the nāda, Kapāleśa is proclaimed;
the bindu ending in 's' (sa) with fire (ra) below, joined with the sixth vowel (ū), is thus celebrated.
O fair-faced one, he who is known as Śikhivāhana should be understood as Saṃhāra,
joined with the sixth [vowel] and endowed with the end of the sixth [group].
The King of Wrath has been fully described—
[the rest is omitted]— and likewise I shall tell you another:
[the syllable] beginning with *ña*, joined with the sixth vowel, and endowed with three feet.
O fair-faced one, it is conjoined with the Bindu at its head, is Vikarāla,
joined with the letter beginning with Śa, and also possesses the sixth vowel below.
Overpowered by the fourteen vowels and adorned with the Bindu and the end of the Nāda,
this is indeed declared to be Manmatha, who is saluted by gods and Siddhas.
By means of this, indeed, all this world—both stationary and moving—is one's own;
it is joined with "Ha" and "Ra" and so forth, situated below the letter "Ū" and accompanied by the nasal bindu.
For this Bhairava is proclaimed as Meghanādeśvara;
he is joined with the letter *kṣa* followed by a nasal drop (*bindu*) and differentiated by the fifth vowel.
Someśvara is proclaimed as the destroyer of birth and death;
it is joined with the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *ya*, and placed below with the letter *ha*.
The radiant one, ending in *la*, beginning with *ra*, joined below with *ru*,
endowed with the point (*bindu*), the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and accompanied by *nāda* and *śakti*.
He is proclaimed as the King of Knowledge (Vidyārāja), the destroyer of great sins;
indeed, this group of eight Bhairavas is celebrated as his retinue.
Likewise, having extracted the world-protectors (lokapālas) preceded by their own names and the syllable *praṇava*,
one should fully conceptualize them along with the words "homage" (*namas*) and "obeisance" (*namaḥ*), together with their weapons.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Extraction of Mantras," in the Svacchandatantra.
Now begins the second chapter:
I shall now explain the ritual of worship (arcana) correctly and in its proper sequence.
Having performed purification, one should then perform a bath with earth and water.
O fair-faced one, having first taken earth from a pure place and purified it with the Astra-mantra,
one should wash the riverbank and place that earth there.
Then, O slender-waisted one, the two parts should be divided by means of the weapon-mantra;
with half of a part, one should likewise fashion the hips, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet.
One should wash [the vessel] according to the rule by performing the yoga three times with intervals;
then, taking half of the remaining portion, it should be consecrated with the weapon-mantra.
O beautiful woman, one should cause [the body] to be illuminated by the sun for seven recitations;
then, having massaged from the head down to the feet, one should perform the ritual bath.
Having emerged from the midst of the water and performed the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) in the proper sequence,
one should perform the salutation to the twilight (saṃdhyā) according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
Thus is the impure bath; now we shall explain the ritual bath:
take that which was previously situated as one part, and from that, divide it into three parts.
On the left hand, in the east, south, and north respectively,
one should then consecrate the eastern portion with the Astra-mantra seven times.

O fair-faced one, having likewise consecrated the one situated in the south with mantras through its faces, and having similarly consecrated the northern one with the deity joined by its limbs; SvaT_2.9.
Having taken the eastern portion, one should cast it in the ten directions;
with the northern portion, however, one should consecrate the water itself.
O lady of excellent vows, remembering Bhairaveśa with an arm’s length [of cloth],
one should veil oneself on the right side.
One should bathe with royal honors using fragrant *āmalaka* and other substances;
furthermore, the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) should be performed with the *Bhairava* mantra.
Having emerged from the midst of the water, one should change that garment;
having performed ritual ablution and established the protective placement (*nyāsa*), one should recollect the root mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, having taken up the *tīrtha* water, one should place it before oneself;
standing there, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*), and so forth, in due order.
O fair-faced one, the Aghamarṣaṇa rite should be performed, followed by the worship of the Sun;
having performed the recitation and offered it thus, one should prostrate.
Having performed the libation for the mantras together with the gods and the sages,
as well as for all the hosts of beings, one should then withdraw the sacred site (tīrtha).
Having recollected the root mantra, thereafter the bath with ashes should be performed,
followed by the bath for removing impurities, with the inner self thoroughly purified through meditation.
Then, having changed his garment, he should perform the twilight worship as before;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual bath while recollecting Bhairaveśa.
One should sprinkle the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the ends of the feet in their respective order with the Bhairava-mantra accompanied by its ancillary limbs.
One should perform the consecration while recollecting the supreme reality;
one should perform the salutation at the twilight [devotions] as before, O lady of excellent countenance.
Then, having gone to the sacrificial hall, one should wash both hands and feet;
having tied the topknot and meditated upon the topknot, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya) according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, O lady of excellent vows, he should take a flower,
pay homage to the Mothers of the Directions, and carefully sprinkle the entrance with water.
By means of the water of Śiva and the Astra-mantra, the expulsion of obstacles shall occur.
Above the door-jamb, one should likewise [worship] the god Gaṇeśa and Śrī.
Having worshipped [the deity] in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense and the like,
and with offerings of water for the guest (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), one should then proceed to the north of the door.
Having worshipped Nandi and Gaṅgā, and Mahākāla to the south,
one should also fully honor Kālindī according to the sequence of the ritual order.
Having recited the Bhairava-weapon mantra and taken up a flower while remaining in meditative absorption,
one should empower it seven times so that it becomes filled with blazing crests of fire.
By the employment of the iron-arrow weapon (nārācāstra), one should enter into the middle of the house;
by that, the entire infinite web of obstacles is warded off.
Then, one should cast the protective mantra in the ten directions;
having worshipped Brahmā in the center with perfumes and flowers in due order.
Then, having sat upon the seat established on the *praṇava*-seat within the southern form, one should assume the previously well-practiced posture situated before oneself.
Having smeared the two hands with fragrance, one should purify them with the Astra-mantra;
having enveloped them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should then drench them with nectar.
Having thoroughly agitated the supreme power (parā śakti), one should then conceive of Ananta;
having assigned the form (mūrti), one should likewise conceive of the faces according to the Svachchanda.
One should assign the five limbs from the thumb to the little finger;
having also visualized the Bhairavas, one should recollect the supreme reality.
Three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) should be performed as the cause for the purification of the body;
having expelled one's own impure wind, one should fill the body with pure [air].
Having performed retention and exhalation, one should cause the self to rest in space—
subtle like a firefly and devoid of the sense organs.
Listen now to how the self itself becomes Śiva—devoid of all objective activity and with its sphere of perception destroyed by Māyā. (SvaT 2.35)
But having grasped the supreme state, O beloved, the body should then be dried up by means of the differentiated withdrawal [mantra] conjoined with the seed-syllable of Rudra.
By that very [seed-syllable], the burning should be performed, joined with fire above and below;
below, it is conjoined with Viṣṇu, having the color of wind and accompanied by the bindu.
For this is known as the purifier; in the rite of immersion, it is remembered as belonging to Varuṇa.
When the nasal drop (bindu) is joined with the head [of the vowel], there then arises the placement of Śakti.
One should bring that [consciousness] back as it was brought forth and flood it with nectar;
for its consciousness has been obscured by impurity and it is dependent upon *kalā* and *vidyā*.
Its self is colored by passion (rāga), likewise fashioned by time (kāla),
further restrained by necessity (niyati), and augmented by the state of being a person (puṃbhāva).
Endowed with the primary intention, possessed of the three qualities,
seated upon the principle of intellect (buddhi), and enveloped by the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).
By means of the mind, the intellect, the organs of action, the sense organs, the subtle elements, and the gross elements—
and by means of the *praṇava*— all that is the cause for the arising of the body.
O Goddess, one should place them in sequence, numbering thirty-one;
O fair-faced one, the six principles (ṣaṭtattvī) connected with the self should be understood here.
The body is fashioned down to the primary earth element,
and the twenty-four principles are indeed devoid of consciousness.
O lady of excellent limbs, all these [images] presided over by a person should indeed always be regarded as sentient; they must always be known as such.
This is declared to be the primordial *pañcaviṃśaka* (the group of twenty-five);
from that, O Goddess, one should place the form, well-characterized by the root mantra.
O Sulocanā, having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the entire thirty-two-syllable Bhairava mantra,
one should thereafter fashion the faces from the head down to the feet.
Thereafter, one should fashion the faces— the upper, the eastern, the southern,
the northern, and the western— according to their proper divisions.
One should arrange the path to be purified according to its divisions of *kalās* as before:
the nine principles (*tattvas*), the three principles, the limbs of *vidyā*, and the three eyes.
The *kṣurikā* [mantra], transcending the groups (*vargātīta*), ignited by fire above and below,
and struck by the sixteen [vowels] within, is indeed the protector that destroys obstacles.
One should first arrange nine [syllables] on the head, the face, and the throat;
then on the heart, the region of the navel, the secret place, the thighs, and the knees.
Having likewise placed [the mantra] at the end of the feet, conjoined with the qualities of one's own meditation,
[one should place] action, knowledge, and will on the right, the left, and in the middle.
For this Bhairava, the king of vidyās and leader of mantras, is thus remembered;
having invoked him in his partless form (niṣkala), one should likewise [invoke] the limbs in their proper sequence.
One should worship the Lord of the gods with perfumes, incenses, various flowers, and diverse kinds of food and edibles, all mentally prepared.
Having meditated upon oneself as Bhairava, one should then perform the ritual in the heart;
having established the bulb (kanda) at the navel, its stalk should be twelve finger-breadths long.
One should visualize [the mandala] as far as the end of the heart; therein, one should contemplate a lotus with eight petals, greatly radiant, adorned with filaments, and possessing a pericarp.
There, O fair-complexioned one, the bulbous root consists of power (*śakti*), while the thorns upon the stalk are indeed those very worlds of the Rudras.
The knot, which consists of *māyā*, is situated on the impure path;
the lotus of *vidyā* is greatly radiant, shining with the seed-syllables in its pericarp.
And the lotuses there, O Goddess of gods, are known as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Having thus meditated upon the auspicious Great Lotus, which consists of all the gods.
First there should be the placement of the power (śakti), and immediately after that, the bulb (kanda).
One should then conceive of the sprout and the arrangement of the stalk as Ananta.
One should sequentially place Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya— consisting of light, exceedingly bright, and radiant with shimmering rays.
White, red, yellow, and black, they are situated in the directions starting from the southeast to the northeast;
these pedestals are in the form of lions, three-eyed, and of terrifying prowess.
The hero should deposit the mantras consisting of Śiva and Śakti;
adharma, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty [are deposited] in the eastern direction and the others.
The northern boundary should be established by the Gātrakas, who are white in color;
and the joining-pins (saṃdhānakīlaka) are like the flax flower (atasīpuṣpa).
O beloved, the Vedas and the Yugas must likewise be known in their proper sequence;
one should contemplate the lower covering as red and the upper as white.
One should understand that darkness (tamas) is in the center; these qualities (guṇas) are thus established.
One should understand the white lotus and should contemplate its filaments.
The [lotuses] at the base, middle, and tip are white, red, and yellow respectively;
the pericarp resembles gold, while the seeds are green.
Having placed Vāmā on the eastern petal, Jyeṣṭhā on the petal facing the southeast, Raudrī on the southern petal, and Kālī in the region of the southwest; SvaT 2.68.
One should place the goddess Kalavikaraṇī on the petal belonging to Varuṇa,
and the goddess Balavikaraṇī resting upon the petal belonging to Vāyu.
One should employ the goddess Balapramathanī in the north,
and one should employ Sarvabhūtadamanī in the northeast.
One should place the goddess Manonmanī in the center upon the pericarp;
O Goddess, the Śakti-maṇḍala, resembling a rainbow, is to be meditated upon.
In the center, one should meditate upon Manonmanī, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns;
having joined the moon with the solar orb on the petal, [one places it] in the filaments.
O Goddess, one should place the circle of fire within the pericarp;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are known as the presiding deities of the circles.
Brahmā has four faces and is red in color; he is adorned with four arms, wears a black antelope skin as an upper garment, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
O Goddess, he holds a water-pot and likewise has a staff in his hand;
the God holds a rosary and has a lotus in his hand, with beautiful eyes.
Having meditated upon Him, who resembles an *atasī* flower and holds the conch, discus, and mace, one should place Him upon the leaves; this destroys all sins.
The god wears yellow garments and is adorned with a forest garland;
his crown-jewel flashes, and he is embellished by a network of tiny bells.
Having meditated upon the high-souled Viṣṇu, who wears divine earrings and is seated upon the throne of Garuḍa, one should place him within the filaments [of the lotus].
White as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, holding a trident in his hand, three-eyed,
ten-armed, large-eyed, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
O fair-faced one, having meditated upon Rudra— clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with the moon, blue-throated, and mounted upon the bull— [one should perform the rite].
One should place [the mantra] that destroys great sins upon the pericarp;
thereafter, one should install the Great Preta, laughing and conscious.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the entire seat of Bhairava, which is red in color, possessed of great splendor, and adorned with three eyes, by means of the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should then visualize the form [of the deity],
shaped like a *kadamba* flower and possessing the luster of the moon.
Above the form, one should visualize the god Bhairava as possessing all parts (sakala),
adorned with the thirty-two phonemes, blazing like a flash of lightning.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should visualize the faces through one's own meditation,
from the head down to the feet, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should conceive of the path to be purified as consisting of thirty-eight divisions of *kalās*,
as well as the nine principles (*tattvas*) and the three principles known as the group of nine called Bhairava.
One should arrange the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga), as well as the eye and the razor;
then one should install the three powers (śaktitraya) in the regions of the right, the front, and the left.
O Goddess of the gods, one should then contemplate the form [of the deity] in the middle region—
the God with fifteen eyes, adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Resembling ten million moons, with a crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
five-faced and large-eyed, adorned with snakes and a cow-nose.
He is adorned with scorpions glowing like fire, resplendent with a necklace,
decorated with a garland of skulls, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The god holds a noose and a goad, carries an arrow in his hand, and wields the Pināka bow;
he grants boons and fearlessness with his hands, and carries a severed head and a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Holding a lute and a hand-drum, with a bell in his hand and bearing a trident,
he displays the majesty of a vajra-staff and holds an axe as a weapon in his hand.
He is resplendent with a variegated, round mallet;
he is clothed in a lion skin and wears an elephant hide as an upper garment.
O Maheśānī, one should meditate upon the god who has eighteen arms, a blue throat, and great splendor, with his face turned upward and possessing the luster of crystal.
The eastern face is yellow, with the luster of a blue lotus petal;
one should know the southern face and likewise contemplate the northern one.
One should contemplate the western [face] as resembling the flower of the pomegranate, like saffron water, and similar in appearance to a mass of moons.
The man who, with a disciplined mind, meditates upon the god Svacchandabhairava, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, will quickly attain perfection.
Then, by means of the supreme seed-syllable, [one should worship] the Supreme, the ultimate cause,
the perfectly tranquil, partless God, who is all-pervading and stainless.

With a joyful heart, O Goddess, I shall tell you how one should invoke [the deity] who is established within the heart, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the end of the subtle sound (nāda).
Having invoked the Supreme Lord, who is unwavering and beyond all causes,
and having established the God according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the imposition of the six limbs.

O Goddess of the gods, one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, and thereafter a welcome; then, with the Niṣṭhurā [mudrā], one should effect the ritual confinement (saṃnidhāna).
Having perfumed him with scents, flowers, and incense, one should worship him;
thereafter, one should display the mudrās three times during the ritual performed at the three periods of the day.
Then, O fair-faced one, having performed the rites of bathing and so forth, and having caused [the disciple] to put on fine garments made of silk cloth; SvaT_2.103.
Having anointed [the deity] with agallochum and camphor, one should adorn [him] with a crown and other ornaments;
one should worship and further embellish [him] with various kinds of pure flowers.
O Maheśānī, having offered the *argha*, one should again display the mudrās,
having prostrated before the god Bhairava, the independent Lord of the universe.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, the ornaments should be placed on the exterior,
starting from the northeast, proceeding to the east, south, and ending in the north.
One should arrange five faces, each endowed with five mouths,
together with ten arms and a crown of the moon.
One should meditate upon their true forms, granting boons and fearlessness,
and place them in the four directions— namely, the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.
The heart, head, crest-lock, armor, and weapon are to be applied according to their respective divisions:
the heart has the luster of the color red, and the head has the brilliance of yellow orpiment.
One should contemplate the Goddess as having a crest resembling a circle of lightning;
one should know her armor to be smoky-grey and her weapon to be tawny-brown.
Resembling the form of light, the eye is situated in the center;
all are remembered as having five faces, ten arms, and being adorned with the moon.
Adorned with various ornaments, anointed with various garlands and perfumes,
and dressed in various garments, they were radiant with beautiful crowns.
Bound with garlands of jewels and adorned with necklaces and armlets,
they have the appearance of sixteen-year-olds, possessing beautiful forms and enduring youth.
The mantras beginning with Bhairava are known as the lords of the seats (pīṭheśas) and the destroyers of the seats;
she who was previously described by me as Aghorī is the supreme Śakti.
Having worshipped Bhairava, one should place her upon his lap;
for the form of Bhairavī is indeed exactly like that of Bhairava.
One should always meditate upon Bhairavī, whose face is slightly terrifying, whose voice is deep and vast, whose countenance is serene, and whose eyes are wide with wonder.
O Goddess, one should place the eight Bhairavas in the second enclosure:
Kapālīśa in the east and Śikhivāhana in the southeast.
In the south is the Wrathful King Vikarāla,
in the southwest is Manmatha, in the western quarter is Meghanādeśvara.
Having placed the Goddess in the northwest, and likewise the Moon-King in the north,
one who is well-concentrated should place the Knowledge-King in the northeast.
They have five faces and three eyes, ten arms, and the crescent moon as their crest;
they are adorned with garlands of skulls and embellished with shimmering rubies.
O Goddess, yellow is remembered as being in the east; red is in the domain of Agni;
in the south is that which has the luster of a blue cloud; and in the southwest is that with the brilliance of fire.
It is dark blue in the western direction, smoke-colored in the domain of the northwest,
with the luster of the moon's orb in the north, and the brilliance of crystal in the northeast.
And in the third [circle], one should likewise imagine the Lords of the World together with their weapons;
I shall state their names correctly and in proper sequence.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, and Samīraṇa; Soma-rāja, Kubera, Īśāna, and Parameśvara.
O fair-faced one, they should be meditated upon in the form of the eight Bhairavas:
the vajra, the spear, the staff, the sword, and likewise the noose.
The banner, the mace, and the trident are indeed the weapons of the world-protectors;
[he should also visualize] the thunderbolt, rich with many colors, and the spear, possessing a luster like gold.
One should visualize the staff as having the luster of split collyrium, the sword as having the radiance of a blue lotus,
the noose as having the appearance of a *kiṃśuka* flower, and the banner as white.
Having worshipped the mace, which has the luster of coral, and the trident, which has a radiance equal to lightning,
one should perform the entire rite of the enclosure and the unification within the leader of the mantra.
The weapons, the world-protectors, the eight Bhairavas,
the five Brahmās, and likewise the limbs— these indeed are the enclosures.
One should pronounce everything in sequence until that which is the Lord within the womb;
furthermore, the joining of the channels (nāḍī) must be performed with the root mantra.
Having visualized [the deity] as far as the limit of the future, one should present the food offerings:
*ghārikā*, *vaṭaka*, *śaṣkulī*, and likewise *modaka*.
One should prepare bowls of sugar-candies and laddus, various kinds of edible foods, rice cooked with *śāli* grains, and lentil soup seasoned with clarified butter.
One should prepare for Kauśalyā cakes made of lentils, as well as honey-topped sweets,
cilakas smeared with ghee, and salted foods.
Various appetizers, both pungent and sweet,
as well as *rasālā*, curd, milk, and various kinds of fermented liquor.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should fill the foremost portion of Śambhu with various kinds of fish and meat, as well as whatever foods are fit to be licked or drunk.
Thereafter, the arghya offering should be presented with well-scented liquor;
subsequently, one should display the mudrā three times during the ritual performed at the three periods of the day.
Then, having performed prostration, one should subsequently perform the recitation (japa),
having taken up a rosary that has been worshipped with perfumes and flowers.
With speech restrained and the mind well-composed, seated upon a lotus throne,
one should recite the root mantra and contemplate it as dissolved into the resonance (*nāda*).
Having opened his eyes and reflected [upon the deity], he should then begin the recitation;
the flow of syllable after syllable should be neither too fast nor too slow.
Those desiring liberation should perform the recitation (japa) while remaining in the day, equalizing it with the vital breath (prāṇa);
that indeed should be known as the withdrawal (saṃhāra), which bestows the fruit of the abode of Śiva.
When the sound, having reached the void, returns once again,
that should be known as the night, lasting until it has returned to the heart-lotus.
This emanation has been fully described as the source of the fruit of all accomplishments;
O fair-faced one, one should always contemplate one's own form as Bhairava.
His obstacles shall perish and his recitation shall become fruitful;
having performed the recitation, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, he should offer it to Bhairava.
O Goddess, by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka), that which abides in the three and is endowed with the triad is declared to be the secret bestower of the threefold accomplishment.
In rites for pacification (śāntika), the recitation is mental; in rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), it is said to be whispered (upāṃśu);
and in rites of sorcery (abhicāra), it is with sound. [The practitioner should face] east, north, or south.
That which the self does not hear is proclaimed to be mental (mānasa);
that which is heard by the self alone is known as whispered (upāṃśu).
O Goddess, that which others hear is said to be "with sound.
The rosary, together with Mount Meru, consists of exactly one hundred and eight beads.
[The rosary] may be made of rudrākṣa, conch, lotus seeds, putrajīvaka, or pearls;
likewise, it may be made of crystal, precious gems, gold, or coral.
O Goddess of the gods, ten rosaries are prescribed for householders;
having meditated upon the thread as the Supreme Śakti, one should then [meditate upon] the beads as the portions of the paths (adhvabhāga).

The path of Śiva is the locus of manifestation; therefore, one should then contemplate that which possesses those attributes (the manifest world), constructing it with twenty-seven, or twice, or four times that number [of elements].

The wise man should not transgress that single [reality] consisting of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), which is formed by the union of all [principles] and resides at the beginning, and which is the cause of both emanation and reabsorption.
O woman of excellent complexion, for those heroes who delight in the posture of a hero,
the great conch-shell rosary indeed bestows the fruit of all desires.
A householder should not perform anything that causes great agitation;
therefore, the best of practitioners should recite using a crystal rosary.
One should accomplish various desires— whether inferior, middling, or superior—
in this way, the all-pervading Bhairava, who resides within the heart-lotus, is to be worshipped.
Having made [the self] both external and internal, one should thereafter begin the sacrifice;
therein, at the outset, there should indeed be an *argha* vessel made of gold or likewise of silver.
Having taken a vessel made of conch, pearl-oyster shell, mother-of-pearl, copper, or even clay,
or one made from the leaf or petiole of a lotus, and having washed it with water, [one should proceed].
O Goddess of the Gods, having smeared [the vessel] with agallochum and sandalwood consecrated by the recitation of the mantra,
and having fumigated it with refined incense, one should then fill it with water.
Having purified it with a cloth filter and reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should strike [the site];
then, having enveloped it with the armor-mantra (*varma*), one should perform the sacrifice right there.
Having briefly sprinkled the collection of materials intended for sacrifice according to the previously stated procedure, one should then commence the sacrifice.
Then, first of all, one should deposit the Śakti, which has the form of space, brilliantly blazing,
all-pervasive, subtle, supported by Śiva, and omnipresent.
One should worship the Goddess illuminated by the syllable Oṃ, ending with a prostration,
and likewise install Ananta, as well as Dharma and Jñāna.
Dispassion and likewise sovereignty [arise] in the sequence beginning with the southeast (āgneyī);
and likewise non-virtue, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty.
O Goddess, [one should fashion] the joining-pins, the lower covering, and the upper part; the lotus with its filaments, the pericarp, and the petals.
The triad of maṇḍalas, the deities, and the powers ending with Śiva;
the form, the network of Brahmā’s kalās, the nine principles, and the three principles.
[He meditates upon] the eight Bhairavas, the Vidyās, the limbs, the eye, as well as the Kṣurikā;
the three powers, the Supreme God, accompanied by the six limbs.
O Goddess, having performed the ritual placement, one should constantly meditate according to the prescribed rule,
having brought it to completion in accordance with the method, with a joyful inner self.
One should perform the welcoming, the offering of water for the feet, and likewise the presentation of the guest-offering,
while obstructing [the obstacle] with a harsh [utterance], recollecting the root mantra.
An extensive worship should be performed with perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth;
thereafter, one should display the mudrās three times during the ritual action at the three periods of the day.
Then, O fair-faced one, the enclosure should be established on the outside;
one should arrange it starting from the northeast, proceeding through the east, south, north, and ending at the west.
O Goddess, the five faces, endowed with the qualities of their respective meditations, are located in the southeast,
northeast, southwest, northwest, and also in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Rakṣas, Soma, and Indra.
The northern limit should be established, and likewise the pentad of limbs;
the eye, indeed, is situated in the eastern direction within the pericarp.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*) and the water for the feet (*pādya*) for all [deities] with their respective mantras;
the practitioner should never mix the flowers with different mantras.
One should not arrange the mantras behind one's back;
they must be given in their proper sequence, and one should never transgress the mantras under any circumstances.
One should simultaneously visualize [the deities] conjoined with their respective mudrās and mantras;
one should constantly perform the offering of water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and incense (dhūpa) for that long.
This procedure has been proclaimed for all mantras alike;
one should visualize the eight Bhairavas together with the world-protectors (lokeśas) and their weapons.

Outside, one should arrange the layout of the cremation grounds (śmaśāna), beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, according to the prescribed rule, starting from the east and extending to the northeast.
And first, indeed, [he visualizes] the powerful Āmardaka, the lord of the cremation grounds,
together with cremation grounds featuring headless trunks and terrifying impaled corpses.
With blazing funeral pyres and the most terrifying howls of jackals,
there is the fire named Agni in the southern quarter, and likewise the one called Kāla in the west.
Likewise, Ekapāda is in the north, Tripurāntaka in the southeast,
Agnijihva in the southwest, and Karālin in the northwest.
In the northeast is Bhīmavaktra; these are proclaimed as the lords of the cremation grounds.
One should satisfy them with fish, meat, and the like, as well as with various kinds of fermented liquors.
One should cause incense, flowers, and likewise incense smoke to be offered to all;
then, having performed prostration and being well-concentrated, one should recite the mantra.
Having offered [the oblation] according to the ritual procedure by means of the practice of exhalation (recaka),
and having performed prostrations with the sound "huḍḍuṅkāra," one should then depart.

Then, well-purified and with water for the guest-offering (argha) in hand, he should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which is endowed with the proper characteristics, with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (astra) near the fire-pit.
Having enveloped this with the Kavaca mantra, one should draw it with a blade of Darbha grass;
then, having lifted it up, O beautiful lady, one should sprinkle it with the Astra mantra.
With that [material], one should perform filling and leveling;
with it, one should also carry out sprinkling, pounding, and plastering.
One should perform the sprinkling and drying with the Astra-mantra itself;
likewise, one should perform the worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and the consecration with the sword.
The vajra-consecration is performed with the weapon-mantra; there are three lines facing east and west, and one facing south and north—this is proclaimed as the vajra.
As quoted, with attribution to the *Svatantra*,
in the commentary on *Mṛgendra/Karmapada* 6:2–4:
"The three lines proceeding toward the east are made into vajras by means of the weapon-mantra."
That which faces south and north is proclaimed as this vajra.

O Goddess, for the purpose of establishing a house, that fire-pit should be covered both inside and out with sacrificial grass (darbha) spread with the tips pointing eastward, using the very same [grass] used for the sword.
On the southern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should prepare a seat of dry cow dung,
a grass mat (viṣṭara) with Darbha grass, and flowers, using the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having established Brahmā by means of the vocative case, one should worship him with his own name joined to the word "namaḥ" at the end, together with his own meditative visualization. SvaT 2.190.
With flowers and other offerings, with fine incense and so forth, and with the *dhruva* mantra in due order,
one should [offer] at the crossroads and in the center of the sacrificial pit with two *darbha* blades and the *praṇava*.
With the two [fingers] of the eastern *saubhya* [mudrā], one should offer a seat (*viṣṭara*) and upon that a flower; one should worship it with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

And having summoned Vāgīśī, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, she who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus and possesses beautiful eyes like those of a woman in her season; SvaT 2.193.
Having meditated upon the Goddess in this manner— endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with all the secondary limbs— one should establish her in the center of the sacrificial pit.

One should worship her— who is lying supine like a woman in her fertile season— with scents, flowers, and other offerings, while recollecting the mantra of Bhava, with one's head directed toward the northeast.
Then, the knower of mantras should display the mudrā for the sake of bringing [the deity] into proximity;
then, taking the vessel of fire, he should sprinkle it with auspicious water using the Astra-mantra.
Having enveloped [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship with the Praṇava alone,
according to the prescribed rule, [visualizing the deity] arising from the forest and so forth, extending from the worlds up to the fire.
Having meditated upon Agni as being like semen, one should worship his consciousness with the *praṇava* and perform the six-limbed worship with the *dhruva* mantra for the sake of immortality.
Having meditated on oneself as Bhairava and having meditated on the fire as being like a seed-syllable,
one should cause it to descend by circling it three times outside the pit with the *dhruva* mantra.
Having cast [the seed] into the womb like a seed with the Bhairava-śivāmbhas,
the wise one, having recited the Astra-mantra and sprinkled it, should cover the womb.
Then, one should place the axle-pit with a blade of *darbha* grass while reciting the *dhruva-mantra*;
likewise, one should arrange [the site] in the four directions using *darbha* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
One should tie a bracelet made of *darbha* grass on the right hand with the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) recited seven times, while remaining mindful of that Weapon-mantra.
Therefore, for the sake of protecting the one whose womb contains fire, there must be the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*).
As it is stated in the venerable *Svatantra*: [quoted in the *Mṛgavāra* ad *Kulapañjikā* 6:9ab].
Having consecrated *darbha* grass with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) seven times, one should bind a weapon-bracelet (*astrakaṅkaṇa*) on the right hand while recollecting the weapon-mantra,
for the sake of protecting that which contains the weapon within.
Furthermore, one should perform worship with three oblations using the heart-mantra.
Having offered three oblations with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) is accomplished;
indeed, one should cause a drop of water to fall here upon the tip of a *darbha* blade while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the *śikhā* [mantra];
likewise, one should offer three oblations with the *uttara* [mantra] and three oblations with the *śikhā*.
For it is indeed the conception of a male; a female is not produced in the womb.
One should perform the *sīmanta* rite with the right hand using the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass.
One should fashion the neck, the shoulders, the waist, the arms, and the shanks;
having thus conceived the various limbs, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) should take place.
One should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and with three oblations offered while holding the head [of the vessel];
one should then divide the fire into three parts—the eastern, the middle, and the western.
Furthermore, through the fire-oblation (*homa*), that which consists of the three principles (*tritattvaka*) [is purified] in the regions of the mouth, heart, and feet;
as it is stated in the venerable *Svacchanda-tantra*: [quoted in the *Mṛgendravṛtti* ad *Kiraṇapañjikā* 6:11c–12b].
One should divide the fire into three parts— eastern, middle, and western—
and [place them] respectively in the regions of the mouth, heart, and feet with oblations of the three principles (*tritattva*).
Then, with five oblations, one should [offer] the heads with the upward-facing [fire] in groups of three each.
Having visualized the five faces— namely the central, eastern, southern, northern, and western—
one should offer oblations three times each with the eastern face.
In the same way, one should perform the expiation for the faces with three oblations;
having assigned an eye to each eye, one should thus assign three [eyes] to each of the faces.
One should perform everything with sesame seeds using exactly three oblations;
then [one should offer for] the collection of kalās, five and then four.
Likewise, eight, three, ten, and eight [limbs] in sequence;
having thus fashioned the remaining [parts] with these, the form of the *kalā* (digit) then comes into being.
Thereafter, one should assign the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their proper order;
one should offer three oblations with the right hand and three oblations with the head.
For the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is thus performed, and then the birth-rite (jātakarma) is described;
one should fan the fire with the Astra-mantra and worship it with the Astra-mantra alone.
One should offer three oblations with the preceding [mantra] and three oblations with the Astra-mantra;
thus, by means of these two mantras alone, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is accomplished.
As it is stated in that very same [text] (*Mṛgavāra*), in the commentary on *Kriyākālaguṇottara* (KP) 6:12c–13b:
"One should fan the fire with the *astra* [mantra], and one should worship it with the *astra* [mantra] alone."
By the performance of three oblations, the birth-rite (jātakarma) is accomplished.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra for immediate purification from the impurity of birth.
Afterwards, one should open the faces [of the deity] by means of three oblations with the Vakra-mantra itself.
The faces are to be purified with the sword through the application of three oblations.
One should sprinkle the three [substances] into each mouth [of the ladle] with the mouths [of the vessel],
and sprinkle the sides of the sacrificial pit with the water of Śiva accompanied by the Astra-mantra.
Having spread out *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward, arranged from south to north,
he likewise places the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the bundles of grass (*viṣṭara*) with their tips pointing north in the eastern and western directions.
With the weapon-mantra (astramantra), they all established Brahmā on the eastern seat,
Rudra on the south, and Viṣṇu on the western seat.
Then, O Goddess, one should first meditate upon Sadāśiva in the north, marked by his own name; one should place the word "Oṃ" (the Dhruva) at the beginning and "Namaḥ" at the end.
They should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and one should contemplate their true forms within them;
moreover, one should worship the Lokeshas above the girdle with the syllable Om.
For the sake of protecting the newborn child, Brahmā and the other deities who have been worshipped,
one should then remove the bracelet situated on the right hand.
Having taken up a flower, one should assign a name to the fire of Śiva;
then, one should perform the ritual service with the *kavaca* mantra using perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth.
Having generated the fire marked with the names of Śiva by offering three oblations with the mouth upwards and again three with the *kavaca* mantra, [he should then invoke] the gods.
One should dismiss Sāvitrī to her own place with the *praṇava*,
having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, and having performed three sets of three oblations (*homa*).
These sacrificial fuels, measuring one cubit in length and numbering twenty-four, are to be offered in the flame for the propitiation of the fire of Śiva.

Having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water using the *astra-mantra*; having veiled them with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should whirl them three times around the *śiva-agni*.
One should wipe them with water using a mantra, then touch them with the tip of a *darbha* blade;
having again rotated them over the fire, one should sprinkle them with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*).
Having touched it with the middle part of a *darbha* blade and having rotated it again over the fire, one should heat it;
then, having cleansed it with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*), one should touch it with the root of a *darbha* blade.
Then, one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face down upon the roots [of the grass];
they should always be worshipped by the wise behind the *darbha* grass, to the south of the fire.
One should perform the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya), beginning with its placement on the fire;
having sprinkled the clarified butter with the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra.

O Goddess, having heated [the materials] in the Śiva-fire with the Astra-mantra and having withdrawn them with the Kavaca-mantra, one should place them after circling them three times around the perimeter of the pit.

Then, taking two tips of *darbha* grass, one span in length and tied together at the middle, he should place the vessel of clarified butter in the womb-position, performing the floating and submerging movements.
This purifier (pavitra) is prescribed as an "up-floating" one, which is joined with a "down-floating" one;
having taken hold of this purifier with the thumb and the ring finger, [one should perform the rite].
One should turn it away three times and likewise face it toward oneself three times,
using the Astra mantra alone for illumination by the fire of Śiva.
Having taken up a handful of *darbha* grass, one should inspect the vessel of clarified butter;
then one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) and thereafter the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having recited the *dhāman* weapon-mantra, the practitioner of mantra should cast that firebrand into the fire;
according to the same procedure involving the *dhāman*, he should sprinkle [the site] with water empowered by the weapon-mantra.
Having consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra by means of Śiva as the state of immortality,
one should worship it with Bhairava through the practice of reciting [the mantra] once.
One should perform the joining of the faces with the three oblations using the [respective] faces;
one should carry out that joining of the faces with the lower face.
In this way, the joining of the gentle face is accomplished;
by means of the application of three oblations, this same procedure applies to the southern face as well.
Then, in the same way, the eastern face should likewise be provided with Śiva;
by the application of three oblations, the junction of the faces is proclaimed.
The upper face is traditionally held to be primary, while the others possess the status of qualities;
for one desiring liberation, the upper face holds primacy in initiation.
Indeed, all the various accomplishments (*siddhis*), beginning with foot-unguents and collyrium,
which culminate in the state of Sadāśiva, one should offer as oblations in the eastern face.
But for killing, eradication, and the like, as well as for inciting enmity and immobilization,
supreme success shall come from performing the fire-oblation (homa) at the southern face.

One should always perform the fire oblation in the north for rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), the attainment of good fortune, the summoning [of desired objects], and the accomplishment of the ascent of good fortune.
In the west, the application of the daily rites is proclaimed;
indeed, the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) should be offered into the western upward-facing [fire].

O beautiful lady, a blade of *darbha* grass should be placed in the center of the clarified butter vessel by means of the *Bhairava* mantra; thereafter, indeed, the preparation of the path is performed.
Having uttered Bhairava, one should cast the *saṃpāta* into the vessel by way of the path;
simultaneously through the three channels, one should deposit three portions into the vessel.
One should conceive of Suṣumnā as situated in the central path, Piṅgalā on the right,
and that which is the fiery energy in the portion of Iḍā as the gentle [lunar] energy on the left.
Having thus conceived [the portion] as one-third, and having filled the *sruva* ladle, he should perform the oblation with the *Bhairava* mantra itself, ending with "to Agni, svāhā. (SvaT 2.251)
Having taken a portion from the share of Agni, one should cast an oblation of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, pronouncing at the end: "To Soma, Svāhā! for the share of Soma. (SvaT 2.252)

One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, beginning with the word *dhāma* and the *praṇava*, using the two mantras known as *agnīṣoma*, preceded by *dhāma* and ending with *svāhā*. (SvaT 2.253)
Having filled the *sruva* ladle from the beginning of the *praṇava* up to the middle of the *ājya*, one should perform the oblation;
for this is the rule in the bright fortnight, while in the dark fortnight it would be otherwise.
The sun should be in the lunar portion, while the designation "fire" remains as before;
one should indeed offer the oblation from the middle between fire and the sun.
Since the moon indeed enters the center of the sun on the new moon day (amāvāsyā),
for that reason, the oblation for the faces [of the deity] is performed by Bhairava for the purpose of consumption.

For the sake of attaining all those purificatory rites beginning with the tonsure (cūḍā) and ending with the initiation into the sacred fire (agnyādheya), one should cause a single full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be offered.
Having uttered Bhairava, Śivāgni bestows all accomplishments;
one should thereafter draw forth the fire, establish it in the vessel, and protect it.
On the northern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and outside the seat (viṣṭara),
one should prepare a vessel (camasa) filled with water there.
One should place there a purifying offering (pavitra) combined with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and sesame seeds;
having invoked [the deity] with the Praṇava and so forth, one should then utter the name of Viṣṇu followed by "namaḥ."
Having established Viṣṇu by means of the very word of address, one should worship him with welcome, a seat, water for the feet, and the arghya offering; thereafter, one should make a request to him.
Whether a sacrifice has been commenced for the sake of an animal or for one's own self by practitioners,
O Blessed One, may there be freedom from defects in our ritual through your grace.
Then, having performed the sacrifice in the fire, one should worship Bhairava;
according to the procedure prescribed for the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should arrange Ananta and the other deities.

Having first meditated upon the five faces, one should visualize the principal face according to whichever mouth is desired for the particular rite, with its dimensions corresponding to those of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should meditate on nine tongues established in each mouth;
eight are directed toward the cardinal directions starting from the east, one is in the center, and those which go to the intermediate directions are for the sake of desired objects.
For the sake of sovereignty, it generates fever; it bestows death and causes enmity with enemies;
it may be used for subjugation or eradication; it grants wealth and bestows liberation.
Bestowing all accomplishments in the center, one should therefore perform the fire-oblation in the center; indeed, with Bhairava alone, for the purpose of arranging the tongues of flame.
Furthermore, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Bhairava mantra,
grasping the tip of the flame at the heart, which is conceived as the consciousness of fire.
Having conceived the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) as residing within one's own heart,
one should imagine the bulbous root (kandaka) at the navel of fire, following the path of the central tongue.
Having meditated [on the heart] up to the heart, one should contemplate a lotus there,
endowed with eight petals, white in color, and of great brilliance.
One should conceive of that as infinite, beginning with Dharma and ending with Caraṇa;
and by means of the syllable Oṃ, one should fashion the form of Agni, ending with Śiva.
The *śikhā* which resides in the heart should again be unfastened with the *dhruva* mantra;
by means of exhalation (*recaka*), one should cast it into the fire—that is the form whose essence is Bhairava.
Having thus conceived [the deity] as having become incarnate and endowed with the thirty-eight kalās,
one should deposit the path to be purified at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.
Having worshipped Bhairava according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
the union of the faces occurs between the two faces of Śiva— the face of Śiva and the fire-face— by means of the two [other] faces.
Having joined them together in this manner, one should become intent on the junction of the channels with the two tongues;
having uttered the root mantra, [the breath] emerges through the nostrils of fire.
O fair-faced one, one should unite the Śiva residing on the sacrificial mound with the [central] Śiva as a single entity,
offering one hundred and eight oblations of pure clarified butter.
One should offer to Bhairava a tenth part [of the total] for his faces and limbs;
one should perform oblations to the eight Bhairavas and the world-protectors with a tenth part.
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer a single full oblation;
likewise, one should offer a full oblation for the purpose of nourishing Bhairava.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, a fire-oblation (homa) should subsequently be performed as desired to rectify any deficiency or excess and to ensure the rite is free from flaws.
A fire sacrifice with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter is praised for granting all desires;
for the sake of achieving wealth and grain, a sacrifice of guggulu resin with clarified butter is recommended.
Vast accomplishment—whether inferior, middling, or superior—is born [from this];
and by means of white lotuses and bilva fruits smeared with clarified butter, one shall obtain prosperity.
O fair-faced one, by means of an oblation of sesame seeds soaked in milk, the rite of pacification (śāntika) is accomplished;
likewise, through [sesame seeds] that are white, red, yellow, and black, there are the rites of pacifying, attracting, and nourishing (pauṣṭika).
And one should perform the rite of killing in due order, O lady of excellent hips;
with jasmine flowers for the sake of obtaining a son, and with *aśoka* flowers for union with a beloved.
A maiden is [attained] with *jātikuṭmalaka* flowers, a *gāndharvī* with those produced from the *bakula* tree,
a *nāgakanyā* indeed with *nāga* flowers, and a *siddhakanyakā* with *siddhārtha* seeds.

O lady of excellent limbs, the lord of men, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, should likewise offer oblations of clarified butter mixed with *caṇyaka* seeds and *phalguṣa* seeds to the celestial nymphs (*apsarasaḥ*).
O fair-faced one, a queen together with her son comes under control;
and a yakṣiṇī is brought under control by means of flowers from the kadamba tree.
One should accomplish [the goal] by means of a *vidyādharī* and *kuyyakas*; there is no doubt in this.
Having bound a deer, one performs a fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds, presided over by lotuses and *bilva* fruits.
With auspicious foods, measured by mouthfuls or by handfuls,
the practitioner, established in the ritual procedure, should perform the oblation in this manner according to the rules.
One who is constantly devoted to worship and fire-oblations attains whatever desires he seeks, exactly according to the word of Bhairava.
Thus ends the second chapter in the venerable Svacchandatantra.
The third chapter:
I shall now explain the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) correctly and in its proper sequence.
With his self thoroughly purified by water, having accomplished what was to be done, and with a serene intellect.
With his body smeared with ashes and adorned with the ornaments of mudrās,
he may wear a crooked sacred thread, be clothed, or be naked.
His limbs are smeared with fragrant perfumes, he is adorned with garlands and wreaths of flowers,
endowed with divine ornaments, serene, and well-cultivated.
Well-perfumed with incense, having consumed excellent betel, and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum,
he stands at the great doorway, meditating as before.
Having worshipped the gatekeepers, one should then perform the scattering of flowers;
having produced the sound of a clap with the application of the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*.
Indeed, through the conjunction of the heel and the lower hand, for the purpose of expelling obstacles:
one should strike those on the ground with the heel, and those in the intermediate space with the palm.
Having thus purified the divine [deities] with mantras, one should then enter the sacrificial hall;
one should arrange protection all around it as before, using the Astra-mantra.
Having concealed the sacrificial hall with armor in the form of an illusion,
O fair-faced one, he then sat down in the southern quarter.
One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) as before, as well as the burning,
purification, immersion, nourishment, and the process of making [the self] complete (sakalīkaraṇa).
As before, one should perform the mental sacrifice within the inner body,
[visualizing] Ananta as the support of Śakti, extending up to the feet of Dharma and the other [qualities].
Furthermore, [the yogin perceives] the limbs as unrighteousness and so forth, the connecting pegs likewise;
the lower covering and the upper [covering] as the filaments and the pericarp of a lotus.
One should offer the lotuses, the spears, the mandalas, and the lords of the mandalas;
one should present the seat ending with Śiva by means of the *dhruva* mantra, which is its primordial form.
The array of the digits of the Brahman-form, the nine principles and the three principles,
the thirty-two-syllable deity, and indeed the eight Bhairavas.
Likewise, one should worship the limbs of the Vidyā, the Goddess Kṣurikā, the three eyes,
the three supreme powers, and the Supreme God endowed with the six limbs.
One should arrange the mudrās, mantras, and ritual substances in their proper places; having thus resolved them, one should arrange them according to the rule and as is appropriate.
One should prepare the petals of the deity by placing Sadyojāta, Vāma, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśa, as has been stated.
Then, one should place the five [deities] beginning with Hṛdaya in the cardinal and intermediate directions, from the east up to the northeast; outside of this is the enclosure of the Bhairavas.
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons, starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
likewise, the weapons and the world-protectors, as well as the eight Bhairavas.
The five Brahmās are indeed the limbs;
one should recite all these enclosures in sequence until reaching the central Īśvara.
Listen now to this union of mantras, which indeed brings about the state of supreme perfection:
from that point, O God, one should utter the deity endowed with the short, long, and protracted [vowels].
One should recite the mantra as long as the sphere of nirvāṇa [is reached],
from the lower power up to the upper, within the interval between the paths of the moon and the sun.
By means of the central path of Piṅgalā, through the sequence of the utterance of phonemes,
one [attains] the five deities, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā.
Having gradually differentiated everything up to the very end of dissolution,
one reaches the state that is waveless, called the pathless, all-pervasive, and beyond the mind (unmanā).
Having presided over that [mandala], one should place it in the heart-lotus in the direct order;
O Goddess, in this same manner, one should install that pervasive [deity] within all the enclosures.
And all of them, presided over by him, bestow the fruits of all desires,
according to their respective forms, structures, and colors as described by me.
In that manner, they should be employed in the mind by means of the mind;
having established Bhairava in his two-fold state within the pericarp.
Resembling pure crystal and adorned with all mantras,
even there it should be known as all-pervading, ineffable, and free from affliction.
Where there is no duality and no conceptualization of mantras and so forth,
one should point that out as the dissolution of the syllable Oṃ, the bindu, and the nāda.
Considering that such a state is difficult to attain, one should never give rise to it— that [state] which has neither top nor bottom, nor directions, nor intermediate directions.
Neither sound nor even space, having meditated upon that, one is liberated;
first there is the mental sacrifice, followed by that which is endowed with material substances.

The teacher who is devoted to sacrifice should always perform [the rites] in this manner upon his own hand, on the sacrificial mound, on the linga, in the mandala, and likewise upon the sacrificial porridge.
Having worshipped properly both in water and in fire, one obtains the fruit of initiation;
however, he who, without performing the mental sacrifice, undertakes another sacrifice [is unsuccessful].
That [impurity] should be known as inauspicious; it does not lead to liberation.
However, when the sacrifice of the self is performed, the purification of the body arises.
One should designate that teacher as being empowered by Śiva himself;
he has indeed spoken of both the mental [burning] and the burning of the self.
Having understood this correctly, he is remembered as the Teacher, the Destroyer of Bonds, Śiva;
wherever he may reside, whoever performs the ritual in this manner [attains him].
Even a killer of a Brahmin would be liberated, how much more so one who is devoted to Śiva,
even if he has fallen into every possible state and is enamored by sense objects.

By worshipping [the deity] even once, one would be liberated; how much more so for one who does so day after day, according to the procedure previously described and following the rules set forth in this tantra?
Even in other tantras, rituals such as sacrifice and the like may be "Kāmika" (fulfilling desires);
they are endowed with various supernatural powers and qualities, and bestow the fruits of various desires.
The perfection of yoga arises and one certainly attains liberation;
even Sadāśiva knows this, as do the gods, the asuras, and others.
Having thus performed the mental sacrifice, one should perform the external one;
contemplating the supreme state, one should first examine the ritual substances.
White sandalwood and camphor, excellent incense, two white garments,
flowers of divine fragrance, sesame, rice, ghee, and so forth.
One should likewise provide mango sprouts, darbha grass, white mustard seeds,
chalk, a ruler, scissors, and a thread for binding nooses.
The water-vessel, the auspicious jar, as well as the fuel, the enclosing sticks,
the sacrificial wood, the tooth-stick, the vessel for the oblation, the large ladle, and the small ladle.
Having taken rice, milk, and many other such items,
one should then take the vessel for the offering (arghapātra) and wash it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship with the Praṇava;
O fair-faced one, one should then fill [the vessel] with water and the other [substances] using the eight-limbed [mantra].
O Dear One, water, milk, flowers, kuśa grass, mustard seeds, and rice—
having prepared all this for the seat with the syllable *praṇava*, one should then project the form [of the deity].
One should worship her, together with the Bhairava enclosures, in due order,
using perfumes, flowers, and incense, preceded by the application of the mantra.
The supreme reality is to be contemplated, and from that one shall indeed become immortal;
likewise, in the ritual for the purpose of cessation, a triad of vessels should be prepared.
Having thus prepared the price for the sacrificial animal, one should likewise prepare the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta),
as well as the conjunction of mantras and the conjunction of the channels (nāḍī) as previously described.
Recalling the root mantra, one should pierce through the heart, throat, and palate, reaching the space between the eyebrows— that peak of sound, the station of the fourth state.
One should pierce through the left, right, and middle [channels] by means of that which stands at the equinox (viṣuvat);
having led it to the supreme *dvādaśānta*, the mantra-body resides in the hand.
By this same method, one should enter that [deity] into one's own heart in reverse order;
by means of one's own exhalation (recaka) itself, one should enter into the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka).
This indeed is the conjunction of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) proclaimed by Śiva;
one should meditate upon the all-pervading Śiva, who is established in the form of the mantra.
Having taken a blade of darbha grass and consecrated it seven times with the Astra-mantra,
one should purify the vessel for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the water of Śiva.
One should wash that [seat] with the Astra-mantra and veil it with the Kavaca-mantra;
one should prepare the seat of Darbha grass with the Dhruva-mantra and likewise arrange the mandala.
One should place the vessel upon it and bring cow-dung and other materials;
these, remaining in separate vessels, should be sprinkled with the water of Śiva consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Having consecrated the cow dung with the Heart mantra, the cow urine with the Head,
the curd with the Crest, the milk with the Armor, and the clarified butter and water of kuśa grass with the Weapon mantra.
One should then consecrate [the materials] with the *dhāman* mantra and subsequently add the cow-dung and other substances;
one should place the cow-dung and so forth into the previously prepared vessel while reciting their respective mantras.
Having joined [the elements], one should subsequently consecrate them with those very [mantras] beginning with the Heart;
then, having conceptualized the infinite embodied form by means of the *praṇava*, [one should worship].
Having worshipped the limbs and the abodes on the outside, one should perform the stationing of the enclosure,
the unification of the mantras, and likewise the rite of immortalization.
Having meditated upon that as the nectar of Śiva and having worshipped it, one should then set it down;
taking a blade of darbha grass consecrated with the Astra-mantra, perform the act of scraping.
As far as the ground extends all around, standing with a gentle face toward the south,
he should then extract the thorn situated down to the edge of the water.
One should contemplate the pure recitation and fill [the vessel] with pearls and other such materials;
the leveling is performed with the Astra-mantra, while the sprinkling is done with the Kavaca-mantra.
Then follows striking with the weapon-mantra, and subsequently cleansing and smearing;
