[this is done] with the weapon-mantra, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and with scented water poured upon it.

One should consecrate the scattering substances with auspicious water joined with the weapon-mantra seven times; having stood facing the eastern direction while reciting the mantra, [one should perform the scattering].
One should scatter grains upwards and downwards and contemplate them as having become weapons;
one should then gather them back with a beautiful white fly-whisk while reciting the weapon-mantra.
Facing toward the northeast, from the southwest up to the northeast,
one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow, with fragrant water, and with the water of Śiva.
Having invoked Śrī with the *dhruva* mantra— she who holds a lotus in her hand, has beautiful eyes,
scatters white flowers, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, gazing upon the sacrificial hall,
she is seated in the Brahma-position, auspiciously facing the door.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should prepare the Śiva-pitcher;
having taken recourse to the northeastern direction, one should [prepare] the mandala with the five products of the cow.
Having smeared it with scented water, one should sprinkle it with auspicious water using the Astra-mantra;
then, having provided the seat beginning with Ananta, one should proceed up to the perimeter of the maṇḍala by means of the Dhruva-mantra.
Having worshipped the jar— which is free from all defects, smeared with sandalwood paste,
and adorned with svastikas and other symbols— using barley, white mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass;
Having wound it with a white thread and filled it with water purified by a cloth,
one should cover it entirely on all sides with sprouts of the mango, the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), and others.

Having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra and gathered it together with the groups beginning with Sahadeva, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra, [the vessel] containing jewels and medicinal herbs.
While recollecting the root mantra, one should place it upon the seat;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Kalās, the Paths (adhvan), Bhairava, and so forth, one should prepare the arghya and other offerings.
Having formed the mudrās, one should worship the heart and other [limbs] upon the petals starting from the southeast;
one should adorn them with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and so forth, and with a white cloth.
On the left side of the water-pot, having sprinkled a mandala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with auspicious water, one should place the seat while reciting the Praṇava.
Having sprinkled the auspicious water-vessel (*vārdhānī*) with the auspicious waters of Śiva,
and having worshipped it like the ritual jar (*kumbha*), one should place it upon the seat.
Having worshipped the water-vessel (vārdhanī) with perfumes, flowers, purifiers, and so forth,
one should recite the weapon-mantra (astra) and lead the vessel before the ritual substances in due order.
Causing an unbroken stream of water to flow in a downward direction,
he should lift it up from that place as far as the corner of Śaṅkara.
The preceptor should then lift up the jar with the Bhairava-mantra;
he should lead it by way of the *vārdhāni* path and place it back down upon that [spot].
One should place the water-vessel behind [the image] while recollecting the weapon-mantra;
then, one should perform a special worship of both [the deity and the vessel] with perfumes, flowers, and purificatory threads.
One should perform the conjunction of the mantras and then the junction of the channels of both;
first, one should arrange the scattered [syllables] together below the vessel.
There were many unbroken missiles—arrows, spears, swords, and mallets;
and numerous other weapons, beginning with discs, sharp-edged spears, and thunderbolts, and ending with tridents.
Pervading the entire abode of Yoga, they remain situated horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
all of them are established as rays of the Vārāhyāstra.
Having joined the Vārāhyā weapon to the disciple’s right hand,
he should place that [hand] upon the ritual jar at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of protecting the rite.
Having offered various kinds of food offerings and having praised him, one should address the Lord:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, I shall complete the sacrifice."
"May your constant presence always be for the sake of removing obstacles.
Having been granted permission and having risen, one should proceed with the *argha* in hand toward the lords of the directions."

One should diligently worship those [mantras], which consist of the arrangement of one's own name and begin with *oṃ* and end with *namaḥ*, using perfumes, flowers, purifiers (*pavitra*), and other offerings.
One should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Indra and ending with Ananta;
then, one should prepare a mandala in the center of the sacrificial ground.
Having first smeared [the vessel] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and then with scented water,
one should sprinkle it with the water of Śiva while reciting the Astra-mantra and perform the veiling rite (avaguṇṭhana).
To the east of the station of Brahmā, having worshipped the gurus and Vināyaka,
one should worship the deities in the north-west, O Goddess, with perfumes and flowers in due order.
Then, having paid homage to these, one should contemplate the command that has been given;
thereafter, one should fashion the Yoga-pīṭha located in the Middle Country.

O fair-faced one, having worshipped Bhairaveśa according to the previously mentioned procedure, together with the purificatory rites (*pavitra*) and so forth, and accompanied by the three enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).
Endowed with the qualities of one's own meditation, adorned with the ornaments of the mudrās,
preceded by the application of mantra and likewise the application of the channels (nāḍī).
One should perform the act of supreme transformation by means of the supreme pervasive [deity];
having offered various kinds of food offerings, one should display the mudrā.
Having performed prostrations and recitation, and having made the offering according to the prescribed rite,
one should afterwards present the bali-offering to the Mothers and the assembly of spirits.
O Goddess of the gods, [one should worship] the lords of beings and the Kṣetrapāla on all sides;
then, O lady of excellent vows, one should bathe, or else perform the ritual dusting (uddhūlana), or sip water (ācamana).
Then, having gone to the fire-pit, one should perform the purification as before and worship Bhairava there according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
One should perform the satiation of the fire with a thousand or a hundred [offerings];
then, taking a flawless vessel, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having washed [the image] with auspicious water, one should veil it with the *kavaca* mantra;
one should smear it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and fumigate it with refined incense.
O you of excellent vows, one should wrap a thread around the neck as a protective armor;
O beloved, one should fashion the maṇḍala with *darbha* grass, which has the nature of the weapon-mantra.
Having sprinkled [the seat] with auspicious waters, one should veil it with the Kavaca mantra;
there, one should install the seat beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva.
One should place the vessel as the embodied form and worship Bhairava residing therein,
together with his three enclosures, using perfumes and flowers in the proper sequence.

O fair-faced one, having sprinkled the hearth with the mental application and with flowers representing the elements, one should then worship it with the Astra-mantra, just as one does the sacrificial pit.
Having placed the cooking vessel there, one should subsequently set the fire beneath it;
having sprinkled the milk and the rice grains with the auspicious waters (śivāmbhas), [one proceeds] in brief.
Having cast it [into the fire] with the mantra exactly one hundred and eight times, O Goddess of Gods, one should cook it slowly, single-minded and composed, while reciting the root mantra.
One should perform the shaking, opening, and so forth with the weapon-mantra;
once it is well-steamed, one should apply the sprinkling of hot liquid and the ritual with the limbs [of the mantra].
O Dear One, one should offer oblations with clarified butter using a *sruva* ladle three times each;
having drawn a mandala on the ground, one should cause [the fire] to descend with the *praṇava*.
One should offer a vessel smeared with clarified butter as a cold libation (śītāghāra),
using the six-limbed Bhairava mantra conjoined with the *vaṣaṭ* call.
Having prepared the mandala near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should lay down a seat of darbha grass;
then, having placed a vessel upon it, one should deposit the residual offerings (sampāta) together with the collection of mantras.
Placing [the substance] in the vessel, while reciting [the mantra], he should cause it to fall with one oblation at a time using the Bhairava-mantra;
indeed, with one hundred and eight superior repetitions, while recollecting the supreme nectar. (SvaT 3.112)
Then, O Goddess, first upon the dust, and likewise upon the knife and the two instruments,
one should perform the sprinkling of chalk, sesame seeds, and clarified butter with the root mantra.
Having divided that sacrificial pap (caru), which is contained in a vessel, into three parts,
one should offer the first portion to Śiva, and the others to the Śiva-fire and the practitioners (sādhakas).
One should offer the second [portion] into the fire, and the third to the practitioners;
having collected the *caru* in a vessel, one should worship it with the Bhairava mantra.
Having brought him [the deity] with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should present him to the abode;
one should present a tenth part [of the offerings] to those residing in the heart and the other enclosures.
In the same manner, one should likewise offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with a ladle into the fire within the jar;
for Bhairava, one hundred oblations are to be offered, and for the limbs [of the deity], a tenth part thereof.
O Dear One, one should cover and set aside whatever remains for the practitioners;
likewise, one hundred oblations are to be offered to Vināyaka during the ritual acquisition of the ground.
Likewise, in this case of acceptance, there should be one hundred and eight oblations for the purpose of expiation when the sequence is either direct or reverse.
O Goddess of gods, if there is a deficiency or excess, one hundred and eight oblations should be performed;
then, O fair-faced one, having worshipped Bhairava, one should request his permission.
Listen to how the ritual for the child should be performed:
having made a small mandala at the door, one should place *darbha* grass upon it.
Having prepared the seat with the syllable *praṇava*, one should cause the disciple to sit upon it,
with feet even, body steady, face serene, and hands joined in *añjali*.
The Guru, facing east, should sprinkle him with the Weapon-mantra using the water of Śiva;
he should strike him on the head with ashes and consecrate him with the Weapon-mantra.
One should arrange three [lines] above the navel and likewise three below the navel;
one should then worship Śiva, together with the limbs of the ritual placement (nyāsa), by means of Bhairava.
Having sprinkled the cloth with the Astra-mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca-mantra;
one should worship it with the Bhairava-mantra and likewise cover its face.
Then, having grasped him with both hands, one should enter behind the curtain;
having placed him facing the deity, one should cause him to offer flowers at his two vital breaths.
Then, having cast [the substance] with the [appropriate] splendor and opened the mouth,
one should show the Cause together with Sadāśiva and the hosts of Vidyās and Mantras.
Freed from the veil of ignorance, the awakened one beholds [the truth],
falling prostrate like a staff upon the earth and bowing down again and again.
Having accomplished his purpose, with a joyful soul, he should raise up the child whose eyes are wide with joy,
take him by the hands, and bring him before the southern form [of the deity].
There, having prepared a mandala and offered a seat with a flower and the syllable *praṇava*,
one should place the child upon it with the upper body erect and facing north.
The Guru, standing facing the east, should perform the sprinkling and other rites;
then, having seated [the disciple], he should carry out the procedure for the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa).
For the sake of attaining a specific fruit, the seeker of liberation or the practitioner,
having smeared his hands with perfume, should purify them with the Astra-mantra.
Having enveloped these two with the Kavaca mantra, one should drench them with nectar;
then, having prepared the infinite seat (Ananta-āsana), one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the limbs of Bhairava.
Having united the self with the void, O Dear One, the body of the disciple should be dried up;
then, having meditated on the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā), one should burn that disciple with the weapon-mantra.
One should visualize the body as burnt, free from smoke and flames;
then, once it has been reduced to ashes and become tranquil, one should drench it with nectar.
One should contemplate the body as being like the sky and consciousness as being like gold and fire;
first, one should perform the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa), and then place the lotus with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Above that, one should meditate upon oneself as auspicious and consisting of light;
having recited the form-mantra (mūrtimantra), one should conceive of oneself as having become that very form.
One should flood [the body] with nectar using the previously extracted mantra;
the deposition of the mantras (mantranyāsa) is performed as before, up to the thirty-eight kalās.
Thereafter, one should deposit the path of the kalās in the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā;
they are crystal-like, black, red, white, and yellow.
Those kalās, beginning with Śāntyatītā, should be known as being composed of the principles (tattvas).
Having invoked them into the locus and likewise assigned the limbs (aṅgas), the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) becomes [established].
Just as one [perceives] the self within the internal organ, so too should one commence the worship;
having uttered the *dhāman*, one should again establish [the deity] both externally and internally.
Having meditated upon the pervasive Lord within the hand of Śiva, and having intensely kindled the collection of mantras,
one should pronounce the sacred abode (dhāman), join [the hands], and place them upon the head of the disciple.
With the hand of Śiva turned downwards, one should touch the heart and the back;
then, having raised [the disciple] and placed a flower in his joined palms, one should do so with the Bhairava-mantra.
Having entered, one should worship Śambhu; having uttered "Śiva," one should cast [the flower];
then, having gone out, one should prostrate like a staff before the God and perform three circumambulations.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, he should pay homage to the Śiva-liṅga situated in the center of the fire-pot and to the one established on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the beginning of the worship of Śiva and the fire-ritual.
Otherwise, he would not be worthy of worship in his original form;
having led him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, [the teacher] should keep him from leaving the hand of the disciple.
Then, in the direction to his right, he should prepare a mandala with the syllable Om;
having offered a seat with the syllable Om, he should place the disciple upon it.
Having seated [the disciple], he should offer a blade of darbha grass into his hand with the Bhairava mantra;
the root-end of the blade held in the disciple's hand should rest against the calves of the preceptor, while its tip remains in the hand.
The central channel, Piṅgalā, has emerged from the body of the disciple;
it has become the sacrificial grass (darbha) here and has merged into the channel of the Guru.
For the purpose of connecting the channels, Bhairava offers three oblations;
through that channel, he should enter the disciple's heart once.
For the purpose of grasping and drawing [the disciple] in, he repeatedly takes hold and releases him;
and since this occurs at the time of initiation, the collection of channels exists for that very purpose.

Then, having performed the *sampāta* rite with all the mantras upon the head of the disciple by means of Bhairava, one should offer an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) with the *dhruva* mantra.
Having uttered the root mantra, one should cast [the oblation] into the fire with "svā";
with "ha," the descent [of the substance] upon the disciple's head is impelled by Śiva.
But as for those mantras residing within the body of the disciple— both externally and internally—
those which reside in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) when worshipped, extending from the primary abode (dhāman) to the end of the enclosures (āvaraṇa).
The simultaneous satiation of these [deities] is proclaimed as *sampāta*;
herein, for each individual mantra, it is performed with three oblations.
Then, having raised the disciple up, one should perform the satiation of the mantra for that purpose;
having offered a hundred oblations to Bhairava, there is an offering of ten [oblations] to the Heart-mantra and the others.
Having arisen with the *dhāman*, one should offer oblations and satisfy [the deities] with the *pūrṇāhuti*;
one should perform the illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantras in sequence, beginning with the *dhāman* and ending with the *astra*.
While reciting the root mantra between two *huṃ* syllables,
one should offer oblations beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *phaṭ*.
The origin of all [mantras], beginning with those of the heart, has been stated here in the context of their illumination;
the illumination of mantras is traditionally taught for the purpose of binding the fetters.
The mantras are indeed the instruments for accomplishing the task of the bound soul (paśu);
the teacher is declared to be the instrument, since he is remembered as being the very form of Śiva.
When a cruel rite is to be performed, one should employ the mantras after having inflamed them;
one should always employ the expressive words in accordance with the nature of the cruel [deity].
One should visualize those of fierce nature as having faces made terrifying by frowns and as being of a harsh appearance;
one should visualize those of gentle nature as being gentle in form when [the rite] is gentle.
Next, I shall describe the ritual of the noose (pāśakarma), using a thread spun by a maiden;
having tripled it and then tripled it again, this is the thread for binding the noose.
Having sprinkled the auspicious water with the Astra-mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should worship it according to the prescribed rule with perfumes, flowers, incense, and other offerings.
Having grasped that [cord], one should extend it from the head down to the big toes;
one should contemplate it as having become the channel (*nāḍī*) of the disciple whose body is held motionless.
The Suṣumnā is the central channel, endowed with all the channels;
it begins with the syllable Oṃ and ends with a salutation by its own name.
Having joined the channel residing within the body of the disciple to the thread,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and veil it with the *kavaca* mantra.

Having sprinkled the water for the *śiva-āmbhas* with the Astra-mantra, one should again offer three *sannidhāna* oblations, consisting of the disciple's own name, the word "pada," and his caste-name, into the disciple's heart.

One should strike it with the flower of the weapon-mantra; thus, consciousness is withdrawn from the heart. By means of the utterance of the syllable *huṃ* and through exhalation (*recaka*), one should enter [consciousness] into the heart.
Having entered through the aperture of the channel, the teacher should cause the disciple to contemplate consciousness as having the form of a *kadamba* bud, resembling a shimmering star.
Having severed that which resides in the heart with the sword-weapon mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and belonging to its respective class,
one should gradually draw it forth by means of the light in the form of a hook until it reaches the power (*śakti*).
Having grasped the *dvādaśānta* and encapsulated it with the heart-mantra,
one should join it to the thread conceived as the channel by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
Having meditated upon the pervasive [deity], one should veil it with the armor-mantra;
one should offer three oblations with the Bhairava-mantra for the sake of its presence.

The second is the body of the thread (sūtradeha), wherein these fetters (pāśas) reside—those which are to be bound and likewise those to be burned; they exist in the locus of the thread, not in a physical form.
The fetters (pāśas) are to be understood as threefold—born of Māyā, of Āṇava, and of Karma;
these obstruct consciousness and consist of the nature of both cause and effect.
Impurity is the cause, while action is the effect;
beyond that, the effect consists of the substratum, namely the body, the worlds, and so forth.
The sign is called "desire," appearing in various forms of causal manifestations;
one should observe these in the sūtra according to the cause of binding and that which is to be bound.
The striking of the nooses should be performed with the respective seed-syllables ending in *huṃ phaṭ*,
preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and one's own name, following the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā.
One should strike the head with a flower; one should grasp [the deity] and apply *hūṃ* and so forth.
Having grasped [the deity] by means of the yoga ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, one should [withdraw them] with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*.
One should join [the soul] to the thread by means of the *dhāman* ending with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*).
In this way, having extracted the bonds such as those of pacification (*śānti*) from their place, one should join them.
One should meditate upon the three kinds of bonds that pervade the path of the five principles;
the supreme power of the Lord, called Kriyā, pervades these three.
Established through the five designations according to the divisions beginning with Śāntyatītā,
one should meditate on the grasping of the supported as having grasped the support for the sake of the bound soul (paśu).
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should satisfy the nooses within the thread by offering three oblations each, according to the sequence beginning with Śāntyatītā.

Therefore, for the purpose of binding, one should inflame the bonds (pāśas) by means of three [mantras] each, using their own names, their generic class, the syllable *phaṭ*, and their abodes (*dhāma*).
However, for the purpose of causing separation from the bonds, there must be an "igniting" (dīpana) of them;
once the bonds are ignited, they become capable of being bound through striking, seizing, and so forth.
One should strike those [deities] residing in the thread with flowers, as if they were residing within one's own body, in due order;
having encased them with the *dhāman* mantra and with their own names, once each.
Regarding binding, this application [is as follows]: one should cause knots to be tied upon the thread;
furthermore, there is the measurement of the binding and the scope of the ritual action.
Abiding in the midst of the thirty-six principles, he experiences enjoyment and not otherwise;
having established the fetters (pāśas) in the vessel, one should offer the *saṃpāta* oblation once.
One should present those [fetters] situated within the pair of vessels upon the sacrificial ground;
having brought them, one should offer them into the jar, saying: "O Lord, protect the fetters! (SvaT 3.189).
One should release the disciple from the *darbha* grass and cause him to place a flower in his hand;
one should then perform worship upon the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), at the *śiva-kumbha*, and at the *śiva-agni*.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
having raised [the disciple], one should indeed offer the five products of the cow and other substances with the Bhairava mantra.
On a pure spot, one should prepare three small mandalas with cow dung;
in one of these mandalas, the child, having been seated, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having sat down in the second [mandala], the wise one should consume the sacrificial porridge (caruka);
having sipped water for purification, he stands in the third mandala holding a tooth-stick.
And having consumed it, O Goddess of gods, one should then cast [the remains] in the east,
the west, the northeast, above, and in the north, which is auspicious.
Know that for anyone else there is impurity; for him, there should be a hundred oblations.
Afterwards, the preceptor should perform the expiation with the Śiva-mantra.
If there is a deficiency or excess in the ritual procedure, one becomes purified through expiation by offering one hundred and eight oblations for the sake of removing mental distraction.
Thereafter, one should satisfy [the deities] with a thousand or a hundred oblations (homa),
and offer the food offering (naivedya) into the fire with a tenth part of the mantras.
O fair-faced one, having performed the special worship, the offering of water (argha), the binding of mudrās,
the hymn of praise, and the instrumental music, one should then consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) and perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
O fair-faced one, having offered the arghya with the mantra of cessation (nirodhārgha),
one should retain it by means of exhalation (recaka) while recollecting Bhairava.
Having filled it with the fist and brought it forth, O fair-faced one, and having worshipped it,
one should take it with the *pūraka* breath and place it within the fire.
Having worshipped [the deity] residing there, one should deposit him into the jar;
having honored Bhairava within the jar itself with flowers and other offerings, one should place him therein.
Having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya), O Dear One, one should touch [the disciple] with cow dung;
then, having sprinkled him with the water of Śiva, one should prepare a bed for the disciple.
O Dear One, for a householder, however, a bed of darbha grass is prescribed, while for an ascetic it is ashes;
the householder should be made to lie with his head toward the east, and the ascetic with his head toward the south.

O fair-faced one, for the disciple stationed there, one should perform the binding of the topknot and provide protection with white mustard seeds, yellow pigment, and other substances, while recollecting the sword-mantra.
Having visualized a protective wall of weapons using ashes, yellow pigment (rocanā), and other substances,
and having enveloped the disciple with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should then cause him to sleep.
Then, having emerged from that very place, one should commence the bali-offering;
the bali has already been prepared with reverence for all beings.
Having gathered that, O Goddess of gods, one should cast it starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
[this includes] the various kinds of spirits who dwell in the divine, terrestrial, and atmospheric realms.

And those dwelling in the depths of Pātāla who are well-disposed toward the sacrifice of Śiva, as well as all beings beginning with Dhruva, and those situated in the directions beginning with Indra; SvaT 3.208.
One should cast [the offerings] while reciting "may they be satisfied" (tṛpyantu) in conjunction with the utterance of *svāhā*;
having worshipped with prostrations, one should then offer perfumes and incense in due order.
From the east to the northeast, and downwards and upwards on all sides,
[he should worship] the field-protectors (kṣetrapālas) situated in the corners, as well as the outcasts (śvapacas) who have fallen [from their status].
Having offered the bali-oblation to all [the deities] and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), O fair-faced one,
and having performed the sakalīkaraṇa, one should consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) in due order.
Accompanied by his companions, the hero— single-minded and concentrated—
should stand within the mandala facing either east or north, each in their respective place.
First, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), consume the sacrificial porridge (caru), and use a tooth-stick;
having thus partaken [of these], one should perform the ritual identification with the deity (sakalīkṛtya) and provide protection as before.
O fair-faced one, one should sleep on the sacrificial ground afterwards together with the disciples,
either through the practice of meditation on Bhairava or while remaining awake in samādhi.
In the *Svacchandatantra*, the third chapter is the "Chapter on the Consecration" (*adhivāsa*).
The fourth chapter:
In order to introduce the initiation (*dīkṣā*) which occurs immediately after the consecration, the venerable Bhairava said:
At the clear dawn, having performed the purification and other rites in the sequence as before,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, one should enter the house.
And the disciple, pure and having sipped water, with flowers in his hand,
then bowed his head to the guru.
Being joyful, he should report his dreams to the guru.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe auspicious dreams as well as inauspicious ones:
among dreams, the drinking of intoxicants and the eating of raw meat; SvaT 4.3.
Smearing oneself with worms and excrement, consecrating oneself with blood,
eating curd-rice, and smearing oneself with white garments.
A white parasol held over the head, a white garland as ornament,
a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, and the royal consecration.
Jewels, limbs, ornaments, and so forth, betel, and fruit;
the vision of Śrī and Sarasvatī, and the embrace of an auspicious noble woman.
Having held a conversation with kings, ṛṣis, gods, siddhas, vidyādharas, gaṇas, and teachers, one attains success in a dream.
Crossing rivers and oceans, traveling through the sky,
as well as the rising of the sun and the blazing of the sacrificial fire.
The sighting of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as the moon's orb;
and likewise, ascending a palace tower or even the pinnacle of a mansion.
Climbing upon men, horses, bulls, young elephants, trees, and mountain peaks;
traveling in celestial palaces (vimānas); and beholding those who have perfected the mantras.
There is gain, as well as the sight of a perfected practitioner (siddhacāra) and of gods and others;
[the attainment of] a pill, a tooth-stick, a sword, sandals, and yellow pigment (rocanā).
Anointed collyrium, nectar, the two Pārata plants, a spear, a water-pot, a lotus, a rosary, and red arsenic; SvaT 4.12.
Having seen blazing perfected substances and those ending with red ochre (gairika) at the end of a dream, one attains success; likewise, one obtains land through a wound.
Victory in battle is like crossing an ocean of blood;
the cremation ground is beautiful, filled with heroes and lords of heroes.
Having obtained from the gods with devotion the sale of great flesh and the distribution of the great noose by means of heroes, vetālas, and siddhas; SvaT_4.15.
Worshipping the deity with his own self, reciting, meditating, and even praising,
he beholds the blazing fire as well-offered and honored.
[He is] the vehicle of the haṃsa, sārasa, cakravāka, peacock, and śabara;
and Bhairava himself, together with the Mothers and the hosts of Rudra and the Mātṛs.
Having seen Bhairava and Bhairavī, one attains accomplishment here; of this there is no doubt.
Auspicious dreams have been described by me; now learn from me the inauspicious ones as well.
Anointing with oil, drinking [poison], entering the subterranean realm,
falling into a blind well, and sinking into the mud.
Falling from trees, vehicles, or carriages, or from palaces and mountains; or the cutting off of the ears and nose, or else of the hands and feet.
The falling out of the teeth, the sight of bears and monkeys,
as well as [the appearance of] vetālas, cruel beings, and likewise the men of Time (kālapuruṣas).
A woman with black hair standing upright, who is soiled and wears black garlands and garments, and has red eyes—should she embrace a man in a dream; ||| SvaT_4.22 |||

There is no doubt that he will die if one does not perform the rite of pacification; furthermore, there will be the destruction of the house and its sanctuaries, as well as of the beds, garments, and seats.
The reckoner [of karma] undergoes self-defeat and the loss of his own substance among donkeys,
camels, horses, jackals, herons, vultures, and cranes.
Mounting upon buffaloes, owls, and crows; engaging in sexual intercourse;
eating cooked meat; and wearing red garlands and unguents.
One whose mind is deranged perceives black and red garments in a dream, as well as laughing, leaping, and wearing withered garlands.
Having seen in a dream the cutting off of one's own flesh, imprisonment, being devoured by a black serpent, and likewise marriage, one does not achieve success at all.
For the impure [offerings] have been thus described; they should be understood by the best of teachers.
The pure [offerings] are to be inferred therein, but one should perform the fire-oblation (homayet) with the impure ones.
One becomes purified from transgressions by reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with the *dhāman*.
Having performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* as before, one should perform the expulsion of obstacles and the rite of protection.
One should perform the encircling as before, [placing] the Śiva-vessel, the Śiva-hand,
having fully worshipped the world-protectors, the Śiva-pitcher, and the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The fire-ritual (agnikārya) is performed as before, including the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
thereafter follows the expiation (prāyaścitta) for the purpose of [neutralizing] bad dreams, as has been described.
Having thus performed the worship and other rites, and having dismissed Śiva from the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should remove the floral remains (nirmālya) and purify the ground as before.
Thereafter, one should perform the daily rites, such as worship, fire-offerings, and recitation;
once the daily routine is completed, one should then perform the occasional rites.
Having smeared [the site] with auspicious waters, one should worship the station of Brahmā with devotion, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter, one should draw the mandala.
One should worship the ritual chalk (karaṇī) with Bhairava;
the falling of the colored powders (rajas) according to their respective domains (dhāman), beginning with white and so forth, is declared in the scriptures.
Once the mandala has been completed, having bathed, one should perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*).
Upon the conclusion of the daily rites, the wise practitioner should perform the occasional rite (*naimittikakarman*).
One should perform bathing and so forth with the preliminary mantras, followed by the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and the rest,
as well as the protection of oneself, the construction of the protective wall with the weapon-mantra, and the worship of the gatekeepers and other deities.

Having established a rampart of weapons for those dwelling on earth, in the netherworld, and in the sky, one performs the expulsion of obstacles and the binding of the directions, followed by veiling with the armor-mantra.
Seated facing north, one should perform the purification of the hands and so forth as before;
then follow the sprinkling with auspicious water (śivāmbhas), the bestowing of the hand of Śiva (śivahasta), and the preparation of the threefold offering (arghatraya).

Having fully worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), one should worship the auspicious jar (śivakumbha) while standing in front of the mandala and sprinkling the mandala with the sword [of mantra].
Thereafter, one should wrap it with armor and consecrate it with the *praṇava* mantra;
by reciting it one hundred and eight times with the *dhāman*, it is purified of the defects of dust.
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra at the four directions and at the door with perfumes and other offerings in due order,
one should visualize the enclosure as the weapon-mantra and then enter the maṇḍala.
Having worshipped the gurus and Vighneśa with flowers and other offerings using the *praṇava*,
one should likewise [offer] the seat for Ananta as before, ending with Śiva, using the *praṇava*.

One should first assign the forms and so forth, extending from the heart-mantra to the end of the enclosure, according to the previously stated rule; having performed worship, one should present the food offerings.
Having offered half [of the oblation] with the *nirodha* mantra, one should indeed cause [the fire] to cease;
then, having performed recitation, meditation, and so forth, one should worship Bhairava situated within the fire.
Having established the junction of the channels at the three locations, one should satisfy the Lord;
having performed the emission of the partless self, one should place it within the vessel.
One should illuminate the [deity] residing in the vase with the left [hand], and then fill it;
for the [deity] residing in the mandala, one should again illuminate it with the left.
One should remember that his splendor enters through the south of the one standing by the fire;
having thus performed the preparatory rite, one should then begin the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having offered the oblation divided into ten parts, one should cast the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
for the sake of purification through atonement, one should perform one hundred and eight [recitations].
Then, with the splendor of the rite that has been completed and transcended,
the preceptor, raising his hand to half the height [of the fire], should subsequently enter the mandala.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord with flowers and other offerings to the west of the *ardhapātra*,
and having first performed obeisance while kneeling upon the ground, he should form the ritual gesture (*mudrā*).
One should announce for the sake of the sacrificial animal: "This supreme sacrifice has been commenced;
whatever was performed in the mandala and at the fire, beginning with the ritual bathing and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana)."
"By your grace, may that abundant and perfect ritual procedure be established here;
now, within the body of the disciple, let there be the process of sakalīkaraṇa and so forth. (SvaT 4.53)
"May the purification of the path extending for a *yojana* be accomplished through your grace.
Having been thus authorized by the Supreme Lord with the words "So be it," the King of Heroes [proceeded].
Having received permission, with a joyful heart, he should step out from the mandala;
taking with him the vessel of water-offerings which was prepared for the sake of the sacrificial animal.
On the southern side of the sacred site, the Guru should cause a mandala to be prepared;
having laid down a seat of *praṇava* made of *kuśa* grass, he should seat the pure disciple there.
Having struck the auspicious water with the Astra-mantra, and having consecrated it with ashes and Kuśa grass in due order,
one should visualize the disciple as having become the very embodiment [of the deity] within the prepared mandala.
Having sat down, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands preceded by the weapon-mantra for burning away [impurities],
as well as the internal and external placement and the concentration on the mantra.
Having meditated upon the God as brilliantly blazing, the Hand of Śiva should be bestowed;
one should cast its splendor upon the head, which destroys the sprouts of the fetters.
Having raised him up from there and led him away, one should cause him to enter the maṇḍala;
having sprinkled his garment with water, one should veil it with the *kavaca* mantra.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and consecrate [the disciple] with the Bhairava mantra;
having bound the eyes with a blindfold, one should cause the disciple to place a flower in his hand.
Standing facing the deity, one should cast a flower without desire;
according to the way the flower falls, one should indeed bestow a name upon the practitioner.
The guru, according to the desire of the seeker of liberation or of the practitioner,
shall open the mouth of that disciple and cause him to prostrate before Śiva.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the mandala and the fire, and having prostrated,
the preceptor stands near the fire-pit together with the sacrificial victim.
In the direction to the left of oneself, one should prepare the mandala with the syllable *praṇava*;
first, there is the joining of the channels, and for that purpose, three oblations are offered.
Having performed the oblation at the point of contact and the minor libation,
one should then offer the full oblation and perform the expiatory fire-sacrifices.
Thereafter, one should offer three oblations with the *dhāman* mantra and the hundred-and-eight [syllables];
likewise, for the extraction of caste and for the attainment of the status of the twice-born, one should use the *dhruva* mantra alone.
Likewise, in the consumption of seed-syllables and in the purification of place and state, one becomes a twice-born;
so too, by means of the *praṇava*, one performs three oblations for the removal of the portion of Rudra.
One should sprinkle the disciple with the Astra-mantra joined with flowers and strike him;
then, having gone out by means of the exhalation (recaka), one should enter into the disciple's body at the heart.
Having recited the auspicious *oṃ* syllable and so forth, and having uttered the *astra-mantra* ending with *phaṭ*,
one should perform the ritual separation of consciousness according to the prescribed rule.
One should sever it with the weapon-mantra and envelop it with the armor-mantra;
having drawn it forth with the hook-mantra, one should cause it to reach the end of the twelve.
The person situated there should be grasped by means of the *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā] and the *dhruva* [mantra];
then, with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the inhalation (*pūraka*), one should correctly enter into the heart.
Having thoroughly refined and liquefied it, one should again expel the person;
then, as he abandons the six deities, he likewise [abandons] his own station.
Having grasped the person situated there and enveloped them with the *bhava* [mudrā],
one should extract them with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and join them to the heart of the disciple.
Having consecrated the sacred thread (upavīta) in this manner with the Bhairava mantra, one should give it to the child;
thus, from the rite of conception until the final funeral sacrifice, the child becomes consecrated in the state of the twice-born.
The attainment of the individual body from the universal class occurs through three oblations;
furthermore, the consecration of consciousness takes place after the final funeral rite (antyeṣṭi).
Having performed [the rite] by means of subtle consciousness, he becomes consecrated in his status as a twice-born;
then, having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations, he should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
For one who is thus consecrated as a *samayin*, there shall be the state of an Arhat in speech,
as well as in hearing, study, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
One whose self is purified through conduct and meditation attains the state of the Lord;
then, for those seeking the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, [the following is taught] for the purpose of purifying the path of initiation.
The subtle ritual procedure that effects the severance of the bonds is now declared.
The Guru questions the disciple who desires the twofold fruit.
Whatever kind of fruit you desire, begin the corresponding means of accomplishment;
the attainment is impelled by the mantra to be mastered, according to the distinction of one's latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
The fire sacrifice (homa) of mantras, mudrās, paths, and substances is considered common;
yet it is differentiated according to the diversity of latent impressions (vāsanā) among disciples as well as the teacher.
In that regard, the practitioner is of two kinds: one established in the Śiva-dharma, whose path is purified by Śiva-mantras and who is engaged with the mantras to be accomplished.
One who possesses knowledge, has been consecrated, and is devoted to the propitiation of mantras—
he is the Śiva-sādhaka worthy of attaining the threefold accomplishment here.
The second dwells on the worldly path, devoted to the performance of sacrifices and charitable works;
performing rituals while longing for their fruits, he remains fixed solely in the auspicious and avoids the inauspicious.
His duty is always the destruction of inauspicious portions by means of mantras;
whether he be a householder or an ascetic, he should remain established in one of the stages of life (āśrama).
The seeker of liberation is said to be of two kinds: the seedless (nirbīja) and the seeded (sabīja).
[This applies] to children, the simple-minded, the elderly, women, those devoted to enjoyment, and those afflicted by disease.
For these [initiates], the seedless initiation (nirbījikā-dīkṣā), which is devoid of the rules of conduct (samaya) and the like, is prescribed;
however, O Dear One, for those who endure the dualities of the wise, it is proclaimed as the seeded initiation (sabījā).
For them, initiation is the bestower of grace, conjoined with the conduct of the rules (samaya);
[so too are] the specific conducts of the rules which are proclaimed in the section concerning Mantra.
These must be protected here with great effort by one who desires the attainment of liberation;
for that [attainment] is to be understood as having a seed, established in both the spiritual son and the teacher.
Whether he be a householder, one in a [specific] stage of life, or an ascetic, having made the formal resolve, he should initiate [the disciple].
Taking a cord of threads representing the fetters (pāśasūtraka), he should suspend it upon the body of the disciple.
The wise one should unite the path within the fire by means of the [divine] abode;
he who stands within the fire of the jar and the maṇḍala is also established within the path of the disciple.
Moreover, the junction of the paths is proclaimed to be situated in one place within the Sūtra,
pertaining to the sixfold path of the common way.
Having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and purified it, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) at the junction of the honeyed [substances],
reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times for the purpose of joining the honeyed substances.
Next is the contemplation of the paths, according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader;
this is the pervasion of the worlds within the principles (tattvas), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva.
And the thirty-six pervasive [principles] consist of the words of the mantra-syllables;
all of them are included within the [thirty-two] principles (tattvas) by virtue of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
Those [powers] beginning with Nivṛtti are indeed remembered as being included within the Kalās;
the seed-mantras (bījāmantra) such as Hṛdaya and the rest are proclaimed to be their designators (vācaka).
One should contemplate the distinct pervasion of each individual *kalā*;
these *kalās*, beginning with Earth, are to be known as those causes beginning with Brahmā.
Having thus meditated upon pervasion, there should be the establishment of the paths;
by means of the *dhruva* mantra alone, one should offer three oblations, and from this, the purification of the paths occurs.
When the deity has been worshipped in the fire and the deposition on the path (adhvanyāsa) has been performed,
one should perform that very same [deposition] starting from the feet, following the sequence beginning with earth (pṛthivī).

"Beginning with *dhāmādhiḥ* and *praṇava*, and again *namaḥ* for *nivṛtti*—this is the mantra for the installation (*upasthāpana*). Having meditated upon the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established throughout the paths (*adhvan*)."
Within the Nivṛtti [kalā], the earth extends for a hundred koṭis;
and within it, there are one hundred and eight worlds at most.
There are twenty-eight words, and a single phoneme is established here;
one should know that there are exactly two mantras, and one should contemplate the six paths.
Having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should offer three oblations into the presence [of the deity].
Therein reside the impurities (mala) in the form of the worlds of Māyā, as well as karma.
The forms of the body and the world are proclaimed to be of the nature of *māyā*;
action (*karman*) is the cause of experience, while desire is the impurity (*mala*) in this context.
In this way, the three bonds situated within the paths (adhvan) are to be meditated upon during initiation;
and for the sake of their purification, initiation is performed according to the prescribed rule.
O Goddess, at the outset one should install Śakti, endowed with the Kalās and Tattvas; having mentally conceived Vāgīśī within the heart, she who pervades all wombs.
From Śatarudra to Ananta, various wombs (yonis) are situated;
by means of the simultaneous state of the menses (ṛtu), one should cause Vāgīśī to be present.
One should worship with flowers, perfumes, and incense in due order using the *dhruva* mantra;
with the syllable *oṃ*, three oblations are offered for the purpose of invoking Vāgīśī.
Having sprinkled the disciple with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, he should strike him while uttering that mantra;
then, having gone [into the disciple] by means of his own exhalation (recaka), he should sever [the bonds] at his heart with a sword.
Then, having drawn that self by means of the *dhāman*, one should place it at the *dvādaśānta*;
having encapsulated that consciousness situated there with the *dhruva* mantra, one should merge it into one's own self through the *mudrā*.
One should fill [the breath] with Bhairava alone, then perform retention (kumbhaka), and thereafter exhale;
having drawn [the breath] from the *dvādaśānta*, one should join it with the Bhavamudrā.
Having meditated upon oneself as the Lord and [upon] Māyā as Vāgīśvarī,
and having joined consciousness within her, one should emit bodies along the path.
For the purpose of experiencing the fruits remaining from the latent impressions of past karma,
[the Lord] simultaneously [produces] diverse enjoyments according to place, time, and body.
Through the power of mantra, such individuals are ripened;
their bodies are divided and they are emitted into the wombs of the Goddess of Speech within the matrices.
And having joined [the disciple] with the *dhāman*, one should offer three oblations;
simultaneously, within all the wombs (*garbha*), bodies of various forms arise.
Fully endowed with the will of Bhairava, [the practitioner] extends [the offering] through the hundred Rudras and so forth to infinity;
within the wombs, he effects the completion of the womb by means of three oblations to Bhairava.
Having performed the oblation, one should then effect the birth again by means of three further offerings;
thus, bodies in all wombs simultaneously attain growth.
Karma is the auxiliary cause for the accomplishment of experience;
in the absence of that [auxiliary], there would be no experience. For that purpose, purification is prescribed. (SvaT 4.119)
When wealth has been acquired, one should enjoy the experience consisting of both suffering and pleasure;
one should dissolve oneself with supreme joy even amidst happiness, sorrow, and the like.
One should perform the oblation in the three [fires] with three [mantras] for each, using the very *dhāman* [mantra];
furthermore, one hundred oblations should be offered with the *dhāman* mantra for the sake of expiation.
But that karma which has the nature of being experienced— characterized by birth, lifespan, and enjoyment—
is purified at the end of its retribution for one established in the world of earth.
The fourteen worlds of saṃsāra, together with the eight [worlds] of formative forces (saṃskāra),
totaling forty-four, will be described on the path of the worlds for the sake of the twice-born.
The womb, the seed, as well as the disposition, the food, and the place—
O Goddess, the purification of these, as well as the attainment of the state of being a portion of Rudra, [is taught].
Having performed an inspection here, one becomes purified through atonement alone;
for whatever objects exist in the form of the world, they are all of the nature of things to be experienced.
When the remainder of the fruits of karma have been experienced, that is traditionally known as "expiation" (niṣkṛti).
It is the cessation [of suffering] through experience; for in the absence of experience, that [cessation] is indeed traditionally known as expiation.
The state of being an enjoyer and attachment to sense objects are proclaimed to be the effects of impurity;
however, the absence of that state of being an enjoyer is that which is produced by the body in that very [state].
By the command of Śiva, the disjunction of that animal victim is performed with mantras;
and three oblations are offered with the *dhāman* mantra for the purpose of effecting the disjunction.
One should also cause three oblations to be offered with the [mantra of the] abode for the severing of the bonds;
the bonds within the body are those pertaining to Māyā, beginning with Kalā and ending with the element Earth.
The forms of bodies and their instruments perish in a thousand ways due to the absence of experience, even though they were intended for the accomplishment of the purposes of the person.
The procedure for the severing of the bonds (pāśa) is performed with mantras enjoined by the ritual rules;
in this way, the disjunction of even the threefold bond is said to be accomplished through initiation (dīkṣā).
Through the dissolution of the remainder of the body,
one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with Śiva alone, accompanied by the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
That consciousness, which resides at the summit of the pure reality (śuddhatattva) and possesses a golden luster,
one should cause to be offered three oblations for its extraction, again by means of the [mantric] radiance (dhāman).
Therefore, having grasped consciousness from that reality while it is joined with impurity,
one should fill it, abiding within oneself, in the heart by means of the mudrā according to the previously prescribed method.
Having retained [the breath], exhaled, and restrained it with the *dhruva* mantra from the *dvādaśānta*,
one should deposit this into the body of the disciple through the opening of the channel as before.
For the purpose of establishing [the soul] therein, one should offer three oblations with the *dhāman* mantra;
then, at the conclusion of the purification of the *kalās*, one should worship Brahmā, the lord of the causes.
Having first invoked [the deity] with its own name and the syllable *praṇava*, one should satisfy it and then offer [the oblation].
One should abandon sound and touch within that [deity], beginning with the *dhruva* [mantra] and joined with the name.
By means of the application of the *svāhākāra* exclamation, one should offer those two into Brahman;
through three oblations each, one should offer the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
One should cause the Śrāvakas to hear [the teaching] using the vocative case;
having worshipped Brahmā and performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should dismiss him.
Having worshipped Vāgīśī with the *dhruva* mantra and having gratified her, he should dismiss her;
then, having offered oblations, he should behold there the pure net of bonds.
Then, one should meditate on the non-existence of that which arises from past karma;
because the seeker of liberation is indifferent [to worldly results], one should not purify the *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion).
For the sake of the practitioner's prosperity, one should purify a single prior karma;
having contemplated that both the prior and future karmas are unified in one, one should then initiate him.
This initiation belongs to the Śiva-dharma; otherwise, it belongs to the loka-dharma.
Even for one who follows the ancient scriptures, it brings about the destruction of unrighteousness (adharma).
This [attainment] should be known as belonging to the worldly sphere (lokadharmin), devoid of the propitiation of mantras;
for upon the dissolution of the commenced body, he indeed enjoys the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Having eaten, he should go upward to wherever he is directed by the Guru;
whether in the Sakala or Niṣkala state, it shall depend on the disciple and the teacher.
Even in Nirvāṇa, one who has been initiated fails because of the absence of karma when there is still a seed;
for he must maintain the bond of the conduct of the pledge.
That noose is not purified at all; it is proclaimed as being "with seed" (sabījā).
However, one should purify the noose of the conduct of the pledge (samayācāra) within the "seedless" (nirbījā) [initiation].
Liberation occurs simply through initiation, always by means of devotion to the Guru;
that second [type of initiation], which bestows immediate liberation, is the seedless (nirbījā). (SvaT 4.148)
At the conclusion of initiation, there shall be purification from the three bonds (pāśa) commenced in the past and future; upon the casting off of the body, the supreme state is attained.
In this way, according to the dispositions of the disciples, the Guru should always bring about various kinds of results through a well-performed initiation.
The power of mantra, which indeed originates from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, is inconceivable;
it should be employed at the time of ritual action by the Guru, preceded by devotion.

Just as one might certainly swallow snares with the tips of horns, the Guru who knows the reality of mantra and is possessed by Śiva effects the swallowing of [the bonds] with mantras in an instant. (SvaT 4.152)
One should perform the joining of the *kalās*, which consists of two forms: pure and impure.
One should utter the pure as short and the impure as long.
Having meditated upon oneness, one should contemplate that which is dissolved and pure;
the cessation of the *praṇava* and so forth is *pratiṣṭhā*, immediately following that.

At the end of that, however, the *namaskāra* is known as the "joining of the digits" (*kalāsaṃdhānaka*). Having invoked, established, and fully worshipped [the deity], one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*).
For this is the joining of the digits; one should observe its pervasion.
From the ankles up to the navel, one should perform the conceptualization of the path within the body of the disciple.
The pervasion of the Foundation consists of twenty-four principles,
fifty-six worlds, and twenty-three phonemes.
It is prescribed as having twenty-one topics to be known and three mantras;
for these are remembered as the primary bonds, which one should contemplate as subtle and infinite within.
However, regarding the purification of the elements and the senses as established in other tantras,
one should always include the six sheaths and the five sense objects within that [purification].
Having established the specific [deity], one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
then, with three oblations to Bhairava, one performs the visualization of Vāgīśī within it.
The invocation by one's own name and so forth, as well as the offering of the *arghya* and the oblation (*homa*), are as before;
likewise, there is sprinkling, striking, cutting, and the seizing by means of attraction.
Having filled [the vessel] with the radiance and having performed the breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should then cut [the connection] and cause [the disciple] to grasp it again;
then, through the sequence as before, [one performs] the entry into the womb and the birth.
Assuming the sovereign form, one should cause [the disciple] to undergo beatings and so forth;
for one established in authority, there is enjoyment, dissolution, and indeed expiation.
The expiation should be performed with the head-mantra (Śiras) in the form of Śiva;
the separation [of the soul from the bonds] is to be offered with the heart-mantra (Hṛd), and likewise the severing of the fetters (pāśa) with the sword-mantra (Asi).
Having performed the extraction of the *pūrṇāhuti* as before by means of Bhairava,
and having established oneself within the body of Sadāśiva, one should perform the rites of separation and so forth.
Established within the self by means of inhalation (pūraka), and remaining there through the process of exhalation (recaka),
one should pronounce the name of Viṣṇu, and having meditated upon and invoked him, one should install him.
One should worship with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, and offer three oblations of libations;
one should always present the essence, which is a portion of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), to Viṣṇu.
Then one should dismiss Viṣṇu and dismiss Vāgīśī;
the junction of the digits (kalā-saṃdhi) is as before, through the application of short and long [vowels].
Within that infinite web of bonds, one should meditate upon non-existence;
the bound soul (paśu), liberated from the two kalās, becomes eager to ascend upwards.
Now, having joined him to that third knowledge, one should purify him;
having established and fully worshipped him, one should offer three oblations.

Having thus brought [the reality] face-to-face, just as before, the pervasion of Vidyā is held to extend from the principle of the Person (puruṣatattva) up to the end of Māyā, including the observation of the paths.
There are seven principles (tattvas) and twenty-seven worlds (bhuvanas);
twenty-six stages (padas) are declared, and seven phonemes (varṇas) are proclaimed.
Having understood the sixfold path through the two mantras, one should perform the conceptualization of Vāgīśī;
having invoked Vyāpinī into all wombs with the Praṇava.
Having meditated upon them as being simultaneously present in their seasonal forms and having worshipped them, one should offer libations.
Then, having sprinkled the disciple with auspicious water, one should strike him with the Astra-mantra.
And by that very weapon-mantra, joined with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
one should enter the heart of the disciple’s body by means of one’s own *revaka*.
Having severed [the bonds] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should draw [the disciple] in by means of the special mantra of attachment (viśeṣāśleṣāstra);
having grasped him from the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta), establish him within oneself as before.
Then, having restrained [the breath] by means of inhalation and having exhaled it,
one should join his consciousness, as before, pervading all wombs.
From the beginning of yoga until its dissolution, and by means of the *dhāman* as before,
the expiation for the Vidyā occurs through a hundred oblations with the *śikhā*.
Then, having invoked Rudra beginning with the syllable *praṇava* and established him, one should worship him;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should place the two fixed oblations (*dhruvāhutī*) upon his form as fragrance.
Having deposited the portion of the *puryaṣṭaka* and dismissed the deity Rudra,
and likewise having dismissed Vāgīśī, the conjunction of the *kalās* is performed as before.
One should employ the vidyā-mantra according to the division of short and long vowels for the purpose of pacification;
however, for the sake of reintegration, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra.
One should perform the invocation by means of one's own name, offer it according to the ritual for pacification,
cultivate the realization of the object of knowledge, and worship with flowers and other offerings.
One should offer three oblations with the root mantra from the principle of Vidyā up to Sadāśiva;
for there is a pervasion of the three principles and likewise of the three phonemes.
The eleven *padas* are to be known, as well as the seventeen cities (*purāṇi*), the two mantras, and the sixfold path; thus these are remembered as the primary bonds (*pāśas*).
One should always cause the many subtle nooses to be absorbed within that;
there, one should fashion Vagīśī according to the previously mentioned rite, [offering] oblations.
Then, worship with the root mantra, followed by sprinkling and striking;
likewise, cutting, attracting, seizing, and the birth of the state of being sustained by yoga.
Likewise, the empowerment, the enjoyment, and the dissolution should occur as before;
all of these are performed with the root mantra by means of three oblations.
For atonement, the preceptor should perform a hundred oblations with the *kavaca* [mantra];
he should effect the separation and the severing of the bonds with the *astra* [mantra].
Having performed the extraction (*uddhāra*), established [the deity] within oneself, and then established [him] therein through the state of non-duality,
one should invoke the Lord by his own name preceded by the *praṇava* and worship him.

Having worshipped, offered oblations, and performed libations, one should offer the intellect (buddhi) by reciting its own name preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*, while identifying it as a portion of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*). (SvaT 4.190)
Having likewise thus offered the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), one should then ask for forgiveness;
having worshipped Vāgīśī and gratified her, one should dismiss her.
One should first apply the *kalā-saṃdhānaka* within the stage beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*);
one should offer three oblations according to the division of short and long [syllables].
One who knows the ritual procedure must perform the concentration on reality (tattvasaṃdhāna) with the Dhruva-mantra;
thereafter, O Dear One, one should establish the Kalā and offer oblations with the Dhruva-mantra.
By performing the application of three oblations while uttering the word for one's own name,
one should invoke Śāntyatītā, establish her, and then worship her again.
Having perceived the pervasion residing in the [lower] paths, those who have reached the Śiva-principle—
namely the Bindu, the Nāda, and likewise the Śakti— are established within the Śiva-principle.
One step is one mantra, proclaimed to consist of sixteen syllables;
one should meditate upon the subtle worlds within the Śāntyatīta [kalā].
O lady of excellent limbs, they are to be purified until those rays of Śiva [reach their goal];
above Śiva, Śiva himself is to be known, wherein one who is united is not born again.
The six paths should be known as one; hear again their enumeration:
the five kalās are to be known, and indeed the thirty-six tattvas.
It should be known that there are two hundred and twenty-four worlds;
herein, there are eighty-one squares, and it is remembered as consisting of fifty syllables and a half.
The mantras are to be known as eleven; this is the mandala of the paths.
When this has been purified, the initiated one attains liberation.
Having invoked Vāgīśī with the *dhruva* mantra, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) as before;
having worshipped her with flowers and other offerings, one should [place] the victim (*paśu*) into her womb as before.
Everything from birth until the end in dissolution must be performed with the *dhruva* mantra;
for the rite of expiation, one should perform a hundred oblations using the root mantra.

One should perform the severing of the bonds of separation as before by means of the *dhruva* mantra; however, it is taught that the state of the soul being situated within itself and within the planet [of initiation] for the bound soul (*paśu*) is effected by the *praṇava*.
Then, having invoked Sadāśiva while reciting the root mantra,
and having established him with a prostration, one should worship him with flowers and offer libations.
One should deposit the mind, which is a portion of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), into the Lord of Causes,
having uttered the Praṇava and so forth, as well as the name "Mind" followed by "namas."
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa), one should subsequently worship [the deities] ending with the names and *svāhā*.
By offering three oblations (*āhuti*), one is purified from the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Then one should dismiss the deity and the causal Sadāśiva;
having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, one should thereafter worship Vāgīśī.
Having honored and gratified them, she, imbued with devotion, should be addressed thus:
"Forgive me, O Goddess of the lords of gods, for I have caused you distress for the sake of the sacrificial victim."
"Now you must no longer obstruct; go, O Goddess, to your own abode.
Having thus dismissed her, the Kalā Śāntyatītā, having gone to dissolution, should be contemplated.
Up to the limit of the support of one's own power, established in the state of the extremely subtle non-existence,
one should indeed offer a hundred oblations with the flame through the differentiation of the reality of the Self.
By means of the yoga of vocalizing with sound, one should offer oblations into the reality of the Self;
this is to be known by the teacher in the great sacrifice as extending up to the level of the principle of Māyā.
O Dear One, for the sake of the rite when there is a deficiency in the ritual procedure, and for the purification through expiation,
one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times into the reality of the Vidyā.
One should perform the oblation within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) by means of the practice of whispered recitation;
one should designate the entire path ending with Sadāśiva as belonging to the principle of knowledge.
Whatever expiation may be required due to the omission or error in the pronunciation of mantras,
that oblation performed within the principle of Vidyā (vidyātattva) shall serve for its purification.
If there should be an occasion for penance due to a deficiency in mental consciousness,
one should perform a fire offering (homa) with the root mantra in the principle of Śiva for the sake of that purification.
Through a mental application, once the end of the power has been reached within the path,
one should perform the severing of the crest at the conclusion of the purification of the three principles.
She stands beyond the paths, supreme, peaceful, incomparable, and free from ailment;
she pervades all principles and is the cause of all causes.
Having meditated [on the deity] at the tip of the child's crest like a drop of water on the tip of a flower,
one should address the scissors with the crest-mantra and cut the crest with that same crest-mantra.
Having handed over the topknot to another, he should depart together with his disciple;
the disciple should perform the ritual bath, and there should be the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) for the Guru.
The Guru may perform either bathing or the smearing with ashes according to his own preference;
having entered [the mandala] and performed the ritual of totalization (sakalīkaraṇa), he should offer oblations to the crest-lock with the Pūrṇāhuti.
Having offered the oblation and gone out, having sipped water and washed the *sruk*, *sruva*, and *kartarī* ladles,
having re-entered and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should perform the worship of the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*).
Then, within the mandala, one should worship the Supreme Lord with flowers and all other offerings; thereafter, one should make a formal petition to Śiva.
O Blessed One, by your grace, having seized and purified a sacrificial animal situated at the eighth station on the path, up to the final cutting of its crest;
I have indeed performed only a small portion of the procedure taught by your mouth;
however, by your power alone, one must swiftly proceed to the auspicious and eternal state.
"Now, O Lord, the task for the application [of mantras] is at your command;
let your command be given, O Master, so that I may unite the disciple."
Having received permission and feeling greatly rejoiced, he should depart from the city;
extending his arm half a cubit toward the fire, he should summon the disciple and sprinkle him with water.
As before, for one seated upon the throne, there is the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa) and so forth,
including the internal placement of the faculties preceded by the joining of the channels.
The worship and libation for the mantras and for Śiva in the fire should be performed by dividing [the offerings] into ten parts, according to the available materials.
Thereafter, one should purify the mantras that reside within the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
by means of a single offering, let their authority be relinquished.
Since the rite of sakalīkaraṇa has never been performed for the sacrificial victim (paśu),
I shall now describe to you the ritual application [for it].

Having understood the measure of the movement [of the breath] as well as the circulation of the vital breath (prāṇa), and the division of the sixfold path as it resides within the single vital breath; SvaT 4.231.
The utterance of *haṃsa* by means of the phonemes, as well as the very abandonment of the causes,
should be known as the void (*śūnya*), the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), the abandonment, the union, and the arising.
Furthermore, having understood that the differentiation of categories occurs again through the attainment of their essential nature,
one should apply oneself to the pervasive presence of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva.
I shall explain its division so that it may be known according to reality:
the movement [of the breath] consists of thirty-six finger-breadths, from the heart-lotus up to the power (śakti).
O Dear One, that which is measured by a time consisting of sixteen *tuṭis*—
listen to me as I describe it correctly according to its divisions as it circulates.
He should abandon one part up to the heart-lotus and the entrance;
the second at the tip of the nose, and the third at the end of the Śakti.
Remaining there, one may turn back as long as one has not found reality;
but once the supreme reality is known, even while remaining there, one is no longer afflicted.
When [the breath] moves downward by means of the power (śakti), then one is unawakened (abudha);
when it rises again from the heart, one is said to be awakening (budhyamāna).
Having attained Śakti, one should be known as a Budha; in the portion of Vyāpinī, there is Prabuddhatā;
but having transcended that, one is Suprabuddha, and then Unmanatva occurs.
There is no time, no movement of the digits, no reality, and no cause;
it is the supreme, pure, perfect nirvāṇa, transmitted through the lineage of gurus.
Having understood that, one is liberated; having gone there, one is not born again.
I shall explain to you how the sixfold path is situated within the vital breath.

Indeed, that which is the perception of consciousness from the feet up to the crown of the head should be known as the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and likewise as the path of the principles (tattvādhvan).
The vital breath, whose continuum is composed of the digits (kalā), always circulates;
Nivṛtti and Pratiṣṭhā operate in the lower part.
Vidyā and Śānti are likewise above; Śāntyatītā is the Adhiṣṭhikā.
Beyond that is the supreme state, the imperishable station situated above it.
In this way, the *bindu* and *kalā* should be understood as being of the nature of *nāda* and *śakti*,
as well as being of the nature of *vyāpinī* and so forth, according to the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader.
All [the levels] are established solely in the vital breath (prāṇa); through the abandonment of the six, there is absorption in the seventh.
Thus has the path of the parts (kalādhvan) been fully explained; now learn from me the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan).
All phonemes, whose nature is sound, exist in this world of moving and non-moving beings;
they abide with five hundred divisions within the scriptures that extend to infinite millions.
From sound, the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to arise; from that vital breath, the phonemes (varṇas) are produced and they dissolve back into it, wherein sound itself has gone to dissolution.
O lady of excellent hips, transcending sound, he is united with reality; O Goddess, being thus united, he is omnipresent and free from both merit and demerit.
Once one has attained the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), one does not look downward again;
for by unrighteousness one goes downward, whereas by righteousness one ascends once more.
Having abandoned duality through consciousness, one becomes all-pervading here;
thus has the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) been fully explained. Now the path of words (padādhvan) is being proclaimed.
Even the eighty-one syllables that abide as the King of Vidyās are essentially phonemes; here, those phonemes abide as the nature of the vital breath.
Therefore, these words therein are [arranged] according to the sequence of the vital breaths;
thus has the path of the words been fully explained. Now, learn from me the path of the mantras.
That which is the eleven-fold mantra-group is established in the *haṃsa*;
and that which is the eleven-fold pada-group moves perpetually within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the bindu;
the half-moon, the nirodhin, the nāda, and indeed the end of nāda (nādānta).
Śakti is pervasive, and Samanā is remembered as the eleventh;
Unmanā is beyond that, and what transcends even that is the stainless state.
The mantras abide thus within the vital breath (prāṇa), and the utterance of the *haṃsa* is likewise described.
The letter *ha*, which is the nature of the vital breath, is traditionally held to be self-impelled and shaped like a horse-shoe (*halākṛti*).
When joined with the letter *a*, and likewise with the movement of the letter *u*,
and joined with the mere measure of the letter *m*, the pronunciation of the syllable becomes distinct.
Through its union with the head, the *bindu* attains a beautiful resonance;
*nāda* is said to be its mouth, for the mouth emits sound.
By this very yoga, the *haṃsa* is called the *puruṣa*;
indeed, it moves through all living beings by way of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
It dissolves into the principle of Śakti; through higher consciousness, it ascends upward.
Having transcended Vyāpinī and Samanā, one should proceed to Śiva by means of Unmanā.
The *haṃsa* situated within the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) does not move; it becomes all-pervasive.
The utterance of *haṃsa*, together with its causes, has thus been fully explained.
The letter *ha* is the essence of the power of vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*), while the letter *a* denotes Brahman;
its renunciation occurs in the heart, and the letter *u* denotes Viṣṇu.
