The letter *ma*, which denotes Rudra, should be abandoned at the throat;
one should abandon that [letter] in the middle of the palate, and the *bindu* itself is Īśvara.
In that context, Sadāśiva is to be described as "abandonment" (tyāga) within the resonance between the eyebrows;
his abandonment is prescribed from the forehead up to the crown of the head.
Śiva, the imperishable, is the signified of those [energies]—Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.
One should cast Śakti into the middle of the head, and above that, one should cast Vyāpinī.
Having abandoned the *samanā* and *unmanā*, through the abandonment of the six, there is dissolution in the seventh;
O Dear One, one should abandon [the states] in this very manner by means of increasingly subtle and subtler states.
Through entities that are gross and even grosser, which bestow various fruits of accomplishment,
the subtle and supreme entity is established as being ultimately non-existence.
The state beyond mind (unmanā) is one nature; another is considered its gross form.
Beyond that is the void, and beyond that is contact.
Sound is light; from that arise the mantras, the causes, and the worlds.
The world, whose nature consists of the five elements, is presided over by these causes.
He who meditates upon the world as having the single form that is about to be described,
attains the state of a Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa), provided he is absorbed in Śiva through meditation upon Him.
And while performing the propitiation of the causes beginning with Brahmā, one who recalls their embodied form according to the previously stated characteristics shall attain identity with them.
The minister and the accomplishment of the mantra arise from recitation, fire-offerings, and worship;
through meditation on the previously described form, they are accomplished here—of this there is no doubt.
Through meditation on the light, the lord of yogis shall attain the perfection of yoga;
when he attains identity with that, he becomes the sovereign of yogis.
Through meditation on sound, one becomes the essence of sound and the fulfiller of all that consists of speech;
and through meditation on touch, one becomes the essence of touch and the cause of the world.
Through the meditation on emptiness, the self becomes empty, pervasive, and omnipresent;
by means of the yoga of equanimous meditation, the yogi shall attain omniscience.
But the Unstruck (unmanī) should always contemplate the supreme, subtle non-existence;
that which transcends all senses and mind is called the imperceptible non-existence.
Having cultivated non-existence through existence, and having rendered existence supportless,
one attains the state of non-existence which is liberated from all limiting conditions.
This is your abandonment of causes; now learn from me the abandonment of time:
the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to consist of sixteen *tuṭis*.
Relying upon two *tuṭis*, each Bhairava remains;
through the division of day and night, they indeed bring about their arising.
The ninth is the supreme deity; from him, your vital energies arise.
One should abandon everything at all times within the breath; I shall explain this to you exactly as it is.
The *tuṭis* are said to be sixteen; they are the instrument of time (*kālakaraṇa*).
Time, established with that as its beginning, pervades the entire realm of speech.
The tuṭi, the lava, the nimeṣa, the kāṣṭhā, and likewise the kalā;
as well as the muhūrta, the day-and-night (ahorātra), the fortnight (pakṣa), the month, and the season (ṛtu).
The solstice, the year, the yuga, the manvantara,
as well as the kalpa and the mahākalpa— he should abandon that [body] at the end of his power.
At the end of the pervasive [kalpa], there is the supreme time; he, as its limb, should abandon that. And that [time] is to be known as the seventeenth, situated beyond the *parārdha*.
O Goddess, even that eighteenth [digit], the *parārdha*, should be abandoned at the end of *samanā*;
for it is the supreme, imperishable pervader of time throughout all time.
It should be joined with the supreme state beyond the mind; there, time does not exist.
It is eternal, perpetually arisen, all-pervading, and one should not abandon its primordial form.
And having attained that which is eternally arisen, one becomes forever identical with it;
thus there is the abandonment of time, and this is called the state of emptiness.
The upper void, the lower void, and the middle void as the third—
these three voids are indeed mobile, located respectively below, in the middle, and above.
The fourth is the pervasive void (vyāpinī-śūnya), and the fifth is in Samanā;
likewise, the sixth is in Unmanā—these six are established as the conventional levels (sāmayāḥ).
All [mantras], even those belonging to the *samaya* [class], grant accomplishment when presided over by reality (*tattva*).
Having abandoned the six voids (*śūnya*), effect their dissolution into the seventh.
That emptiness, however, is supreme and subtle, devoid of all states;
it is called "non-empty" and "empty," and emptiness is said to be non-existence.
That is designated as non-existence where all entities have come to an end;
it is the supreme state of mere being, utterly tranquil, an indescribable reality that persists.
And wherever the gross [elements] such as sound and the rest are situated,
there also the supreme void remains, pervading everything.
O Dear One, that very same [reality] becomes gross by virtue of its gross limiting adjuncts;
though one, it is established through the distinction between the gross and the subtle.
Having attained that, one achieves identity with it; there is no doubt in this matter.
The state of emptiness has been fully explained; now learn from me the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
One should know that the first [state] is equal flavor within the self; the second is to be known in the mantra.
One should make the third reside in the channels, and one should make the fourth reside in the power (śakti).
The fifth is proclaimed in Vyāpinī, while the sixth is in Samanā;
O Goddess, the seventh is ordained as the state of equalized flavor (samarasa).
Having first gathered the disciple’s self according to the previously mentioned procedure in due order,
one should subsequently join it with one's own self and contemplate it as having become thoroughly blended.
Having performed inhalation and retention, one should restrain [the breath] with the *samāna* wind;
O Goddess, as many channels as there are situated transversely, upwards, and downwards.
Drawn together by the equalizing breath, they become unified;
within them, those winds also attain a state of equal flavor within the vital breath (prāṇa).
The channels, however, remain unified within the *suṣumnā*;
then one should indeed utter the mantra and contemplate it as dissolved into the *nāda*.
The mantra, the self, and likewise the channel—thus they become of one flavor;
then, in the left, right, and middle, one should release the resonance (nāda).
And that path is the Setubandha, having gone upon which one is not born again—
wherein Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself [reside].
These attain equality here; otherwise, they remain separate.
When one utters that sound within it as long as possible, one reaches dissolution.
The Nada situated in the midst of Śakti is indeed ordained as being of the nature of Śakti;
everything there consists of Śakti, and everything becomes of one flavor (samarasībhavet).
Having reached Vyāpinī above that, one should attain identity with all;
she is called "Vyāpinī" because she pervades everything on all sides.
Beyond that, having pervaded the level of Samanā, one should again attain identity with it;
and she is to be known as all-pervading, established in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
Having abandoned the sixth, which is the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), one should then proceed to the seventh;
having attained that, there is indeed identity with it—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
And he [is present] in all beings, in their dispositions, essences, and senses,
whether stationary or moving, and existing as conscious or unconscious.
Pervading the entire path, it remains in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya);
indeed, it forcibly causes even the minds of yogins to tremble.
For one whose state consisting of the knowable is stable, full, and all-pervading,
the mind does not waver, even while situated in all conditions.
Wherever the mind goes, one should contemplate that very object as the knowable;
for having moved, where could it go, since everything is composed of Śiva?
Abiding amidst all objects and within the domains of the senses,
wherever one may examine it, nothing whatsoever is found that is not auspicious.
Having thus understood the state of equal flavor (samarasa), one would never be deluded;
he whose disposition is thus in every respect shall also become omnipresent.
Thus has the state of equal flavor (samarasa) been explained; now understand from me the equinox (viṣuvat).
The first is the equinox of the vital breath (prāṇa-viṣuvat), and the second is to be known as the [equinox] of the measure (mātra).
The third is the channel-equinox (nāḍiviṣuvat), the fourth is the tranquil one,
the fifth is the power-equinox (śaktiviṣuvat), and the sixth is indeed called time (kāla).
Now the seventh division, the equinox of the principles (tattva), is described:
by joining the self and the mind to the vital breath (prāṇa), one becomes the equinox.
In the vital breath, that which is called the Viṣuvat is said to be the Mantra-Viṣuvat;
one should recite the mantra as long as the mind does not become distracted by anything else.
Through the division of the higher and the lower, that which consists of mantra is so described;
it is called the "Mantric Equinox. Now learn from me that which resides in the channels.
Among all the channels, that which is situated in the center should be known as Suṣumnā; it goes from the navel to Śiva by means of Śakti.
There, one should cause the sound (nāda) to flow; this is called the equinox of the channels (nāḍī-viṣuva). Now I shall explain to you that which is tranquil and likewise the equinox.
In each solstice, the movement is six finger-breadths; there are causes for every single finger-breadth.
Having set aside those causes from below, there are indeed only six causes.
But in the seventh [state], it is indeed utterly tranquil, with the range of the senses completely stilled;
one who is tranquil is to be known as "stabilized" (stimita), and "stabilized" is considered to be motionless.
"Immovable, waveless, steady, and full on all sides—
having established such a state of being, the initiations should be performed by the teachers."
Understand from me this tranquil Viṣuvat, which has power as its limiting adjunct:
when the Nāda situated in the middle of the power moves above the Nāda.
Now, understand from me that which is called the time of the Śakti-Visuvat:
the sixteen *tuṭis* which are established at the end of the breath.
The time [of that] was said by me to be merely the twinkling of an eyebrow at its end;
divide that again into three parts according to the distinction between the higher and the lower.
Another is the sixteenth up to the time [of the seventeenth], and the seventeenth is the supreme;
but that time which is both supreme and non-supreme, O Dear One, is the eighteenth Lord.
Having thus divided time into three parts, the vital breath (prāṇa) should then be released;
the other [breath] resides at the head of Śakti, and the second is in Vyāpinī.
The third is at the place of Samanā; it is known as the equinox of that time. This is declared as the sixth, and the seventh is called Tāttvika.
O Goddess, being free from mental fluctuations, one should then apply oneself to the Self therein;
for when joined with that, the self indeed becomes identical with it.
O Goddess, that which is called the Reality (tattva) stands beyond all as the Equinox (viṣuvat).
Having known the Equinox to be of such a nature, who would not be liberated from bondage? (SvaT 4.333)
The equinox has been thus described; now hear about the differentiation of the categories, as well as renunciation, experience, and union in the supreme state.
The eleventh category of objects should be known as ending with the Transmental (unmanā); it is the supreme state.
One should pierce through [reality] with the spear of knowledge; knowledge is that which makes the object of knowledge known.
Since it is an incomparable cognition that makes things known, it is an illumination like a lamp;
just as someone with a lamp in hand might perceive and then take up an object.
In this way, one should cause the object of knowledge to be established within that knowledge by means of knowledge;
for knowledge, O lady of excellent vows, is declared to be the characteristic of the reality of the object of knowledge.
The characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is declared to be the quality (guṇa), and the art (kalā) is always the reality (tattva).
There is no reality without a quality, and no quality without a reality.
People everywhere grasp at qualities, but the reality is never grasped;
for it is grasped through inference and through direct sensory experience.
Through scripture, however, [the truth] is obtained by means of the relationship between proponent and opponent;
it is said that "scripture is knowledge," yet there are infinite millions of treatises.
All scripture consists of sound, and sound is proclaimed to be Haṃsa.
The yoga of Haṃsa has been explained previously; now the enumeration of its measures (mātrās) is stated.
The application of its measure is as follows: from the heart and so forth, it extends one span (vitasti) above the navel and six finger-breadths below the throat.
The heart, however, is located in the middle region and measures four finger-breadths;
there Brahmā is established by means of the twenty-four principles (tattvas).
Know that the throat is eight finger-breadths [in length]; Viṣṇu is established there, conjoined with the eight principles (tattvas). Above that is four finger-breadths.
Rudra, relying upon the principle of Māyā, resides at the base of the palate;
the space between the eyebrows is proclaimed to measure two finger-breadths.
There, O Goddess, Īśvara resides, endowed with two principles;
and eleven finger-breadths above that is the Lord Sadāśiva.
Endowed with the two principles, he goes as far as the aperture of Brahmā;
one finger-breadth above that is Śakti, and there Śiva is established.
When only the skin remains, the pervasive [state] is said to be Samanā, and beyond that is Unmanā;
but further than that is the Supreme Reality, which is devoid of all means of valid cognition.
Now the number of measures (mātrā), the count, and the yoga of the Haṃsa are being told:
the letter *a* and the letter *ha*, these two, abide as one.
There is no distinction between these two, like that between wind and space;
it should be known as a single entity, which proceeds from the heart.
The syllable *ukāra*, indeed having two measures (*dvimātra*), should be articulated in the place of the throat;
the syllable *makāra*, indeed having three measures (*trimātra*), should move within the middle of the palate.
The *bindu* consists of half a *mātrā*, for it is said to be half a measure;
O Goddess, its utterance is prescribed to be between the eyebrows.
From the remainder of that, there is the half-moon, which should be one-quarter [of the measure];
and the *nirodhin* is half a quarter; one should utter these at the end of the forehead.
The Nāda, consisting of sixteen parts, should rise as far as the crown of the head;
the Śakti, consisting of thirty-two parts, should rise to the end of the thirty-six [tattvas].
The pervasive [power] consists of sixty-four parts and stands beyond Śakti;
above it are Samanā and Unmanā, while the supreme, imperishable [state] is without measure (amātra).
The number of measures (mātrā), the yoga, and the measure (pramāṇa) have been fully proclaimed.
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, one should then differentiate the categories of reality (padārtha).
One should cause [the deity] to burst forth by means of the pain of the *mātrā*s, together with the visualization of the *mudrā*;
for the mantra is indeed the power of gnosis (*jñāna-śakti*), and the *mudrā* is of the nature of action (*kriyā*).
And existence is said to be the mind; that mind is preceded by the intellect (buddhi).
Furthermore, the Supreme is to be reached through the mind, being presided over by the power of will (icchā-śakti).
Wherever there may be a desire, knowledge proceeds there;
through the connection of action and instrument, the utterance of reality occurs.
For one devoid of ritual action and its instruments, there can be no utterance at all;
and that [action] is traditionally held to be threefold according to the distinction of the instruments.
The wise one should utter the reality with one instrument,
and then, with the second, he should obstruct the channels and the gateways.
Having performed the third divine *karaṇa*, one should indeed utter the *tattva*;
having performed inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should block all the gates.
For when the gate of the anus is blocked, the others are indeed blocked; therefore, one should contemplate that single gate as flowing upwards.
O Dear One, those channels and lotuses of the knots that are directed downwards are completely obstructed by the *kumbhaka* [retention] and blossom forth on all sides.
Now, listen to the description of the procedure for that:
the tongue should be joined to the palate, yet slightly above it, without touching it.
Having slightly opened the mouth, one should not touch the lips;
likewise, the rows of teeth should remain untouched here, and the gaze should be free from looking upward or downward.
Having held the body erect, it is called the divine posture;
having assumed the divine posture, perform the utterance of reality.
And when the breath, having been retained, is exhaled very slowly,
[it purifies] the channels and the lotuses of the knots that are situated within the body.
Propelled by the exhaling breath, they become upward-streaming;
then, piercing the knots with the spear of gnosis, one should cause them to emerge completely.
Having pierced the knot of the heart-lotus, thereupon a sound arises;
through its union with space, it becomes like the resonance of a bell.
O fair-faced one, the sound ceases when it reaches the throat;
however, as it pierces the region of the throat, the sound vibrates with the resonance of "dhuga-dhuga."
O lady of virtuous vows, when the vital breath reaches the middle of the palate,
a "ghumaghum" sound arises from the knot at the palate as it pierces through.
Thus have those experiences been described as the vital breath moves, O lady of excellent vows;
these three are said to consist of eight digits each, arranged one above the other in sequence.
Wherever that vital breath (prāṇa) may abide, the self (ātman) attains its corresponding state;
it assumes that very form in accordance with the nature of its location.
When [the breath] reaches the middle of the eyebrows, O Goddess, a bursting sound arises;
for one who pierces the *bindu*, the sound becomes a humming *dhuma-dhuma*.
O Dear One, how can there be liberation—both external and internal—for one who possesses the *kapir* along with the *nārikīla*, together with the undivided *bindu*? (SvaT 4.376)
O Goddess, having pierced the drop, one should then pierce the half-moon;
as the half-moon is being pierced, a tingling sensation arises in the forehead.
Having indeed pierced the half-moon, one should pierce the obstructing [channel];
as it is being pierced, its sound resounds with a *simi-sima* vibration.
O Goddess, these three locations are endowed with five sets of five kalās;
therein, at whichever place the vital breath (prāṇa) moves, he resides.
The self becomes of that very form and attains each respective state;
then, having pierced through the obstructing [state], the wise one should proceed to the Nāda.
A subtle sound, equal to the resonance of a bamboo flute, arises there; it pierces the abode of the internal sound (nāda), the Brahma-aperture which is very difficult to penetrate.
As the aperture of Brahmā is being split, a sound resonates clearly;
the vital breath, situated within the Śakti, resembles the sound at the end of a bamboo flute.
One should indeed pierce that power which is difficult for all yogins to pierce;
and when that power is pierced, then [the distinction between] the auspicious and inauspicious becomes stilled.
Then, O Goddess, having pierced the Śakti, that which remains becomes the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī);
its experience there is like the touch of an ant.
O Goddess, these three places are endowed with five sets of five kalās;
wherever the vital breath moves, it attains that very form.
Wherever one may abide, one shall attain that very state;
therefore, indeed, by means of great effort, having pierced through, one goes to the supreme goal.
O Goddess, having indeed pierced through the pervasive [power], one should abandon the mind in the state of Samanā;
by abandoning the mind with the mind, the individual soul (jīva) attains isolation (kevalatā).
In that state, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed solitary, endowed with the activity of self-knowledge,
completely liberated from all bonds, and having the nature of pure existence alone.
Transcending all stages of the paths, consisting solely of pure consciousness,
he perceives neither any other state nor even the supreme state whose nature is Śiva.
Freed from both the higher and the lower, the Self is established within its own self;
this is the pervasion of the Self, and beyond that is the pervasion of Śiva.
By those who, without knowing the supreme reality, have merely imagined the state of Śiva as being devoid of all temporal adjuncts through the total destruction of bondage; (SvaT 4.391)
Those who worship the self do not go to the supreme Śiva within the Śaiva system;
colored by the principle of the self, they attain the state of the principle of the self.
Therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, the self (ātman) must be abandoned;
then, the principle of the self (ātmatattva) must be abandoned, and one should apply oneself to the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
That [state] is to be known as *unmanā*; "mind" (*manaḥ*) is said to be volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Volition arises sequentially as cognition, whereas *unmāna* exists simultaneously.
Therefore, that indeed is the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā), because no other exists beyond it;
for in this [knowledge], one simultaneously attains the supreme qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
Because it brings about the realization that the nature of phenomena such as sensation is the supreme self,
and because it leads to the relinquishing [of grasping] regarding that supreme self, it is therefore called "knowledge" (vidyā).
Abiding therein, one should manifest the supreme splendor, which is the ultimate cause;
when that supreme splendor is manifested, one abiding therein attains the state of Śiva.
Just as a flame might be seen in the sky within a well-kindled fire,
so too the Self, residing within the body and the vital breath, dissolves into that state.
In that very same way, the highest of teachers should maintain the conceit:
"I alone am the supreme *haṃsa*, Śiva, the ultimate cause."
That animal-souled one, having become absorbed in my vital breath and attained a state of equal flavor (samarasī),
I unite with the supreme Śiva through the application of the ritual action of mantra.
Thus, he who knows this in its true essence as being like fire within the center of the body—
just as [the flame] transcends the crest of the fire, so too is he joined to the Supreme.
O Goddess, one who is joined to that supreme reality and endowed with qualities such as omniscience becomes the one Śiva, undivided from all things in every respect.
The three principles are known as supreme, while the other resides within the path;
it consists of the differentiation of categories and the application of abandonment and experience.
Having understood all this as previously stated, one should apply oneself to reality (tattva).
O Sovereign of the Gods, hear now the pervasion of reality in brief.
Having bound oneself to the seat of the principle of *vidyā*, one stands upon the seat of the principle of *bindu*;
possessing a body composed of *nāda* and *śakti*, and endowed with the pervasive operation (*vyāpinī-karaṇa*).
Moving together with the realization of omniscience, that [energy] flows to the very end;
her body is filled by that which is declared to be the supreme triad of principles.
That other body is gross, fashioned from the thirty-six principles;
yet there is also the supreme triad of principles, which is devoid of all paths of the principles.
By that, her body, which is devoted to the path of reality (tattvādhvan), was completely filled;
thus does one who practices this conduct whose essence is Śiva act.
Because he moves in the company of Śiva, he is called an Ācārya; through seeing him, conversing with him, touching him, or even remembering him, [one attains purification].
The pervasive power of the Lord certainly exists; there can be no downward movement for that [power].
Therefore, even a creature who has killed a Brahmin, when conjoined with that [power], becomes Śiva.
Therefore, there is none equal to him in this world of the moving and the unmoving;
Śiva, acting for the benefit of the worlds, exists in the form of the Ācārya.
Therefore, one should not exercise a human intellect regarding the teacher,
the mantra, the knowledge of Śiva, and Śiva himself.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the Lords of Knowledge who are the leaders of the wheels do not create any distinction whatsoever among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras.
Those who are appointed to the office of teacher are all remembered as Śivas;
those lowest of men, however, who see them otherwise than in their primordial nature [are not].
They are cooked in hell for what is called three years;
one who seeks Śiva must not engage in conversation with such a person.
Having engaged in conversation with him, one also goes to hell;
therefore, by one who desires liberation, all should be regarded as equal to Śiva.
By his command, the attainment of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation indeed occurs for the teacher and for thousands of millions of lineages of his own kin.
Through the thorough knowledge of both cognition and the object of cognition, he will deliver all beings;
such is the teacher who knows the aforementioned methods and understands the nature of existence.
By means of this single *pūrṇāhuti* alone, he unites the sacrificial victims with the Supreme;
now I shall describe to you the ritual procedure for the *pūrṇāhuti*.
With the upper body erect and the neck straight, he stands with feet even;
at the level of the navel, the base of the sacrificial ladle (sruk) is placed evenly, with its tip facing upward.
O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* ladle upon the *sruc* with its bowl facing downward,
and having offered a flower at the tip of the *sruc*, one should join both hands together with the *darbha* grass.
Having grasped it with the fist and with both hands with great effort,
O beloved, the right hand should be in front and the left indeed behind.
Having grasped [the vessel] with both hands in the manner of palms turned upward,
one should then drench it with ghee and perform the act of self-consecration.
I alone am the supreme reality, according to the division of the higher and the lower;
for reality is indeed one everywhere, and one should not conceive of any other state of being.
O fair-faced one, the sixfold path which has been deposited here in the jar is likewise conceived as common within the mandala, the fire, and the interior of the disciple.
Having placed that path within the *sruc*— situated in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and located in the midst of the channels (*nāḍī*)—
and having balanced it in the flow of the breath, one should discharge the stream with the *sruc*.
By means of the *vasudhāra* application, one should cast [the oblation] into the fire,
leading the base of the *sruk* ladle from the region of the navel to the range of the tip of the nose.
In whatever manner one should release the stream [of breath], in that same manner one should exhale the vital breath (prāṇa).
That prāṇa, consisting of the sixfold path, also attains the state of phonemes (varṇatā).
There exists nowhere any object of knowledge other than these sixfold sounds;
therefore, they remain established as things to be abandoned or adopted within the supreme contemplation of mantra.
Through the phonemes, there is the sixfold cause; by abandoning the six, there is dissolution in the seventh.
These are the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu*.
The Half-moon, the Obstructress, the Sound, and the Upward-moving;
then the Power, the Pervasive One, and beyond that, the Equal One (Samanā).
O lady of excellent limbs, the infinite web of bonds,
which resides within the mantra and is characterized by what is to be abandoned, is pervaded up to the limit of the *samanā* by the six causes.
Here, above the bonds (pāśa), the Self is indeed like space, stainless as a point (bindu) within consciousness;
through the fragrance of the qualities of the Śiva-principle, it beholds the attributes of Śiva.
Having abandoned the observation of the bonds, that which is indeed the observation of one's own true nature is the pervasion of the Self; the pervasion of Śiva is otherwise than that.
When one meditates upon those objects which are qualities such as omniscience as being all-pervasive,
this pervasion by Śiva occurs within consciousness in the form of its cause.
Therefore, the nature of the subject (dharmī) is indeed taught as Śiva, the peaceful;
he is beyond the mind (unmanā), yet graspable by the mind, for one who is established in self-awareness is unmanā.
Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with the nature of pure awareness;
then, like a bound soul (paśu), one attains the state of Śiva and is liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
And when another is appointed, he should again fill the *sruva* ladle with that substance through the opening of the *sruc* until it is offered into the fire.
One should contemplate the external kumbhaka within the supreme reality;
through the state of arresting the external, there arises a state of aesthetic identity with Śiva.
Otherwise, O Goddess, it would not exist like the force of a river in the ocean;
for the Sindhu, though situated within the waters of the sea, becomes one with the ocean.
Furthermore, the Self does not undergo division within the ocean of Śiva;
one should prescribe that this state lasts for as long as it takes to fill the sacrificial ladle.
But by this very time, through the external practice of *kumbhaka*, the all-pervading Self becomes Śiva by virtue of its state of essential oneness (*samarasatva*).
Thereafter, one should bestow the qualities by means of six subsidiary oblations;
just as when kingship has been attained, one is consecrated with water-pots.
And those qualities of his are proclaimed upon the surface of the earth by bards;
likewise, once the state of Śiva has been attained, the wise man should bring forth [those] qualities.
Become indeed omniscient, svāhā! And likewise, become completely satisfied; become one whose awakening is beginningless, and thereafter, one possessed of the power of sovereignty.
Likewise, one who possesses unimpaired power and infinite power should then bring forth all those qualities and recollect the root mantra.
One should offer oblations using the application of the word *svāhā*, preceded by *oṃ hūṃ* joined with the term for the self (*ātmapada*), and ending with "to the Omniscient One" (*sarvajñāya*).

O observer of excellent vows, one should offer three, five, ten, or even just one [oblation] with sesame seeds or with clarified butter; thereafter, one should perform the consecration with the root mantra.
Having stirred the supreme nectar of power (*para-śakty-amṛta*), one should cause it to fall upon the head of the disciple;
it should enter the door of the fourth state (*turya-dvāra*), for one should contemplate it as being both external and internal.
The body is dried up by the fierce powers of the mantras, such as the "burning of the remainder" (śeṣanirdahana) and others; for that purpose, there is the consecration.
Before the completion of the initiation (dīkṣā), one should cause the disciple to place a flower in his hand;
then, having released the *darbha* grass, [the flower] should be offered into the Śiva-fire, the water-pot (kalaśa), and the Guru.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
having accomplished what was to be done, with a joyful soul, one becomes one who has crossed over, utterly stainless.
With eyes wide open and tranquil, one should contemplate oneself as satisfied;
this is the initiation leading to Nirvāṇa, whether it be seedless (nirbījā) or with seed (sabījikā).
One should perform the consecration for those whose initiation is "with seed" (sabījikā);
one should appoint those who possess learning, virtuous conduct, and proper behavior to the office of teacher.
Then, O auspicious one, immediately following the yoga of Śiva, the consecration of the preceptor is performed with five jars smeared with white sandalwood paste.

Having worshipped [the image] like a Śiva-vessel with jars filled with water containing gems, purified by prosperity, growth, and the like, and filled with medicinal herbs and unbroken rice grains; SvaT_4.456.
One should place the five principles, beginning with earth, into the five [petals] by means of white lotuses emerging from the mouth, joined with mango sprouts.
O Great Goddess, one should again place the *kalās* within the *kalaśas*;
one should deposit those five *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti, into them here.
Each individual jar should indeed be pervaded from Ananta up to Śiva;
one should worship the god Bhairava with all the ritual requisites in due order.
O Dear One, each individual jar should be consecrated by Bhairava, endowed with the six-limbed enclosure and joined with the concentration of the mantra.
Recalling the Supreme Reality with exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], [he should perform this] in the west, north, south, east,
as well as in the northeast.
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rule, the wise one should perform the consecration;
he should designate a pedestal in the northeast of the sacrificial hall.
There, having prepared a mandala adorned with swastikas and other symbols,
covered above by a canopy and beautified by banners;
There, O Goddess, one should place a seat made of *śrīparṇī* and sandalwood;
having placed there the seat of Ananta, one should install the Child who has become the embodied form.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, standing facing the northeast,
one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and then rebuke [the obstacle] with sour gruel and rice.
With lumps of earth, ashes, and cow dung, combined with sprouts of dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, curd, and water, and accompanied by the ritual waving of lamps (nirājana).
Having thus rebuked him according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the consecration to be bestowed;
or, having recollected the abode [of the deity] within the jar containing the earth and other elements, one should sprinkle [the disciple].
Having meditated in sequence upon the vases, the preceptor, being well-composed, should be consecrated;
then, having caused him to put on other garments, he should be worshipped thereafter.
Having entered the southern form, one should prepare the yoga-pīṭha;
having established [the deity] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should establish the authority.
The uṣṇīṣa, crowns and the like, the parasol, sandals, the throne,
as well as elephants, horses, palanquins, and so forth— all the insignia of royalty without exception.

Having given a knife, a pair of scissors, chalk, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a bundle of *darbha* grass, a book, a rosary, and so forth, those established in the four stages of life [should be initiated].
"By the path of grace for those to be initiated, initiation and its exposition must always be performed by you; from this day forward, this is your duty by the command of Śiva. (SvaT 4.472)
Having raised [the disciple] and grasped his hands, one should cause him to enter the mandala;
then, having knelt upon the ground, one should worship Bhairava.
"Having thus requested the Blessed One, O Lord, I have been consecrated by your command,
established in the station of an Ācārya, and acting according to your authorization."
That which was to be done has now arrived; the exposition of the meaning of the Śiva-tattva must be performed by the instructor in the presence of Śiva.
Having emerged from the temple onto the mountain, one should offer the path of the kalās;
having performed the satiation of the mantra, one should offer five oblations for the kalās.
Having offered the five [oblations] into each of the five [fires], the Guru,
having performed the worship with the *argha* offering and so forth, should prostrate and announce [the completion] to the Lord.
The master has been consecrated by me; for that purpose, one should satisfy the mantra and mark the right hand with the five limbs, beginning with the heart-mantra.
One should mark the *darbha* grass with the fire of Śiva, beginning with the youngest [finger],
place a flower in the hand, and cast it into the mandala-fire.
Having prostrated like a staff before Bhairava, the jar, and the fire,
he who has obtained authority becomes joyful in soul and endowed with both visible and invisible fruits.
That Guru is indeed equal to Śiva, bestowing the fruit of the abode of Śiva;
at the conclusion of the rite of pacification (śānti), there is the initiation of prosperity (bhūti-dīkṣā), which consists of the state of Sadāśiva.
She is to be known as possessing the nature of Śiva, whereas otherwise she possesses the nature of the world;
she is proclaimed as possessing the nature of Śiva for those practitioners for whom she is intended.
Having performed their consecration, one should appoint them to the state of a practitioner (*sādhaka*);
this is the consecration of the practitioner, which follows after the initiation into the Vidyā.
That initiation of knowledge (vidyādīkṣā) exists according to the distinction of latent impressions (vāsanā);
however, no distinction of karma is found anywhere throughout the entire path.
All those actions that have been performed and have passed away,
having purified them according to the rule, they remain as five parts.

At the time of the *yojanī*, however, there is a distinction for the practitioner: it is the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), whereas the subsequent *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) is not to be conceived as residing in one place.
For the sake of the practitioner's prosperity, one should first purify a single rite;
having uttered the entire abode (dhāman), one should deposit it within the body of Sadāśiva.
Having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva in the form of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha),
one [attains him] endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) through the application of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Upon the attainment of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, having offered eight oblations with the root mantra using its own specific name, one should consecrate the practitioner.
One should perform [the ritual] with five jars; one should place Nivṛtti and the others in three [jars], Śāntyatītā in the fifth, and Śānti in the fourth.
Having enclosed [the mantra] with Śānti and the five [elements] beginning with Earth,
one should subsequently place the sādhya-mantra into each individual flask.
Having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) by means of the limbs of the Vidyā, one should then assign the enclosure of the Vidyā-limbs;
thereafter, one should consecrate each individual flask with exactly eight hundred recitations.
Having placed the seat within the outer mandala with the syllable *praṇava*,
one should establish the practitioner there and then perform the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Having rebuked [the disciple] as before, one should sprinkle him with all the *sādhya* mantras;
then, facing the eastern direction, one should bathe him with the three jars beginning with Nivṛtti.
Afterward, having taken the jar of the Śāntyatīta [level], one should sprinkle the disciple;
then one should take the Śānti [jar] and perform the consecration with the two joined together (saṃpuṭa).
This is the initiation of the practitioner, performed in both direct and reverse order;
having initiated him, one leads him in and places him in the southern form.
Having offered a seat with the syllable *praṇava*, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa should be performed;
for the sake of the practitioner's entitlement, one should prepare the rosary and other implements.
Having given the ritual manual of mantras, a rosary, chalk, an umbrella, and sandals— provided they are devoid of the *uṣṇīṣa*— and having entered into the presence of Śiva, [he should proceed].
"O Supreme Lord, having informed you, this practitioner has been prepared by me;
may success come through your command, by means of the threefold devotion."
Thereafter, one should give the mantra to be accomplished, accompanied by water and flowers;
it should be placed in the hand of the practitioner for the sake of his success.
Having prostrated and received both [the master and the disciple], one should place the mantra within the heart;
the disciple, with a joyful countenance, and the master, likewise filled with joy.
In the fire-chamber, being attentive, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) of the collection of mantras,
or the libation of the mantra to be accomplished, either a thousand or even a hundred times.
Having thus satisfied [the deity], one should cause a flower to be placed in [the deity's] hand;
having worshipped the God who resides in the three [places], one should then perform three circumambulations.
Having prostrated with a mind endowed with devotion, one shall obtain the fruits beginning with *aṇiman*.
Having raised the practitioner up, one should say: "Protect the pledges (*samaya*) with diligence."
O Goddess, at the conclusion of the initiation, these [verses] should be recited by the wise;
thus, O fair-faced one, having completed the initiation in this manner at all times.
Listen to how the sacrifice of one's self must be performed:
whether it be through gnosis or by nature, according to the will of the Master.
One should perform this very subtle, scientific procedure according to the following rule:
the conceptualization of the Path and Vāgīśī is joined with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other substances. (SvaT 4.507)
One should simultaneously deposit the path pervaded by the five digits;
having performed the worship, fire-oblation, ritual services, and so forth, one should apply oneself to the Self.
Through union with the consciousness of the disciple, one should simultaneously deposit the paths;
having worshipped that [consciousness] with flowers and other offerings, one should offer three oblations for the sake of yoga.
O Goddess, one who is firm in his vows should simultaneously perform the oblation with the root mantra during conception, birth, acquisition, and the dissolution of enjoyments.
O fair-faced one, three oblations are to be offered for each ritual action;
the expiation is to be performed separately for the five locations, the kalās, and the self.
The expiation is proclaimed to be one hundred or half of that;
for those who sever the bond of separation, there is a simultaneous manifestation by means of the very abode itself.
When the extraction has been performed and [the soul] is established in the reality of the Self, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
one should then unite the Self with the reality of Śiva, the supreme cause.
Having brought forth the qualities as before, make them immortal as before;
this is for the sake of the completion of one's own initiation and for the cessation of transgressions.
Then, by means of the form of consciousness, characterized by a single simultaneous utterance,
there is indeed the [severing] of the bonds of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted all at once through Bhairava.
The eternal state is subsequently proclaimed as the subtle initiation;
one should perform the special worship and the fire-oblation according to one's capacity.
One should worship Hara with instrumental music, song, fine dance, and so forth, as well as with hymns of praise;
then, having performed three circumambulations of the pitcher, the fire, and the maṇḍala.
Having performed a prostration with eight limbs, one should address the Supreme Lord:
"O Blessed One, for the sake of the sacrificial victim, you have been invoked by me."
Therefore, O Lord, O God, you should always forgive me, who abide by the prescribed rule; for though I am without desire, my worship may fall short of the ritual as taught by the Teacher.
It would not be excessively voluminous with collections of ordinary materials;
rather, it is the ritual procedure that has been composed by me, relying solely upon devotion.
"O Lord, may all that become fruitful for me through your great grace;
with a gracious countenance and joyful heart, you should consider the boon granted. (SvaT 4.521)
Then, having sat down, O Dear One, one should perform the withdrawal of the sacrifice in due order;
having made a request for the first portion, one should take it and place it protected by the weapon-mantra.
Then, having performed the special worship and the offering of water (argha), one should again perform prostration;
thereafter, taking up half [of the vessel] for the cessation [rite], one should offer the argha from both the left and the right.
Having offered [the oblation], one should dismiss the deity while recollecting the mantra of the abode;
having performed exhalation (recaka) for oneself, one should cast a flower toward the deity.
Having gathered the mantras situated at the sides by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā],
and having visualized them as flickering like lightning, one should deposit them within the body of the abode (*dhāmadeha*).

One should cause [the disciple] to grasp the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) of Bhairava, which is dissolved in the form of the point (bindu); and one should cause him to grasp the point as residing in the power of sound (nādaśakti), which is the very form of power (śaktirūpa).
Having encapsulated the form of the Śakti with the pervasive Praṇava on both sides,
one should grasp it with the Saṃhāriṇī and join it at the end of the twelve.
Having placed [the deity] in the heart by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should contemplate it as abiding in its own place,
in its manifest (sakala), unmanifest (niṣkala), and both manifest-and-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala) forms.
O Dear One, one should thus recollect that [mantra] residing in the heart as being in a state of dissolution within the mantras;
for this is the procedure for dismissal, and in this manner one should worship in the fire.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should cast the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having given half [of the remainder] for sipping water (ācamana), one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
By means of the practice situated within the maṇḍala, through exhalation and inhalation,
one should collect the assembly of mantras and arrange them in their proper places.
Then, for the sake of the daily rites, one should awaken the fire;
O Dear One, one should remove the remains of offerings and sweep away the dust.
Then, having entered, he should sprinkle that ground with auspicious water;
then, having gone outside, he should perform the bali-offering for the spirits as before.
Having sipped water and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, he should then offer libations to those who bear the liṅga;
thereafter, the disciple should worship the Guru with the full extent of his available wealth.
The governor of a district (deśādhyakṣa) [should give] a hundred villages; the lord of a province (maṇḍaleśa), half of that.
One who enjoys a hundred [villages] should indeed give five, and likewise one who enjoys twenty [villages] should give one village.
The enjoyer of the village should give a field, but the enjoyer of the field should give twenty;
whatever may please the Guru, all that one should offer.
Then, avoiding any deceit regarding wealth, he becomes free from debt;
thereafter, one should cause him to hear the rules (samayas) in the tantra issued by Bhairava.
Afterwards, the Cumbaka, with speech restrained and a tranquil mind, should partake of the *caruka* together with the practitioners, each situated separately in his own vessel.
It should be given in due sequence; from that, one shall attain accomplishment.
By this very procedure, those who have been initiated, O Infinite One, [attain] their boons.
O beloved, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others,
all of them possess equal dharma when they are engaged in the Śiva-dharma.
O fair-faced one, all those who wear matted hair and whose bodies are smeared with ashes, who eat from a single row [of vessels], are declared to be the *samayins*.
There is one [form] for the sons, and likewise one for the practitioners;
there is one for the magnetizers, regardless of distinctions of prior birth.
That lineage of Bhairava is known as one alone, auspicious and imperishable;
having taken recourse to this tantra, one should certainly not proclaim a prior [lower] birth.
O Goddess, for sons, practitioners, and likewise for those bound by the observance (samayin),
a man becomes liable to expiation if he proclaims his former birth.
He is cooked in hell for three days for Rudra, five days for Keśava, and for one fortnight for Pitāmaha.
Therefore, one should become free from lack of discernment if one desires the supreme goal;
for through discernment, O Goddess of Gods, accomplishment and liberation will certainly come to pass.
In the *Svacchanda Tantra*, the fourth chapter [ends].
The fifth chapter:
"O Sureśāna, O Parameśvara, the initiation into the *kalās* has been explained."
Please graciously explain the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) in brief.
O Pārvatī, for the sake of what is dear to you, I shall briefly explain how the thirty-six principal principles (tattvas) are to be purified.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall now explain to you how all things, from the earth up to Śiva, are purified along with their respective pervasions and corresponding attributes.
I shall now explain in due order those syllables of the Vidyārāja, characterized by the number nine, which are the designators of the principles (tattvas).
The letter *ū* is traditionally taught as the designator for everything from the Earth principle up to Pradhāna;
and the letter *ya* indeed belongs to Puruṣa, who is conjoined with the principle of Rāga.
O fair-faced one, one should know the *niyāmikā* to be endowed with the *vidyātattva* through the letter *va*; one should conceive of *kāla* and *kalā* through the letter *la*. (SvaT 5.6)
The principle of Māyā is [indicated] by the letter *ma*; the principle of Vidyā by the letter *kṣa*;
the principle of Īśvara by the letter *ra*; and Sadāśiva by the letter *ha*.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, the Śakti should be deposited with the Praṇava;
one should purify Vyāpinī and Samanā right there above.
Having purified [the self] in due order with the root mantra, O observer of good vows,
one should unite the self with the supreme reality, which transcends the state of *unmanā* and pervades all.
In that which is without appearance, supreme, peaceful, sovereign, imperishable, and unborn, the thirty-six principles have been declared; now we shall explain the nine principles.
Primordial Nature (prakṛti) and the Person (puruṣa), as well as Necessity (niyati) and Time (kāla);
likewise Illusion (māyā), Knowledge (vidyā), the Lord (īśa), Sadāśiva, and Śiva. (SvaT 5.11)
Having purified [the elements] according to the rule, one should apply oneself to the pervasive self;
when the five principles (pañcatattvī) are to be purified, the mantras of the faces are their designators.
One should purify [the elements] from the earth up to space in that sequence;
for as far as the pervasion of the *kalās* extends, so far indeed does that of the *tattvas*.
Now I shall explain the three principles (tattvas) as they are to be purified, O fair-faced one.
The letter A is proclaimed to be the designator of the principle of the self (ātmatattva).
One should know that [the letter 'u'] marks the end of Māyā; the letter 'u' also marks the end of that which is called Vidyā.
That should be known to extend up to Sakala; however, the letter 'm' belongs to Śiva.
The *kha-svara* (the sound *kha*) is the designator of the *śiva-tattva*, which is the nature of space (*kha-rūpa*).
Having purified [the elements] in due order, one should unite them with the supreme reality (*para-tattva*).
The initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) has been fully described as established in four divisions;
now I shall explain the supreme initiation (paradīkṣā) exactly and in due order.
Regarding the syllables of the Vidyārāja, which are characterized by the number nine,
I shall now describe to you their arrangement according to their individual divisions.
Having fashioned a city with nine naves, characterized by nine lotuses,
the wise one should draw a dwelling nine cubits in size, exceeding [that] by eight joints.
That [mandala], divided into seven parts and further partitioned into southern and northern sections,
should first be divided into squares and marked therein with fish-shaped figures.
One should draw forty-nine squares with a thread;
in the central square, a thread measuring thirty-two finger-breadths [should be placed].
O Great Goddess, having drawn [the mandala] divided into four parts,
one should fashion the pericarp in the first part and the filaments in the second.
On the third [layer], one should mark the junctions of the petals, and on the fourth, the tips of the petals;
having drawn eight lines in the cardinal directions and likewise in the intermediate directions.
One should rotate four circles, each measuring four finger-breadths,
having placed a thread in the center between two lines for each direction.
Then, having rotated the foremost thread according to the method of the half-moon,
the wise one should lay down the central thread situated upon the filaments.
Having first established the eastern petal, one should likewise establish the others;
then, having drawn twenty-four filaments, [one proceeds].
One should place a very beautiful circular line at the front of the petals;
within that, a square of the same proportion must be made.
O Dear One, having first established the Brahma-line by means of the sun situated at the equinox,
one should then establish the cord extending east and west using a gnomon.
Having fixed a gnomon in the center measuring twelve finger-breadths,
one should rotate it around the sides to draw a line measuring sixteen finger-breadths.
In the forenoon, one should mark the shadow situated in the west with clear indicators;
O Dear One, when the sun is situated in the west, one should mark the eastern shadow.
O fair-faced one, one should mark the northern and southern points with a fixed line;
then, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus together with its pericarp.
Having taken the squares of the directions, characterized by the number eight,
the remaining ones are to be erased, O lady of excellent hips, by joining every other one.

Then, O Goddess, one should draw eight lotuses in the directions on the outer perimeter, as well as the doors; one should likewise fashion the *śobhā* (ornamental arches) measuring half the width of the pathway.
One should draw the ornamentation of that same measurement up to the edge of the cheek;
likewise, the neck is of that same measurement—this is proclaimed as the door.
The city is known to have nine naves through the division of eight doors;
having bathed according to the rule, O Goddess, the Guru should enter the abode.
Having performed the ritualization of the body (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and so forth according to the previously stated procedure,
one should then worship the god Bhairava, the Supreme Lord.
O woman of excellent complexion, having offered a seat with the *praṇava* (OM) ending with "Śiva," one should worship the god Svacchanda, the Supreme Lord, in the center.
According to the previously described procedure, one should place the letters, accompanied by the six limbs,
upon the eight petals starting from the east and proceeding in order up to the northeast.

"O fair-faced one, one should understand that Sadāśiva is represented by the letter *ha*, and so forth, up to the end of Prakṛti; in the center [of this], there is the conceptualization of the Lord of the Seat (*pīṭheśa*)."
One should worship the eight deities situated in the pericarp of the lotus of the directions;
in their place, Bhairava is to be worshipped, while the remaining [deities] are worshipped with the [corresponding] syllables in due order.
And one should purify [the elements] from Prakṛti up to Śiva, O beautiful goddess;
beginning from the northeast direction, one should purify the central seat.
One should unite [the soul] with the supreme reality, Śiva, the ultimate cause;
in this way, one should likewise purify the phonemes, the mantras, and the worlds.
One should rely upon the procedure of the *kalās* starting from Kālāgni up to Śiva;
thereafter, O Dear One, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the pledges (*samayas*) arising from the tradition of the Tantra.
One should not revile the god Bhairava, nor a scripture originating from another source;
one should likewise not revile Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, or the Vedas themselves.
Since all [these paths] originate from Śiva and bestow the fruit of liberation,
one should not disparage the Smārta dharma, which shows the path of right conduct.
The deities beginning with Brahmā, the Mothers, Cumbaka, Giri,
the Vīras, the Sisters, the cows, and likewise the hosts of spirits.
One must not damage the property of the deity as established in the Siddhānta;
nor, O Supreme Goddess, should one eat the food of the Guru if it has not been given.

O fair-faced one, one should not feel aversion toward those who consume liquor, meat, fish, and other such things, nor toward those who follow proper conduct or lack it, provided they bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin).
One should always consume the *caruka* and constantly worship the gurus;
O Great Goddess, one must not touch the ritual implements with one's foot.
One should constantly contemplate the Saṃhitā and always cause the devotees to hear it;
one must not neglect the daily rites, O fair-faced one, nor the performance of the Sandhyā ceremonies.
One should not recite the manual of the scriptures in the presence of those who have not been initiated;
one should always worship the God three times a day, remaining devoted to recitation and meditation.
Constantly observing the commitments (samaya) with the desire for the fruit of both [self and others'] welfare,
I shall therefore explain the initiation of consciousness (vijñāna-dīkṣā) in its proper sequence.
Having taken up that disciple-self, which is purified solely through the internal movement of the vital breath, one should join it with one's own life-force.
Having likewise uttered the *abhimāna*, one should then perform [the rite] as before;
thereafter, one should purify the path of the disciple by means of the *udghātas*.
Then, O lady of virtuous vows, one should utter the principles beginning with earth,
each one in its proper sequence, according to its nature as both distinct and non-distinct.
The first *udghāta* is traditionally taught as the vocalized utterance of syllables accompanied by the deities, through the conjunction of the *bindu* with *śakti*.
O Goddess of gods, that which is free from the three deities and endowed with the end of the fourth is proclaimed as the second *udghāta*.
The third upward thrust (udghāta) occurs from the half-moon [center] into the nirodhinī; it is the prolonged utterance of the syllable *haṃ*, conjoined with the *bindu*.
O Goddess, when the two breaths have been split apart, then that which is at the end of the resonance (nāda) occurs;
O Mistress of the Gods, that is proclaimed as the fourth breath-exertion (udghāta).
That very utterance of the syllable, established at the end of the pervasive [state], is the *udghāta*; O Goddess of the Gods, it is proclaimed as the fifth.
Then, having performed five suppressions, the wise one should purify the earth;
it is purified in this way by ending with the syllables A, U, and M, and not otherwise.
Then, when the earthly element has become pure, it should be contemplated by yogins as having become water together with the self through yoga.
When [the disciple] has become like water, the mantra-practitioner should again utter that same [mantra] four times;
joined with *dhāraṇā* and ending in the nasal drop (*bindu*), he should contemplate it within himself, having drawn it from the disciple.
When the mass of water has been purified, one should contemplate it as having become fire;
within those [masses], the three strikes of fire remain in a state of cessation.
From that, fire ceases to exist, and the wind is purified by two upward thrusts;
one should contemplate it as dissolving into space by means of the upward thrust.
When the wind has ceased, one should then join that void with a single upward thrust;
that is to be known as the Pervasive (Vyāpinī), established at the end of the fifth [breath].
Then, in the Samanā [state], the Self is said to be all-pervasive with respect to the principles (tattvas);
thereafter, it is all-pervasive with respect to the Self; and after that, it is again all-pervasive everywhere.
For the knower of yoga, the Self established at the end of the principles (tattvas) should, by means of a single upward breath (udghāta),
be joined to the supreme reality, which transcends the mind and pervades all.
O Goddess, listen as I explain the application regarding the supreme reality;
O Goddess, one should utter the mantra in its short, long, and protracted forms, which is the highest.
Through the division of the higher and the lower, one reaches the supreme reality as far as it extends:
the three deities conjoined with the *bindu*, the half-moon, and the *nirodhikā*.
And Nāda conjoined with Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, and Unmanā;
and Unmanā and the Supreme, the all-pervading, immutable Śiva.
Having understood the entire procedure for these [mantras] in its entirety and in the proper sequence, the practitioner of mantras should then apply them; otherwise, he should not apply them at all.
The triad residing in the bindu is within the sound, and the fourth is indeed the bindu itself;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are said to be the phoneme consisting of three measures.
The Lord Bindudeva resides in the throat, where sound arises;
therein, sound abides within the power of action (kriyā), and is thus remembered as the power of action itself.
O Goddess, that sound, having been impelled, proceeds from the palate;
having moved slightly further, that sound proceeds to the end of the nose.
O Supreme Goddess, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) should be understood with effort;
it is the sound situated in the head, located as far as the forehead.
The phoneme residing within those [vowels] is proclaimed as their *udghāta*;
those who remain there, being devoid of the knowledge of Śiva, turn back.
The *bindu* is established in five ways; [then there are] the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) and the obstructor (*nirodhikā*).
Beyond that is the *nāda*, which should be uninterrupted.
When the mouth is slightly opened, the god of gods, Sadāśiva, becomes fourfold; this is known as the sound that carries great velocity.
The fifth is not the sound "va," for it is remembered as upward-moving;
its past power is established as fivefold.
O Goddess, there contact occurs; therein the knower of the Self is as before.
Beyond that is Vyāpinī, established in five ways.
O Supreme Goddess, one may sometimes perceive a touch localized on the tip of a hair, or perhaps not; that [power] is declared to be all-pervasive, yet it is not knowledge.
One should not allow the mind to dwell even upon that which has just passed;
by ascending to the state beyond the mind (unmanā), one then becomes a pure self.
O best of gurus, one should unite the disciple’s self with the state of Unmanī;
being thus engaged therein, in the supreme peace, he shall attain great tranquility.
The tradition transmitted through the lineage of gurus has been revealed;
the means for union with the supreme reality has been explained to you.
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, one should perform all rites:
the path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of the creative energies (kalādhvan), and indeed the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
O Dear One, by thus purifying the path of the phonemes, mantras, and words,
this initiation of retention (dhāraṇādīkṣā) must indeed be performed here by the yogi.
Or, O Goddess, it may indeed be well-performed by one who has attained mastery over mantras.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of Initiation into the Principles," in the Svacchandatantra.
The sixth chapter begins: O fair-faced one, [now follows] the description of the practitioner who is endowed with the conduct of the observances (*samaya*).
Various accomplishments arise for one who has taken refuge in mountain caves.
On a well-purified patch of ground, entirely free from debris,
secluded, solitary, and delightful, one should there worship Bhairava.
O observer of excellent vows, by reciting one hundred thousand syllables of Bahurūpa and joining them with the five *praṇavas*, success is certainly attained through that recitation.
One is liberated without a doubt by the piercing of the *praṇava*:
[it consists of] the short, the long, the protracted, the subtle, the ultra-subtle, and the supreme Śiva.
Having known the Praṇava in its fivefold way and having pierced through it, there is liberation without a doubt;
the Praṇava exists in five states, conjoined with the Haṃsa.
Whatever verbal composition exists in the world is established in the knowledge of Śiva;
and that knowledge of Śiva resides therein as the *haṃsa* conjoined with the *praṇava*.
Without union with the *praṇava*, the individual soul (*jīva*) remains alone;
yet, joined with its own nature (*prakṛti*), it does not abide in isolation.
Likewise, the individual soul (jīva) functions within the body as it is permeated by the sixth [breath];
when impelled by that [sixth], it then moves upward.
Even though that reality is directly perceptible, those who are deluded by the great māyā do not recognize it, unless there is an instruction from the scripture.
And the sixth should be known as the upward-moving [wind], abiding in the face of its own nature;
unmanifest, residing within one's own body, it functions as a subordinate quality.
But when the Lord is devoid of qualities, solitary, and beyond time, there would be nothing to be known; he is indeed absolute and partless.
He has no form or body, nor color or action;
how can he be grasped, being subtle, ungraspable, eternal, and immutable?
For this reason, O Goddess, the sixth seed-syllable is employed;
joined with five groups of five, it is both with parts and without parts within the body.
But when the yogi who contemplates yoga grasps that [object],
he should meditate upon it as mere existence, even though it has been brought forth by yoga.
When he performs creation, the *bindu* proceeds upwards;
and above the *bindu* is Śiva, the Peaceful One, the supreme cause.
Therein the drop (bindu) attains dissolution; that place is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Through the conjunction with the sixth vowel and through practice, one shall obtain it before long.
O Goddess, its qualities are traditionally held to be six and five;
it should be known as qualified and with parts (sakala), while Śiva is without qualities and without parts (nirguṇa and niṣkala).
The one with parts (sakala) is conjoined with the planets, while the partless (niṣkala) is established in pure being;
when that which has parts is being recited, the partless is indeed recited.
By the Lord, for the sake of providing the means for the gods and asuras to perform sacrifice,
his entire form was manifested in two states.
The first is the natural form, and the second is the modified;
both the natural and the modified are joined with the sixth.
Regarding those categories previously explained, he repeatedly breathes therein;
by means of this [breathing], he proceeds, and by that [same means], he returns.
The Praṇava exists in five states; it consists of three syllables and has three deities.
Endowed with Bindu and Nāda, the Praṇava is thus fully described.
The letter A, the letter U, and the letter M as the third—
these three phonemes are proclaimed to be the three deities beginning with Brahmā.
Through the union of Bindu and Nāda, there are Īśvara and Sadāśiva;
these indeed are the five Praṇavas, while Haṃsa is always endowed with Prāṇa.
The Supreme Self is Śiva, the Haṃsa, conjoined with another;
beyond the five Praṇavas, I shall speak of them once again.
O Goddess, Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samanā, Niṣkala,
and likewise Unmanā— these are proclaimed as the five Praṇavas.
Beyond that, the supreme *haṃsa* abides pervading everything;
these indeed are the five *praṇavas*, according to the division of the higher and the lower.
Constantly impelled by the supreme and the non-supreme *haṃsa*,
they indeed proceed everywhere, bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
But when joined with these five, he consists of the five *praṇavas*;
yet, abiding therein, he is of a single form and is traditionally known as being partless (*niṣkala*) in reality.
Through connection with that, its seed— which causes all seeds to sprout—
proceeds from which the abode of gods and asuras arises.
In that state, O Dear One, both mantras and phonemes find their firm foundation, and not otherwise;
those who understand this are liberated like a snake shedding its skin.
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find reality;
but once the city of reality is known, one is never born again anywhere.
A man has not yet accomplished his purpose so long as he does not find the Haṃsa;
one should declare him to have accomplished his purpose when it is joined with the Praṇava.
Having understood the utterance from that, one should utter it, O fair-faced one;
O Goddess, the utterance of the Haṃsa is declared to be threefold.
The third [syllable] is joined with the letters *ha* and *o*, followed by the *bindu* at the end;
its utterance through the placement of emanation (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*) is called the yoga of withdrawal (*saṃhārayoga*).
In this very sequence, the wise one should utter the mantra;
having established the triad within the *bindu*, he should then open the mouth.
Then, when the mouth is slightly opened, one should recognize the Nāda;
it is fivefold as residing in the Nāda, and again fivefold as residing in the Śakti.
In the pervasive [energy], there are fivefold states: those of the *samanā*, the *niṣkala*, and the *unmanā* self;
and the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattvaṃ*) stands pervading all.
Knowing this, people who know the principle of Śiva are liberated;
otherwise, those who remain fixed within the *bindu* are not liberated at all.
The form of light resides in the *bindu*; the form of sound resides in the *nāda*;
that which resides in the *śakti* is the experience of touch; and above that is the form of emptiness.
The pentad beginning with Brahmā and their void—that is their state;
they are established everywhere through the division of the higher and the lower.
Samanā transcends emptiness, while Unmanā is the pure self;
the supreme reality, which transcends all, abides pervading everything.
The deities should be understood as having the nature of mantra because of their quality of being the *bindu*;
abiding therein, they accomplish all activities, without a doubt.
The reality is indeed the Unmanā state, while the Samanā state is the Void itself;
likewise, there are Touch and Sound, and immediately after that, Form.
O fair-faced one, the preceptor must recognize that all [deities] reside within the nature of the mantra;
abiding therein, they bestow the yoga of knowledge.
But at the time of ritual action, O Goddess, one should recite all [the mantras] together with their heads, hands, and other limbs, endowed with the partless (niṣkala) [essence].
One should meditate on all [the deities] as consisting of light, bestowing the perfection of sound.
Those residing in power (śakti) are said to be givers of power; those residing in the void (śūnya) are remembered as the pervasive ones (vyāpaka).
O fair-faced one, those [levels] up to Samanā indeed bestow knowledge in succession;
above that, they grant absolute liberation (kaivalya); and in the state of Unmanā, they are omniscient.
All those who have been described by me are pierced by means of reality;
having known that, they all bestow both accomplishment and liberation—of this there is no doubt.
I have explained to you the reality conjoined with the five *praṇavas*,
preceded by the five *praṇavas* and joined with ten thousand *oṃkāras*.
O observer of excellent vows, by reciting this mantra in its many forms ending with the salutation,
one attains accomplishment through a hundred thousand repetitions according to the count of syllables.
One should always recite the mantra joined with the *praṇava* at its beginning;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should again perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part [of the recitations].
Human flesh combined with meat from the city and thoroughly drenched in ghee;
from that, one attains accomplishment—whether inferior, middling, or supreme.
By reciting [the mantra] three hundred times,
one becomes equal to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the gods, as well as to the Siddhas, Daityas, and lords of the Uragas.
He becomes one who bestows fear and one who takes it away; he is the performer of curses and favors.
He robs even Time of its pride and can cast down even the mountains.
One may shatter the *bilva* diagrams and even cause the elephants of the quarters to tremble;
one may likewise subdue Brahma-rākṣasas, vetālas, cruel grahas, and vināyakas.
O Goddess, by remembering [this], one destroys [all obstacles]—one who is otherwise invincible even to the gods;
even ordinary rites are accomplished through a hundred thousand recitations.
I shall explain them correctly and in due order:
Mohanā, Sahadevā, Bhūdhātrī, and Cakralāñchanā.
One should nourish [the deity] together with Rāmavallī using one's own seed-syllable;
this supreme means of subjugation should be given in food and drink.
Furthermore, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp the root of the *uḍumbara* tree under the asterism of Puṣya;
when joined with the faculty of the self, this is the supreme means of subjugation.
The impurities of the ears and eyes, saliva, blood,
along with the sense organs and earth-cadamba, should be offered with milk at night.
It should not be given when one is away from home, for she will die in separation;
[there are] sixty seeds of gold and sixteen moon-crystals.
O beautiful woman, he to whom you give [this practice] joined with the "Naragoda" [mantra],
this Kāpālika yoga follows after him as he goes.
The root of the white Arka, Mañjiṣṭhā, the head of a sparrow,
Kuṣṭha grown in a house, and one's own blood combined with the [relevant] organ.
This supreme means of subjugation should be administered in food and drink;
likewise, the *mohanā* plant, combined with *mayūraśikhā*, acts as a captivating agent.
When joined with the senses that have attained the self, it is the supreme means of subjugation;
likewise, *lajjālukā*, *gorambhā*, and the rite of *caṇḍālī*.
That [mantra], mixed with the feet of the Lord of Nagas and endowed with its own seed-syllable—
this divine, supreme yoga is bestowed upon whomever, O lady of excellent vows.
Endowed with sweetness, he remains in control for as long as his lifespan lasts;
chickpeas, black gram, and mung beans have emerged through the lower opening.
Vomited matter, ghee, semen, female menses, as well as the impurities of the heart, urine, blood, hair, and saliva, O fair-faced one. (SvaT 6.69)
Putrajānī, Kṛtāhvā, and Nāgendrapada joined together;
Mohanā, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Dhātrī likewise stand together as one.
O fair-faced one, under the Puṣya asterism, one should employ this yoga, which is honored by the gods, for those who are arrogant;
it should be administered in food and drink.
I shall now describe the rite of eradication for enemies who are arrogant in spirit:
[one should use] the feathers of a crow and an owl, as well as the urine of a donkey and a camel, and earth.
Having fashioned an effigy, the wise one should smear it with the blood of a crow;
he should also insert the feathers of a raven and an owl into its anus.
One should bury that at a crossroads and then,
having ignited the funeral pyre fire upon it, one should perform oblations there with crow feathers, O lady of excellent vows.
One should take [the seeds] together with wandering birds, processed with donkey urine,
and having inscribed the name of the person for whom it is intended, beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *ra*.
At the conclusion of the mantra, one should recite that which is placed at the end with the visarga;
the enemy, afflicted by disease, will wander the earth like a crow.
Having fashioned an image of the enemy out of oil-cake, neem leaves, clay, yeast, and husks, and having wrapped it with *akṣa* flowers;
One should bury that [image] in a cremation ground after kindling a fire upon it;
then, one should perform a fire-offering (homa) with flowers from the *vibhītaka* tree while reciting the name of the person [against whom the rite is directed].
Even one who is equal to Kāmadeva shall indeed become an enemy and be loathed,
by means of guggulu mixed with priyaṅgu creepers and pierced with clarified butter.
O Goddess, by offering oblations of sesame seeds mixed with *jātī* buds and anointed with the three sweets, one becomes fortunate and wins over eight hundred women.
Even a man devoid of beauty attains good fortune by offering oblations of sesame seeds mixed with salt and anointed with the three sweets, which are dear to [the deity].
Within seven days, a woman who is proud of her beauty comes under one's control;
[this is achieved by using] mustard seeds and salt soaked in honey, milk, and ghee.
One should offer oblations mixed with *nāma* (the name); by this, one may swiftly attract that person.
Taking the *rocanā* of a man and the ichor of an elephant, [one should perform the rite].
Having meditated upon it and empowered it with this mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times;
then, whether it is given for bathing, as an ointment, in wine, or as perfume, [the desired effect follows] for whomever it is bestowed.
