He quickly becomes submissive, a giver of wealth and likewise a giver of life;
or else, he will certainly kill one's own enemy swiftly.
Taking two skull-bowls, one should write the name of an enemy who is filled with hundreds of injuries, ungrateful, and evil-minded.
That [substance], placed within a skull-cup joined together, is infused with the charcoal of poison,
combined with blood, and interspersed with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Having gone to the great forest of pretas, one should then worship at will with offerings of black garlands; thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
Having petitioned the god Bhairava, "Strike down my enemy," and being authorized by the god, he took those two heads.
Having gone there, O Great Goddess, seated upon a skull-throne,
he remained stationed there, filled with wrath and facing the south.
Having recognized his own form as Bhairava— terrible and most fearsome—
the wrathful mantra-practitioner should utter the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables.

O illustrious lady, then, reciting the name of the enemy in reverse order with the syllable *anta* at the end, and having uttered the two syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, one should strike violently against the *kādi*.
O Goddess of the Gods, when it has been ground into powder bit by bit, it perishes completely within seven nights; this application is irreversible.
In this way, this Lord of the Lords of the Kings of Mantras performs hundreds of thousands of applications arising from other kalpas as well.

O Goddess, for the purpose of pacification, one should offer milk as an oblation to the deity who has entered the *anuloma* sequence and is established at the end of the *vauṣaṭ* utterance; this brings about benefit.
The syllable *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed for nourishment (*āpyāyana*), while *svāhā* at the end is for the rite of subjugation (*vaśakarma*);
and for the purpose of satiating (*tarpaṇa*) mantras, as well as in worship (*arcana*), it is traditionally taught that they should end with *namaḥ*.
For this, O Goddess, has been taught for the sake of the wise practitioner who is endowed with the proper time and portions of ritual action; it brings happiness without any hardship.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the section on the five *praṇavas*, in the *Svacchandatantra*.
The seventh chapter:
"O God, O Maheśvara, by your grace, the ritual action has been understood by me."
And tell me, O Lord of Gods, about the divisions of time in detail.
O beloved, time is to be understood here as twofold: the solar and the spiritual.
O beloved, [this applies] when the hour, the constituent factor, the ascendant, the auspicious conjunction, and the excellent day are all favorable.
In the mass of the decrease of light, however, there is the southern and northern solstice,
as well as the eclipses of the moon and sun, and likewise the seasons.
The fortnight, the month, the time-periods, the equinox, and the transition between zodiac signs— the arising of merit and demerit, O Goddess, is proclaimed as this solar [time].
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I explain the internal [body]:
it is the body composed of the six sheaths, conjoined with the elements and their subtle counterparts.
His body is presided over by mind, intellect, ego, the organs of perception and action, the guṇas,
all the principles (tattvas), and likewise by the gods.
Therein, the self and the power of the Lord, moving indeed through the channels as the vital air (vāyu),
are situated in the center of the navel, within the bulbous root (kanda) below the navel and the generative organ.
From that [center], O Dear One, channels emerge sideways, upwards, and downwards;
situated there like a wheel, ten channels are the principal ones.
There are seventy-two thousand channels;
from them others have emerged, and from these yet others, emerging again and again.
As many as there are hair-pores, so many channels are said to exist;
just as the leaf of a Palāśa tree is pervaded everywhere by its fibers.
In the same way, the bodies of all living beings are pervaded by channels;
they are always filled with vital winds and moved by the power of the Self.
O fair-faced one, through the distinction of their separate activities and the distinction of their movements,
there is a differentiation of names according to the various modes of movement and activity.
The differentiation of the channels and the vital winds should be known by the thousands;
O fair-faced one, ten principal channels have been described.
O Goddess of the Gods, among those [channels],
listen to me regarding the names and functions of the winds that are situated within the channels.
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā as the third;
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
these are declared to be the ten principal channels (nāḍīs) that carry the vital breath (prāṇa).
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.
O beloved, the winds and the channels are situated like a wheel;
O fair-faced one, by moving within them, one attains both accomplishment and yoga.
And for one who recites it, O lady of excellent limbs, he shall attain the perfection of recitation;
O Goddess, the triad of channels is said to be superior even to the ten.
The two [energies] consisting of *bindu* and *nāda* are indeed situated in the middle; they are known as being of the nature of *śakti*.
They are declared to reside in the heart-cakra, bringing benefit to practitioners.
The vital breath indeed moves through those [channels] according to the division of day and night;
I shall explain that to you by dividing it clearly, as it truly is.
Drawn forth by the power of the Lord, these three— wind, vital breath, and the self— reside together and circulate everywhere without distinction.
For it carries [the breath] both downward and upward, causing all the channels to flow;
through the various distinctions of its functional states, it manifests the forms of the phonemes in manifold ways.
O beloved, from seventy-two thousand [drops] ten indeed arise;
O lady of excellent hips, that one alone is established as the element of ten million.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of the out-breath (*apāna*) and the in-breath (*prāṇa*),
abides in the chest of living beings, constantly filling itself in relation to exhalation and inhalation.
Because it performs the act of breathing (prāṇana), it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa.
Now I shall describe to you the movement of day and night within the prāṇa.
The sixteen *tuṭis* within the vital breath have indeed been described by me previously; however, in the external world, they are proclaimed as *lavas* by means of time.
O Goddess, by means of those four [periods], the movement within the vital breath (prāṇa) is ordained;
O Goddess, by those same four watches (prahara), a day comes to be.
Night is to be known by four [units], and a day-and-night by eight;
Śiva is through Dharma, while Haṃsa is the Sun, the Haṃsa endowed with radiance.
The Self (ātman) is indeed called Haṃsa; the vital breath (prāṇa) is endowed with the nature of Haṃsa.
From its arising comes the Kāla-kāla (the Time of Time), and from that arises the rising of the planets.
The constellations, the zodiac signs, the stars, and likewise the degrees—
all these indeed rise within the vital breath during a single day and night, O lady of virtuous vows.
O Dear One, I shall now explain to you the division of the rising of day and night:
it flows from above the heart down as far as below the throat.
When one finger-breadth has passed, the first watch is said to be over;
the second is to be known as having begun above that, and midday occurs at the middle of the palate.

In this regard, O lady of excellent vows, human recitation and meditation performed [with the gaze] three finger-breadths above the tip of the nose shall indeed grant liberation, as long as it is maintained.
O lady of excellent complexion, this third watch shall indeed occur at the end of Śakti;
the fourth watch is proclaimed as the end of the day.
But at the end of the fourth [tuṭi], O Goddess of gods, the sun of the vital breath is always set;
therefore, O Beloved, the twilight of setting here consists of half a tuṭi.
Having lingered for that duration, it then proceeds downward once more;
and that, O Goddess, is established as the rising of the moon and the night.
By means of the application of the sequence previously described, he moves in this manner through the watches;
and at midnight, it is prescribed once again in the same way regarding the palate.
When [the breath] reaches the heart-lotus, that is the time of dawn;
O lady of excellent hips, half a *tuṭi* thereafter constitutes the morning twilight (*pūrvasaṃdhyā*).
Therefore, he shall again become the very rising of the sun;
indeed, O auspicious one, he shall always move according to the sequence as before.
During the day the sun should move, and during the night the moon should move;
this, indeed, is the rising of the moon and the sun that has been proclaimed by me to you.
The planets, beginning with Mars, indeed move in this manner according to their respective divisions;
O Dear One, they also rise within the vital breath during every watch.
Whichever watch (velā) or turn (vāra) it may be, he should perform [the ritual] for two watches;
Rāhu moves with the Moon, and Ketu moves with the Sun.
Those who are the planets are indeed the nāgas, and they are the eight guardians of the world;
they are the eight embodied forms, and they are the eight lords of the hosts.
And those five groups of eight Rudras, as well as the other eight Yogas,
and those eight Vidyeśvaras beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
All the principles (tattvas), beginning with Sakala, are situated here beyond [the individual soul];
and all those eight Bhairavas previously mentioned are likewise established here.
Having presided over the planets and so forth, they cause the rising of all things;
together with the zodiac signs and the lunar mansions, they rise day and night.
At midday and at midnight, the rising of Abhijit occurs;
therein, the desired fruit shall accrue to practitioners in this world.
This division of day and night has thus been explained to you by me;
now I shall explain to you the fortnights, months, and years.
By means of an internal day-and-night, a *kāṣṭhā* is established externally;
by means of an internal month, there is likewise an external *kalā*.
In that regard, O lady of excellent complexion, thirty days and nights constitute a month; and with twelve such months, there is then one external *ghaṭikā*.
Three hundred and sixty Ahorātras are declared to be one year; externally, that same duration is indeed a Ghaṭikā.
Sixty ghaṭikās indeed flow externally during one day and night;
those same sixty, by way of internal movement, are recorded as years.
Now, O lady of excellent hips, I shall tell you again the number of breaths within them:
twenty-one thousand six hundred.
By means of the external day and night, the number of breaths within the lord of the seasons (the year) is fully explained; that must be understood by the practitioner.
The practitioner who knows the supreme reality is always absorbed in the *praṇava*;
for him, this recitation is prescribed as that which bestows the fruits of both accomplishment (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mukti*). (SvaT 7.56)
Success is achieved in the downward flow when [the breath] has reached as far as the heart-lotus;
O virtuous one, liberation indeed occurs in the upward flow within the supreme reality.
Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eye is cast elsewhere,
the vital breath always proceeds effortlessly.
There is no one who utters it, nor is there any one who obstructs it;
the Haṃsa, dwelling in the chest of living beings, utters itself spontaneously.
This enumeration of months and years has been told to you by me;
hereafter, I shall describe the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
O beautiful goddess, that which has been described as a day and night within this vital breath (prāṇa), that very thing constitutes two fortnights; now I shall explain the month to you.
Half a *tuṭi* is proclaimed as the rest, both below and above;
those fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) which are said to be in the middle are thus proclaimed.
At the first rising, from the heart-lotus, half a *tuṭi* shall be the day;
and during the second half of the *tuṭi*, when she moves, it is night.
O fair-faced one, in this very day and night, the zodiacal signs, planets, and lunar mansions arise in their proper sequence, just as before.
A fortnight is prescribed as consisting of fifteen *tuṭis*.
When there is a decrease in the lunar days (*tithi*), it should be known as a debt; when there is an increase, it becomes wealth.
Cough indeed constitutes debt, while exhalation is called wealth;
through the upward movement during the dark fortnight, there occurs withdrawal and depletion.
Indeed, performing cruel deeds there, one may attain success;
however, O lady of excellent vows, auspicious deeds performed during the dark fortnight do not succeed.
O fair-faced one, that *tuṭi* which is prescribed as the entry of power (*śakti*) into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) should be known as the new moon (*amāvāsya*) in the dark fortnight.
In the middle and upper portion of Śakti,

that which is proclaimed as half a *tuṭi* should be known as the junction of the fortnights (*pakṣasaṃdhi*), consisting of the half of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the first day of the lunar phase (*pratipad*).
Indeed, there, by the cutting of the lunar day (tithi), an eclipse of the sun occurs;
at that time, O Goddess, the lunar disc appears within the solar disc.
In that interval, O fair-faced one, Rāhu becomes a seeker of nectar;
the moon pours forth nectar, and Rāhu swallows it.
Having drunk [the nectar], he abandons that *ālamba*; then he is said to be liberated. In the world, this is taught as the "eclipse of the sun."
When these three planets— Rāhu, the Sun, and the Moon—
are seen in conjunction, that shall be a great eclipse.
That time shall be the most meritorious of all times for all the worlds;
therein, bathing, as well as giving, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth [yield great fruit].
O Goddess, whatever is performed by practitioners shall yield infinite fruit;
and having bypassed that very half-tuṭi, the rising of the bright fortnight occurs.
From the womb of Śakti, emanation proceeds downward; from that, growth is produced.
And beginning from that point, auspicious actions and prosperities arise.
For one who is engaged in meditation, mantras, and so forth, success is certain; there is no doubt in this matter—once the Haṃsa of the vital breath has reached the first *tuṭi* below.
The first half of the day is said to be day, and the other half of a *tuṭi* is night;
[therein reside] the zodiac signs, the planets, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants, the astrological conjunctions (*yoga*s), and the lunar phases (*karana*s).
In the same manner as before, through the sequential application [of yoga], they arise day and night;
that [first day] is to be known as the first lunar day (pratipad), and the moon becomes one digit (kalā).
On the second day, however, the second [tuṭi] increases in sequence;
and in this manner, starting from the lunar days (tithis), it proceeds until the fifteenth tuṭi.
The practitioner should recognize the full moon day as the specific lunar date; on that day, worship, recitation, and meditation become complete and fruitful.
And when the moon becomes full within that [fortnight], O lovely-eyed one,
that half-tuṭi of hers is known as the junction (saṃdhyā) of the fortnight.
Half of that [day] is the full moon, established with the half of the first day of the lunar fortnight;
within the center of the junction of the heart-lotus, there occurs the seizing of the moon.
In this world, the lunar eclipse is said to occur without the sun;
and in that very [eclipse], there is great merit through meditation, fire-offerings, recitations, and so forth.
O Goddess of the gods, during both fortnights,
the eclipses of the moon and the sun bestow various supernatural powers upon the diligent practitioner.
And liberation itself, O auspicious lady, is free from both sides;
indeed, by abandoning both sides through the previously mentioned method.
Always abiding in the state beyond the mind (*unmanī*), supported by the supreme transformation,
one should abandon everything below and, established in meditation, apply oneself [to yoga].
For him there is liberation, of this there is no doubt; otherwise, he would become a possessor of supernatural powers (siddhi).
In both cases, indeed, the grasping of all embodied beings occurs.
Thus has this been fully explained, O fair-faced one, up to the duration of life;
now, within this very context, the internal day-and-night and the arising of the year are described.
From the heart-lotus up to the top, six zodiac signs are situated;
each occupies six finger-breadths, starting from the heart-lotus as far as the Śakti.
For in every finger-breadth here, five lunar days (tithis) are established;
its first half is the day, and the latter half becomes the night.
Those thirty lunar days which consist of six times five are the monthly days and nights;
by those thirty days and nights, a month is said to have two fortnights.
Indeed, at the rising of the lunar mansion in the month, during the movement of the breath upwards and downwards,
the transit (saṃkrānti) is situated in Capricorn, arising from the heart as the place of origin.
Having abandoned six finger-breadths below, it again transits into the water-pot (kumbha);
having abandoned two finger-breadths above the neck, it again transits into the fish (mīna).
Having abandoned [the breath] from the throat upwards as far as the palate, one should then transition into Aries;
the transition extends as far as the nose, for it is exactly six finger-breadths.
This indeed is the equinoctial transit established in the north;
it brings about great prosperity through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and meditation.
Having abandoned the tip of the nose, the swan of breath should move into Taurus;
having abandoned six finger-breadths, it should then transition into Gemini.
O lady of excellent vows, transmigration is said to occur through the path up to the end of Śakti,
beginning from Capricorn and ending with Gemini.
In this [system], the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is devoid of success pertaining to this world;
bathing, meditation, giving, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth [are likewise ineffective].
Whatever has been performed by practitioners and others in many thousands of ways, one does not obtain it in this life; it manifests only in the next world.
The days increase there from Capricorn until Gemini;
at that time, he withdraws the vital energy from this world of moving and unmoving beings.
The Haṃsa, having drawn it forth with its rays,
should cause that which was previously grasped— the ancient form existing within the womb— to abide within the womb in its manifold aspects.
Starting from Cancer, it rains everywhere;
starting from that [point] at Capricorn, one should perform meditation, fire-oblations, recitation, and so forth.
For the sake of attaining the next world,
that which has its fruit immediately following it would be the vow of mantra-grasping and the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*).
One should begin everything for the sake of one's own accomplishment of mantra starting from Pisces;
even among external trees in the world, they are impelled by the six seasons.

The mantras, impelled by the practice of vows and other rites, come to delight in the flowers as an illumination for the one whose weapon is the flower (the God of Love), in accordance with the proper time.
Blazing with the awakening to the objects of knowledge, they are the achievers of accomplishment and liberation;
their nature consists of internal sound and form, impelled by the tasting of the six flavors.
The swan, however, being inflamed by awakening, takes refuge in the fish at the throat;
for it is there that the perception of sound becomes clearly manifest to him.
O Goddess of the Gods, from that time forward, everything proceeds for him through recitation up to the end of the couple; from that, perfection is born.
Accompanied by Haṃsa and situated in the power of the Bindu, facing downwards through the gates of accomplishment,
he rains [the nectar] within the palate from the beginning of Cancer until the end of Libra.
From the throat downwards, the embodied one should cause [the breath] to proceed from the heart-lotus in all directions;
therefore, for the sake of attaining the self and for nourishment, one should practice it here.
O Dear One, because creation arises during the period born of the southern solstice,
the *haṃsa* should move from below the power (*śakti*) into the heart at the time of Cancer.
Having abandoned six finger-breadths, it indeed enters Leo;
then, having again abandoned six finger-breadths, it enters Virgo once more.
Having thus abandoned [the path] from the tip of the nose to the palate, it becomes the equinox;
this is said to be the transition of Libra (tulā-saṃkrānti), and it becomes the southern equinox.
Therefore, one should undertake the practice performed here in this life which grants all desires,
as well as victory over death, peace, and nourishment.
Therefore, that food consisting of the six tastes, having passed below the throat, nourishes the body;
then, having bypassed six finger-breadths, it moves again toward the scorpion [the lower part of the small intestine].
Having left two finger-breadths above the throat and four finger-breadths below the throat,
and having bypassed the scorpion [node], the transition of Sagittarius is said to occur.
Six finger-breadths below [the navel], situated within the bow, the Haṃsa moves in the heart; having moved as far as the lotus of the heart, it rises upward.
Thus, one should always practice these twelve [observances] during the transits [of the sun] into Capricorn and the other signs;
by this very sequence described, [one attains] the lifespan of all embodied beings.
Success pertaining to this world and the next is classified as inferior, middling, and superior;
the two paths have been described, while the attainment of liberation is free from both.
Always abiding at the end of the two solstices and at the limit of the Unstruck (unmanī),
one situated therein shall indeed attain the perfection of liberation through recitation and meditation.
"Having gone to liberation, one shall not return; such is the vow of Bhairava.
Now listen further to the arising of the twelve-year cycle within this arising of the year."
Since the rising of the months begins in the year of Caitra,
practitioners should therefore commence the mantra practice starting from that point.
O fair-faced one, that [period] of twelve years should be known as beginning from the month of Caitra;
I shall describe its characteristics and the distribution of the vital breath within it.
In that regard, O lady of good vows,
O beloved, that day and night which has been described by me should be divided into twelve parts within a year.
Twelve of those days and nights indeed constitute one year;
by multiplying those [years] by five, twelve years shall become one season (ṛtu).
By doubling that very [time], it is ordained as *kāla*;
by tripling it, this constitutes an *ayana*, and by sextupling it, a year (*vatsara*).
Just as twelve transits (saṃkrānti) are proclaimed here in a year,
so those years are proclaimed [to occur] in the vital breath (prāṇa) at the arising of the twelve-year cycle.
In twelve years, however, there are days and nights; learn their number from me:
four thousand, three hundred, and twenty.
O Goddess, I have explained to you the arising of the twelve-year cycle within this vital breath;
now, once again, I shall explain to you the arising of the sixty-year cycle right here.
O fair-faced one, those sixty-year cycles beginning with Ānanda should be known;
and they [occur] within a single vital breath (prāṇa) moving downward and upward, O beautiful goddess.
I shall explain to you, O Goddess, how they proceed according to their respective divisions:
whoever would propitiate the mantra beginning with Ānanda, O Goddess.
O Goddess of the gods, his bliss arises together with the mantra;
at the age of twelve, one should divide that [bliss] fivefold throughout day and night.
Sixty years are proclaimed to be five days and nights;
when those are multiplied by six, they are proclaimed there as one month.
And by those twelve [digits], O Goddess, one year is constituted;
this measurement is proclaimed for each finger-breadth plus a fifth part.
With six finger-breadths, those [energies] arise for fifty years; they rise up to sixty years.
From the heart-lotus up to the end of Śakti, there occurs the arising of thirty years.
From the base of the *śakti* up to the heart-lotus, there occurs the emergence of thirty years;
I shall now state the number of days and nights contained within those sixty years.
Twenty thousand, one thousand, and six hundred days and nights are reckoned in a sixty-year cycle, O fair-faced one. (SvaT 7.138)
I have explained to you that the arising of sixty years is contained within a single breath,
as well as the eclipses of the moon and sun, and the fortnights, months, and solstices.
O fair-faced one, [this occurs] at the beginnings of the ages, at the ends of the ages, as well as during the year,
during twelve years, and also during sixty years.

Whatever has been performed externally at the [appropriate] time through bathing, giving, sacrifices, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, as well as through the yoga of knowledge and so forth— [all that is rendered fruitless].
O beautiful lady, when this has been spoken, one obtains that great fruit;
having understood the movement of the breath-gander (*prāṇahaṃsa*) in its course, one should devote oneself to it in that single [moment].
The movement [of consciousness] becomes clearly self-perceivable through mastery over the movement in the channels;
or else, it is thus exceedingly augmented by means of recitation alone.
The practitioner of mantra understands the yoga; having understood it, he shall attain omniscience.
Furthermore, I shall explain it again according to the division of the three channels.
During the southern and northern solstices, as well as during the equinoxes,
this *haṃsa* moves through this world of the moving and the unmoving in such a manner.
Abiding within in the form of Time, fashioning the world through its constituent parts (kalās),
he has the three channels as his support and is established in the three paths.
Pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas), established in a threefold state,
overcome by the six causes, and endowed with the triad of powers (śaktis).
Pierced by will, knowledge, and action, and situated between the moon, the sun, and fire,
the channel in the right nostril is indeed known as Piṅgalā.
The *iḍā* is indeed situated on the left, while the *suṣumnā* stands in the middle;
the path of the gods (*devamārga*) is on the right, and likewise the path of the ancestors (*pitṛmārga*) is on the left.
The middle path is that of Śiva; having gone there, one is not born again.
On the right is the waking state of the sattva quality, while on the left is the dreaming state of rajas.
In the middle, darkness (tamas) is to be known, as well as the state of deep sleep (suṣupti);
Brahmā and Īśvara reside on the right, while Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva reside on the left.
In the center, Rudra and Śiva are proclaimed; the supreme Śiva is beyond all.
Jyeṣṭhā resides in the south-east, Vāmā in the north, and Kriyā likewise in the north-east.
Raudrī and Icchā are situated in the middle as the supreme power (Parā) and the supreme-non-supreme (Parāparā);
the Sun is established on the right, while the Moon shines on the left.
In the process of digestion and in its capacity as an illuminator, the fire remains indeed in the middle;
for it causes all that is to be digested—arising from the qualities of soma and the others—to be cooked.
By his own power, he should reveal the stainless supreme reality,
as well as all the zodiacal signs, the planets, the lunar mansions, the yogas, and so forth.
They move in succession precisely along the path of the moon and sun;
and all of them, O beloved, enjoy the sun and the moon in turn.
They indeed consist of the nature of the Moon and the Sun, established upon the three paths;
the Sun blows and burns, while the Moon rains down nectar.
Since the world, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, is composed of the moon and the sun,
the southern path of the sun is known as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
That which is called the left is indeed the northern course (saumya), while the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is there;
the equinox (viṣuvat), consisting of the moon and the sun, issues forth from both nostrils.
There are five transits in the north and indeed five in the south;
between the southern and northern [paths], there are two equinoxes due to the transit.
The southern path belongs to the Sun and is renowned for the accomplishment of malevolent rites (abhicāra);
likewise, the northern path belongs to the Moon and is used for nourishment, prosperity, and pacification.
When it moves from the south to the north, and from the north to the south,
that is the southern and northern transit, and it is established in this very way.
When the channel shifts from the southern to the northern one,
it remains there for half [a cycle] and flows through the middle toward the north.
That is declared to be the equinox; however, during the northern course, it is the northern [equinox].
O fair-faced one, when he moves from the north toward the south, that is the [southern] transition.
O beloved, it carries [the breath] there for half [a year], and for half it carries it to the south;
thus, up to the southern equinox, it is born from the southern solstice.
In that state, whatever worship, recitation, or fire-offering is performed becomes a bestower of liberation;
established therein through the yoga of meditation during initiation, the Guru indeed grants release.
Externally, O fair-faced one, this occurs within day and night; internally, however, the haṃsa of the vital breath undergoes twenty-four transitions.
Twelve [muhūrtas] are said to be in the day, and indeed twelve are recorded in the night;
one equinox occurs in the forenoon, while the second occurs at midday.
The third occurs in the afternoon, and the fourth at midnight;
thus the Viṣuvat is said to be fourfold, bestowing liberation within a single day and night.
The *haṃsa* always carries nine hundred [breaths] for each of the twenty-four transitions, according to the nature of the equilibrium of the elements.
This is declared to be the measure;
when it flows otherwise, then it indicates both the desired and the undesired.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, for his own sake or for the sake of others, the yogi should perform the visualization when the first rising of the sun has arrived.
From that point on, the hero, a yogi whose mind is well-restrained and who is established in the yogic posture, should investigate both life and death.
O Dear One, recollecting his own life-breath situated within the *suṣumnā*,
he should then remain perfectly tranquil, with his mind focused solely on the vital breath.
Indeed, at the time of the transition of the vital breath, it flows while situated solely in Piṅgalā;
O Goddess, having recognized this as the equinox (viṣuvat) in the flow, one should determine the [auspicious] time.
O lady of excellent vows, one's lifespan should be known as one year for every single day and night;
he shall live for two years for every two days and nights.
In this case, three years are [attained] by three [days], four years by four;
five years by five days, and six years likewise by six [days].
With seven [lines], one lives for seven years; with eight, for eight days;
with nine, for nine years; and with ten, for ten years.
O beloved, by means of eleven days alone, a yogin lives for eleven years;
by twelve days, he lives for twelve years.
If [the breath] flows for seven watches (yāma), one lives for six months;
if it flows for six watches (prahara), one indeed lives for three months.
O Goddess, with a lifespan of two and a half months, he lives for one month with four watches [of breath] remaining. SvaT 7.181.
If it flows for three watches, one lives for half a month;
he whose [wind] flows for two watches lives for eight days.
If one should carry [the breath] for one watch, one may live for four watches;
if one carries it for half a watch, one shall live for two watches.
Immediate death occurs for him in whom the *haṃsa* moves through the three paths, from the moment it is observed that the Lord of Time has indeed entered the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (SvaT 7.184)
O beloved, having observed the month, the fortnight, the day, the year, that very day, and so forth,
with such diligent effort, certainty will arise at that time.
Thus have I explained to you regarding the time of the northern course;
now learn from me the knowledge of death even for one who is not disciplined, concerning the vital breath.
O Goddess of the Gods, when one who has placed his thumb into the ear-canal no longer hears sound, one should predict his death within six months.

In the midst of a great noise, when one hears only the supreme sound— the rustling of bark garments and the chirping of birds— and does not hear anything else for one month, O Dear One, he shall live.
Listen to me regarding Utpāta, Kāṇa, and Mṛtyuyoga:
when the vital breath flows through the opening of the mouth during the five transits (saṃkrānti).
One should declare that yoga to be an uprooting; it moves from one place to another, and thus loss of wealth, agitation, and an increase in disease arise.
The destruction of the home of a friend and the loss of one's vital energy occur when the single right nostril is active during the period excluding the sun's southern course.
Through the flow of the eight transits (saṃkrāntyaṣṭaka), that indeed becomes the yoga of the one-eyed;
[the afflictions are] fistula-in-ano, hernia, eye disease, and jaundice.
Painful piercing, boils, suffering, and disorders of the chest also occur;
these are the thirteen transits through the left nostril.
Fever, headache, pain, hemorrhoids, stiffness, dysuria, urinary disorders, and jaundice arise. (SvaT 7.194)
O lady of excellent vows, residing in the *iḍā*, it provokes a disease through phlegm;
on whichever day of the lunar cycle it is observed, [the result occurs] on the following day.
One is afflicted by all diseases, whether on the left, on the right, or on both sides;
furthermore, another tactile cognition occurs below the nose as well as above it.
When [the breath] touches above while moving upward, there are the aforementioned afflictions of disease;
when it flows through the right [nostril], there is verbal abuse and being overwhelmed.
When she touches the middle casket in the center, she attains the state of overwhelming others;
when she flows as one, migrating in many ways here and there, she moves.
When the Haṃsa of the vital breath flows through the Suṣumnā during its slow movement, then there will be worship, great honor, and gain for him.
There shall be gain of land, Dharma, sovereignty, and the arrival of beloved ones;
one should carry out exactly twelve transits, starting from one of the two equinoxes.
Then, one should predict death within exactly one year;
at that time, each transit (saṃkrānti) diminishes by one, and thus one month is diminished.
O lady of excellent hips, there is one transit at which thirty breaths arise and perish;
this should flow externally day after day for thirty days.
O fair-faced one, at the end of the month death shall occur; indeed, it happens instantly.
O lady of excellent complexion, this has been fully explained by me to you as the *mṛtyuyoga* (the conjunction of death).
Whether one practices for a year, a month, a fortnight, a lunar day, or at a specific time,
one should prescribe that very same time from which one began.
The wise know the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) through the channels of Iḍā and Suṣumṇā;
thus has this auspicious [process] been described to you regarding the time arising from the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
Thus, having understood that death and misfortune arise from the body when [the time] has come, the yogi shall conquer death and all misfortunes without exception.
Having meditated upon Kāleśa-Svacchanda, or the Haṃsa who is the Lord of all,
situated within the path of the nostril's opening, he can create and withdraw the universe.
Abiding there, situated within all beings, one should contemplate everything;
by meditating on that which resides therein, the Lord conquers death, for he does not contemplate that which resides elsewhere.
For one engaged in meditation, omniscience arises within six months;
however, the knower of yoga who is disciplined regarding time understands the three times.
O Maheśvarī, by reciting or even meditating upon the Kālahaṃsa mantra, one indeed becomes the very form of Time; autonomous, one moves like Time itself.
Having slain death and abandoned old age, freed from all diseases and fears,
one possesses higher knowledge, hearing from afar, reflection, and vision.
Through the conquest of time, one shall always attain all sovereign qualities;
by meditating on the right nostril, one shall obtain the sovereignty of Brahmā.
Therefore, he knows their lifespan, their equal vigor, and the past;
he becomes a knower of the future and possesses strength equal to Viṣṇu on the left.
Equal to that is his sovereignty and his lifespan; he becomes a king among yogins and knows everything—past, present, and future—from within.
By means of the yoga of constant meditation, one shall attain equality with Rudra;
one becomes equal to him in lifespan, strength, vigor, form, and sovereignty.
Through the supreme state of Brahmā, one shall attain the station of Īśvara;
through the supreme state of Viṣṇu, one shall attain the sovereignty of Sadāśiva.
By meditating upon that which is the supreme state of Rudra, one becomes Śiva;
thus is known the victory over death—the victory of one who meditates on the nectar of immortality.
Having meditated upon the sixteen-petalled heart-lotus, white and in full bloom, situated within the hollow of the channel-opening like a lotus stalk, and endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās).
One should contemplate oneself in the center of that [lotus], possessing all limbs complete, with a form shaped like a pericarp, as stainless as pure crystal, resembling the full moon.
Above that, in the great ocean of the nectar of Śakti, is a second lotus filled with the nectar of the waves abiding in the glorious ocean of immortality.
And that downward-facing lotus has a pericarp like the full moon;
in its center, one should contemplate a swan, provided with a drop and a crest at its base.
One should contemplate divine nectar raining down from all sides,
and one should contemplate that it has entered through the aperture at the top of one's own head.
One should contemplate oneself being flooded and filled by that white, abundant, and thick nectar which destroys death.
One should constantly contemplate the entire body as being filled with nectar through the openings of the channels connected by lotus stalks.
Thus, one whose self is eternally disciplined becomes equal to Amṛteśa;
having abandoned disease, death, and old age, he sports with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā).
Thus, through that meditation on nectar, there shall be victory over death at its appointed time;
or else, established in the supreme reality, one is not afflicted by any times whatsoever.
One should contemplate the supreme reality, which is free from the movement of time,
liberated from parts and stains— the partless, supreme state.
The reality of the Self is indeed partless, whereas the body is called a stain;
it is conjoined with the six causes and endowed with all the principles (tattvas).

The phoneme (varṇa), the point (bindu), and likewise the resonance (nāda), conjoined with the pervasive power (vyāpinī-śakti) and extending as far as the limit of the level of the Equal One (samanā), is called the support of the impurity (kalaṅka).
For the supreme Self is that which is to be supported; the state beyond mind (unmanā) is said to be intent upon that.
At the end of that is the supreme reality, devoid of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
It is all-pervasive, auspicious in every way, within all things, and facing in all directions;
it abides in the reality of the five pentads and is endowed with eighteen qualities.
But if one knows that which is supreme within this [reality], then one is liberated from bondage;
likewise, the causal factors, the mantras, and the digits (kalās) such as cessation (nivṛtti) and the rest.
The Bindu, the Half-moon, the Nirodhī, the Nāda, and the Ūrdhvaga;
the Śakti, the Vyāpinī, the one whose self is the Samanā, and likewise the Unmanā.
O fair-faced one, this group of five fives has indeed been explained to you;
now learn from me the thirty-six principles and their qualities.
Ego-sense, intellect, and mind, as well as the objects of the senses;
grasping, contact, the substratum, and power is remembered as the eighth.
These eight qualities are the eight Bhairavas; thus, the group of eight Bhairavas consists of these qualities.
Furthermore, the vital breath (prāṇa), the swan (haṃsa), and likewise Śakti—these are the eighteen qualities.
Among these, that supreme reality is devoid of any support for vocalization;
free from both the syllable and the non-syllable, the supreme reality is beyond letters.
How can there be liberation in syllables? How can there be space in a flower?
[Liberation exists] only as long as it is uttered by speech, and only as long as it remains in writing.
To that extent he is to be known as having parts (sakala), yet he is partless (niṣkala) and devoid of differentiation;
he is liberated from creation and dissolution, and free from action and time.
When there is downward movement, there is emanation; upward movement is said to be withdrawal.
One who is born through downward movement becomes dead indeed through the upward [movement].
Having abandoned both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), one should indeed abide by way of the reality-practice (tattvavṛtti).
And that reality-practice has been explained as being devoid of all adjuncts of the paths (adhvan).
Freed from the reality-path and its phenomena, and devoid of causal factors,
the yogi abides in the state of reality (tattvavṛtti), having abandoned all undertakings.
Freed from passion and hatred, and devoid of despondency and joy,
he should never long for sense objects nor ever revile them.
One should always be equal toward enemy and friend, and equal toward a Brahmin and a dog-cooker;
one should be a constant seer of equality and remember everything as being composed of Śiva.
One should always remember oneself in that very same way, in every respect;
likewise, one should remember all the principles (tattvas), the elements (bhūtas), the castes (varṇas), and those which are known as the mantras.
By means of this contemplation on Śiva, they indeed remain perpetually under his control;
and he, O lady of excellent vows, performs neither merit nor sin.
Having accomplished what was to be done, his mind is serene; he has no further task remaining, for he is always complete in this world and in the next.
Freed from both dharma and adharma, and devoid of merit and sin,
for him there is indeed nothing that is edible or inedible, nor anything that is drinkable or undrinkable.
For him there is nothing impure, nor indeed anything pure, O lady of virtuous vows;
for he is eternally independent, devoid of all dependence.
He has no sacred field, no place of pilgrimage, no ritual observance, and no restraint;
his field is the Supreme Power (parā śakti), from which everything is brought forth.
O Goddess, since all the paths proceed while remaining established therein,
it is indeed the supreme, peaceful holy site, eternal and pervading the bliss of the universe.
That by which this infinite universe is pervaded through its universal powers, and through which there is constant detachment from saṃsāra—this is proclaimed as *yama*. (SvaT 7.252)
Discipline is constant meditation, which is single-minded devotion to the supreme reality;
one should not contemplate one's own birth, nor one's lineage, nor one's kinsmen.
One should practice the state of being all castes, yet not abide within the [fixed] castes;
one should always abide by the dharma of others through the cultivation of others.
He is omniscient and completely satisfied, perfect by his very nature;
he is independent, with unimpaired power, and rests upon that which is without beginning or end.
For primordial awakening is indeed incomparable, devoid of time and occasion;
it is liberated from movement and exhalation, and is free from day and night.
One should not keep watch during the day, nor should one sleep at night anywhere;
rather, one should abide in one's own true nature, free from both day and night.
In this way, indeed, the yogin proceeds; he shall attain supreme equanimity, and time shall not reckon him even in hundreds of millions of eons.
He for whom this contemplation is always present is liberated even while living;
for Śiva is eternally contemplated, and time cannot affect Śiva.
The yogi, by means of the yoga of freedom (svacchanda-yoga), moving with a gait of freedom,
being joined to the state of freedom, shall attain equality with the Free One (Svacchanda).
One who is truly self-willed should always wander at will;
such indeed are the signs of death, as well as other portents (riṣṭas).
Through yoga, the lord of yogis knows those [elements] contained within the *nāda*;
having conquered them by means of yoga according to the aforementioned sequence.
O lady of excellent vows, hear from me concerning those external signs which an unyoked one or even a non-yogi perceives here as portents of death.
If one's palate, lips, and throat become dry, the complexion suddenly turns ashen,
and the shoulders undergo a collapse, such a person will meet death within six months.
He who day after day sees a blue,
white, green, or black circle in the sky will die within half a year.
One who sees the sun devoid of rays, or the moon bereft of its splendor,
or sees the stars and the moonlight as black, has but six months of life remaining.
He who indeed sees in a dream a golden-colored person, or one that is tawny, or even black, lives for six months.
For one who sees the shadow of his own headless body, he has six months of life remaining;
likewise, [one who dreams of] anointing with oil, drinking it, or wearing red garlands and ointments [has the same fate].
When one indeed sees red garments or black ones in a dream,
along with ghosts, piśācas, rākṣasas, dogs, jackals, and pigs;
Surrounded by vultures and crows, buffaloes, camels,
and donkeys, he undergoes the devouring of his limbs and is led away naked and utterly distraught.
Furthermore, he who sees [these signs] in a dream lives for one year:
[if they appear] on the Śaṅkhāvarta, in the middle of the arms, at the ankles, or at the vital joints.
He for whom this vibration does not occur will certainly meet his death;
[for he perceives] the orbs of the moon and sun within the body, as well as the fixed pole star and Arundhatī.
That man who does not see the Mahāyāna will certainly die;
that which has entered the cavity of the palate is called the Mahāyāna.
The tongue is said to be Arundhatī, and the tip of the nose is called Dhruva;
at the corners of the eyes, when pressed by the fingertips, are the mandalas of the Moon and the Sun.
If one does not see this even in the sky, that man will certainly die;
he may suddenly become stout, and suddenly indeed become thin.
Extremely angry and extremely terrified, he lives for one year [seeing] a black man wearing black garments, with a metal staff raised in his hand.
Furthermore, having seen a man facing him in a dream, if his heart dries up at that very moment immediately after bathing, his life span is only three months.
If his body is not even slightly warm, he lives for only one season;
if a rainbow appears at night, or a meteor during the day, or lightning is seen in a cloudless sky [he will die].
Even if a burning sensation occurs in a region that has not been scorched by fire, he lives for only one month;
likewise, he whose eyes are watering and who cannot clearly hear sound [will die].
One whose life has reached its end for one month does not perceive odors and suffers from muteness;
indeed, his face resembles a red lotus and his tongue becomes black.
He whose limbs display various colors, whose heart weeps,
and who experiences trembling of the palate and the navel, lives for only half a month.
He who is a leader among those with visible crow-noses does not smell the smoke of a lamp;
he does not recognize what was seen before—he lives for four months.
He who does not see the beneficial drop (bindu) constantly following the mouth,
yet constantly suffers from hiccups, lives for only one year.
O Dear One, these external signs and those which are the portents of death are [overcome] through worship, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, and concentration.
By performing the ritual of protection, one conquers; of this there is no doubt.
How, then, does the purification of the channels and the mastery of the vital winds occur?
"O Lord, tell me of the locus, the form, and the sound, as well as the ritual action;
O Beloved, this is the supreme essence of yoga, more secret than the secret."
Listen now to that yoga in its true essence, which has not been taught to anyone:
on a highly auspicious spot of ground, not near fire or water.
In a place devoid of sand and gravel, free from withered trees, silent and without insects or anthills, and entirely avoided by calamities; SvaT_7.288 //
In that holy place, a dwelling for the most righteous,
one should practice yoga there after having worshipped Bhairava, the God of gods, together with Vināyaka.
Having paid homage to the former teachers, being disciplined and devoted to meditation,
one should assume the *svastika*, the *padmaka*, or the *bhadra* posture.
Having performed the burning and purification of the meditation belt (*yogapaṭṭa*), which has a handle and a half-moon, as is comfortable,
one should then flood it with nectar.
Then, the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa is performed with both the external and internal [mantras];
thereafter, the inner sacrifice (antaryāga) is to be performed as before, and likewise the supreme [mantra] is to be recited.
One should practice the Haṃsa-svacchanda mantra tenfold by way of yoga—
transcending the bindu and having the form of the light at the end of sound.
Having formed a mental resolve upon the object of conceptualization, one should indeed meditate on that which is all-pervading;
it should be filled by the right nostril and exhaled by the left alone.
This is the purification of the channels and of the path of the way to liberation;
through exhalation, inhalation, and retention, prāṇāyāma is traditionally said to be threefold.
These are common to the exterior, but furthermore there are three within;
one should exhale by means of the internal [wind], and fill by means of the internal.
Having performed a steady breath-retention (kumbhaka), one should perform three internal movements:
from the navel to the heart, and [the withdrawal] of the mind from the domain of the senses.
The fourth, however, is known as *supraśānta* (perfectly tranquil) *prāṇāyāma*;
when the retention of the breath is complete, one draws [the breath] into the navel while breathing out.
One should slowly release the breath through the left nostril;
the Vāyavī concentration is at the thumb, and the Āgneyī is in the middle of the navel.
The earth-element concentration is at the region of the throat, while the water-element concentration resides in the uvula;
the space-element concentration at the crown of the head is remembered as that which brings about all accomplishments.
It is accomplished through one, two, three, four, or five counts of exhalations;
however, when the vital breath is completely restrained, it goes to the crown of the head and returns.
This is declared to be the "expulsion" (udghāta), which should always be understood by yogins;
through well-maintained breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), attachment and aversion are abandoned.
One should burn away evil through the *dhāraṇās*; in *pratyāhāra*, there is the restraint of the senses at the heart, the anus, the navel, the throat, and likewise at all the joints.
For these, beginning with Prāṇa, are established; now hear from me their forms and sounds:
[Prāṇa] resembles molten gold and is red like an Indragopaka insect.
The appearance of the five [Buddhas] is like milk and like crystal;
their sound is sweet as a bell, bronze, or thunder, and their great resonance is like the cry of an elephant.
This terminology is taught for the five [winds] beginning with prāṇa:
speech, laughter, song, dance, the movements in battle, and the arts.
Craftsmanship and all activities are merely the movements of the vital breath;
it should cause food and drink to enter and discharge their waste below.
The apāna wind will cause blindness and diseases of the ear;
the samāna wind brings to equilibrium what has been eaten, licked, and drunk.
Agitation, hiccup, and likewise sneezing are the activities of udāna;
so too are perspiration, horripilation, piercing pain, burning sensation, and the breaking of the limbs.
These are the functions of the vyāna; it perceives touch as well, being situated in the thumbs, the knees, the heart, the eyes, and the head.
The Nāgas and others are of many forms; learn from me their function:
they produce delight and agitation, as well as desiccation and terror.
Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta as the fifth,
Atinidrākara, and another, Yojaka, and Dhanañjaya.
The contraction and cessation of the breath, as well as the gurgling sound upon its departure—
these are the manifestations of the five [winds], beginning with Nāga, at the time of death.
And Dhanañjaya does not depart at all upon the upward exit after abandoning the body;
rather, he contracts it like a tortoise and dries up the physical frame.
One should first conquer the vital breath; when the breath is conquered, the mind is conquered.
When the mind is conquered, for one who is at peace, the supreme reality shines forth.
One should meditate on the prāṇa and apāna in the anus, the prāṇa and samāna at the navel,
the prāṇa and udāna in the throat, and the prāṇa and vyāna as pervading the whole body.
One should restrain the [winds] beginning with Nāga, which are joined with the vital breaths, in their own respective locations;
and as for the duration of that restraint, listen as I describe it to you. (SvaT 7.317)
One should meditate on that [wind] starting from the *tāla* [measure] until five hundred have passed;
thus the wind is surely conquered for the rites of transference and egress.
His divine luster, auspicious fragrance, and wisdom increase;
divine vision, divine hearing, and divine speech arise within him.
One may traverse the worlds like the wind and behold the Siddhas and the gods;
the attainment of whatever is conceived by the mind proceeds, and the eightfold qualities manifest.
With all desires perfectly fulfilled and free from all dualities,
he becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra and is equal to Śiva.
Having joined the prāṇa and apāna breaths together, endowed with ten million short [syllables],
at the foundation of the navel, O lord of yogins, sweat and trembling arise.
Furthermore, one should restrain the prāṇa and apāna residing within the heart;
through the union with the long-pointed [state], one falls to the ground at that very moment.
Likewise, one should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) situated here in the throat;
through the union with ten million plutas, there then arises the state of dreaming.
By means of the yoga of the drop (bindu) at the center of the eyebrows, one should effect the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
there, deep sleep arises, and in an instant, one awakens.
Having resorted to the aperture of the crown of the head, one should begin the meditation on the partless;
as he practices in this way, the sign of realization will then arise for him.
The piercing of the ant-thorn pierces the upper door,
having sequentially pierced all those [channels] up to the state of *unmanī*.
O Goddess, having abandoned the aforementioned characteristics, one should proceed with spontaneous freedom;
indeed, the state of *unmanā* arises within this very body for the practitioner.
He may transfer [his consciousness] into the bodies of others, and he is not afflicted by hunger or thirst;
indeed, he perceives everything that has occurred and will occur throughout the three worlds.
That [knowledge] becomes direct perception for him, and omniscience arises;
through the application regarding internal time, there is both knowledge and consciousness.
All this has been fully explained; now learn from me the constituent parts as well.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
The eighth chapter:
O Goddess, I shall describe the sixfold division in due order.
The portion of existence, the portion of intrinsic nature, and the portion of the falling of flowers.
Another part is known as mantra, and the attainment of that part is twofold:
the recollection of the deity and the innate state; know that to be the true nature.
I shall describe their respective natures and activities in due order:
one who is devoted to the Vedas is a portion of Brahmā; now learn from me the portion of Rudra.
He was a devotee of Rudra, possessed of excellent character, and always devoted to the scriptures of Śiva;
he was a portion of Viṣṇu and a devotee of Viṣṇu, while being a portion of the Moon and of pleasing appearance.
One who delights in all the gods is peaceful; one who is a portion of the Yakṣas accumulates wealth;
one who is greedy and eats with pride and refinement is known as a portion of Vāyu; and one who is fickle is considered a portion of Wind.

He moves with the confidence of a serpent, possesses the nature of a nāga, and sleeps for long periods; he harbors long-standing resentment, has a foul-smelling mouth, and always has a craving for the milk of female elephants.
O fair-faced one, the Gāndharva is always a singer and a devotee of Śiva;
the living being who is a portion of a Vidyādhara is known as a lover, while he who is a portion of a Daitya is known as a hater.
One who has a portion of Kāma is handsome, fortunate, and beloved by courtesans;
one with a portion of a Rākṣasa is cruel, merciless, hostile toward the gods, and [harsh] toward the twice-born.
The portion of the Piśāca is a seeker of deception; during the day it is fearful and timid;
the portion of Agni is harsh, intense, a consumer of heat, and likewise tawny.
And Tejasvin, the son of Savitṛ, was always devoted to the dharma of public works;
compassionate and permeated by the spirit of Śiva, he constantly performed sacrifices.
O fair-faced one, all the gods, when empowered by the limbs of Bhairava through their own meditation, recitation, and fire-offerings, bestow the fruits of their own accomplishments.
All the Bhairavas are traditionally held to bestow the fruit of all accomplishments;
their essential nature has indeed been declared for the benefit of practitioners.
O beautiful goddess, the name should be determined by the falling of the flower;
that mantra will be mastered by him if he should worship it alone.
O Goddess, I shall explain in brief the attainment of one's portion:
the practitioner who performs the fire-oblation of the "sky-going" [substance] and the banner.
O you of excellent vows, even that mantra which has reached its end will indeed be accomplished for him;
and even a mantra that lacks any parts, O fair-faced one, [will succeed] through the signs of knowledge.
Then, having first performed the sacrifice, one should cause the oblation (homa) to be made in the fire;
and having performed the ritual for the disciple according to the previous procedure and in accordance with the rules.
By means of the application of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should unite [the disciple] with the eternal state;
meditating upon the supreme reality (paratattva), one should accomplish whatever is desired by the mind.
Having counted the portions of the mantra, one should grasp it with thorough deliberation;
I shall now describe, in brief, that which is inferior, middling, and superior.
One should recognize the inferior enemy, the middling one who appears as an ally,
and that which is accomplished and well-accomplished is proclaimed as the supreme.
Having separated the syllables of the mantra, provided with their vowels and nasal dots (bindu),
one should likewise join the syllable of one's own name below it.
O Goddess, starting from one’s own name and proceeding until the syllable of the mantra is reached, one should determine that [syllable] upon which it falls as the first [syllable].
I shall now describe briefly that which pertains to the lines on the fingers:
one who is successful (*siddha*) is indicated by the first joint, and one who is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by the second.
In the third [case], he is well-accomplished; in the fourth, he is to be known as an enemy.
Having abandoned both the enemy and the one to be accomplished, [the object] should be given by the Cumbaka.
O fair-faced one, he who is purified by his own *aṃśaka* is Bhairava here; he is the perfected form, the well-perfected, and the bestower of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
Having worshipped that [deity] situated in the center, one should place the central [deity] in that position;
for the God is remembered as being omnipresent and residing within all things.
He is the bestower of both spiritual accomplishment and liberation; in the ultimate sense, he is not the letters.
This supreme secret, more hidden than the hidden, has been explained to you along with its mysteries.
Therefore, for the purpose of introducing the Tantra, I shall briefly explain that which has descended from Śiva, the supreme cause, in an invisible form.
The nature of sound (dhvani), however, is extremely subtle, perfectly pure, and endowed with radiant luster. (Note:
However, it should be noted that when Kṣemarāja refers forward to this passage in his commentary on Svacchandatantra 1:1–4b, [he cites it as follows].)
He quotes it as follows:
"As he will say:
From the supreme cause, Śiva, who is tranquil and whose form is unperceived..."
The scripture, which is of the nature of resonance (*dhvani*) and extremely difficult to obtain, has emerged;
that very same [scripture] exists in another form through Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, the great-souled one of the five mantras,
having quickly deliberated upon the goals of human existence, [established] the various means of accomplishment individually.
From the worldly level up to the state of Śiva, for the sake of both higher and lower manifestations,
[these states exist] within their respective spheres of objects for those who are fit to receive such grace.
Bound by the *anuṣṭubh* meter into thousands of millions of billions of parts,
the Lord Sadāśiva himself, abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple, [revealed it].
Through sentences consisting of preceding and following words, that knowledge was imparted by the Lord to [the disciple] according to the difference in the foundational systems (tantra),
by the will of Śiva.
This Vidyā was previously taught with due reverence by [Śiva] to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), ending with Māyā and Niyati; from them, it was likewise obtained by the Rudras.
The knowledge that is most difficult to attain was received by Śrīkaṇṭha from Īśvara;
by him, too, it was proclaimed below [to his subordinates], namely to the Rudras, by the will of Īśvara.
Having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule from the Pradhāna up to the end of the Śatarudra,
my own initiation and likewise my consecration were performed in the same manner in the past.
O Goddess of the gods, this Tantra, which accomplishes all aims and was formerly bestowed by Śrīkaṇṭha, has now been handed over to you by me along with its full authority.
You too should offer [the oblation] to Skanda and Rudra according to the prescribed rite,
as well as to the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, and to the Vasus, the Mothers, and the Sun.
O Supreme Goddess, having gathered the Nāgas and Yakṣas in the world,
speak [this] to the sages, and from the sages, even among human beings.
Thus, this supreme, divine tantra, which is a casket of the jewels of accomplishment, must be kept strictly secret by you; it should not be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the section on the *aṃśakas*, in the Svacchandatantra.
Now, hereafter, I shall proclaim this supreme secret.
O lady of excellent vows, I shall tell you that which has not been declared to anyone.
O beautiful lady, while the god Mahābhairava was sporting,
[the mantra] that effects creation and destruction emerged from his heart.
His body has the form of the fire at the end of an aeon; his roar is like the sound of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution;
his fangs resemble a mass of lightning; and the radiance of his matted locks is equal to a blazing flame.
His eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire; he has hollowed-out sockets and is most terrifying;
his chest is broad and expansive, and he wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
His crown is shimmering with rubies, he is adorned with serpent-earrings,
he displays the majesty of a necklace of snakes, and his bracelets and anklets are made of serpents.
Clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with a girdle of serpents,
his garment covered by an elephant hide, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Five-faced, mounted upon a corpse, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
adorned with a garland of skulls, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The god holds a noose and a goad, with his body bent by a bow and arrow;
he carries a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, radiant with its throbbing lower lip,
it is saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and is difficult even for the gods to attain.
In this way, one should fully proclaim that god Bhairava, the Svachchhanda;
by remembering him, the god destroys even the most formidable mass of sins.
The mantra of this [deity] has been previously described as consisting of thirty-two syllables;
one should recite the mantra dissolved therein, preceded and followed by the five *praṇavas*.
I shall explain its ritual procedure in brief, but not in detail;
it should be performed on a previously mentioned site that is purified and possesses auspicious characteristics.
Having drawn the mandala there with the auspicious pigments previously mentioned, in a place strewn with heaps of flowers and perfumed with incense and fragrances; SvaT 9.13.
Having made it well-measured and level on all sides, square in shape, and measuring one cubit, two cubits, four cubits, or eight cubits; SvaT_9.14 //
Having established the directional divisions as before, O fair-faced one,
one should draw a lotus in the center, provided with four gates, eight petals, and a pericarp, and distinguished by its filaments.
Having drawn a beautiful wheel of thirty-two syllables on the outside,
and having likewise made it well-proportioned, one should draw a circle on the exterior.
One should arrange a square area adjacent to that, with a pathway on the outside;
the gate should be fashioned according to the measurement of the central lotus, as previously described.
With his body smeared with ashes, adorned with the ornaments of mudrās,
wearing matted hair as a sacred thread, naked, and with his senses fully restrained.
O Dear One, with a conch and an arghya vessel in hand, having consecrated his body through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having deployed the weapon-mantra all around, one should worship Bhairava.
One should [worship] that very same manifest deity, the independent Supreme Lord, as the Form established upon the seat of the *praṇava*, by means of the syllable *haṃsa*. (SvaT 9.20)
O Goddess, one should invoke with that which is supremely radiant, free from affliction, and formless; likewise, one should invoke the heart, the head, and the crest-lock.
One should likewise assign the armor (*varma*), the eyes, and the weapon (*astra*) by means of that very [mantra];
as well as the installation (*sthāpana*), the presence (*saṃnidhāna*), and the worship beginning with the half-cessation (*nirodhārdha*).
O fair-faced one, everything—both that which has been mentioned and that which has not—must be performed by him alone;
Bhairava, situated in the center, should be worshipped together with the six limbs.
Then, one should place the goddesses residing on the petals with thirty-two syllables,
beginning from the eastern spoke and continuing until they are established at the end.
I shall state their names, numbering thirty-two:
Aruṇā, Ghoṣā, the goddess Devī, Revatī, and Bhogadāyikā.
Sthāpanī, Ghorasaṃjñā, Rakṣā, Bhārabharā,
Ghorarūpā, Ravā, Ghoṇā, Rati, Tārā, and Rūpiṇī.
Bhayahāni, Caṇḍā, Sarvadā, Varā, Takṣakī, Śārvī, Barbarā, and likewise Sarvagā.
Raudrī, Bhrāmaṇī, Nāginī, Manoharā,
Stambhanī, Roṣaṇī, Drāvā, Rudrā, and Praśāsinī.
The goddess who removes fear should be known through those thirty-two [syllables] in sequence:
first the Praṇava, then the letter, followed by the name of the goddess, and likewise the word of salutation.
This procedure, however, must be performed for all [the goddesses] by one who knows the ritual rules:
first, the four [squares] in the east are golden-hued, possessing a radiance equal to a rainbow.
One should visualize [the deity] with four faces and four arms, holding a vajra in his hand, full of pride, adorned with a garland of skulls, and laughing loudly.

One should always remember the deity of the southeast as having the luster of red color and holding a spear in his hand; one should remember the deity of the south as black-colored, extremely terrifying, and holding a staff in his hand.
One should visualize the deity of the Nairṛta direction as blue, with the luster of a blue lotus, holding a sword in his hand;
one should contemplate the deity of the western quarter as dark-green, holding a noose in his hand.
In the northwestern direction, there is a smoke-colored [deity] with a banner in hand, very restless;
in the north, one should know [the deity] to be white, bearing a mace and a shield.
Likewise, in the northeast, one should visualize [the deity] with the luster of crystal and holding a trident in his hand;
he who is thus intent on meditation should constantly practice this cycle.
O lady of excellent hips, within half a year, his threefold accomplishment shall come to pass on Mahendra,
Malaya, Sahya, Pāriyātra, and likewise Arbuda.
O beloved, [it is likewise] on the Vindhya, on Śrīparvata, and on Mount Kola;
O fair-faced one, at Kurukṣetra where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā converge.
Established at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and Brahmāvarta, as well as in the most meritorious Antarvedī and likewise on the Narmadā; SvaT 9.38.
In a very fertile region of the earth, delightful with clusters of lotuses,
in whichever specific places the Blessed Lord Śiva, the Self-Existent One, [manifested].
In those places, O Goddess of the Gods, one who is established in discipline, has conquered the senses,
restrained speech, and possesses a tranquil mind, should be devoted to the recitation of a hundred thousand syllables.
Subsisting on vegetables, eating fruits, and devoted to meals of wild rice and the like;
intent upon worship at the three times of day, he is further dedicated to the fire-ritual.
The Great Being, whose self is cultivated and who is conversant with the methods of protection,
shall achieve success in his mantra and accomplish all that is moving and unmoving.
The fire of time (kālāgni), the hells, the netherworlds (pātāla), Hāṭakeśvara,
the seven worlds together with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and beyond that, the five groups of eight (pañcāṣṭaka).
The eightfold divine womb, ending with Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
as well as Niyati, the principle of Time (Kāla), Rāga, Vidyā, and Kalā.

Through the power of the King of Mantras, everything— the principle of Māyā, the principle of Vidyeśvara, the principle called Sadākhya, and that which is within the sphere of Śakti— is accomplished without effort.
One shall quickly accomplish the previously mentioned rites—whether inferior, middling, or superior;
there is no doubt here, according to the word of Bhairava.
Then, having relied upon the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra) endowed with the six limbs,
and having joined him with the [appropriate] birth-yoga, one should place him upon the lotus of eight petals.
O Great Goddess, devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, one should perform the worship according to the previous rule while meditating upon Svacchanda, the Supreme Lord.
O Goddess, one attains all desired objects; there is no doubt about this.
Now, regarding the methods of protection, one should employ the Aghora mantra as follows.
I shall speak accordingly; listen with one-pointed mind, O beautiful lady, after having drawn the wheel endowed with thirty-two spokes.
O fair-faced one, it should be joined with the filaments of the navel and made perfectly level;
having taken yellow pigment (gorocanā) combined with prepared lac-dye, [one should draw it].
O Goddess of the Gods, one should draw the King of Vidyās, situated within the pericarp and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, using a green blade of *dūrvā* grass. (SvaT 9.52)
O Goddess of gods, one should draw the object to be accomplished (sādhya) within that [mandala] ending with the power (śakti);
O lady of excellent hips, it is placed between the letters *ka* and *ṣa*, positioned within the eyes and so forth.
Having encircled it with the letter *ī*, O Goddess, one should place it within the spokes;
then, within its interior, one should write the deity previously mentioned and the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Having performed that within the womb of existence (*bhavagarbha*), one should envelop it with that which is called the letter *ī*;
O lady of excellent limbs, one should do this three times while relying upon the yoga of meditation.
O fair-faced one, having restrained [the breath] upwards with the syllable *kroṃ* and having sprinkled it with the moon,
one should worship it with flowers and incense.
And one should wrap that birch-bark, which is without holes, free from blemishes, and even, with a five-colored thread, O fair-faced one. (SvaT 9.57)
One should then strike it with the scum and place it in the midst of honey,
O beloved, when [the person] has been seized by death and overtaken by time.
"Having recognized one who is marked by the signs of death, one should inscribe this protection;
thus his death shall not occur—so Bhairava has declared."
O lady of excellent hips, one should write the name of whichever person is within the womb of Kapālīśa upon a birch-bark leaf with the juice of *rocanā*.
Situated in the middle of an enclosure formed by the syllable Oṃ, and sealed with the letters of the eyes,
by the application of the Vauṣaṭ-syllable, death does not occur for him.
O Goddess of the gods, one should interlace the name of the person to be accomplished with the word *śikhī*;
one should then apply the syllables of fire (the letter *ra*) both below and above the syllables of the name to be accomplished.
Indeed, a burning sensation arises for him; if one visualizes the target blazing, with the syllable *phaṭ* and others recited at the beginning and end, for seven days, [the result follows].
At that very moment, a burning sensation arises according to the word of Bhairava;
for [the mantra] restrained by Krodharāja resides within the center of the Śmaśānapaṭa.
O fair lady, one should write [the mantra] with ink from a cemetery mixed with poison and blood,
inserting the name of the person interspersed with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Through the application of the mantra "māraya" (kill), one who is endowed with a cruel nature will die within seven nights, even if he is well-protected by various safeguards.
O Great Goddess, [the mantra] is formidable, with nooses positioned above and below;
O Mistress of the Gods, it is interlaced with the name of the target and the utterances "huṃ phaṭ."
If one does not appease [the enemy] without effort, fear will arise from that enemy;
O fair-faced one, having joined the name of the person to be acted upon with the god of love (Manmatha).
Beginning with *dhruva* (om) and ending with *svāhā*, accompanied by red visualization—
O lady of excellent limbs, [the practitioner] stands here facing that direction, [addressing] such-and-such a person.
One should perform recitation and fire-offerings so that [the person] comes under the control of such-and-such;
they come under control within seven days—this is the certainty of the scripture.
At the conclusion of Meghanāda, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended,
enclosed between the letter *ya* at the beginning and end, and accompanied by the mantra ending in two *phaṭ*s.
Having placed this [image] in the abode of the pretas, one should worship Bhairava there with *akṣa* flowers, O lady of excellent hips, while standing facing that direction.
O Goddess, it swiftly expels him; there is no doubt about this.
O Mistress of the Gods, it is joined with the King of the Moon (S) at the beginning, middle, and end.

O beautiful goddess, having written the name of [the person] together with the *vaṣaṭ* syllable and the seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should place it near [the deity] and set it in the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*).
By practicing for seven nights and reciting eight hundred times at the three periods of the day,
one quickly accomplishes even that which is difficult to achieve and shall obtain abundant wealth.
O Goddess, one should utter the designation of the Piśāca, ending with the Wrathful King (Krodharāja), consisting of five limbs and endowed with a cruel nature.
One becomes insane immediately through [neglecting] the fire-oblation and the recitation;
I shall now proclaim the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], so listen with a one-pointed mind. (SvaT 9.77)
Having taken a birch bark leaf that is smooth, without holes, and free from blemishes,
one should draw upon it an eight-petalled lotus together with its pericarp.
O Goddess, O slender-waisted one, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished in the very center of its pericarp, and encircle it in the eight directions with the Svachchhanda mantra.
Having encircled it with the Praṇava, one should thus write [the mantra] upon the petals;
on the eight petals, one should also write the name of Aghora beneath each.
It should be said: "O Lord, protect me who has come to you for refuge!
First, the arrangement of the three syllables, and immediately after that, the Svachanda."
One should write the birth-name of the person to be accomplished with the syllables interspersed;
