then, one should apply the arrangement of three syllables ending with *vaṣaṭ*.
Having kneaded it with beeswax, one should cast it into the midst of milk;
supreme peace arises. Now hear another [method] from me.
O lady of excellent hips, having placed the name between *juṃ* and *saḥ*, joined with the *praṇava* at both ends, one should cast it into the three sweets.
One attains supreme peace and is no longer afflicted by death or disease;
O fair-faced one, having taken a birch-bark leaf and *rocanā* [yellow pigment], [one should proceed].
One should draw what is called the "Mātṛkā-interlaced" [diagram] with blades of dūrvā grass;
within its inner core, however, one should make it interlaced with the vowels.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, having written the name of the person to be accomplished within the womb,
one should subsequently encircle it with the *dhruva* mantra and then with the letter *va*, O beloved.
One should write the letter *sa* and the letter *kṣa* immediately thereafter;
then, O virtuous one, encircle it again with the letter *ṭha* and the seed-syllable of Māyā.
O Goddess, one should restrain with the goad the protection that destroys death—
[the protection] conjoined with Svacchandabhairava and joined at the beginning with the syllable Om.
Endowed with the Vaṣaṭ-syllable, smeared with camphor powder,
and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should cast it into the three sweets.
Supreme peace arises; there is no need for deliberation here.
Alternatively, having fashioned a pill, one should wear it on the neck or on the arm.
"Bhairava spoke thus: 'Disease shall not arise for him,' and he [taught] the three-syllable root mantra endowed with the *vaṣaṭ* class."
For one who always consumes food, water, and drink after having consecrated them with mantra, death does not occur; such is the word of Bhairava.
Now, O Great Goddess, when a practitioner has been defiled by a low-born woman,
he should employ the Aghora mantra together with the root mantra in that situation.
And having assumed for himself a form of Bhairava that is most terrible,
formidable with its fangs, and adorned with a garland of flames.
With serpents dangling and playing about him, holding a sword in his hand, most terrifying,
endowed with his former form, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
O Great Goddess, one should visualize that which has been stepped upon as being bitten;
one should contemplate the poison as being consumed by those intensely blazing flames.
O Goddess of the gods, at that very moment he becomes free from poison;
whoever performs such meditation upon the planets shall be liberated in an instant.
Moreover, O Great Goddess, when a certain person is unskilled in meditative concentration, he then renders [the poison] poisonless in an instant by means of antidotes.
Taking two young boys together with a female nāga,
one should [use] the black root of *gokarṇikā* combined with the root of the plant called *soma*.
One who eats [the poison] ground with raw cow's milk will become free from poison;
likewise, by means of the root of *gonimba*, the state of being free from poison is produced.
One should grind the root of *aśvamāra* with water;
it should be administered as a drink or as a nasal drop (*nasya*), and then one becomes free from poison.
One should grind the root of *āragvadha* with water;
when administered as a drink or as nasal drops, one then becomes free from poison.
One should employ the essence of madhuka as a nasal drop or for drinking;
thus one shall become free from poison, according to the word of Bhairava.
One should employ the root of *jambulāsika* in a drink or as a nasal drop;
O Goddess, one will then become free from poison—of this there is no doubt.
O beloved, one should prepare a fine powder of ṣaḍbindu, paṭa, and dates,
and having combined it with peacock bile, one should form it into pills.
Having encased it with the three metals, one should place it on the hand or around the neck;
poison does not affect him, even if he has been bitten by great serpents.
One who has been afflicted by poison should drink medicinal elixirs mixed with clarified butter;
for it is the certain conclusion of the scriptures that poison will not take effect upon him.
In this way, there are also other yogas fashioned by one's own will,
as well as Kālāgni, the hells, the netherworlds (pātālas), and Hāṭakeśvara.
One whose self is purified should bestow [the initiation]; they will attain success, there is no doubt in this.
For everything is set in motion by the Supreme Lord according to His own will.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Svacchanda Tantra.
The tenth chapter:
O Mahādeva, this path has been indicated, but not yet described.
Out of your grace, please explain that for the benefit of practitioners.
I shall now fully explain the path for the benefit of practitioners.
Now, below Kālāgnirudra, the cauldron (kaṭāha) is situated.
Its thickness is ten million yojanas; above it are the worlds, numbering ninety-nine crores, as well as a thousand cosmic eggs.
Seventy million, one hundred thousand, ten thousand,
as well as arbudas, vṛndas, and likewise kharvas.
"Countless lotuses," and so forth—
of these many [beings], the leader here is indeed Ananta, the Supreme Lord.
By that [pure state], the pure eggs (aṇḍas), together with the *ūhakas* and the supports of the powers (*śakti*), are purified; they are numbered at thirty-two.
Accompanied by retinues of millions upon millions, they are endowed with incomparable qualities;
they are crowded with floods of divine limbs and possess eyes made lovely by the play of their eyebrows.
Resplendent like ten thousand suns and adorned with arches and watchtowers,
there is no one there who suffers, except for the suffering born of the god of love.
There indeed the heroes sport with women in playful fashion,
dwelling in various worlds that exist in the form of wombs.
Thus have the worlds been described; all those worlds inhabited by the residents of the intermediate realms attain purification once Ananta has been purified.
Then, Kālāgni, stationed above by Śrīkaṇṭha,
carries out his office as one who follows his command.
O beloved, he remains accompanied by many tens of millions of Rudras;
now I shall fully declare the measurement established by Śiva.
O lady of excellent hips, listen to how this occurs in terms of *yojanas*:
the Great Principle (*mahat*) is perceived as ten times more gross than the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).

The "Great One" (mahat), which consists of two-fifths of the [total] and is preceded by the elements (bhūtādi), is called gross (sthūla). Furthermore, the dimension of the Great One is perceivable through mental states (bhāva) but is not visible to the eye.
That which is seen as a tenfold subtler particle than the *bhūtādi* when the sun shines through a lattice window is called an atom (*paramāṇu*).
The aggregate of eight atoms is known as a *trasareṇu*; that is called a "lotus-dust" (*padmarajas*).
Eight *trasareṇus* are prescribed as one hair-tip (*vālāgra*),
and likewise eight hair-tips are proclaimed to be one nit (*likṣā*).
They know that eight *likṣās* make one *yūkā*, and eight *yūkās* become one *yava*;
O lady of excellent hips, eight *yavas* make a joint, and that is the measure of a thumb, or a finger.
A span (vitasti) is said to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) in measure;
two spans make a cubit (hasta), which consists of twenty-four finger-breadths.
A bow-staff (*dhanurdaṇḍa*) consists of four cubits (*hasta*), as do a *nālikā* and a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
Two full thousand bows are designated as a *krośa*.
Two *krośas* make one *gavyūti*, and two *gavyūtis* make one *yojana*;
by this measurement of *yojanas*, O illustrious lady, [the world is reckoned].
O observer of excellent vows, his lion-throne is greatly radiant, two thousand units in width and one thousand units in height,
upon its great pedestals.
There dwells the Lord of Gods, Kāla, who has twelve eyes;
he is white, red, yellow, and black, four-faced, and possessed of great power.
Then Raktāṅga and Karāla, with tawny eyebrows, beards, and eyes,
have flames in their mouths, flames in their matted locks, and flames on their body hairs, blazing intensely.
The extremely intense flames of his weapons blaze within his hands;
he is radiant like a flaming mountain, resplendent with blazing tongues of fire.
The great-souled one indeed has ten arms; he carries a sword and a shield, holds arrows and a bow in his hands, and likewise bears a noose and a goad.
Holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and bearing hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
his body shines brilliantly for a million yojanas.
His world, measuring ten million yojanas, blazes intensely;
it is filled with Rudra maidens and with Rudras bearing flaming tridents.
It was surrounded by various celestial palaces blazing with light;
ten million flames issued forth from it upwards.
Above that, O Goddess, O fair-faced one, there are fifty million [yojanas];
no one dwells here, as it is enveloped in smoke and heat.
Beyond this, O lady of excellent hips, the hells are proclaimed;
fifty crores, O Goddess, have been described in their proper sequence.
O fair-faced one, I shall fully declare the principal [mantras], numbering one hundred and forty; listen as they are recounted by name.
Avīci, Raurava, and Mahāraurava;
Tāmisra and Andhatāmisra; Saṃjīvana and Sujīvana.
Padma, Mahāpadma, and likewise Kālasūtra;
Sūcīmukha, Mahākāya, Kṣuradhāra, and Asiparvata.
Asitāla, Druma, Drumamastaka,
the renowned Drumārāma, and likewise Kumbhīpāka.
Ambareṣa, Aṅgārarāśi, Tīkṣṇatuṇḍa,
as well as Vajratuṇḍa, Śakuni, Mīnodara, and Kharodara.
Sandaṃśa, Vajrakāya, and Medaka, O fair-faced one;
Uṣṭragrīva, Mahākāya, Vetāla, and Vaḍavāmukha.
Asṛkpūyahrada, Bhramara, Maṣaka,
Saṃgraha, Kapāla, and Taptakavaca.
Gajapāda, Mahāvaktra, the one called Kūrma, Nakula,
Pīḍana, Kumbhīra, Krakaca, and Śūla.
Anaṅga, Aṅgārodgāra, Pradīpta, Trimukha,
Pañcavaktra, Śatāsya, Jalauka, and Biladhūmaka.
Molten lac and pitch, terrible in form and exceedingly cruel;
the breaking of bones, putrid flesh, and indeed the impure substance of fat.
Ulūka, Paraśu, Daṇḍa, and likewise the one named Kāka;
Socchvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, and likewise Vṛkāsya.
Aśvāsya, Gopalāda, Aloka, Dahana, Śvavaktra, Davāgni, Kṣārakūpa, and likewise Tamas; SvaT_10.43.
There is Ahīnāñcaya and Taptapāṣāṇa,
as well as Virūpa, Rūpavān, Citrin, and likewise Citradhara.
The buffalo and the rākṣasa have black, tawny, and red faces;
likewise, there are the hunchback named Utaptataila, the thunderbolt, the rain, and the mallet.
Musala, Anātapa, Yamalādri,
Krimikūṭa, Bahuśākha, Śalmali, and Phaṇī.
The iron shackle, the iron rope, and the iron cage;
the piercing of the body, the serpent, the scorpion, and Time itself.
Vajrakaṇa, Kaṭāha, Paṭṭa, and Saṃkula,
as well as Ghora, Ajagara, and likewise Mahāvaitaraṇī.
Gṛdhra, Kurara, Kukkuṭa, Pramardaka,
Kardama, Durdura, Lamboṣṭha, and Vajranāsika.
Cipiṭa, Khañjarīṭa, Śavala, and Nīla;
then Kāka, Kaṅkumukha, and after that, Śivārāva.
Gajanāda, Mahānāda, and likewise Siṃhanāda;
Mahāgrāha, as well as Nakra, Mūṣika, Kīṭa, and Sāgara.
Head-downward, three-fold whirl, likewise the crushing by a wheel;
the lead-smeared, the pit of lead, the sugarcane press, and the creeper on the mountain.
Kaṭaṅkaṭa is renowned, as is Taptavāluka;
these extremely terrible hells are proclaimed to be triangular.
And for the purpose of casting down those living beings who delight in evil deeds,
as well as the deceitful sinners who perform cruel acts.
[This applies] to those of the most base and merciless castes, whose very souls delight in harming others,
who take pleasure in the wives of others, and who revile the scriptures of Śiva.
For those who steal the property of the gods, for killers of Brahmins and fathers,
for killers of cows, for the ungrateful, and for those who betray the trust of friends;
For those who seize the golden land, who have abandoned purity and right conduct,
who are devoid of compassion and courtesy, and whose minds are intent on malice and falsehood;
The hells, however, are declared to be for those who abide in the paths of unwholesome action;
for worlds devoted to virtuous action do not fall into hell.
I shall explain that in brief, according to the facts and in proper sequence:
truthfulness, patience, non-violence, purity, ritual bathing, and freedom from deceit.
He who possesses compassion and freedom from greed does not go to hell;
he is peaceful, self-controlled, joyful in soul, free from egoism, and equanimous.
Being free from malice, free from envy, and devoid of longing for the prosperity of others;
being without jealousy, without pride, devoted to Śiva, and free from fickleness.
Delight in recitation and meditation, steadfastness, the avoidance of miserliness,
vows, observances, self-study of scripture, and the state of possessing three staffs.
Faithfulness in all things, straightforwardness, modesty, self-respect,
brilliance, tranquility, contentment, and the avoidance of unpleasant speech.
Constantly acting with circumspection, the restraint of the mind and ego,
freedom from hypocrisy, freedom from deceit, absence of guile, and the nature of wisdom.
Devotion to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, seeking refuge with cows and Brahmins,
offering oblations into the fire, giving gifts, and attending upon those possessed of knowledge.
Delight in solitude, meditative absorption, contentment within oneself alone, lack of involvement in the affairs of others, and indifference toward those who are innocent; SvaT 10.66.
Freedom from anger and freedom from indolence—these qualities have been proclaimed. He who cultivates these states is fit for immortality.
Even those bonds of human nature that are proclaimed to be infinite perish for embodied beings who are righteous and devoted to the conduct of Śiva.
Therefore, having understood this, one should apply the mind to the Dharma,
so that one's consciousness becomes undeluded, free from conceptual construction, and stainless.
He goes to the supreme worlds and does not see the hells—
he whose intellect is undeluded and who is free from sin toward all beings.
He who is free from guile and possesses inner strength does not see the hells—
he by whom the sense-faculties have been conquered and whose mind remains under control.
By the victory of that [yoga], all the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, are conquered;
for one whose intellect remains steadfast whether in one's own affairs or in the affairs of others.
"This alone is true wisdom; the rest are merely readers of books"—thus has this Tantric principle been stated in brief.
There is no limit to the number of others who are not followers of the Tantras;
however, those who delight in the Śiva scriptures and are devoted to their gurus [are different].
But for those who know the supreme reality, no evil shall accrue.
Now, learn from me the principal among these hells.
The thirty-five hells are proclaimed to be of four types;
thus, in brief, they are said to number one hundred and forty.
When those thirty-five or thirty-two [deities] have been purified, those fifty million [beings] are purified by means of those purifications.
O fair-faced one, that pure [number] shall be four hundred;
indeed, by means of three purities, they become exactly thirty-two purities.
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall state the names of those three:
the well-known Avīci and the terrible Kumbhīpāka.
And Mahārauravarāja is their location; learn it from me:
they are situated respectively in the lower, middle, and upper parts.
I shall explain their pervasion to you correctly and in due order;
O Dear One, one should purify Avīci, which is situated as the eleventh among the hells.
O Goddess, by means of the self, one should purify Kumbhīpāka, the twelfth [hell], and likewise that known as Mahāraurava; of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, I shall briefly describe the thirty-five [hells]:
Avīci, Kṛmisaṃcaya, and likewise the river Vaitaraṇī.
Loha, Śalmali, and Asiparvata;
Socchvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, Pūtimāṃsa, and Parastathā.
Molten tin, the pit of alkaline brine, and likewise the smear of lac—these are included within Avīci; now hear concerning Kumbhīpāka.
The Crushing of Bones, the Sawing with a Saw, the Pit, and Kaṭaṅkaṭa; the Mixture of Fat, Iron-Mouthed, and the Copper-Smeared are thus proclaimed.
Kumbhīpāka is to be known, as well as Tīkṣṇāsi;
Tapraloha is to be known, and likewise Kṣuradhārapatha.
Aśani, Sutapta, and these twelve are proclaimed;
the eleven [others] within them are to be known as the terrible hells of Kumbhīpāka.
And after Mahāraurava, learn from me [the names of] Kālasūtra,
Mahāpadma, Kumbha, Saṃjīvana, and Ikṣuka.
The noose, the ambara-īṣaka, and likewise the iron band;
the staff-machine, the impure one, and another of terrible form.
Mahāraurava is situated above these;
[and there are] the Avīci, the Kṛmi hells, and the most dreadful Kumbhīpāka.
One should contemplate the impurities contained within the Mahāraurava hell;
furthermore, learn from me the measurement of the thirty-two hells.
The height of each is recorded as ninety-nine lakhs;
they should be known to be thirty-two in sequence, with intervals of exactly one lakh between them.
Above these, O fair-faced one,
stands the Lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas, endowed with the qualities of yogic sovereignty and power.
His city is proclaimed to be nine million [yojanas] in extent;
above that, I shall describe the netherworlds (pātālas) in brief.
Ābhāsa, Varatāla, Śarkara,
Gabhastimat, Mahātala, Sutala, and beyond that, Rasātala.
The eighth is to be known as golden, endowed with all desired objects;
from Ābhāsvara up to the golden [heaven], I shall describe the measure to you.
Each of these supreme cities has a height of nine thousand [yojanas],
and the distance between each one should be known as numbering one thousand [yojanas].
All their worlds are indeed shaped like umbrellas;
they are endowed with all objects of desire and possessed of every excellence.
With the peaks of golden ramparts crowded with parasols and banners, resounding with networks of small bells, and adorned with archways and watchtowers; SvaT_10.100.
With gateways and windows adorned with divine garments,
and filled with the sounds of singing and musical instruments such as lutes and drums.
With masses of rows of various celestial realms, resplendent with all kinds of jewels, and with palaces possessing lofty peaks and a radiance equal to moonlight; SvaT_10.102.
With excellent gardens along the streets and roads, always endowed with flowers and fruits,
sweet with the cries of cuckoos, and frequented by peacocks and bees.
[The ponds] were crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, adorned by ruddy geese,
resounded with the cries of cranes, and decorated with clusters of lotus plants.
They were adorned with ponds abounding in clear water and with oblong lakes,
and guarded by men of massive stature and great strength and prowess.
[They were] enriched with the very nature of all sovereignty, endowed with all auspicious marks,
[provided] with divine garments, excellent betel, and divine fragrant ointments.
Those practitioners who are devoted to the worship of Śiva, by his grace, [become] endowed with divine ornaments and crowns adorned with jewels.
O Great Goddess, they enter Pātāla, which is frequented by the Siddhas;
there they obtain mercury, divine elixirs, and the substances of the Siddhas.
And others, full of desire, constantly sport with hosts of divine women who possess forms at will and move with the gait of rutting elephants.
Adorned with all kinds of ornaments, highly skilled in the arts of love, dressed in divine garments, and bent by the weight of their breasts; SvaT_10.110.
With waists that were slender, with serene faces, and with long, tremulous eyes;
with hips adorned with small bells, and beautified by necklaces and armlets.
O Goddess, thus have those who dwell within the netherworlds been described to you— those whose limbs are smeared with fragrant perfumes and adorned with girdles and waist-bands.
O fair-faced one, it is said that there are three classes of asuras, nāgas, and rākṣasas, each residing individually in one of the netherworlds (pātāla).
In the seven netherworlds (pātāla), one should know there are likewise other lords of the worlds:
Bala, Atibala, Balavat, and Balavikrama.
Subala, Balabhadra, and Balādhyakṣa are proclaimed;
by these being pure, these inhabitants of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) become pure.
And that which is above is proclaimed as the golden Pātāla;
there dwells that god Hāṭaka, the Supreme Lord.
Surrounded on all sides by thousands of millions of cities,
he is attended by divine hosts of Siddhas and Udras, and encircled by sisters and mothers.
[He is endowed] with yoginīs, the daughters of yoga, and Rudras together with their daughters;
with mantras equal to perfected substances, and with wish-fulfilling gems and elixirs.
Indeed, one should cause those whose minds are absorbed in that state to enter the temple of Hāṭakeśa, which is truly enriched by perfected vidyās.
Therefore, that Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, is called Hāṭaka;
above that, however, are twenty thousand yojanas.
O fair-faced one, the earth is declared to be a skull-bowl on all sides;
therefore, the Blessed Earth is filled with various provinces.
In its center, O fair-faced one, is the great Meru made of gold;
I shall describe to you the extent of that mountain from top to bottom.
It rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high;
it is planted sixteen thousand yojanas deep below.
The width at its base is the same as that; the width at its summit is double that.
Above it is a divine assembly hall named Manovatī.
It measures fourteen thousand yojanas in extent;
it is richly adorned with all kinds of beautiful jewels and is attended by thousands of women.
Endowed with all manner of enjoyments, it belongs to the great-souled Brahmā;
it is crowded with Siddhas and Vidyādharas and surrounded by Ṛṣis.
In its northeastern quarter, the Jyotiṣka peak is remembered;
it resembles ten million suns and is served by the foremost of the Gaṇas.
Endowed with flowers of all seasons, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
crowded with thousands of women, and possessed of every sovereignty.
There dwells the Blessed One, the three-eyed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign;
for he is surrounded by the world-protectors and is the leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
One should know that to be my own portion, saluted by gods and siddhas;
it exercises its authority, impelled by the will of the Supreme.
Fourteen thousand yojanas below the assembly hall of Brahmā,
there is a circular mountain range (cakravāṭa) on all sides.
The eight heavens have been described; there the world-protectors reside. To the east of Indra is the famous city named Amarāvatī.
Likewise, Tejovatī is proclaimed as the city of Citrabhānu in the southeast;
in the south is the city named Saṃyamanī, belonging to Yamarāja.
Kṛṣṇāṅgārā is proclaimed as belonging to the Lord of the Rākṣasas in the southwest;
to the west, that of the Lord of Waters is remembered by the name Śuddhavatī.
O beloved, to the northwest is the city of Vāyu, named Gandhavahā;
and to the north is the city of Soma, named Mahodayā.
In the northeast is the city of King Īśa, named Yaśovatī;
O Goddess, hear now of the twenty-six cities to the north of these.
To the south of Amarāvatī is the city of the Apsarases called Kāmavatī;
it is golden, belonging to the hosts of Siddhas, and indeed situated to the south of that [city].
To the south of that city is another auspicious city of the Ādityas, known by the name Aṃśumatī, adorned with rubies.
The divine Kusumāvatī is renowned as the silver city of the Sādhyas;
to the west of Agni lies Revatī, the city of the Viśvedevas.
To the west of that city, O Goddess, is the divine city of Viśvakarman;
to the west of Dharmarāja, it is known as the city of Mātṛnandā.
There the Mothers play, reeling from their drinking of honey-wine;
to the west of that city of the Rudras is the golden city named Rohitā.
There, the Rudras bearing tridents are the attendants of Yama;
to the west of that [city] is to be known the city named Guṇavatī.
To the east of Nirṛti lies the city named Piṅgalā, which belongs to the eleven Rudras and is characterized by walls and gateways of vajra.
O Goddess of the gods, the Piśācas known as Svakarmasaṃjñās reside there;
near the north of the southwest quarter, the city known as Kṛṣṇāvatī is remembered.
In that very place dwell the rākṣasas known as Nistriṃśas;
and on the northern side of that is the golden city Sukhāvatī.
Mitra dwells right there, surrounded by many servants;
to the north of that as well, there is an extensive golden mountain named Gāndharvī.
There dwell Gandharvas surrounded by divine maidens;
their number is proclaimed to be ten thousand koṭis.
The Siddhasenā belongs to the Bhūtas, while that of Varuṇa is to the south;
the one named Hema belongs to the Vasus, and that of Varuṇa is also to the north.
To the north of that, O Goddess, is the city named Siddhavatī;
it is proclaimed as the city of all the Vidyādharas.
O Goddess, to the south of Vāyu, there is a city known by the name Siddhā;
there dwell the Kinnaras in cities possessing the splendor of gold and the sun.
To the east of Vāyu is the golden city of Gāndharvī, belonging to Citraratha,
the preeminent king of the Gandharvas, which resounds with the celestial music of the Gandharvas.
The Blessed Lady herself resides there, adorned with the musical notes of the scale,
clothed in the three musical modes (grāmas), and embellished by the girdle of the musical notes (jāti).
Her limbs are variegated by *mūrchanās* and *tānas*, she arises with various *tālas* and *kalās*,
she is endowed with primary and secondary characteristics, and she is veiled by the middle [channel].
There, the goddess Sarasvatī was being sung of by Gandharvas,
served by Nārada and other sages, and attended by Nāgas and Kinnaras.
To its east is Citrā, belonging to Tumburu and Nārada;
and to the west of Soma is the city of the Guhyakas, known as Pramadā.
To the east, by the very name of Soma, is the city Citravatī;
belonging to the great-souled Kubera, it is variegated and composed of all kinds of precious minerals.
Surrounded by twenty-six thousand koṭis of yakṣas, the glorious and supreme one dwells in unsurpassed enjoyments.
To its east is the city named Śubhā, made of Jāmbūnada gold;
there indeed dwell the Karma-devas, who have attained divinity through their own actions.
To the west of the king of the gods is the glorious city of Viṣṇu;
there dwells the illustrious Lord of Śrī, who resembles the flax flower.
Janārdana, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and wears yellow garments, resides there;
to the south of Īśa is the city named Padmavatī.
Of Brahmā, who is seated upon a great lotus, who wears a garland of lotuses,
whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, and who is born from a lotus.
To its south, O Goddess, is the city named Kāmasukhāvatī;
there, O Queen of the Gods, the two Aśvins as well as Dhanvantari reside.
North of Amarāvatī, there is a city renowned as Mahāmeghā;
that divine abode of the Vināyakas is established there.
Ten thousand times ten million [of them] are likewise heroic and auspicious;
they are Vināyakas, greatly radiant, with a splendor like the blazing of fire.
For the sake of slaying the Asuras, Meru was fashioned by me from my thumb;
thus, it is surrounded above and below by such excellent cities.
And those cities which are proclaimed to be all around Meru— O beloved, they are all filled with thousands of millions of cities.
Completely filled with all sovereign powers, resplendent with every kind of jewel,
they are crowded with divine women and thronged with divine men.
O Goddess, Ānanda is ever present in every city of the gods,
with celestial palaces, cities, and groves, and with the pavilions of the four gardens.
With parasols, banners, and flags; crowded with elephants and horses;
with sounds of joy from duels; and with the blasts of conchs and kāhala trumpets.
O Goddess, the temple of the gods is always filled with songs and dances for those men in the meritorious land of Bhārata who are devoted to sacrificial rites and works of public utility.
Those men who worship Tryambaka even once go to Mount Meru;
well-sprinkled by the waters of the Gaṅgā, they sport there as the best of gods.
O best of gods, please graciously explain in brief how she arose from the Gaṅgā and is honored by the Suras and Siddhas.
O lady of excellent vows, I shall also tell you of the origin of the Gaṅgā;
for in ancient times, that great goddess was my wife, the mother of the world.
O Mother of the World, formerly my eyes were covered by your fingernails with your own tears, and then you opened them once again.
O beloved, as water flowed from the mouths of the leaders of the attendants through your fingers,
the Gaṅgā issued forth in ten streams upon my skull-enclosure.
Seven indeed are established there: one is situated in Viṣṇupura, the second is above the world of Brahmā, and the third goes to Satyaloka.
And she indeed remained once more in heaven within the lunar orb;
then, having emerged from the moon, she established herself in the city of Kāśī.
Then, O Goddess, being praised by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others,
I [sent] the highly meritorious river Gaṅgā out of a desire for the welfare of mortals.
"O Mahādeva, having brought her down, release her into the world of mortals.
Then, O Sovereign of the Gods, that Aparājitā was addressed by me.
"For the sake of the welfare of the worlds, come, O beautiful goddess!
Having arrived, you shall go again to the summit of Meru upon my head."
Emerging from that, O Queen of the Gods, she flows toward the ocean in four directions:
in the east she is designated as the Sītā, and in the south as the Suvahā.
Sunandā is in the western quarter, and likewise Bhadrasomā is in the north;
O Great Goddess, Mandara is known as Gandhamādana.
Vipula, Supārśva, and the others from the east to the end of the north are declared to be the supporting pillars (viṣkambhas);
now learn from me their respective colors as well.
White, yellow like turmeric, blue, and with the luster of pomegranate juice—
near the eastern Viṣkambha is the forest named Citraratha.
There is a pond named Aruṇodaka, adorned with lotuses,
and near Gandhamādana is the great forest called Nandana.
In its center is the Mānasa lake, covered with lotuses;
near Vipula, however, is the great Vaibhrāja forest.
In its center is a pond of pure water called Sitoda,
and near its own flank is a forest named Pitṛvana.
Within that [city], however, is the great and beautiful Bhadra lake;
listen as I describe its four wish-fulfilling trees.
Then, on Mount Mandara, there is a Kadamba tree situated at its summit,
extending for a thousand yojanas and rising five hundred yojanas with its branches.
It shines, beautifully in full bloom, with flowers the size of jars;
on the summit of Gandhamādana, the Jambū tree is said to be of that same size.
The juice arising from the mass of its fruits should be known as being like nectar;
by that, O beloved, the river Jambū was produced, flowing with great force.
Having circumambulated Meru, he enters his own Jambū tree at its root;
from contact with that [tree], gold arises which serves as an ornament for the gods.
Therefore, it is known in the world as Jāmbūnada, the supreme ornament;
there, the trees, creepers, shrubs, birds, beasts of prey, and so forth [are all golden].
All those who dwell there are made of Jāmbūnada gold, as are the others;
likewise, even in that vast region, there is a tree known as Ketumāla, which is an Aśvattha.
After Indra had conquered the asuras, he suspended a garland of jewels there;
therefore, that land is known as Ketumāla, frequented by the siddhas.
Nyagrodha is proclaimed to be equal to Supārśva;
Meru, endowed with manifold qualities, is thus briefly described.
O beloved, I shall describe in brief the regions situated at its sides:
from the center of Meru, there are fifty thousand [yojanas] in each of the four directions in brief.
Jambudvīpa, extending all around to the edge of the salt ocean,
is indeed divided into nine regions separated by mountains.
And in the southern direction, three mountain ranges are to be known;
those three are Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat.
And further to the north are Meru, Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān;
these six mountains indeed extend from east to west.
Nīla and Niṣadha are proclaimed to measure one hundred thousand [yojanas],
while Śveta and Hemakūṭa are recorded as ninety thousand.
Himavat and Śṛṅgavat, extending for eighty thousand [yojanas],
reach as far as the salt ocean and are two thousand [yojanas] in width.
Himavat, joined with Kailāsa, as well as Triśṛṅga together with Jārudhi,
and the white Śṛṅgavān, resembling the moon, shine forth brilliantly.
Niṣadha is blue, composed of sapphire; Hemakūṭa has the luster of rubies;
and Himavat is golden, with the appearance of snow.
To the east of Meru, O Goddess of the Suras, the mountain Mālyavat shines forth for thirty-four thousand yojanas.
Extending from south to north, its width shines at one thousand [yojanas];
likewise, on the western side, there is Gandhamādana, equal to that.
Nīla, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana are each forty thousand yojanas in height.
In the four directions from Meru, there are two boundary mountains each;
Jaṭhara and Hemakūṭa are situated in the eastern part.
Kailāsa and Himavat are situated on the southern side,
while Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are the two mountains on the western side.
Jārudhi and Śṛṅgavān are situated to the north;
all around Meru lies the delightful region known as Ilāvṛta.
Below the Cakravāḍa mountain range, extending nine thousand yojanas in width,
it is square on all four sides throughout its entirety.
There, neither the heat of the sun nor the rays of the moon prevail,
for the world is illuminated by the radiance of Meru.
The people there possess the luster of fresh lotus petals and are exceedingly delicate;
subsisting on the juice of jambu fruits, they are entirely free from old age and death.
Their lifespan is proclaimed to be thirteen thousand years;
they consist of gods, gandharvas, siddhas, rishis, and vināyakas.
And this Ilāvṛta is surrounded by innumerable hosts such as the Gaṇas, Mothers, Sisters, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and others.
To the east of the ocean and south of Gandhamādana lies the region known as Ketumāla, which possesses the highest of all qualities.
The people there are exceedingly beautiful, dark as the petals of a blue lotus;
having drunk the juice of the jackfruit tree, they live for ten thousand years.
Jayanta, Vardhamāna, Aśoka, Hariparvata,
Viśāla, Kambala, and Kṛṣṇa— these are the seven principal mountain ranges there.
To the east of Mālyavat and to the west of the ocean lies the region known as Bhadrāśva; there, too, the lifespan is ten thousand years.
The people there resemble the moon and subsist on the fruit of the black mango;
they are the Kaurañjas, the Śvetaparṇas, the Nīlas, and likewise the Mālāgrakas.
And Padma is likewise declared; there are five such mountain ranges of the [five] families, which are recorded as being thirty-two thousand [yojanas] in extent from east to west.
Thirty-four thousand [yojanas] extend from south to north;
these two regions are known as the abodes of the inhabitants of Kuru-varṣa.
Those worlds are called the Kurus; there the inhabitants eat the fruits of the Kuru trees.
They live for thirteen thousand years, remaining in perpetual youth.
Men and women, resembling the *śyāmā* flower, glossy and handsome, give birth in pairs, free from the fear of separation.
The ground consists entirely of jewels and is strewn with Himalayan sand;
it is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas in length and shaped like a bow.
There, the two mountain ranges of the family are Sūryakānta and Indukānta;
and right there is the wish-fulfilling tree named Kuru, radiant with flowers.
That most beautiful region should be known by its name as Kuruvarṣa;
and having entered the salt ocean in the northern direction of that [region], one finds it.
The Moon Island (Candradvīpa) is proclaimed to be five thousand yojanas in extent;
likewise, having entered the salt ocean in the northwestern direction.
O fair-faced one, it is exactly four thousand yojanas;
the auspicious island is proclaimed to be ten thousand yojanas.
It should be known as having an auspicious form, bestowing the fruits of all desires;
there, people live for ten thousand years, consuming divine nectar and fruits.
In the region called Candra, too, there is a lifespan of ten thousand years; those who subsist on fruits live there.
Between Śveta and Śṛṅgavān, it should be known that there is a golden land.
Having consumed the fruit of the *lakuca*, people there, resembling the moon,
live for thirteen and a half thousand years by that measure.
To the north of Nīla and likewise to the south of Śveta is the region named Ramyaka, where the inhabitants subsist on the fruit of the banyan tree.
Dark-complexioned like the petals of a blue lotus and free from old age and disease,
their lifespan is proclaimed to be twelve thousand years.
The region Ramyaka, nine thousand yojanas in extent, and Hiraṇmaya are situated to the north of Hemakūṭa and to the south of Niṣadha.
Harivarṣa is thus described; the beings there have the luster of silver, live for exactly twelve thousand years, and subsist on sugarcane juice.
And that [region] is exceedingly beautiful, extending nine thousand [yojanas],
situated to the south of Hemakūṭa and to the north of Himavat.
The region named Kimpuruṣa is there;
its people have the luster of gold, and subsisting on the fruit of the Plakṣa tree, they live for nine thousand years.
Its width there is proclaimed to be exactly nine thousand [yojanas],
situated to the south of the lord of the Himalayas and to the north of the salt ocean.
The region known as Bhārata is small there, and its happiness is said to be meager;
the people are terrified by the fear of disease, suffering, and lacking in prosperity.
Some are handsome and others are ugly; some are fortunate and others are unfortunate;
some possess enjoyments while others have meager enjoyments, and likewise others are utterly miserable.
Fair-complexioned, dark, as well as black, tawny, and white-brown—
according to the distinctions of color and caste, and in accordance with their various respective duties.
In the land called Bhārata, the four castes and even those born of the lowest orders are produced;
there are also islands and other sub-continents endowed with their own respective local languages.
The wise and likewise the foolish, those skilled in arts and sciences, as well as yogins and men of knowledge, the most virtuous and others who are sinful— [all these are equal].
O beloved, some are born as beggars while others are born as givers; many men are constantly born as servants and slaves.
However, one quality remains there: the acquisition of auspicious and inauspicious fruits.
Even when [the other qualities] have perished, a certain state consisting of the three ages (yugas) still exists.
O fair-faced one, it should be known that the land called Bhārata possesses four ages;
whatever action is performed there, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [bears fruit accordingly].
By that [power], O fair-faced one, the worlds from Śiva down to Avīci abide;
likewise Mahākāla, Ekāmra, and so forth.
Ten million sacred fords (tīrtha) are said to yield the arising of great merit,
as do five hundred rivers there, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
Understand that it is nine thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a bow;
O beloved, nine divisions are recorded there, separated by oceans.
For each individual continent, a thousand [yojanas] are proclaimed;
it should be understood that five hundred are land and likewise five hundred are water.
They are not to be approached by one another; hear their names from me:
Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimat.
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Vāruṇa,
as well as the island known as Kumārikā, are proclaimed as the ninth.
Starting from Bindusaras, the region called Kumārī is proclaimed to extend for a thousand yojanas, containing various castes and stages of life.
O fair-complexioned one, O beloved, those qualities previously mentioned that exist in the world of Bhārata reside right there in the world known as Kumārī.
In that very place, seven beautiful mountain ranges are to be known:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śaktimān, and Ṛkṣaparvata.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these are the Kulaparvatas that shine forth;
O beloved, there are six secondary islands situated in the midst of the southern ocean.
Aṅgadvīpa, the one called Yava, Malaya, the one named Śaṅkha,
Kumuda, and Varāha— thus they are proclaimed.
It is said that on the island of Malaya there is a mountain named Malaya;
at its foot is indeed Trikūṭa, and Laṅkā is situated upon it.
It is made of gold, brilliant, adorned with four gardens,
constructed with variegated walls, and embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
There, Rākṣasas of infinite wealth and great strength and prowess take their pleasure with celestial maidens, being devoted to those young women.
There, on Mount Malaya, the best of mountains, is the Agastya-peak;
there is the most meritorious hermitage of Agastya, radiant as crystal.
There, beings who are otherwise mutually antagonistic play together without fear;
no pestilence arises there, nor does untimely death occur.
There is no old age, nor sorrow, nor fear of calamities anywhere;
no one speaks untruth, and there is neither passion nor hatred anywhere.
By the power of Agastya, ignorance has been cast far away;
there indeed dwell heroic sages who have established their ascetic toil in the yoga of knowledge.
O Great Goddess, those devoted to recitation, study, fire-offerings, worship, and praise are constantly intent upon the propitiation of Tryambaka, the Great God.
Accompanied by Agastya, all those who proclaim liberation and worldly prosperity remain there with purified souls, capable of both inflicting curses and bestowing grace.
Jambudvīpa extends for one hundred thousand yojanas all around;
outside of it lies the salt-water ocean, extending for one hundred thousand yojanas.
It stands threefold in circumference, indeed in the shape of a circle;
there the mountains have entered, terrified by the fear of Vṛtra’s enemy.
I shall describe those twelve of great heroism in brief:
Vṛṣabha, Dundubhi, and Dhūmra entered from the eastern side.
Candra, Kaṅka, and Droṇa entered through the north;
then Aśoka, Varāha, and Nandana as the third.
Other mountains there have entered the salt ocean:
Cakra, the one named Maināka, and the third, Balāhaka.
O lady of excellent hips, the mountains have entered from the south;
between Cakra and Maināka stands the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha).
Jambūdvīpa has been fully described; now its origin is being told:
there was a Manu named Svāyambhuva, and his son was Priyavrata.
Then ten sons were born to him, preeminent in heroism and strength:
Agnīdhra, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vapu.
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, Satra,
Medhā, Satra, and Agnibāhu— these are the three who have gone forth as renunciants.
Those remaining in the seven islands who were consecrated as mighty ones,
as well as the Agnīdhras in Jambudvīpa— these are remembered as his nine sons.
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Hari, Ilāvṛta,
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Ramyaka, and Hiraṇmaya.
The ninth is named Kuru; these are remembered as the lords of the nine regions.
Born indeed from Agnīdhra, they were heroes of exceeding strength and prowess.
O Pārvatī, the nine regions here are marked with their names;
the son of Nābhi was the highly heroic Vṛṣabha, who was devoted to dharma.
His son was the powerful Bharata;
it is after his very name that this most excellent region is to be known as Bhārata-varṣa.
Furthermore, O beloved, eight sons and another daughter were born to him;
here in Bhārata, within these eight continents, eight sons were established.
The ninth is called Kumārī; these islands were proclaimed by Bharata after the names of those [daughters] whom he bestowed upon Kumārī.
Jambudvīpa, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali,
Gomeda, and Puṣkara— these are the seven continents, O Pārvatī.
Now, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe the oceans to you:
the salt ocean, the milk ocean, the curd ocean, the ghee ocean, and likewise the sugarcane juice ocean.
The seven oceans are proclaimed as Madyoda, Svādūda, and the rest;
Jambudvīpa is recorded as being one hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
It should be known as circular; outside, it is equal to that salt-water ocean. Thus, by doubling in size in this manner, the oceans are situated surrounding the continents.
And Agnīdhra is proclaimed in Jambudvīpa, O fair-faced one;
Medhātithi by name is in Śāka, and Vapuṣmān in the land known as Kuśa.
Then Jyotiṣmān is remembered as the king on Krauñca, Dyutimān on Śālmalī;
Havya is the name on Gomeda, and likewise Savana on Puṣkara.
The time for those dwelling in Śāka and Gomedha is equal to the Tretā Yuga;
likewise, the conduct of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) of the inhabitants there should be understood in that same way.
Medhātithi had seven sons who were consecrated as rulers in Śākadvīpa:
Śānta, Abhaya, Aśiśira, Sukhada, Nandaka, and Śiva.
Kṣemaka and Dhruva—these are the seven regions known by their names; now learn from me concerning the mountains as well.
Gomeda, Candrasaṃjña, Nārada, Dundubhi,
Somaka, Ṛṣabha, and Vaibhrāja are the mountain ranges of the family.
Sukṛtā, Anasūyā, and Sumukhī as the third;
Vipāśā, Tridivā, Kumbhī, and likewise Amṛtanālikā.
These very great rivers, having issued forth from these mountains,
have emerged starting from the east and entered the Ocean of Milk.
But those people in Śākadvīpa subsist on milk and eat fruits;
they are all like moonstones, handsome, and pleasing to behold.
Endowed with all sovereign powers, they sport with celestial women;
formerly, seven sons were established by Vapuṣmat in Kuśa.
Śvetalohitajīmūta, Harita, Vaidyuta,
Mānasa, and Suvrata are marked by the very names of the rain-clouds [of their respective regions].
Kumuda, Auvada, Vārāha, Droṇa, Kaṅkata,
Mahiṣa, and Kusuma— these are the seven Sīmanta mountains.
Śvetatoyā, Kṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, Locanī,
Vīvṛtā, and Vivṛndā— these seven are indeed the best of rivers.
Those rivers of purifying waters entered the curdled milk;
meanwhile, the people there lived happily, consuming curds and fruits that tasted like nectar.
All of them, devoted to divine enjoyments, sport together with their wives;
these seven sons of Jyotiṣmān were established in Krauñcadvīpa.
Udbhijja is proclaimed, as well as Veṇu, Maṇḍala,
Rathakāra, Lavaṇa, Dhṛtimat, and Suprabhākara.
And Kapila—these are the kings, marked by the names of the [rain] seasons:
Vaidruma, Hemanābha, Dyutimān, and Puṣpadantaka.
Kuśala and Harimarda—these seven are the Kulaparvatas (principal mountain ranges).
[The rivers are] Mahī, Dhātā, Śivā, Apāpā, Pavitrā, and Saṃtatadyuti.
And Dambhā—these seven rivers are thus enumerated; O beloved, all these sin-removing streams flow into the Ghṛtoda ocean.
All the people dwelling there are handsome and preeminent in splendor;
subsisting on food consisting of ghee and ambrosial fruits, they are well-satisfied yet tormented by passion.
Accompanied by women with eyes as long as lotus petals, they sport;
these seven radiant sons were consecrated on the Śālmala continent.
Manonuga, Uṣṇa, Pāvana, Andhakāraka,
the sage named Dundubhi, and Kuśala— these are remembered as such.
The names of those seven [mountains] are indeed, in order, the seven:
Krauñca, Vāmana, Andhakāra, and Divākṛti.
Dvibindu, Puṇḍarīka, Dundubhi, and the Kulādris;
Pauṇḍarīkā, Kauśikī, Gaurī, Siddhā, and Kumudvatī.
Sandhyā and Rātrī are renowned; these rivers, which emerge from the mountains, have been described in brief as flowing toward the Ikṣurasārṇava ocean.
The people dwelling there who drink the juice of sugarcane possess divine splendor; they are peaceful, handsome, and speak kindly.
Havyarāja consecrated his seven sons in Gomoda— a place crowded with various women and the source of all sensual pleasures.
Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Marīcaka,
Kumuda, Unnata, and Mahābhadra are thus remembered.
The regions are marked by their names according to their own measurements:
Udaya, Kesara, Jaṭhara, and then Surāvata.
Śyāma, Ambikeya, and Meru—these are the mountains that mark the boundaries;
likewise Gabhastī, Sukumārī, Kumārī, and Nālinī.
The Veṇukā, the Ikṣu, and the excellent river Dhenukā—
these holy rivers, carrying auspicious waters, flow with the juice of wine.
O fair-faced one, the inhabitants of that world eat fruits as sweet as nectar and drink the nectar of wine.
They shall have all their desires fulfilled, be handsome, and free from disease;
they shall be accompanied by various groups of young women who are proud of their beauty and youth.
O beloved, they constantly enjoy themselves, languid with passion and intoxicated by drink;
therefore, in that place called Puṣkara, Savana is the leader.
Two sons of his, renowned by that name, were established upon the mountain called Puṣkara;
it is circular in shape and known as Mānasottara.
O lady of excellent hips, its height is fifty yojanas and its width twenty-five; it is endowed with all kinds of jewels.
In the center of Dhātakī is King Mahāvīta, and outside is King Nṛpa;
they are free from envy, the thirst of passion, and calamities.
All those people there will be happy during that two-year period;
however, O fair-faced one, it should be understood that the mental [mandala] is wheel-shaped.
I shall now describe to you the cities of the four world-protectors located there:
the city of Hara is called Ekasārā, and the southern city is Saṃyaminī.
Sukhāhvā and Vāruṇī are the two [oceans] of Soma;
the ocean of sweet water (svādūda), multiplied by Puṣkaradvīpa, is situated at the end.
Furthermore, there are two hundred million, five hundred and three thousand, and fifty yojanas.
O fair-faced one, the measurement from Mount Meru up to the Sweet-water Ocean is thus proclaimed;
beyond that, O lovely-faced one, is the golden ground extending for ten koṭis.
Beyond this is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand yojanas in extent, circular in shape like a bracelet, existing for the sake of the gods' recreation.
O fair-faced one, it is proclaimed to be one hundred thousand yojanas in height,
endowed with all kinds of jewels, and golden in color.
O beautiful goddess, the sun shines within that [mandala] and not outside;
the world-protectors and the Rudras of unfailing power reside there.
Viruja, Vasudhāmā, Śaṅkhapāt, Kardama,
Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and Bhājana.
In the bright abode of the Siddhas and immortals, made of Jāmbūnada gold,
[the sequence proceeds] starting from the east, gradually as far as the domain of Īśāna.
The world-protectors indeed stand there protecting these subjects;
in its center, O lady of excellent hips, are the fourteen wombs.
Stained by their own karma, beings act in various forms;
above Lokāloka, however, is the southern course of the sun.
Likewise, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is proclaimed there as being to the north;
it is midnight in Amarāvatī and sunset in the city of Yama.
It is recorded that at midday it is in Vāruṇī, and at sunrise it is in Saumya;
and at the very moment its rising is seen in Amarāvatī.
Then the sun sets in the western quarter; such is the course and return of the sun. Its northern path is the *suvīthī*, and its southern path is the *ajavīthī*.
Indeed, this path of the ancestors and the gods has been described by me to you;
outside of it lies a terrible darkness, difficult to behold and devoid of living beings.
Thirty-five crores, nineteen lakhs,
and forty thousand yojanas are recorded, O fair-faced one.
The Garbhoda ocean is known to be equal in measure to the seven oceans;
it is joined with the shell of Brahmā’s egg at the center of Meru.
Fifty crores are to be known in each of the ten directions;
thus, this great earthly realm is to be understood as consisting of one hundred crores.
Henceforth, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall declare the measurement;
or rather, O Great Goddess, [I shall do so] everywhere according to the sequence.
Now, regarding the purificatory rites at the time of initiation, learn from me their sequence:
one should cause the Power (śakti), the Principle (tattva), the World-sphere (bhuvana), and the Womb (yoni) to enter [the disciple].
Having performed the ritual offering of incense for them in due order,
one should likewise [offer it] to Ananta, Kālāgni, and the hells in their proper sequence.
Then one should purify the netherworlds (pātāla) in successive order from below upwards;
thereafter, O fair-faced one, one should perform the service (upasthāna) for the Bhuvarloka.
Then, having worshipped the goddess Vāgīśvarī with flowers and other offerings,
one should sprinkle the bound soul (paśu), strike it, and separate it [from its bonds].
Cutting, as well as attracting, seizing, and then uniting; likewise, the empowerment for conceiving a fetus and for giving birth.
Yoga, enjoyment, and dissolution, as well as the purification of the womb—
these fourteen I shall explain in brief and in their proper sequence.
They know the Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājāpatya, and Brāhma as the eighth.
By means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), animals, birds, wild beasts, and likewise other reptiles are to be purified in the path of Śiva (śivādhvan).
The fifth is the stationary [realm], and the sixth is that born from the human womb;
together with those belonging to the divine womb, this is declared to be the mandala of saṃsāra.
One should purify the fourteenfold [world] within the earthly realm (bhūrloka);
for it is here, within the sphere of the earth and the other levels beginning with Māyā, that the Self transmigrates.
Therefore, it is called *saṃsāra* (wandering), because one wanders here and there;
and situated in the midst of the path, one experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion.
Joined with the three bonds and presided over by the power of Vāmā,
[the soul] proceeds on the path of emanation and reabsorption through the instrumental cause that is Īśvara.
Again and again, in the midst of the path, he is joined with the auspicious and the inauspicious;
those snares within the path, moreover, should be known to be infinite millions in number.
As long as one remains in the state of non-reliance through the distinction between the primary and secondary qualities,
from that very point one should understand that the path is the cause of bondage.
That which is called the fourteen-fold circle of transmigration has indeed infinite divisions, which are distinguished according to the variety of karma.
For in the two Karmavallis, there are infinite factors such as karma, the Lord (Īśa), and so forth;
indeed, the self is bound by the self, and the self must liberate itself by the self.
Just as a silkworm, like an insect, firmly encloses itself within its cocoon, so that it is no longer able to free itself from it; so too is this [the case for the mind].
Likewise, all transmigrating beings are bound by their own fetters;
like animals caught in snares, they are not capable of liberating themselves.
As long as Śiva does not perceive his own self by himself,
[beings] are liberated from the bondage of fetters through the descent of Śiva’s power.
Otherwise, they do not know at all their own nature, which is utterly stainless,
innate, pure, incomparable, and free from affliction.
Deluded by the delusion of impurity and bound by the various forms of karma and so forth,
they remain hidden therein, just as fire exists within wood.
Just as fire, once clearly extracted by means of the churning stick, perceives its own nature as radiant and perfectly stainless; so too [does the practitioner perceive the Self].
For other beings as well whose eyes are overwhelmed by darkness,
he illuminates objects by destroying the gloom with his rays.
In that same way, O Goddess, the Self perceives its own beginningless nature through the power of the churner; it is not otherwise under any circumstances.
O Goddess of the gods, Manthaka here is indeed Sadāśiva himself;
having assumed the body of the Ācārya, he is ever established in bestowing grace.
The mantras should be known as being like the friction-sticks for churning, and the path here is like the fire-drill wood;
Vāgīśī, residing in the womb, should be known as the smoke, like impurities and the like.
The Self is indeed to be known as fire, while the supreme Śiva is its awakener;
just as fire, once awakened, becomes utterly stainless and intensely radiant.
Just as a piece of wood does not enter [the fire] again once it has been extracted from the path, so too the Self,
freed from impurity, karma, kalās, and the rest, is devoid of exhaustion.
Even while remaining there, one would not be bound, because one is exceedingly pure,
just as copper is freed from its blackness through the union of mercury and fire.
But when separated by those who know reality, gold attains its true nature and never again becomes copper; likewise, the Self never [returns to its former state].
The power of the mantra, which consists of aesthetic flavor, should be understood as action, like fire;
and he who knows that should be known as Śiva, whose body is the form of the teacher.
The Self, O Dear One, should be known as being like gold, while impurity should be known as the dross;
thus, through the application of mantra, substance, and ritual action, [the Self is purified] upon the support of fire.
Indeed, when the self has been purified by a Guru who is learned in the Tantras, it no longer undergoes impurity;
it attains the stainless state of Śiva.
Having understood this, O lady of excellent limbs, the initiation should be performed as it was in the past;
one should purify the primary bonds which were previously described by me.
But those bonds which have become subordinate qualities are also purified by virtue of that;
and indeed, that which was previously described by me as being of fourteen kinds [is likewise purified].
O Goddess, that maṇḍala of saṃsāra must be purified upon the surface of the earth;
I shall explain all of that in due order, as it is to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva.
One should primarily purify everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
likewise, the worlds of Brahmā, Prajāpati, Soma, and Indra.
Furthermore, the Gāndharva, the Yākṣa, and likewise the Rākṣasa,
the Paiśāca, the Sthāvara, and the Mānuṣa should be purified in their respective order.
Among stationary beings, the saptacchada tree; likewise, among serpents, Vāsuki;
among birds, Garuḍa; and among wild animals, the lion.
One should purify cattle by means of their cow-origination, and one should purify human beings;
one should likewise purify those born of the lowest castes, Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Brāhmaṇas.
O Goddess, one should purify the offices [of initiation] by means of the five Brahmans through the application of ten oblations, from the lowest castes up to the Brahmins.
A Brahmin has forty-eight entitlements: the conception rite, the rite for a male child, the parting of the hair, and the birth ceremony; SvaT 10.386.
Naming, the rite of departure [from the womb], the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony—
O lady of excellent hips, these eight are declared to be purified by this very [rite].
O Goddess, when these have been withdrawn, he is then born as a twice-born;
this is proclaimed as the ninth bond of the vow, and it is designated as the "limb."
I shall explain the constituent parts in their proper order:
the girdle, the tooth-stick, the deerskin, and likewise the *tryāyuṣa* [three-fold longevity].
O fair-faced one, they know that the twilight rites, the worship of fire, and alms-gathering are indeed the seventh;
and these are seen as the restrainers at the time of initiation.
They know Bhauteśa, Pāśupatya, Gāṇa, Gāṇeśvara,
Unmattaka, Asidhāra, and Ghṛteśa as the seventh.
These seven vows of the celibate students (brahmacārin) have been observed;
they are to be understood as the vows of conduct, proclaimed as being constituent parts [of the practice].
Indeed, together with these, there is one ninth [rite], the binding of the vow;
it is taught that this sevenfold set of vows is actually contained within it.
O fair-faced one, these fourteen vows are to be offered in this manner;
the four Vedic vows are likewise to be offered, without a doubt.
The four Lords of Vows (Vrateśvaras)— namely Aiṣṭika, Pārvika, Bhautika, and Saumika— are the regulators of the religious student (brahmacārin).
One should know that the thirteenth [initiation] is the vessel for the Vedas;
from that, O beloved, follows the gift of a cow, which is the fourteenth.
Having bathed, one who has attained knowledge should marry a maiden;
having fashioned a wife out of darbha grass, he should perform sacrifices together with her.
That which is to be known is the fifteenth; thereafter, the sacrificial fires follow in sequence.
They call these the occasional (naimittika) portions, which I shall explain in due order.
The Aṣṭakās, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrāyaṇī,
as well as the Caitrī and the Āśvayujī— these are the seven cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas) in their respective order.
Together with these, one should understand them by the enumeration of twenty-two:
the Āgneya, the Agnihotra, and after that, the Darśa.
The full moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī) is likewise to be known, as well as the four-monthly sacrifice (cāturmāsya);
the animal sacrifice (paśubandha) is specified, and after that, the sautrāmaṇi.
O beloved, these seven are declared to be the Havis-sacrifices that purify;
together with these, one should understand the twenty-nine sacraments.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśika,
the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma as the seventh.
The Soma-sacrifices are declared to be thirty-six in number:
Hiraṇyapāda is the first, and likewise Guhyahiraṇyadhṛt.
Hiraṇyameḍhra, Hiraṇyanābhi, and Hiraṇyagarbha;
likewise Hiraṇyaśrotra, Hiraṇyatvak, and Hiraṇyākṣa.
The ten sacrifices are proclaimed as having golden tongues and horns;
here, each one indeed produces clarified butter by the hundreds.
All these thirty-seven [offenses] are purified by a thousand [recitations];
thereafter, one should perform the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) in due order.
When all these have been performed, one then becomes a householder;
thereafter, by performing that thirty-eighth [stage], one becomes a forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Then, having undertaken the life of a wandering mendicant and performed the funeral rites, one thus attains the state of a Brahmin.
Therefore, I shall now briefly describe the eight qualities of the self.
Compassion toward all beings, patience, freedom from envy,
purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness— these are even beyond this.
Freedom from miserliness and freedom from longing—these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self;
and in brief, there are forty-eight formative factors (saṃskāras).
When these have been purified, O observer of excellent vows, even those who are innumerable become pure;
therefore, having indeed performed the final oblation (anteṣṭi), one should bestow qualities upon the disciple.
Having offered five oblations for each of the five [deities] with the Brahma-mantras in due order,
one should then direct the winds upward with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
By the word "upward" (ūrdhva), that karma which is proclaimed to be impure is designated;
one should apply the fetter to that [karma] and not to anything else.
Therefore, one should not perform the extraction, nor should one lead [the disciple] anywhere;
rather, one should apply the ritual action there according to the prescribed sequence.
Then, for the sake of one's own enjoyment, the powers beginning with *aṇimā* should be attained by the Brahmās in due order through the application of five oblations.
By the word "upward" (ūrdhva), that which is based upon the Bhūrloka is to be understood;
for one who is engaged in that [practice], the rite must be performed there, and never in any other place.
As long as karma has not been exhausted, how can there be liberation?
Therefore, by the term "yoga," one means the single-minded contemplation of each respective karma.
O Great Goddess, [the rite] is averted; thereafter, one should offer the expiatory oblations with Śiva through eight hundred offerings, and then [offer for] the lords of the worlds.

Having purified the inhabitants within the worlds and the worlds themselves in their proper sequence by means of the fire-oblation (homa) alone, one should likewise perform the disjunction and the severance.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and the *samuddhāra*, as well as the *tatsthatva* in due order,
one should offer the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the causes of deficiency or excess.
In this very sequence, one should purify everything up to the abode (dhāman).
Bhūrloka has thus been fully described; now learn from me about Bhuvarloka.
From the surface of the earth up to the sun, the measurement is one hundred thousand [yojanas];
in the middle, there are ten wind-paths, numbering ten thousand each.
In the first wind-path, I shall describe the clouds as they are situated:
fifty yojanas above [the earth] is the wind named Ṛtarddhi.
He who increases the nourishment of the plants as well as their strength, and who,
being imperishable, causes the entire earth to flourish and brings it to fullness.
By day he is indeed the Haṃsa, the wind that brings happiness to human beings;
because he supports the vultures (gṛdhra), he is known as Gṛdhradhara.
The wind named Prācetasa is produced by the Pracetasas;
it indeed destroys the trees and sometimes sets them all in motion.
The fire named Prācetasa stands together with that very [wind];
when it burns houses, it is designated as such.
Happy he dwells in the ocean; he is not satiated by water-food.
Beyond a hundred yojanas, he is called Senānī Vāyu.
And while this wind blows, silent clouds accompanied by lightning dwell there;
remaining at a distance of only one *krośa* from the earth, they discharge their waters.
Beyond a hundred yojanas, the clouds known as *sattvavāha* are said to exist;
they rain down fish, frogs, and tortoises during these foul days.
Beyond a hundred yojanas, a mass of wind is proclaimed;
in that [region], disease-inflicting clouds rain down poisonous water.
From that, the afflictions that act as Māras arise for all embodied beings;
above that, however, stands the unfailing wind-god Devīya.
There, those clouds of Mārakās are firmly established in the Amogha [wind];
indeed, the wind named Vajrāṅga is situated fifty yojanas away.
In that [region] are clouds named Tūpala, which rain down tūpala stones;
at exactly that many yojanas from there is the Vaidyuta wind.
And the clouds of lightning dwell in that Vaidyuta region;
there, due to the agitation of the wind, that great thunderbolt is produced within them.
Fifty yojanas above that, the mountain Raivata is said to be located;
there, the wind named Puṣṭivaha rains down nourishment for embodied beings.
In the Saṃvarta [kalpa], there are clouds that bring disease; raining down the waters of disease, those clouds indeed remain for fifty yojanas over that region.
The wind named Viṣāvarta is situated fifty [yojanas] above;
in it are established the clouds named Krodhodaka.
They will be full of anger and passion, as well as full of strife;
they will bring about the destruction of kings and likewise the ruin of their subjects.
And when those clouds rain there, they produce rain;
[the clouds] are Aghoṣya, Megha, Vajrāṅga, Vaidyuta, and likewise Raivata.
Saṃvarta and Viṣāvarta are winds of terrible velocity;
indeed, the divine Piśācas born from the body of Skanda dwell below.
It is recorded that there are thirty thousand koṭis of Skanda’s followers;
they indeed worship the son of Hara with divine flowers.
The thirty thousand koṭis of formidable Vināyakas, born from Mahādeva, are established in that wind.
Those of cruel deeds who steal the earned merit of men who have not disciplined themselves— like elephants [stealing] from the wind, even though it possesses a vajra-like body.
Resembling crushed collyrium, they are terrible and renowned as the Tāpanas;
they are the lowest among the Vidyādharas, moving through the mind and the wind.
Those who have accomplished vidyās, human beings, and vetālas and the like from the cremation ground,
having attained siddhi, are established in this wind.
In that Vaidyuta [region], the Apsarases dispatched by Vāsava always reside there for the protection of the city of the earth.
Whether in fire, in water, or in battles from which they do not retreat;
or when dying for the sake of recovering cattle or liberating prisoners—these are the best of men.
Then they proceed upwards by means of celestial palaces marked with jewels,
filled with banners and ponds, and resounding with divine bells.
They lead them away in celestial chariots surrounded by thousands of women;
on Mount Raivata, those great-souled ones are indeed established as Siddhas.
Having mastered the gorocanā, collyrium, ashes, sandals, deerskin, and so forth,
those great-souled ones become perfected beings capable of assuming any form at will.
Those great-souled ones dwell there, established in divine perfection;
even during the great wind of universal dissolution, they are remembered as hosts of Vidyādharas.
Those ten and thirty crores were adorned with divine ornaments;
they were anointed with divine perfumes and decorated with the splendor of divine garlands.
Clouds born of smoke from the fire-element are known to bring cold and overcast weather;
mingled with the wind, they move like a boat upon a whirlpool of poison.
Therein are those skilled in the Gandharva arts who share the nature of Gandharvas,
as well as birds capable of assuming any form at will, who know the methods for playing the flute and the lute.
The clouds named Brahmajā, born from the breath of Brahmā,
are situated above Durjaya at a height of one hundred yojanas.
There, indeed, are the guardians of Indra named Durjayas;
they remain stationed there, relying upon the wind called Parāvaha.
Ten crores of clouds named Puṣkarāvartaka, born from the lotus-born [Brahmā], are proclaimed to be endowed with great heroic power.
The wings that were severed from the great-souled mountains by Śakra,
Parāvaha carries them away like an elephant carrying men.
In that [realm], there are gandharvas named Vāyugamas who dwell in the sky;
eleven koṭis of them have been proclaimed.
Those clouds named Jīmūtas, which arise from the life-force of the gods,
are supported by the second wind, Āvaha.
In that [region] are ten classes of Vidyādharas named Jīmūtaka;
from there comes the wind called Āvaha, where the Droṇas take their abode.
In that regard, the Droṇas are proclaimed as the protectors of the clouds;
indeed, they were created by me in the past for the welfare of all living beings.
Above that, arising from the skull, are the clouds named Saṃvarta;
the wind named Mahāparivaha is their support.
Thus, in the first wind-path, the clouds indeed move together with the winds;
there, the Siddhas and the lords who travel within the clouds have been described.
In the second path of the wind, the Mothers who are daughters of Agni are to be known;
endowed with virtues, they dwell there, presided over by the power of Rudra.
And in the third path of the wind, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas dwell,
fully perfected through the enjoyment of their own karma and presided over by all the Siddhas.
And here on the fourth path dwell the deities of weapons:
iron arrows, discuses, bows, spears, tridents, javelins, missiles, and mallets.
O Goddess of the gods, on the fifth path dwell Airāvata and the others:
Airāvata, Añjana, and the great elephant Vāmana.
Supratīka, Gajendra, and likewise Puṣpadanta;
Kumuda, Puṇḍarīka, and Sārvabhauma as the eighth.
O Goddess, those renowned as the elephants of the quarters are stationed in their respective directions;
on the sixth path of the wind, O Goddess, dwells the mighty king of birds.
He is renowned as Garuḍa, exceedingly invincible and possessed of great prowess;
in the seventh [layer], however, is the celestial Gaṅgā, followed by various aquatic creatures.
That meritorious [river] with divine nectar-water is proclaimed to be threefold;
it wanders through the midst of the sky, circular on all sides.
The celestial Gaṅgā, renowned as the constant festival of the gods,
shines like a garland of flowers resting upon the head of the sky.
There, [he was honored] by the highly fortunate Siddhas, by the hosts of Vidyādharas,
as well as by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the Maruts.
By the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Pitṛs, gods, and great seers, as well as by the Rākṣasas and Guhyakas, all intent upon divine praise; SvaT_10.477.
By high-souled beings praising, muttering prayers, and singing;
by those dancing and leaping about, amidst the sounds of divine drums.
With the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums, the resonance of lutes, and the notes of flutes impelled by the vital breaths of the mind; SvaT_10.479.
With lotuses having stalks of beryl and petals of gold,
fragrant with filaments made of rubies and reaching the size of great wheels.
The great river, the support of the Dharma, adorned with hundreds of celestial palaces and divine forests, appears as if it were dancing, O best of rivers.
Emerging from my eye is indeed that supreme Kriyāśakti,
the goddess Mahāmandākinī, who is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Constantly adorned by billions of great celestial palaces situated without any gaps,
this blessed goddess eternally abides in the expanse of the sky.
There, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, this [teaching] fell from my head onto the peak of Mount Meru and descended upon the surface of the earth.
That Gaṅgā is also imperturbable, remaining supported by the wind;
its width is proclaimed to be a full hundred yojanas.
Its circumference is then ten million [yojanas]; auspicious and possessing great velocity, it stands as if revolving, perfectly circular on all sides.
Having filled Dhruva, that goddess remains in an exceedingly wonderful state;
she is holy, flowing with divine nectar, and the destroyer of all sins.
In the eighth [region], however, the King of Bulls dwells together with his consort and Nandana;
he is unimpeded and is Dharma itself made manifest.
And here, on the ninth path, resides the Prajāpati named Dakṣa;
he is Brahman itself, dwelling there directly, presided over by the power of Brahman.
O Goddess, on the tenth path of Vāyu reside Vasu, Rudra, and Divākara;
here also are Aṅgāraka, Sarpi, Nairṛta, and Sadasatpati.
Sadasaspati, Budha, Dhūmaketu, the renowned Jvara,
Aja, Bhuvaneśa, Mṛtyu, and likewise Kāpālika.
The eleven Rudras are traditionally known as the source of the fulfillment of all desires:
Dhātṛ, Dhruva, Soma, Varuṇa, Anila, and Anala; 10.492.
Pratyūṣa and Pradoṣa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus;
these are indeed declared to be the Vasus—now learn from me concerning the Ādityas.
Āryamā, Indra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, and Viṣṇu the wielder of the bow;
and Mitra is likewise proclaimed—the one who is not the youngest as being the youngest.
Vivasvat, Parjanya, and Dhātṛ are indeed remembered as the twelfth;
they know these to be the descendants of Kaśyapa, and from among them [arose] that treasury of splendor.
The divine object arising from nectar is accompanied by all the gods;
upon that chariot is the wheel of sacrifice, and the pole consists of all-encompassing knowledge.
The seven horses are the seven vowels, which resound with the sound of the *hūṃ* of the Vedas;
the serpents are their yokes, and Aruṇa is indeed their charioteer.
His bed is truth, while the speed of his chariot is that of the wind;
the body of the Sun-god, however, measures nine thousand yojanas.
His triple-mandala shines radiantly throughout the three worlds;
this supreme power of knowledge blazes forth, taking the form of the sun.
By means of the application of the month and the day of the week, they move by the will of Śiva;
these wander throughout the Bhuvarloka for a full day and night.
Then the Moon, situated above the Sun at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas],
nourishes the entire world by raining down streams of nectar.
The power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva shines forth in the form of the moon;
above the moon, at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas], resides the circle of the constellations.
Two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that is situated the son of the Earth (Mars);
two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that is situated the son of the Moon (Mercury).
The preceptor Surācārya is situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] above him;
and the descendant of Bhṛgu (Śukra) remains two hundred thousand [yojanas] above him as well.
Two hundred thousand [yojanas] above that, Saturn moves with ease;
at a distance of one hundred thousand, I shall describe the sages in brief.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci are proclaimed as the sages (ṛṣis).
For by means of restraint and observance, these [deities] are capable of both cursing and bestowing grace;
they are afraid of causing pain to others and are heroes in the investigation of the scriptures.
All of them have raised the sword of wisdom, which removes the veil of ignorance;
as masters of mantra, yoga, and ritual action, they are armored and invincible.
Endowed with the qualities of the power of yoga and intent upon the worship of Śiva,
from them, O Goddess, there are fourteen fixed stars (tārakas), numbering one hundred thousand.
O woman of excellent complexion, their bodies were fashioned for Dhruva;
Brahmā himself, in another form, was appointed to the station of Brahmā.
O Goddess, the multitude of luminaries bound to that [center] revolves perpetually;
yet it should be known as motionless when presided over by the power of Śiva.
From the terrestrial mandala up to the end of Dhruva, there are fifteen million [yojanas];
I shall describe here, in brief, the layers of wind situated therein.
The seventh [layer] extends from the cloudless sun, the moon, the constellations, and the circle of planets,
up to the region designated by the seven sages, ending at the Pole Star (Dhruva).
The heavenly world (svarloka) is proclaimed to extend from Āditya up to Dhruva;
here indeed resides King Mahendra, honored by the gods.
Surrounded by ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, and hosts of apsarases,
those devoid of knowledge perform the agnihotra sacrifice or other ritual offerings.
Men go to the heavenly world (svarloka), but they return again to the human realm;
above the heavenly world, however, there are two koṭis of yojanas.
And eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas], O fair-faced one, is Maharloka;
there indeed dwell the ṛṣis and the Siddhas, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, Janaloka is situated above Maharloka at a distance of eighty million yojanas.
Ekapāda, Jahnu, Kapila, Āsuri,
Bhautika, and Vāḍvali are the inhabitants of Janaloka.
Likewise, O beloved, twelve crores above Janaloka is declared to be Tapoloka,
which is filled with sages and lords of yoga.
Sanaka, Sananda, Sanatkumāra, Sanandana,
Śaṅku, and Triśaṅku are the inhabitants of the world of Tapas.
