O fair-faced one, there are fifty-six padmas, twenty lakhs, and [five] crores,
starting from the end of the Bhūrloka up to the Satyaloka.
O fair-faced one, this number of worlds has been declared;
O beloved, it consists of sixteen crores measured from above the world of austerity (tapoloka).
Satyaloka is fully described as the place where Brahmā himself resides;
there the blessed Lord sports, surrounded by twice-born ones who are equal to himself.
Perfectly accomplished through the knowledge of karma, firmly established in non-duality,
they have attained the state of bliss and reached the state of bliss.
The Rigveda itself was present there in embodied form, with a luster like that of sapphire,
its limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments.
To its east stands the Ṛgveda, blazing with its own splendor;
to its north is the Yajurveda, resembling pure crystal.
Wearing divine earrings, with a massive body and mighty arms,
the eternal Sāmaveda stands in the western quarter.
Wearing red garments, glorious, with a radiance like that of a ruby,
he bears a garland of flowers and is adorned with various wonderful ornaments.
Likewise, Atharvāñjana stands to the south,
dark-complexioned like collyrium, with tawny eyes, a red neck, golden hair, and a massive body.
The six auxiliary limbs, the Itihāsas, all the Purāṇas, as well as the Vedas, the Upaniṣads, Mīmāṃsā, and the Āraṇyakas; SvaT 10.531.
The utterances of *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, as well as the secret doctrines,
and the *gāyatrī* reside there where the four-faced God resides.
The abode of enjoyment belongs to Brahmā; from there, O beloved, one should go to the Supreme Brahman, situated ten million yojanas above Satyaloka.
Known as the Brahmāsanam, it has the luster of *japā* flowers and vermilion;
situated in the center of a red lotus, it possesses a brilliance equal to a ruby.
Four-faced, master of the four Vedas, following the course of the four ages,
Brahmā is surrounded by those who know Brahman and attended by sages.
Endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, he is the agent of the sixfold creation and the bestower of the connection between dharma and its fruits in age after age.
He is the creator of beings in the animal realm and the hells, as well as of divine beings together with humans;
indeed, he is the creator of all beings among gods, asuras, and men.
Above that, O fair-faced one, is a distance of two crores of yojanas;
[there dwell goddesses] resembling blue lotuses and possessing a luster like sapphire.
The city of Viṣṇu is remembered as being beyond the world of Brahmā;
it is endowed with all objects of desire and resplendent with every kind of jewel.
With stairs and pillars made of emerald, crowded with blue banners,
expansive with canopies of bells, and adorned with beautiful yak-tail whisks.
She was surrounded by groups of maidens who resembled the petals of blue lotuses,
their deer-like eyes startled by the sound of the god of love’s bow.
Resounding with the tinkling of anklets, stumbling with soft, languid movements,
and shattered by hundreds of strikes from the arrows of the God of Love;
That Blessed One, Viṣṇu, whose eyes are like lotuses, is attended by those whose white eyes roll about due to the exhaustion of intense intoxication.
Having a form like sapphire and the luster of a blue lotus petal,
four-armed and large-bodied, with a broad chest, he holds a mace.
Wearing a crown, earrings, and a conch, and intent upon protecting his subjects,
that Blessed One is served by hosts who possess their own prowess.
And those devotees of Viṣṇu who are constantly devoted to meditation, worship, and recitation,
they— possessing immeasurable prowess— go to that abode of Viṣṇu.
Seven crores above that, the world of Rudra is situated;
it resembles pure crystal and is adorned with courtyards and gardens.
It was majestic with rows of palatial mansions consisting of a thousand stories,
and endowed with *puṣpaka* celestial chariots as pure as swans, jasmine, and the moon.
With groves and garden thickets radiant with flowers of every season,
the breezes were pleasant to the touch and bore the fragrance of incense and camphor.
It is filled with rivers, streams, and lakes, and adorned with clusters of lotus ponds;
it is the most excellent, the bestower of boons, the most preeminent, and the one of supreme complexion.
Vasiṣṭhā, Varāhā, and Varārohā as the seventh—
these are indeed declared to be the Gaṅgās that always carry one to the world of Rudra.
They were adorned with white lotuses rich with a hundred thousand petals,
possessing stalks resembling sapphire and fragrances extending for a yojana.
Abounding in clusters of thousands of women, grey with heaps of flowers,
these noble ladies resemble the autumnal moon and are as soft as fresh butter.
With beautiful brows, foreheads, and faces, slender waists, and languid with intoxication,
they possessed hair resembling a swarm of bees and fragrant with the scent of musk.
With long-hanging earlobes and eyes as broad as lotus petals,
they possess lips resembling pomegranate flowers that bear the fragrance of blue lotuses.
With shanks resembling plantain stalks, with arms as tender as lotus fibers,
with feet shaped like the sprouts of the aśoka tree, and with feet comparable to lotus petals.
With claws resembling *ketakī* flowers, with teeth radiant as pearls,
and naturally rich in exquisite fragrance, they seemed to be dripping with nectar.
They are always adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; with clusters of crest-jewels, girdles, and upper-arm bands, as well as with intensely red flowers.
With breasts resembling water-jars in shape, elevated, well-rounded, with full sides and resting upon thick necks; SvaT_10.559.
Bowed under the weight of a succession of teachers, adorned with strings of pearls,
they rival the gait of royal swans and possess the grace of elephants in rut.
Their gentle strides falter, made resonant by the tinkling of their anklets;
their eyes are tremulous with playful arching brows, rich in the charms of laughter and dance.
As if gladdening the limbs of the Rudras dwelling there,
[the women] reeled, overwhelmed by intoxication and possessed by the seizing-grahas of passion.
Though noble women such as these, distressed by fear of their own husbands, might cause joy to the lords of the hosts merely by embracing them while reeling, [they do not attain this state].
With eyes like those of terrified deer, they came into the embrace of their husbands,
and embracing them with all their limbs, they drank in their faces with their own mouths.
In the abode of Rudra, the daughters of Rudra sport together with the Rudras;
and the Rudras themselves possess such forms, preeminent through the power of knowledge and yoga.
With crowns and variegated earrings blazing with great jewels,
with armlets, bracelets, girdles, and ornaments of flowers and garments.
Adorned with necklaces of pearl strings and upper garments of sacred threads,
they possess massive bodies and broad chests, have three eyes, and hold tridents in their hands.
Resembling ten thousand moons, grey with the powder of camphor,
all of them are praised by gods and siddhas, exceedingly gracious, and bestowers of boons.
Having obtained boons by force, those ten-armed ones with the moon upon their crests are satisfied;
there, neither death nor old age exists, nor is there the sorrow born of separation.
Free from the fear of saṃsāra, they sport together with maidens;
when their office has ended, the Rudras are surrounded by the Rudrakanyās.
By the will of Śrīkaṇṭha, all go to Śiva at the dissolution of their bodies;
having gone there, they are not born again even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
By such innumerable beings, traveling in celestial chariots,
mounted upon great bulls and elephants, or riding excellent vehicles such as lions and horses;
It is surrounded by hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Rudras;
in its center is the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], with lion-gates and excellent archways.
It is surrounded by ramparts and turrets resembling clear pearls,
and is attended by the hosts of gatekeepers Nandīśvara and Mahākāla.
Resounding with networks of small bells, crowded with banners and flags,
and adorned with clusters of canopies and parasols from which pearl necklaces hung down.
It is adorned with the splendor of bells and chowries, further beautified by mirrors,
and with jars placed at the doors, joined with jewels and sprouts.
The courtyard of the world was adorned with svastikas and leaf-patterns, fashioned by experts in the science of painting and made radiant with powdered minerals.
It was strewn with hundreds of lion-thrones, adorned with jeweled altars,
and provided with gate-towers, watchtowers, chariot-paths, streets, and winding corridors.
It is beautifully adorned with doors fitted with various and abundant precious gems,
and with exits, elegant windows, and cornices possessing the luster of crystal.
With pillars joined by staircases, radiant with diamonds and lapis lazuli, and with domes resembling the full moon adorning the summits; SvaT_10.580 //
With thousands of grounds radiant with the luster of pearls,
and with theaters for dramatic performance, richly adorned and filled with the sounds of dancing and singing.
With pavilions richly adorned with various jewels and filled with circular assembly halls,
it was crowded with throngs of Rudras seated there and multitudes of Rudra-maidens.
It was adorned with delightful artificial elephants and beautifully decorated moon-chambers;
it was perfumed with incense sticks and sprinkled with saffron water.
It was covered with variegated cloths, strewn with heaps of flowers,
and filled with the sound of musical instruments, the roar of victory, and the blaring of trumpets.
With flutes, lutes, and clay drums; with *gomukhas* and mouth organs;
with small drums, cymbals, and the sound of conchs and kettledrums.
With the sound of kettledrums, the beating of hand-drums,
the great noise of slapping hands, and the resonant roar of lions;
With the shouting of the hosts of attendants, with sounds like the thundering of clouds,
with the hymns of bards, and with the resonance of the Sāmaveda;
With the sounds of the *huḍuṅkāra* and loud laughter joined with the resonance of song, with the sound of the bull’s joyful bellowing, and with the noise of elephants and horses; SvaT_10.588.
Resounding with the sound of waist-bands and anklets, the great city seems to sing;
it is the glorious temple of Śaṅkara, which bestows all prosperity.
There, the Blessed Lord Rudra, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra,
is constantly bathed in the Gaṅgā, clothed in divine garments and raiment.
His limbs were smeared with the fragrance of the earth, he was well-honored by the flowers of Śrī,
and he was praised by Sarasvatī and the foremost of the seven musical notes.
The full moon itself stands as his parasol;
the Gaṅgā, the Tuṣita heaven, and the umbrella are all present, and all the suns serve as lamps.
His seat is occupied by Puṣpadanta, Gaṇeśa, and others;
likewise by Kapila, Karkaṭa, Vimarda, and Kaṅkaṭa.
Vikrama, Dṛḍha, Niṣkampa, and likewise Niṣkala—
these eight are declared to be the Haras, three-eyed and of immense prowess.
Having the forms of lions, possessing great splendor, with manes fierce and radiant,
they are endowed with the power of mantra which assumes the form of a spear and is possessed of yogic sovereignty.
That seat was disclosed by those of great energy and preeminent strength;
there, Rudra, adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, sat upon the Bhadrāsana.
Complete with all the primary marks, adorned with all ornaments,
the god has three eyes and ten arms, and is decorated with a crown of matted locks.
With a full chest and thighs, broad shoulders, and mighty arms,
he sits in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), grey with the powder of camphor.
His hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he likewise bears all weapons;
his hands and feet are exceedingly soft and marked with the sign of the hundred-petaled lotus.
With fingers adorned by the luster of moon-like nails, with well-knit knees and ankles, and with feet that are evenly elevated; SvaT_10.600.
He was honored by the Gaṇas and Rudras, who were themselves worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
and on all sides, he was fanned with chowries and whisks by the wives of the Rudras.
The glorious one, fanned constantly, possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons;
his self is thoroughly satiated by the nectar of gnosis, and he bestows the sovereign power of yoga.
Constantly meditated upon by yogins, with a serene face and eyes,
he appears as if laughing with the rays of his stainless wisdom.
Having destroyed the darkness of ignorance, he reveals his supreme form;
surrounded by Rudra and the hosts of Mothers, he is the bestower of all happiness.
Seated upon his lap is the Goddess, with the radiant luster of molten gold,
worshipped by hosts of yoginīs, practitioners, gods, and kinnaras.
Complete with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
she eternally bestows the perfection of yoga and grants both liberation and worldly prosperity.
Umā, with her beautiful eyes, is eternally facing the God;
she is Śakti in another form, and Hara is likewise the possessor of Śakti.
And by the will of Śiva, Brahmā performs the creation and dissolution within the cosmic egg;
yet those who are intent on the worship of the Liṅga are devoid of initiation and knowledge.
They go to the abode of Hara, which brings the bliss of all sovereignty;
freed from old age and death, they are devoid of disease and sorrow.
O Goddess, they do not descend again into the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra;
rather, beheld by Śrīkaṇṭha, they go upward from there to attain auspiciousness (śiva).
The world of Rudra has been fully described; now listen, O Umā, to what lies above that, as each successive world is situated with an ever-increasing degree of excellence.
Below the Brahmāṇḍa and above the world of Rudra,
the city of Daṇḍapāṇi is to be known, surrounded by various hosts of Rudras.
But the Blessed One Daṇḍapāṇi, endowed with the power of mastery over yoga,
held the staff with the very palm of his hand by the will of Śiva.

And he reveals the path to liberation, which is so difficult to pierce, having been propitiated according to the prescribed rite through meditation by the will of Śiva; thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
I shall describe in brief those Rudras who exist in the seven worlds: Śarva, Rudra, Bhīma, Bhava, and likewise Ugra.
Likewise, you are Mahādeva and Īśāna, the lord of the world of Rudra;
Brahmā resides in the world of Brahmā, and Viṣṇu indeed in the city of Viṣṇu.
Rudra, abiding in the world of Rudra, is remembered as the leader of all;
from Kālāgni up to Daṇḍapāṇi, there are ninety-eight crores [of deities].
O lady of excellent hips, this path has been described in yojanas;
O fair-faced one, the shell (kaṭāha) is both below and above the Brahmāṇḍa.
O fair-faced one, it is established in a solid form with a measurement of ten million yojanas,
and it extends fifty million yojanas upward from the surface of the earth.
And fifty yojanas should be known [in depth] all around;
thus, one hundred koṭis should be known as that which is called the earthly reality (pārthiva-tattva).
It should be known to extend to a hundred Rudras; it is golden, perfectly circular, possesses a strength exceeding that of diamond, and is impenetrable even by the gods.
O fair-faced one, one should pierce [the target] by means of the application of the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ*;
O slender-waisted one, I shall now describe the hundred Rudras in brief.
In groups of ten, throughout the ten directions on all sides,
I shall describe them in successive order according to the sequence beginning with the east.
Kapālīśa, Udyojabandhana, Vajradeha, Pramardana,
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa.
Having attained the power of Indra, these great gods, endowed with sovereign might,
move about, being highly honored by Indra himself.
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara,
Jvalana, Uddahana, Babhru, Bhasman, Antaka, and Kṣayāntaka.
Having fully mastered the power of Agni and being endowed with sovereign might,
these great gods, who are highly honored by King Agni, move about freely.
He is Yama, Death, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and he who is designated as the Creator;
he is the uniter and the disuniter, as well as Dharma and the Lord of Dharma.
Having overcome the power of Yama,
these great gods, endowed with sovereign might and highly honored by King Yama himself, roam about freely.
The slayer of Nairṛta and Marut, with a cruel gaze and terrifying appearance,
has hair standing erect, distorted eyes, and smoke-colored, reddish fangs.
Having overcome the Nairṛta forces,
these great gods, endowed with sovereign power and highly honored by the Lord of the Nairṛtas, roam about.
Bala, Atibala, the mighty Pāśahasta,
Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka.
Meghanādī and Sunādī are thus briefly proclaimed;
having overcome the power of Varuṇa, they are endowed with sovereign power (prabhu-śakti).
The great gods who wander about are well-honored by Varuṇa and Indra;
[the winds] are swift, light, possessing the speed of wind, subtle, sharp, and terrifying.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana—
having overcome the power of Vāyu, they are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods who wander about are well-honored by Vāyurāja; he is the lord of treasures, possessed of beautiful form,
fortunate, and his body bears matted locks.
Lakṣmīratnadhara, Kāmī, Prasāda, and Prabhāsaka,
having overcome the power of Saumya, are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods wander about, well-honored by King Soma;
then there is the omniscient Lord of Vidyās, whose vision is wisdom and who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Śarva is the lord of the gods, the eldest, the protector of beings, and dear to Bali;
authorized by Īśāna, the gods, honored by the immortals, carry out their activities.
The great gods who roam about are presided over by the power of Īśa:
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and the one named Māruta.
Grasana, Uḍambara, Īśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭraka,
endowed with the power of the Lord, having overcome the strength of Viṣṇu.
The great gods who wander about are well-worshipped by Ananta;
they are Śambhu, Vibhu, the leader of the Gaṇas, the three-eyed one, and the lord of the thirty gods.
Saṃvāha, Vivāha, and Trilocana, desiring Nala,
having overcome the power of Brahmā, were endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods who wander about, being well-honored by Brahmā himself,
are said to have a retinue of one thousand for each.
Known as the hundred Rudras, they abide pervading the cosmic egg;
they are innumerable thousands, extending in directions such as the zenith and the rest.
The gods, who move everywhere according to their own will even throughout the kalpas and manvantaras,
are the Rudras stationed in the ten directions, beginning with the east, ten in each direction.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe each of these presiding lords individually:
situated to the east of the Egg is the one known by the name Śveta.
Endowed with hundreds of Rudras, he possesses great heroism and prowess,
like the sun with its blazing and most intense rays.
In the southeast is the one resembling fire, renowned by the name Vaidyuta;
he too, O Rudra, is surrounded by hundreds of those with the brilliance of lightning.
To the south of the Egg is Mahākāla, resembling the fire at the end of an eon;
O Goddess, he stands there surrounded by hundreds of Rudras of immeasurable prowess.
The son of Nirṛti, named Vikaṭa, surrounded by a hundred followers,
stands there with great majesty like a second sun.
In the west, that Rudra who is renowned as Mahāvīrya,
surrounded by the hundred Rudras, remains there with his immeasurable prowess.
In the northwestern direction of the Egg, the glorious and mighty Vāyuvega,
endowed with great strength, stands here surrounded by a hundred [attendants].
To the north of the one named Subhadra, surrounded by a hundred [attendants],
the one of great strength stands here, endowed with the power of great heroism.
Surrounded by rays of light, the valiant one stands there;
he is the Rudra named Vidyādhara, established in the northeast.
Surrounded by the hundred Rudras, like the moon-king encircled by stars,
he remains there, endowed with great heroism and strength, possessing infinite valor.
Below, another Kālāgnirudra is situated here as the second;
he stands surrounded by hundreds of Rudras stationed there, O fair-faced one.
Surrounded by hundreds [of attendants], like the sun with its rays,
Vīrabhadra, encircled by the Rudras, was stationed above the cosmic egg.
The eleventh [is] Mahākāya, arisen from the wrath of Rudra;
thus these great-souled ones here are each accompanied by a hundred.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent vows, these ten are surrounded by the hundred Rudras;
the retinue of these great-souled ones is beyond counting.
For these stand surrounding the cosmic egg, just as honey-bees surround honey,
or as a kadamba flower is encircled by its filaments.
For that egg was thus surrounded by Rudras of immeasurable prowess with houses adorned with various jewels, featuring archways and watchtowers.
It was adorned on all sides with variegated objects made of Jāmbūnada gold,
crowded with celestial women, and endowed with everything that fulfills every desire.
This universe has been described as having cast off the snare of bonds,
yet it remains submerged in the great ocean of birth, disease, old age, and death.
Covered by the impurity of the three qualities (guṇas), crowded with various castes,
overcome by the ignorance of the fettered (paśu), and agitated by the three states of existence (gatitraya).
The realms of existence are indeed impermanent for all disputants;
yet, being deluded, they do not understand the distinction between the higher and the lower.
In the past, the golden egg, which is the form of the world and consists of destruction,
was created for the welfare of the group of souls who are pervaded by the Māyā of the Lord.
Then, above that, the principles beginning with Water and ending with Śiva are established in ten ways through a progressively ascending union.
Above that is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and above that the intellect (buddhi) is established in a hundredfold way;
O lady of excellent complexion, the primordial matter (pradhāna) should be known as being a thousandfold above that.
The human [scale] is ten thousand; destiny is recorded as one hundred thousand.
Beyond that, O lady of virtuous vows, it continues up to ten million, which is a *kalā*.
Māyā, however, exists pervading all that is mobile and immobile in ten million ways; Vidyā, possessing ten times the qualities of Māyā, is established by pervading Māyā.
This [level] is pervaded by Īśvara with a hundred-fold ten-millionfold increase;
Sādākhya extends for a thousand million, and above that are Bindu and Nāda.
Indeed, the Śakti remains pervading a multitude of yojanas;
O Goddess, the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī) remains established having pervaded the entire path.
Therefore, O lady of beautiful countenance, the Śiva-tattva is to be known as immeasurable;
I shall now describe the worlds (bhuvana) in their proper sequence, beginning from the water-tattva.
The form and the dissolution, as well as the manifold expansion of the worlds,
which is not seen by the cognitions of the ignorant whose vision is deluded by wrong paths.
That which is not [attained] by the Sāṃkhyas, nor by the Yogins, nor even by the Pāñcarātrikas;
nor by the proponents of inherent nature (svabhāvavādins), nor by the proponents of karma.
Nor [should one debate] with those who propound doubt, such as the naked Jains (nagnakṣapaṇaka) and others;
nor with those who speak of the elements (bhūtavādin), nor even with worldly people.
Nor by those who contemplate the self, nor by those who propound logical reasoning,
nor even by the Vaiśeṣikas who are devoted to the six categories.
Nor by those who speak according to logic and employ reasons and examples,
nor by those who maintain the doctrine of a single birth, nor even by those who maintain the doctrine of oneness.
"The Lord is not well understood by people through deceitful doctrines"—
for those who speak thus, there are three hundred such arguments.
Furthermore, for the sixty-three other disputants whose minds are deluded and who are afflicted by the cataract of ignorance, this [work] is the supreme means for opening their eyes.
For those submerged in the mire of saṃsāra, it is the supreme raft for crossing over;
for those blinded by the darkness of great delusion, it is the supreme dispeller of darkness.
This divine nectar of knowledge, which extends throughout the nine worlds, has been obtained by me as a wonder issuing from the mouth of the Supreme Lord.
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess, to this wonderful and diverse form:
the infinite multitude of worlds is established through its uninterrupted continuity.
It has a dense covering like a honeycomb or a web;
it resembles the nests of fish and conchs, and is situated like the seeds of the dāṣīmī plant.
The multitude of ancient cities resembles the filaments of the kadamba flower;
it is like the camp of Mahāsena’s army, or like a grove of trees in a forest.
O fair-faced one, there are endless worlds, continuous and infinite,
possessing various forms, diverse, and composed entirely of all kinds of jewels.
Some are circular, some are long, some are shaped like half-moons,
others are shaped like men, and still others are shaped like svastikas.
Forms shaped like mountains, those with the appearance of herds of elephants,
others shaped like arrows, and those with the form of flames.
There are forms of great celestial palaces (mahāvimāna) shaped like tridents,
others shaped like drums (muraja), and ancient cities with triangular shapes.
O fair-faced one, there are forms of great beings shaped like a hundred peaks,
as well as others with a thousand peaks and whirlpools.
There are other peaks numbering ten million and innumerable summits;
some are circular, some are square, and others are triangular.
There were divine variegated banners and divine bells upon victory standards,
enriched by the sounds of kettledrums and the resonance of divine songs.
The sounds of divine drums and the resonances of great flutes,
the noises of various musical instruments, and all the worlds at all times.
They are white, with the luster of crystal, shaped like rubies,
having the color of moonstones, and resembling strings of pearls.
O lady of excellent complexion, some [of these] have the color of lac juice,
some the color of the indragopaka insect, and others resemble sapphire.
They have the color of blue lotuses and resemble masses of lightning;
they have the color of the rising sun and resemble the interior of a lotus.
Others have the luster of the moon and resemble ten million moons;
others have the color of the midday sun and resemble ten million suns.
They have the luster of *aśoka* flower clusters, resemble yellow orpiment,
possess the color of Indra’s bow, and are as white as cow’s milk.
They have the luster of vermilion and saffron, resemble gorocana pigment,
possess the color of molten gold, and are like smokeless fire.
Some worlds are white like conch shells,
while others are of various colors and possess diverse forms and shapes.
Beyond these, O Goddess, is the all-pervading supreme state,
immeasurable, incalculable, and inaccessible to all disputants.
Without the grace of the Lord, this knowledge is not obtained;
nor indeed does the state [of realization] arise for embodied beings without having received initiation.
But when, due to a specific cause, the power that brings about liberation arises,
one should, by the will of Śiva, attain the auspicious initiation consisting of knowledge.
Then, through the divine nature of mantra-yoga, the bound soul (paśu) shall attain liberation;
otherwise, it does not reach liberation even by means of hundreds of [other] knowledges.
He to whom everything has been revealed by Śiva, who possesses infinite forms—
he alone attains liberation, being Śiva, the Great Lord of All.
Therefore, this supreme knowledge was previously taught by me to you;
it is like a boat for the crossing over of those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Beyond the ointment of great illusion, unknown within the sphere of the ignorant,
infinite, supreme, unshakeable, and easily realized— the Supreme Lord.
"O beloved, listen with a one-pointed mind to this nectar of knowledge which I shall proclaim— the wondrous [teaching] that was vomited from the mouth of the Supreme Lord and obtained by me."
Indeed, above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there stands a group of eleven,
belonging to the eleven Rudras who possess a brilliance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the divine world of the Goddess situated above,
which consists of sapphire and is perfectly circular on all sides.
In that place resides the Blessed Goddess Bhadrakālī;
she dwells there, dark as a blue lotus, with a luster like smooth saffron.
Adorned with two earrings in the form of solar discs,
she shines like the twilight on a full-moon night, radiant with both the moon and the sun.
And a great necklace shines, situated between her two breasts,
like a river flowing between two mountains of black collyrium.
And the divine throne, composed entirely of vajra and adorned with celestial jewels, is supported by four lions of immeasurable prowess.
On the brilliantly shining seat, the goddess possesses a luster like that of pure collyrium;
she stands upon a white peak of the Himalayas like a dark blue cloud.
Her divine girdle, composed of every kind of jewel,
shines forth like a night at dawn when adorned with yellow garlands and silken garments.
Her third eye, situated on her forehead,
shines resplendent like the sun risen at dawn, adorned with a web of rays.
With her white parasol held aloft,
she shone like the night illuminated by the moon situated above a dark cloud.
Surrounded by thousands of millions upon millions of women,
she was like the crescent moon enveloped by the stars in the vault of the sky.
The women have the complexions of white and blue lotuses, or are dark like gold; some are as dark as the buds of the *priyaṅgu* flower, while others are as fair as the moon and in the prime of youth.
Possessing forms as pure as lotuses, with full hips and breasts,
they were skilled in the techniques of amorous gestures and expressions, and proficient in dance and song.
Sitting near that goddess, the women there take delight in the sounds of lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and other bamboo wind instruments.
Know thus, O fair-faced one, that the world named Jaya exists,
which is known in the world as Durgā and resides within the interior of the cosmic egg.
In former times, Viṣṇu, having propitiated the Supreme Lord through ascetic penance,
brought her down for the sake of slaying the great-souled Mahiṣa.
And with that single horn, the Blessed One Himavat mountain was cast aside like a dry leaf and destroyed by the Blessed Lady.
That Goddess destroys him, like the risen sun dispelling darkness;
that Goddess exists through the names and forms of all the goddesses.
Concealed by the yoga-māyā, she is a maiden who brings the world into being;
she is described elsewhere as inconceivable and immeasurable.
Accompanied by Viṣṇu, the Goddess appears again and again in every kalpa,
assuming various names and forms as his sister.
In every Manvantara and likewise in every Yuga,
she acts for the protection of the worlds, bestowing benefit like a mother.
Thus has been described the world named Jaya, O fair-faced one;
those who are devoted to it and have received initiation into its mandala go there.
O fair-faced one, this cannot be attained through austerity, nor by those skilled in statecraft who bestow abundant sacrificial fees, nor even by various kinds of gifts.
Through the grace of the God of gods, whose crown is marked by the crescent moon,
they obtain initiation and attain the mandala of universal monarchs.
Indeed, through seedless initiation (nirbījadīkṣā), it grants liberation to embodied beings;
that supreme initiation of liberation is proclaimed according to the rule.
O fair-faced one, to whatever extent initiation is performed for men in the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa), they attain a corresponding state within this world.
O beloved, I shall describe to you all the worlds, their lords, and their respective arrangements in due order; listen with a one-pointed mind.
O Goddess of the gods, in Bhadrakālī resides the supreme deity born from the wrath of Rudra,
numbering ten million and possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon.
His voice resounds with a roar like that produced by a mass of clouds at the end of an eon;
he possesses a hundred arms, great splendor, and is adorned with divine ornaments.
Bearing the moon upon his head, he is dark with a luster like blue collyrium;
resembling the neck of a peacock, he is somewhat pale and somewhat red.
It has the color of a blue jay or a cloud, resembling the flower of the linseed plant;
it resembles sapphire and is somewhat like the appearance of a bumblebee.
His form resembles pure collyrium, and he is accompanied by the eleven Rudras,
as well as by thousands of millions of great-souled Rudras.
The world of that deity is renowned by the name Vijaya;
it is divine, resembling sapphire, like all vajras, and vast.
O woman of excellent complexion, it is surrounded by ten thousand times ten million Rudras,
along with other multitudes of intermediate worlds.
He was surrounded on all sides by divine Rudras of great heroism, who were dark like the petals of a blue lotus and resembled the neck of a peacock.
With praises, auspicious rites, songs, dances, and the sounding of musical instruments—
such as small drums, flutes, lutes, kettledrums, cymbals, and horns.
With kettledrums and trumpets, with conchs, dundubhis,
and pīlukas, with clay drums, taṭṭarīs, cymbals, and murajas likewise.
With the sounds of maunda, kāhala, and ṭaṅka drums, with Tamil drums, ghaṭas, and the like; with musical instruments, leaping rhythms, clapping, shouting, and cymbals.
By means of the bhūtas and hosts of bhūtas, by the Rudras, through their chatterings and recitations,
as well as by those meditating, those chanting, those running, and likewise by their various activities.
And by other high-souled beings who were emitting the cries of peacocks and cuckoos, and displaying various playful modulations of sound.
Enveloped by those [beings] with elephant faces, lion faces, horse faces, and auspicious countenances, he of great splendor was like the sun surrounded by its rays.
The Blessed One is attended by those with the ears of cows, those with the faces of cows, others with the faces of leopards and bears, as well as those with the faces of tigers and monkeys.
Vīrabhadra, possessed of great splendor and radiant like the fire at the end of an eon,
has a vast seat for that deity composed entirely of vajras.
Extending ten yojanas and square in shape, it shines with the brilliance of fire;
there it resplends, surrounded by eight lions of terrifying prowess.
In this regard, those of meritorious deeds who remember Maheśvara—
whether they die in water, among the winds, in fire, or by decapitation— [attain the goal].
O Goddess of the gods, they attain the sovereign awakening of Vīrabhadra, who possesses great splendor;
for he is the great enclosure above this world.
Furthermore, the mother was thick and stood like a rainbow;
that auspicious canopy was situated between them.
And there dwells that Great Being, measuring only the size of a thumb-tip;
there, indeed, its diameter is said to be ten million yojanas above.
O Dear One, the watery enclosure is threefold the width of the transverse [dimension];
everything is enveloped by that which spreads across the great ocean.
It is renowned as Rudrāṇḍa, O beloved, and as Rudrāloka;
it is the abode of Vīrabhadra and likewise the dwelling place of Bhadrakālī.
It is adorned by thirteen other worlds and is continuously embellished by various divine hosts of Rudras.
O beloved, the egg of Vīrabhadra is indeed like the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
beyond this, I shall describe the great world of the Earth.
In this world of mortals, the eternal Goddess Dhātrī resides,
having attained an incomparable golden state and remaining established therein as the foundation.
It was surrounded by many celestial palaces of the universal monarchs,
and it was filled with hosts of beings and teachers who were devoted to that supreme goal.
He was surrounded by hosts of Rudras within the multitude of worlds, accompanied by the sounds of hundreds of musical instruments enriched with the resonance of divine songs.
In the center of this world, [he] resembles the rising sun;
divine, he has the hue of a red lotus and the luster of an *aśoka* flower cluster.
A divine, multi-storied palace made of ruby stands there;
in its center is the Blessed Lady Dharitrī, the sustainer of the world.
She is eternally adorned with a hanging garland of red flowers,
and her cheeks are embellished with the form of the orbs of the sun and moon.
Clad in yellow golden raiment and adorned with a great necklace,
she stands upon the back of a tortoise extending for a hundred yojanas.
She has four faces and eight arms, adorned with divine ornaments;
she is endowed with beauty and youth, and is skilled in dance and song.
Thirty million divine women born of the mind, adorned with celestial ornaments, attend upon her, surrounding her on all sides.
Desiring their welfare, Śarva created them for that purpose;
they resembled molten gold and were adorned with divine ornaments.
Adorned by a raised parasol being held over them,
they stand before that mountain of great splendor, the great Mount Meru.
Sitting there, worshipping that goddess, the lord of the mountains remained,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus and resembling a dark-blue cloud.
The great mountain named Nīla, clothed in yellow garments and possessing great splendor,
was like another enemy of Kaiṭabha due to his exceedingly beautiful form.
The Lord of Mountains, being attended by divine cities,
appears like the moon to the north of him, adorned with various ornaments.
The great mountain named Śveta is radiant and possesses a white parasol;
to its north is [the mountain] resembling the sun, adorned with a crown and other ornaments.
Clad in yellow garments, glorious, and renowned as Śṛṅgavān,
he was like another god of love with his exceedingly beautiful form.
I shall also speak with the right [hand]; listen attentively, O beloved!
He possesses the radiant splendor of the moon and is adorned with divine ornaments.
Clad in white garments, glorious and renowned by the name Niṣadha,
he resembles molten gold and is adorned with divine ornaments.
With an exceedingly radiant body, like a second Grandfather (Brahmā),
the glorious one wore yellow garments and was adorned with yellow garlands and unguents.
The lordly Hemakūṭa mountain, possessed of great splendor and like a collection of all radiances,
shines like the sun enveloped by the twilight.
Resembling a pale white cloud, similar to a conch shell or cow's milk,
wearing white garments, glorious, and adorned with divine earrings.
With a great parasol being held over his head,
he who was renowned as Himavat appeared like a second sun.
Gandhamādana, resembling an indragopaka insect, is situated in the west;
glorious and wearing red garments, he is like the sun resting upon the mountain of setting.
Resembling pure crystal, wearing white garments, and auspicious,
there is a glorious mountain named Mālyavat, adorned with a crown and earrings.
It is surrounded by these and other mountains,
including Lokāloka at its edge, as well as other principal mountain ranges.
The goddess who possesses a divine form is indeed the body of the Supreme Lord;
she is the state reached by the yogi who, having abandoned his vital breaths, performs concentration upon the subtle element of smell.
They attain such a form, the supreme body of the Earth;
beyond this, O Goddess, lies the great oceanic world.
Divine and composed entirely of vajra, it is endowed with hundreds of various wonders;
its color is like that of a blue lotus, and it is perfectly circular in every respect.
In the center of this world, however, is a mandala resembling the moon,
measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in circumference all around.
In its center, however, is a person of golden complexion and great splendor,
wearing a crown, earrings, and garlands, adorned with divine ornaments.
He is the supreme body of the Lord Varuṇa, the ocean;
and having surrounded that high-souled deity on all sides, [they stood].
Endowed with beauty and youth, they constantly attend upon her;
the goddess wears white garments and is anointed with white perfumes and unguents.
She wears a white sacrificial thread and is adorned with white garments;
a white parasol is held over her head.
To his north stands indeed the Gaṅgā, his supreme body;
she is the goddess wearing blue garments, anointed with blue perfumes.
And to his south is the Yamunā with a blue garland around her neck;
these and other great rivers surround him of great splendor.
And the eight oceans, O Goddess of gods,
surrounded by their own rivers, always worship with devotion that supreme form of Varuṇa.

Various lakes and sacred fords, as well as those devoted to them, are established right here; having properly performed meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*).
Having reached the supreme source of the waters, that is the supreme body of Vāruṇī;
beyond this, O woman of excellent complexion, I shall describe the world.
It is renowned as Śrīniketa and known as Padmagarbha;
it is filled without any gaps by hundreds of clusters of celestial palaces standing close together.
It was adorned by the lords of the worlds, by the Rudras, and likewise by the hosts of Rudras;
it was beautified by divine lakes and by long ponds.
And with lotuses the size of chariot wheels, adorned with jewels and gold,
having stalks of lapis lazuli, and fragrant with divine scents.
It was beautifully adorned with those various, blossoming vajra-stamens, which were soft, radiant, and resembled the orb of the moon.
It was adorned on all sides with various gardens resounding with the songs of diverse birds, and with trees that grant every kind of desire.
With divine pleasure-mountains made of various jewels that exist in the mind, and with celestial women possessing the loveliness of divine youth; SvaT_10.805.
It is adorned by divine women rich in gestures, emotions, and amorous play,
and with various jeweled lotuses and white petals, O lady of excellent vows.
It was adorned with those mounted upon lordly elephants who uttered hymns of praise and auspicious sounds,
and it was filled with celestial women singing and dancing.
In that divine realm, possessing a radiance equal to the interior of a lotus,
there is a divine mandala resembling the autumnal moon, filled with rays of light.
In its center is the Blessed Lady Śrī herself, the Illuminator of the World,
whose splendor surpasses that of thousands of millions of moons.
But the splendor of splendors shines forth simultaneously in one place—
that which is peaceful like nirvāṇa, captivating all through its bliss.
The supreme goddess is embodied, her form is unfailing;
she extends for a hundred yojanas and possesses a radiance like the rising sun.
Upon a lotus made of moonstone, with a vajra as its filaments and pericarp,
possessing ten million petals, most divine, and endowed with the qualities of fragrance and flowers.
Seated here perpetually upon a lotus throne, the Blessed Lady, possessing a radiance equal to the interior of a lotus, is endowed with supreme majesty.
Bearing upon her chest a beautiful garland of great jewels hanging down,
she shone like the moonlight along the path of the triple-streamed river.
She wore earrings that resembled the solar disc upon the surface of her cheeks, which was shimmering with the movement of radiating rays.
Wearing a girdle from which clusters of rays radiate,
she is golden-hued, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with a magnificent necklace.
She shone with a moon-like parasol being held over her,
and was accompanied by songs from the Gandharvas born of Rudra’s mind.
That slender form of the Supreme Goddess was surrounded [by her retinue],
she who was attained by the powerful Viṣṇu after propitiating her through ascetic penance.
The river was given by the pleased Rudra onto the chest of Viṣṇu;
that blessed goddess became established upon half of Viṣṇu’s body.
By one quarter of the god Indra she resides in heaven;
by half of that quarter, O Goddess, she is established among earthly beings.
Half of that [power] resides among humans, pervading them through its forms;
it is proclaimed to be twofold: of its own nature (*svarūpā*) and capable of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpā*).
O you of excellent vows, that subtle and immovable body remains there during the Rudra-krīḍā incarnations at Prayāga and other such sites.
And one who dies especially on Śrīparvata shall go to that world;
even though other regions exist, this is the destiny described for them.
Having attained such a goddess, [consisting of] the sovereignty of *aṇimā* and so forth,
she becomes eightfold and divine, and remains even among the gods.
Even among those who have attained accomplishment, that goddess is said to be the supreme accomplishment,
for the sake of which the lords of the thirty gods, such as Tāraka and others, waged war.
Terrible deeds beyond counting have been performed by those desiring to attain that sovereignty;
indeed, countless battles have been waged by universal monarchs.
O fair-faced one, that which has been thus described as the bondage of the ignorant is traditionally held to be the supreme Śrīpura, exactly as it is.
Henceforth I shall declare; learn from me the world-system:
it is known as Sārasvata and is remembered as Gāndharva.
And the city of Padmagarbha, O observer of excellent vows, is said to be ten million yojanas in measurement all around.
Divine, consisting of every kind of jewel, and endowed with all sovereign powers,
it is filled with auspicious celestial palaces of various forms made of diverse gems.
There were also Gandharvas and Mānasas singing in many ways,
as well as others dancing, with various groups stationed at his side.
It was crowded with beautiful women and Gandharvas;
in its center, O Goddess of Gods, was an auspicious [throne] resembling the autumnal moon.
A divine, circular mandala, filled with a garland of rays, exists;
in its center stands the Blessed Lady, Sarasvatī herself.
The Goddess, clad in yellow garments and possessing eyes as broad as lotus petals, surpasses the splendor of a thousand autumn moons.
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing a golden sash, and bearing divine earrings.
Bearing upon her breast a great necklace with the luster of the moon,
she was adorned with a pair of earrings from which clusters of shimmering rays radiated.

The auspicious goddess Mūrcchanā has the three *grāmas* as her waist, the seven notes (*svara*) as her body, the *tānas* as her rising hair, and she bears the *aṅgas* as her growing limbs. (SvaT 10.837)
The feet, the seat, the palm-like soles, and the power of the syllables of song;
likewise, the fingers and the joints are the auspicious marks, O fair-faced one.
Seated upon a supreme, divine throne, surrounded by the lords of the hosts of spirits,
she stands resplendent like the auspicious stability of the entire world.
She was surrounded by the celestial maidens of the Mānasa lake and by the Gandharvas of the Mānasa;
likewise, Hāhā, Hūhū, Citraratha, Tumburu, and Nārada were there.
Viśvāvasu, Viśvaratha, and those skilled in divine song,
having mentally composed their selves and abandoned desire for the fruits of action, [attained liberation].
O you who are worshipped by the gods, those embodied beings who, having meditated upon the retention of speech, release their vital breaths, indeed attain that station of Sarasvatī.
Those best of men indeed attain the world of Sarasvatī;
for this Goddess Sarasvatī is truly the supreme form of the Lord.
That Goddess, who exists in a state beyond all else for those dwelling within the interior of the cosmic egg,
stands upon a single foot in the world of Brahmā.
In the realm of Śakra it is half of that, among the Gandharvas half of that,
among the Siddhas half of that, and among the Kinnaras half of that.
Half of that [number] is for the Nāgas, half of that again for the Yakṣas, and half of that for the Piśācas; indeed, she remains stationed among them in those respective portions.
He remains among humans possessing thousandth-parts of the powers of the Piśācas;
having performed severe austerities by means of those [powers] and having propitiated the wielder of the Pināka bow, [he attained this state].
That goddess, embodied and adorned with her own splendor,
was brought down for him as he recalled the vowels from the beginning of the kalpa, long ago at the dawn of Brahmā.
Because she emerged from the vowels, she is indeed Sarasvatī;
she resides in all the scriptures and is established in the poetry of poets.
That Goddess who resides eternally in Vālmīki and in Vyāsa, and who increases the wisdom and intellect of all the sages; SvaT_10.850.
She indeed possesses all knowledge, is omniscient, and is worshipped by the gods;
her city is proclaimed to be in the northwestern direction of Mount Meru.
This supreme world of Sarasvatī, which is her most excellent body, has been proclaimed by me to you, O Goddess.
In this very same reality that is to be attained, listen indeed to the most excellent of worlds:
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, and likewise Naimiṣa.
Āṣāḍhin, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍin, Bhārabhūti, and Lākula—
these, O Dear One, are known as the Eight Secrets (Guhyāṣṭaka) residing within the enclosure of water.
Therefore, I shall now describe the principle of fire (tejas-tattva) above that in brief;
O fair-faced one, I shall describe the world of Agni therein.
And it bore the brilliance of *aśoka* blossoms on all sides,
possessing the hue of full-blown *kiṃśuka* flowers and resembling the *japā* flower.
In the center of this world, there is said to be a circular mandala of fire-like radiance, possessing a splendor equal to the risen sun.
In its center, however, is the Lord Śivāgni, the supreme cause;
having descended into the midst of the cosmic egg, he remains eternally in a ninefold manner.
In the mouth of that Rudra, the Supreme Self,
Svayambhū Nīlalohita himself resides in the form of the tongue.
But he alone, O Great Goddess, is the Supreme Lord Kālāgni;
I shall describe his form—listen attentively, my dear.
Having the luster of the petals of a red lotus and a brilliance equal to rubies,
he is glorious, wearing red garments, and adorned with red garlands and unguents.
His beautiful face was adorned with two earrings possessing the brilliance of the sun,
and he shone with a great, radiant necklace resting upon his chest.
Wearing a crown and earrings, radiant, he is called the mouth of the gods;
the Lord himself is seated upon a seat composed entirely of vajras.
Like a forest fire ignited by the friction of bamboos on a mountain peak,
there are ten thousand times ten million Āgneya lords of the Gaṇas.
From the southern mouth of this self-existent Svayambhū as he breathed forth,
there emerged the Rudras, possessing the brilliance of the sun, for the welfare of all the worlds.
Therefore, those great-souled ones constantly attend upon that fire,
as do various divine women who are experts in celestial song.
The Gaṇas, the Rudras, the hosts of Bhūtas, and the Kiṅkaras by the thousands—
he is indeed recited as Śivāgni, the supreme lord of all oblations.
In the ritual procedures for fire-offerings, that which is always offered by those who know the rites—
having performed the fire-related concentration (dhāraṇā)— they go to that Agni who is Īśvara.
He exists pervading everything, both as one and as many;
he is the source of all luminous bodies, and from him the sun was born.
And he is manifested in many ways during the kalpas, manvantaras, and so forth;
and on the surface of the earth, he appears divided by fifty different types of births.
Thus has the great Āgneya world been correctly described;
hereafter, I shall describe the lords of the worlds within that world.
And Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpa, Āmrātakeśvara,
Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
The extremely secret [teaching] has been fully explained in sequence from the east to the end;
now, above that is the wind-enclosure, wherein resides the imperishable wind.
Therein, O fair-complexioned one, is the world of Prāṇa, which belongs to Vāyu;
it is as white as a conch shell, cow’s milk, or the autumnal kunda flower and the moon.
In that divine realm, endowed with hundreds of divine wonders,
there was in the center a divine mandala with a radiance like the autumn moon.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the midst of that divine [mandala], which is filled with garlands of rays and illuminates the ten directions, resides the supreme body of Vāyu.
Wearing a crown and earrings, radiant, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
his limbs variegated by various ornaments, and decorated with wonderful garlands and unguents.
Wearing variegated garments, glorious, and adorned with great necklaces—
these are the gods named Mārutās, numbering one hundred crores and possessed of great strength.
They worship the Great-Souled One, whose form is Vāyu and who possesses great splendor—
the omnipresent Lord who pervades bodies as one and as fivefold.
Divided sevenfold and again sevenfold, extending transversely and doubling in size,
that supreme body of the all-pervasive Lord shines as one through his divine mandalas.
Having meditated upon this very single self of the vital breath (prāṇa) as tenfold, and having performed concentration (dhāraṇā) upon it, the yogis indeed abandon their vital breaths.
"Great-souled ones, having become like the wind and taking on the form of space, enter that [state].
Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, has the world of Prāṇa been described to you."
I shall describe the Rudras who are the lords of those worlds in their proper order:
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākala, and likewise Kanakhala.
Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Māhendra, and Bhīma as the eighth—
this which is more secret than the secret must indeed be understood with diligent effort.
But in space, like space itself, pure and stainless as clear crystal,
he abides in the central region, subtle in form, imperishable, and eternal.
The yogi engaged in the concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā) is united with that state.
Regarding this space, I shall declare those Rudras who are established therein.
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, Mahālaya,
Gokīrṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu as the eighth.
This group of eight purifiers has thus been proclaimed in brief. Outside of this is the ego (ahaṃkāra); therein, learn from me the Rudras.
Chagalāṇḍa, Duraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara,
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara.
The eight Sthāṇus are proclaimed to extend from the east to the northeast;
situated in the Middle Country is the Lord Rudra, the Sovereign of Ego (Ahaṃkāreśvara).
White, red, yellow, black, and the brilliance of crystal—
these are the colors that have been briefly described to you among the five groups of eight.
White, red, black, blue, dark-grey, and cloud-colored;
yellow and white are to be known [as the upper clouds], while those below possess a smoky luster.
The hundred Rudras are fully described as three-eyed and holding tridents;
all have the crescent moon upon their crests and are accompanied by the Rudrāṇīs.
The worlds of the hundred Rudras should be known as being lotus-shaped, endowed with various jewels, and possessed of enjoyments and sovereignty.
O Dear One, above the covering of space and below the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra), there should be cities in the shape of tortoises on all sides, five in each group of eight.
I shall now proclaim the worlds; listen again with a one-pointed mind.
First, however, is the great and expansive mandala of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra).
O Goddess, it stands like a canopy for many millions of yojanas,
white, red, black, yellow, green, and with the luster of crystal.
O Goddess of the gods, it is circular on all sides like a canopy;
for there, O lady of beautiful countenance, Śarva alone is the sovereign lord.
From that, impelled by Śarveśa, the earth is born;
above that maṇḍala is the maṇḍala of the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra).
O beloved, it is green, dark like an emerald, and resembles the wing of a blue jay;
for there, O fair-faced one, Bhava alone is the sovereign lord.
Therefore, the waters issued forth, impelled by Bhava;
and above that mandala is the mandala of the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra).
Resplendent with the brilliance of shimmering sunbeams and possessing a luster equal to a ruby,
Rudra Paśupati alone abides there.
Therefore, that light emerged by the will of Paśupati;
O Supreme Goddess, that light pervades all the worlds.
Above that mandala, O beloved, is the mandala of the subtle element of touch;
the mandala of wind has a luster equal to the dawn-red.
Resembling the shape of a canopy and perfectly circular all around—
that very mandala, O Goddess, is where Īśāna is established.
Therefore, O Dear One, the wind has emerged, impelled by the will of the Lord;
from that [wind] arise the five vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth, while the Supreme is the pervader of that wind.
That one [mandala] also becomes manifold, divided sevenfold and again sevenfold;
above that mandala, however, is the mandala of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra).
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with a luster like clear water,
its form resembling a canopy and perfectly circular on all sides.
Bhīma alone remains there as the sovereign;
therefore, the great sky emerges from that, impelled by the will of Bhīma.
O Dear One, it pervades all worlds and transcends both the higher and the lower;
therefore, above that mandala, the solar mandala is spoken of.
Resembling a thousand suns, it blazes forth on all sides;
radiant with rays like a canopy, it is perfectly circular in every direction.
For Rudra alone remains there as the sovereign;
from him, O fair-faced one, the suns emerge in every kalpa.
Above that maṇḍala, however, the moon-maṇḍala is said to exist;
its orb is equal in brilliance to thousands of millions of moons.
But Mahādeva alone remains as the sovereign lord;
therefore, the moons and other luminaries are impelled by Mahādeva.
Countless thousands have emerged in every eon;
therefore, above that maṇḍala, it is called the Vedamaṇḍala.
With a splendor equal to ten million moons, perfectly circular all around,
it stands like a celestial canopy, presided over by Ugreśa.
That [stream] was indeed obstructed by Vāmā;
from it, thousands of sacrificers have indeed emerged and remained throughout kalpa after kalpa.
From Brahmā, impelled by his fierce austerity,
there arose the various Vedas and sacrifices from that Brahmā whose path is infinite.
Therefore, these sacrifices and the fruits of sacrifice proceed,
together with austerity, charity, and so forth, being governed by the power of *vāmā*.
Thus, these eight bodies are proclaimed as the supreme (parā);
the non-supreme (aparā) ones, however, abide pervading the entire cosmic egg of Brahmā.
Beyond these, there is also the mandala consisting of the instruments,
which is white, red, black, yellow, and green in color.
The five lords abide in the mandala consisting of the instruments;
from that, indeed, the karma-deities proceed for all embodied beings.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth—
from these [arises] that which is called the Illuminator (prakāśaka), which beyond that resembles the sun.
From that, indeed, the five faculties of cognition proceed:
the ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose, in their respective order.

The function [of the sense organs] is the perception of objects; they are situated within the spheres of light, are eternally presided over by their respective lords, and are impelled toward those very objects.
Beyond these, there exists a circle of light rays resembling the lunar disk, equal in its extent and circumference on all sides.
From that indeed proceed the five objects for all embodied beings:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
Beyond these, moreover, is the gentle orb of the Moon;
from that, the mind has emerged by means of its five rays.
"Citta," "cetas," and "manas" are the terms for that which sets in motion the senses such as hearing;
its lord is the Moon of great splendor, by virtue of his gentle radiance.
Above that maṇḍala, however, beyond it,
is a great maṇḍala resembling the hibiscus flower and like the rising sun.
And as before, one should measure it as a complete circle;
from that mandala, O Goddess, [emerges] with a luster like the dawn at twilight.
Like fire accompanied by smoke, this ego-sense indeed proceeds;
it is the internal organ residing within the self, by which this world is colored.
Like a blind, intoxicated elephant, the forest fire creeps forward;
its presiding deity is indeed Rudra, by whom he is always impelled.
O Goddess, Chagalāṇḍa and the others were previously described by me to you;
now, following the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the obscuration of the intellect (buddhyāvaraṇa) is explained.
Listen now to the description of the world of the eight classes of divine beings, which possesses a splendor equal to the radiance of thousands of millions of suns.
The world named Kakubha has a splendor equal to the dawn-red twilight;
it is filled with joyful women who are the very embodiments of the mind.
There dwell Piśācas whose radiance is equal to the glow of the dawn;
ten thousand times ten million are those who reside there.
The great lord among the piśācas, named Svananda, is valiant;
his complexion is like the dawn-red at twilight, and his form resembles the bandhūka flower.
Adorned with earrings, decorated with necklaces and armlets, wearing a crown,
bracelets, and a diadem, he is auspicious, clothed in golden garments of fine silk.
He was surrounded by a vast multitude of spirits standing at his sides,
who assumed various divine forms and were adorned with celestial ornaments.
Endowed with divine garlands and ointments and possessed of divine sovereignty,
he of great splendor was surrounded by [beings] like the Great Host (Mahāgaṇa) by its attendants.
Hereafter, I shall describe the great realm of Rākṣasa,
which resembles the throat of a cuckoo and is like a dark blue cloud.
In that divine world, endowed with celestial sovereignty,
there was indeed the great Karāla, lord of the Rākṣasas, resembling natural collyrium.
Wearing a crown and earrings, radiant and of great splendor,
he shines like a majestic mountain fire amidst a forest, resembling pure black collyrium.
Ten thousand koṭis of rākṣasas named Muditās,
possessing the luster of bees and clouds and endowed with great radiance, dwell here.
Hereafter, I shall describe the great realm of the Yakṣas,
which is entirely made of Jāmbūnada gold and resplendent with divine jewels.
In that auspicious world, which is produced from enjoyment and sovereignty and is perfectly circular on all sides,
there dwells the king of the yakṣas named Subhadra.
Shining with the color of molten gold, adorned with a crown and other ornaments,
he is accompanied by thousands of millions of yakṣas of immeasurable prowess.
Surrounded by all of them, Śarva shines like Śarva with all his hosts.
Hereafter, I shall describe the great world of the Gandharvas.
Resembling yellow *kauśītakī* flowers and possessing a luster equal to that of *campaka* blossoms,
there indeed dwells one named Surūpa in that divine world, O beloved.
He is like the lord of the Gandharvas and gods, resembling Mount Gandhamādana;
he has the luster of molten gold and the radiance of the rising sun.
With his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments,
he was surrounded by ten thousand times ten million gandharvas.
The Gandharvas named Svakāntās, adorned with variegated garlands and ointments, resemble fragments of realgar as well as yellow orpiment.
All of them wear variegated garments and are adorned with variegated ornaments;
beyond that, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the station of Indra.
Above that is the realm known as Bṛhadbhoga, which grants all desires;
it is white like a conch shell or cow’s milk, resembling the autumnal kunda flower and the moon.
In that divine world, which is endowed with hundreds of celestial wonders,
resides the Lord named Vibhūti, the Great Indra and Sovereign of the World.
Resembling the orb of the moon, adorned with strings of pearls,
wearing white garments, glorious, and anointed with white garlands and unguents.
His crown is blazing, he is adorned with two radiant earrings,
and wearing necklaces and armlets, he is white and decorated with a white turban.
The gods known as the Bhūtijas are indeed endowed with supreme prosperity;
they wear crowns and earrings, and are adorned with divine garlands.
Ten thousand times ten million gods, known as Indras,
surround him of great majesty, like the moon surrounded by the stars.
The auspicious world named Manoja is like the autumnal moon;
it resembles white clouds, is radiant, and possesses the brilliant luster of a pearl necklace.
There indeed resides the supreme Moon, named Amṛta;
he resembles pure crystal, is glorious, and wears white garments.
Adorned with earrings that resemble blazing light, he shines resplendent;
his limbs are anointed with divine perfumes and decorated with celestial ornaments.
In that regard, those rays known by the name Raśmivyūhasamaprabhā should be understood as divine and gentle, arising from the splendor of the Moon.
There are indeed ten thousand times ten million [worlds] of those of gentle splendor;
beyond this, O Goddess of the Gods, is the great world of the Prājās.
In that divine world, you are the Lord of Creatures,
possessed of immeasurable splendor, universal in form, universal in color, and adorned with all ornaments.
The Universal Soul was surrounded by gods of universal form,
ten thousand times ten million Viśvas of immense splendor.
Surrounding the Great-Souled One, they attend upon him in splendor;
thus, it should be known that the Brahma [light] is like a conch shell or cow’s milk.
There the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) resides, gentle-eyed and seated upon a white lotus;
he is glorious, wearing white garments, white garlands, and white unguents.
Wearing a white sacred thread and adorned with great necklaces,
he is accompanied by ten thousand times ten million [beings] whose radiance is equal to the orb of the moon.
Surrounded by the Brahma-deities like the sun amidst autumnal clouds,
[he beheld] the realms of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Indra.
Likewise, O beloved, the realms of Saumya, Prājeśa, and Brāhma—
these indeed are the abodes and cities of those born of the gods.
For, descending [into the world], they come into being while meditating upon their own self-born [nature],
impelled by the command of the Supreme Lord and urged on by Māyā.
And constrained by the necessity of Brahmā, whose birth is manifest,
they are manifested at the beginning of creation in manifold ways through names and forms.
O lady of excellent hips, they do not abandon the abode even in part;
one should purify the self together with the eightfold city and the senses by means of mantras.
Having thus purified the five groups of eight, the eight forms, and the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) in due order with diligent effort, one should thereafter [purify] the eight Krodhas.
Saṃvarta, Ekavīra, Kṛtānta, Jananāśaka,
Mṛtyuhantṛ, Raktākṣa, Mahākrodha, and Durjaya.
Their worlds indeed possess the hue of blue lotus petals;
each one has a retinue of one hundred million times ten thousand.
Above the eight Lords of Wrath (Krodheśvaras) resides the great group of eight Splendors (Tejoṣṭaka):
Balādhyakṣa, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Tridaśa, and Tripurāntaka; // SvaT_10.979 //
Sarvarūpa, Śānta, Nimeṣa, and Unmeṣa—
this retinue is said to consist of fifteen thousand.
These Agnis and Rudras are indeed remembered as being black in color due to their brilliance;
their worlds are variegated and shaped like tortoises.
Beyond this, the unsurpassed eightfold yoga has been fully described:
the Uncreated (Akṛta), the Created (Kṛta), the Raibhava, and the Brāhma.
Furthermore, the Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Auma, and Śraikaṇṭha worlds—
there the yogins sport with these realms that possess the luster of crystal.
Then the Blessed Mother of the World appeared in person;
you are Umā, the immeasurable, the self-born source of the universe for the entire world.
Resembling molten gold and possessing the radiance of the rising sun,
she resides upon a beautiful, great jewel-encrusted throne supported by eight lions.
In that place extending a hundred yojanas, adorned with divine garlands and pure ornaments,
dwells the goddess Divyakuṇḍalinī, resplendent with great necklaces.
At the forefront of victory is the highly fortunate Vijayā, possessing a form as excellent as Śrī;
and Jayā, radiant like the interior of a lotus, adorned with every ornament.
And Nandā, whose eyes are like lotus petals and who is adorned with necklaces and armlets;
and Sunandā, whose limbs are variegated with all kinds of ornaments and who is captivating to the mind.
Surrounding her on all sides, thirty thousand and three hundred million female doorkeepers stood in attendance.
Various divine and noble women always attend upon them;
there is also a single koṭi of celestial palaces belonging to the Rudras of immense splendor.
They are known as the Aumās, or otherwise as the Vaimānas;
they worship that Goddess, their Mother, just like sons.
Having descended into the midst of the egg together with me, O fair-faced one,
that eternal [Power] has manifested for the sake of favoring the worlds.
In the first aeon she was Jaganmātā, in the second Jagadyoni,
in the third she was named Śāmbhavī, and in the fourth Viśvarūpiṇī.
In the fifth [kalpa] she was named Nandinī, and in the sixth she was Gaṇāmbikā;
in the seventh kalpa she was Vibhūti, and likewise in the eighth she was Subhūti.
Ānandā was in the ninth kalpa, Vāmalocanā in the tenth,
Varārohā in the eleventh, and Sumaṅgalā in the twelfth.
In the thirteenth aeon, O Goddess, she is proclaimed as Mahātanu;
and in the fourteenth aeon, she is celebrated by the name Anantā.
Bhūtamātā is remembered as the fifteenth, and Uttamā as the sixteenth;
Sahasradhārā is the seventeenth, and Satī was formerly the eighteenth.
In the kalpa of Cākṣuṣa Manu, you were the auspicious daughter of Dakṣa;
yet, due to Dakṣa’s contempt, you formerly cast off your own body.
Having remained there until she had again filled this digit of the moon,
she was once more propitiated by Himavat and made his own daughter.
O Goddess, having performed most difficult and wondrous austerities,
you have become one whose limbs are covered in hair (aṅgaruhā) after regaining me as your husband once more, my beloved.
O fair-faced one, I, whose abode is Kailāsa, am together with you;
you are the body of my left side and are never separated from me.
At Dakṣa’s sacrifice, she was born again under the name Bhadrakālī;
she is another form of Ekānaṃśā, Satī, who emerged from Śiva.
Having reached this cycle of four ages, during the Dvāpara Yuga, she was born as Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā together with Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying Mahiṣa.
Known by various synonymous names such as Kātyāyanī and Durgā,
she is the bestower of boons upon devoted human beings and is affectionate toward her devotees.
Previously you descended upon the summit of the Vindhya mountain;
from here onwards, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall describe the world-realms.
It is renowned as Sucārvi, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns;
it has the form of a peak of Kailāsa and the luster of pure crystal.
Surrounded by millions of great celestial palaces belonging to the universal monarchs,
in that divine world there was one whose splendor was equal to ten million suns.
He has a thousand arms, feet, faces, and eyes;
he is the Lord of Umā, the Master of the World, the supreme bestower of grace upon all.
Indeed, the entire place of enjoyment is situated there on the left side,
extending for a hundred yojanas and adorned with various jewels.
Upon a supreme, divine seat covered with celestial rugs, resembling a hundred suns in brilliance,
and variegated with jeweled lotuses.
Seated there, possessed of great splendor, surrounded by eight bulls,
wearing golden garments and fine silken clothes, and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
He wore two earrings that were brilliantly blazing like the orb of the sun,
shimmering with clusters of rays and dense with light.
Wearing upon his head a crown variegated with divine jewels,
it was exceedingly brilliant, most fierce, and resembled the peak of Mount Kailāsa.
His great necklace, Pralamba, was thick with radiating rays,
like a waterfall falling from a peak of the Himalayas into the Ganges.
With thirty thousand crores and likewise three hundred crores [of attendants],
who were trident-bearers with matted hair, three-eyed, and adorned with divine ornaments;
He was surrounded by Rudras assuming various forms as well as hosts of spirits,
and encircled by divine and mental women.
He was indeed surrounded by hundreds of millions of celestial palaces;
and all seven Mothers, possessing beautiful forms and adorned with various ornaments, were present.
Surrounding the Great-souled One, they stood encircling him on all sides—
women with the luster of Brahma-lotuses, adorned with divine ornaments.
O Goddess of gods, she stands in the southeastern direction like another Śrī;
O fair-faced one, she resembles a conch shell or cow’s milk in the northeastern direction.
The goddess Māheśvarī, of great splendor and honored by the gods, stands there;
and Kaumārī, radiant like the interior of a lotus and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
In the northern direction, O Goddess of gods, she is attended by Kāminī;
she resembles a smooth blue lotus and is adorned with necklaces and earrings.
In the southern direction, she worships the Supreme Lord;
she is renowned as Vaiṣṇavī by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Resembling a dark blue cloud and adorned with all ornaments,
O Goddess of the gods, Vārāhī stands present in the western quarter.
White as a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon, and adorned with necklaces and earrings,
that goddess Indrāṇī stands present in the eastern direction.
With a terrifying face, blazing and adorned with all ornaments,
Cāmuṇḍā worships the Supreme Lord in the southwestern direction.
For they do not abandon the God who is endowed with all states of being;
having been brought down by Brahmā, they [reside] in the human world as partial incarnations.
For the sake of slaying the Asuras and for the welfare of human beings,
Brahmā, the sustainer of the world, performed most formidable austerities.
For the sake of slaying Ruru, I too have brought them down;
however, other supreme ones remain established in the highest heaven, acting according to their own will.
Worshipping him according to their own will through the distinction between the higher and the lower,
Umā herself becomes sevenfold through various transformations of name and form.
Thus that Blessed One, the God, surrounded by his Mothers,
remains there with supreme splendor, illuminating the world.
Above him likewise are the eight forms of that wise one:
Śarva, Bhava, the Lord Rudra, and Paśupati; 10.1031.
Īśāna, Bhīma, Mahādeva, and Ugra—
by means of these forms, Śarva brings about the supreme creation.
Earth, water, fire, air, space, and the sun,
as well as the moon and the sacrificer— these eight are known as this creation.
But they abide in that [state] with their whole being, whereas elsewhere they abide only partially;
thus the Lord is situated above the world of Brahmā.
And on the summit of Meru resides Īśāna; furthermore, he is sought after as the eightfold yoga, known by the name Śrīkaṇṭha and likewise having his abode on Kailāsa.
He remains pervading [the universe] through his eight forms, beginning with Śarva;
for those who fully practice the qualified yoga of Maheśvara, [he abides thus].
And through devotion, celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint,
those wise ones, having perceived the Self residing within the body, proceed here to that [state].
And having beheld his mandala with supreme devotion,
the wise ones— self-restrained and liberated from duality— go there.
And above them, moreover, stand twelve Suśivas:
Vāma, Bhīma, Īśa, Śiva, and likewise Śarva.
The Lord of the Vidyās, the Sole Hero, the Holder of the Fierce [Power],
Īśāna, the Consort of Umā, Ajeśa, and Ananta as well.
Likewise, Ekaśiva and the twelve Suśivas are remembered;
all are like saffron in color and possess a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Established within the various worlds shaped like conch shells,
above that is the Lord Vīrabhadra, the sovereign of the mandala.
Having attained union with that, one rejoices together with him.
Beyond this, O Great Goddess, they know the group of eight Mahādevas.
Mahādeva, Mahātejas, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Udbhava,
Ekapiṅga, Ekeṣaṇa, Īśāna, and Bhuvaneśa, preceded by Puraḥsara.
In the group of eight Mahādevas, there are Śivas accompanied by [consorts] the size of a thumb;
they are liberated from the collyrium of Māyā and are esteemed by the Supreme Lord.
The lords of the worlds have been described by me as residing in the seat of the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).
Now, above that is the principle of the qualities (guṇatattva), which is established therein.
The three divine lines of gurus stand separated by their qualities;
the first line, of darkness, is situated above.
Their names are now told correctly and in due order:
Śiva, the Lord Vāmadeva, and the powerful Caṇḍa.
Prahlāda, Uttama, Bhīma, Karāla, Piṅgala,
Mahendra, Dinakṛt, Pratoda, and Dakṣa.
Kalevara is renowned, as well as Kaṭaṅkaṭa;
Ambuhartā, Nārīśa, Śveta, and indeed the Ṛgveda.
The Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, as well as Atharvan the very auspicious,
Virūpākṣa, Jyeṣṭha, Vipra, and likewise Nārāyaṇa.
Gaṇḍa, Nara, Yama, Mālī, Gahaneśa, and Pīḍana—
this is declared to be the first row, remembered as consisting of thirty-two Rudras.
Above Rajas, however, the second row is said to consist of Śukla,
Dāsa, Sudāsa, Lokākṣa, and Sūrya.
Suhotra, Ekapāda, Gṛha, Śiveśvara,
Gautama the Lord of Yogins, and another, Dadhibāhu.
R̥ṣabha, Gokarṇa, and the god Maheśvara; Guhyeśāna, Śikhaṇḍin, Jaṭin, Mālin, and likewise Ugraka.
Bhṛgu, Śikhin, Śūlin, Sugati, Supālana,
Aṭṭahāsa, Dāruka, Lāṅgalin, and Atidaṇḍaka.
Bhāvana, Tathābhavya, and Lakuleśa—these are declared to be the thirty Rudras; this is the second, most excellent row.
And above Sattva, the third row is said to consist of Deva,
Aruṇa, Dīrghabāhu, Atibhūti, and Sthāṇuka.
Sadyojāta, as well as Jhiṇṭhi, Ṣaṇmukha, Caturānana,
Cakrapāṇi, the one named Kūrma, and likewise Ardhanārīśvara.
Kapālī, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and likewise Vaṣaṭkāra,
as well as Vauṣaṭkāra, Svāhā, and Svadhā are proclaimed.
