Saṃvartaka, Bhasmeśa, and Kāmanāśana—these are the twenty-one Rudras; this is the third row.
Endowed with the power of the yoga of gnosis, the supreme teachers sport,
liberated from the snares of saṃsāra and devoid of great delusion.
All the gurus have three eyes, are as pure as clear crystal,
are omniscient, omnipresent, and bestow grace upon the worlds.
The divine worlds of all are shaped like elephants;
now learn from me about those Rudras who exist up to the limit of the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the intellect (buddhi).
O fair-faced one, there are two hundred and seven worlds;
others who exist within them have not been mentioned by me, O fair-faced one.
Above the qualities (guṇas), however, Pradhāna is proclaimed;
I shall describe in brief those Rudras who reside therein.
And Krodheśvara, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, Krūradṛk, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikheda, Sahita, and Īśvara.
But in the case of the primordial nature (prakṛti), O Rudra, those of great heroism are proclaimed [to reside there];
that which is the ultimate limit of the qualities (guṇas) is here called Pradhāna.
Therefore, learn from me the worlds within the principle of Puruṣa:
Ambā, Salilā, Oghā, Vṛṣṭi, and Tārā together with [her consort].
Sutārā, Sunetrā, and Kumārī after that,
as well as Uttamāmbhasikā— these nine are proclaimed as the Tuṣṭis.
Tārā, Sutārā, Tārayantī, Pramodikā,
Pramoditā, Modamānā, and Ramyakā after that.
Likewise, irresistible will (*prākāmya*), lordship (*īśitva*), and that which is called mastery (*vaśitva*),
as well as the power of determining things according to one's desire (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*)— these are remembered as the group of eight beginning with *aṇiman*.
Now, listen to this regarding the three rows of teachers and disciples above:
Maskarī, Pūraṇa, Kṛtsna, Kapila, and Kāśa.
Likewise, Sanatkumāra, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, and others are portions [of him];
as well as Kaśyapa, Nāsiketu, Gālava, and Bhautika.
Śākalya is also proclaimed, as well as the supreme sage Durvāsas;
and Vālmīki, the best of gurus, along with Parāśara and Gālava.
Pippalāda, Saumitri, Vāyuputra, and Bhadantaka—
those beginning with Maskari and ending with Bhadanta— are proponents of both the seen and the unseen.
The first row is held to consist of twenty-two excellent gurus:
Jahnu, Tṛṇabindu, Muni, and likewise Tārkṣya.
Dhyānāśraya, Dīrgha, Hotṛ, Jāgara,
Agastya, Vasubhauma, and Upādhyāya are proclaimed [as the teachers].
Śukra, Bhṛgu, Agni, Rāma the son of Jamadagni,
Adhvaga, Sthūlaśiras, Bālakhilya, and Manu are thus proclaimed.
Vajrātreyas, Viśuddha, Śiva, and Cārurathānuga,
ending with Jahnvādicāru— this is held to be the second row.
Hara, Jhiṇṭhī, Pratoda, and Amareśa as the fourth;
Kṛṣṇapiṅgeśa, Rudra, Indrajit, Vṛṣaka, and Śiva.
Yama, the renowned Krūra, Gaṅgādhara, Umāpati,
Bhūteśvara, Kapālīśa, and likewise Śaṅkara.
Ardhanārīśvara, and likewise Piṅgala as another;
Mahākāla, Saṃvarta, Maṇḍalī, and Ekavīraka.
Likewise, there is another renowned one, the eternal Bhārabhūteśvara;
and there are twenty-five sages beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru.
The twenty teachers beginning with Hara and ending with Dhruva are traditionally recorded;
this is declared to be the threefold lineage of the sages, comprising both teachers and disciples.
O Goddess, hereafter I shall describe to you the eightfold science of the channels (nāḍīvidyāṣṭaka):
Iḍā, Candriṇī, Gaurī, Śānti, and likewise Śāntikarī.
Mālā, Mālinī, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā;
then, O Goddess of the Gods, the group of eight forms (vigrahāṣṭaka) is described above.
The effect and the instrument, as well as that which produces pleasure and pain;
knowledge and the goal to be accomplished, as well as the means and the cause—these are renowned.
Now I shall describe the nooses of the body and the tenfold Dharma as it has been taught:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from deceit.
Absence of anger, service to the guru, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness—
such is the tenfold dharma by which a man is called a practitioner of dharma.
One should perceive the sixteen transformations known as the secondary qualities (parabhāva), which exist as established therein:
taste, smell, form, touch, and likewise sound.
The five subtle elements have been declared; now learn from me the sense organs:
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are known as the organs of action.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose is recorded as the fifth;
these, O Goddess of the Gods, are the organs of perception, while the mind is recorded as the sixteenth.
The bonds of the body are thus fully described; therefore, they know the qualities of the intellect (buddhi) to be virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, which follows after that.
Likewise, non-dharma, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery—
I shall explain these, along with the threefold egoism, in their proper sequence.
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi [evolvents], in their respective order—
understand from me how their purification occurs at the time of initiation.
One should purify darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva) in successive order;
likewise, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
And the objects of the senses have been fully described; they must be purified with great effort—namely, desire, anger, greed, delusion, and malice.
Birth, death, old age, disease, hunger, thirst, and likewise craving;
as well as despondency, fear, pride, and even exhilaration.
Passion, hatred, mental instability, anger, falsehood, and malice;
deceit, the quality of stinginess, unrighteousness, and lack of self-mastery.
And those who are adventitious must be understood; learn from me the fetters of the Gaṇas:
the goddesses Nandī and Mahākālī, as well as Gaṇeśa and the Bull.
Bhṛṅgī, Caṇḍīśvara, and Kārttikeya is remembered as the eighth;
Ananta, Tritanu, Sūkṣma, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śivottama.
Śikhaṇḍin, Ekanetra, and another, Ekarudra—
one should purify the bonds consisting of the Vidyeśvaras at the time of initiation.

Those [defilements] mentioned here, those not mentioned, and those whose characteristics are described in other tantras—all these must be purified within the *puruṣa*; by that, the individual (*pudgala*) shall be liberated.
Now, one should know that above [that] is Niyati; learn from me the Rudras who reside there:
Vāmadeva, Śarva, and likewise Bhava and Udbhava.
Vajradeha, Prabhu, Dhātṛ, Krama, Vikrama,
and Suprabheda as the tenth— these are remembered as the Śaṅkaras within Niyati.
That lotus which is situated in the heart— the Self is established therein—
with destiny as its petals, ego as its filaments, and the intellect as its pericarp.
In the reality of time, Śivā is to be known; I shall describe her in brief:
she is the pure, the awakened, the fully enlightened, the profoundly tranquil, and the supreme syllable.
Śiva, Suśiva, Dhruva, Akṣara, and Śambhurāṭ—
these ten, O fair-faced one, are to be known as the Śivas within the principle of Time (kālatattva).
The Śaṅkaras are said to have a golden luster, while Śiva resembles crystal;
O illustrious lady, such is the retinue assigned to each one.
One crore and sixteen thousand other worlds are all said to be shaped like tortoises.
Henceforth, learn from me concerning Hari and Hara within the principle of attachment (rāga-tattva):
Suhṛṣṭa, Suprahṛṣṭa, Surūpa, and Rūpavardhana.
Manonmana and Mahādhīra are proclaimed as the Lords of Heroes (Vīreśas);
I shall now declare which other Rudras are established within the principle of passion (rāgatattva).
Kalyāṇa, Piṅgala, Babhru, Vīra, Prabhava,
Medhātithi, Chhandaka, Dāhaka, and Śāstrakārin.
Likewise, these five disciples and ten teachers are established;
above that is the principle of Vidyā—now hear of the world therein.
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, Raudra, Kala, Vikaraṇa,
as well as Balavikaraṇa and Balapramathana.
Sarvabhūtadamana and likewise Manonmana—
O Great Goddess, these three great deities reside within the principle of Kalā.
Mahādeva, of great splendor and great light, is possessed of majesty;
O lady of beautiful countenance, the principle of *kalā* has thus been explained in brief.
O Great Goddess, these Rudras have three eyes and the moon as their crest;
they are surrounded on all sides by thousands of crores of Rudras.
Resembling pure crystal, they are endowed with the power of yogic sovereignty;
those who are red in passion are to be known as those whose strength in the yoga of knowledge is preeminent.
Their houses are indeed shaped like parasols and variegated with jewels;
above them is Māyā—this I shall describe in brief.
Having pervaded the path both below and above, she abides in her universal form;
therein dwell the twelve highly fortunate Rudras of great power.
O Goddess of the gods, Gahana, Asādhya, the Lord Hariharaprabhu, Daśeśāna, Trigala, and likewise Gopati; SvaT_10.1124.
In the lower casket, O fair-faced one, within the principle of Māyā,
Kṣemeśa— the lord of Brahmā— and likewise Vidyeśāna are to be known.
Vidyeśa, Śaiva, and Ananta is said to be the sixth;
these Rudras are proclaimed to reside within the enclosure of the upper Māyā.
Among these, however, the Lord Ananteśa, the Master of the World,
having brought about manifestation, acts according to his own will, O Sovereign.
The twelve Rudras are proclaimed by the first division as being omniscient, the makers of all things, and intent upon both restraint and grace.
I shall now describe how the Rudras are established within this principle of Māyā, according to the division of the three categories.
And then, O Goddess, Gopati is situated at the lower knot;
above the knot reside Viśva, Trikala, and Kṣema.
Brahmā, Adhipati, and Śiva as the fifth;
below and above is Ananta, and the fetters (pāśas) are likewise situated here.
O Goddess, it has indeed been explained previously that from this [lineage] the family of sages arises;
she is the womb and Vāgīśvarī herself, born of whom one is not born again.
Oṃkāra, Sādhyadhātṛ, and thereafter Damaneśa;
they say that Dhyāna and Bhasmeśa follow, and after those come the Pramāṇas.
They call the fivefold meaning "the secret," and beyond that, "Rudrāṅkuśa";
[these consist of] the Heart, the Characteristics, the Array, and the Attraction.
And likewise, the eighth is proclaimed here as Ādarśa;
these, O Goddess, are surrounded by thousands of crores of Rudras.
Variegated with diverse colors and adorned with various ornaments,
they take delight with thousands of different women according to their husband's wish.
All of them have three eyes and carry tridents; they wear matted hair, the moon, and crowns;
their power and majesty are undiminished, and they hold authority over the principle of Māyā.
Established within the various worlds that exist in the form of wombs,
beyond this lies Māyā, which deludes all living beings.
With their intellects deluded by that [ignorance], which is the enemy of enmity-less [peace], proponents here dispute, saying, "This is reality; this is not."
But those lowest of men who are not devoted to their guru, the gods, the sacred fire, and the scriptures, abandon the true path and are led swiftly onto a wrong path.
Those who know only the investigation of fallacious reasoning and rely upon dry logic—
Māyā indeed causes them to wander, for they desire liberation where there is no liberation.
Severed by the sword of Śiva-initiation, it shall not sprout again;
thereafter follows the Great Vidyā, the source of the arising of all vidyās.
She alone, the imperishable treasury of the dissolution, origination, and manifestation of the world,
is proclaimed as the Supreme Goddess Vāgīśī.
And that Vidyā, though divided into eight groups, is indeed the Mātṛkā itself.
I shall now describe the worlds in their proper order and sequence.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Raudrī, Kālī, Vikaraṇī,
as well as Balavikaraṇī and Balapramathanī.
Damanī and likewise Manonmanī are the subduers of all beings;
they have the appearance of molten gold, possess five faces, and are three-eyed.
Possessing unfailing vigor, they are omniscient and abide everywhere at all times;
endowed with all-knowledge, they are all adorned with every ornament.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of all sovereign powers,
there are seven principal crores of mantras that are established.
Each one has a retinue numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions;
they sport in divine worlds that are shaped like lotuses.
Triguṇī, Brahmavetālī, Sthāṇumatī, Ambikā, Parā,
Rūpiṇī, Mardinī, and Jvālā— these seven are their respective Īśvarīs.
The Vidyārājñīs have been fully described; one should purify them at the time of initiation.
Their external principle is that of Īśvara; now hear from me concerning their worlds.
Endowed with the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras), free from illusion and stainless,
he is indeed the agent of maintenance and dissolution, and the bestower of liberation and sovereignty.
His seat, moreover, is vast, measuring a thousand petals;
three and a half crores of mantras are situated upon that seat.
Abiding there, the Lord God, the bestower of boons, faces in every direction;
he has five faces, great splendor, ten arms, and three eyes.
The gentle deity is white as cow’s milk, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
clad in celestial garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Complete with all the primary marks, adorned with all ornaments,
holding a trident in his hand, with the moon upon his crest, and decorated with a crown of matted locks.
With a serene countenance and lovely appearance, bestowing the sovereignty of yoga,
and with hands granting boons and fearlessness— this one is to be meditated upon by the masters of yoga.
Upon her lap rests Vidyā, who is the support of all sciences;
she is clothed in divine garments and adorned with divine garlands and unguents.
Adorned with divine garlands of flower-strings and strings of pearls,
resembling pearls in appearance, she has five faces and three eyes.
When propitiated according to the prescribed rite, she always grants knowledge to the wise;
she shines as if smiling, due to her gaze upon the face of Maheśvara.
I shall now describe the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) in order, starting from the east and ending with the northeast:
Ananta, Sūkṣma, and likewise Śivottama.
Ekanetra and Ekarudra, as well as the celebrated Trinetra,
Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin, are to be known as the Vidyeśvaras in their respective order.
Therefore, understand from me that form and its state reside therein as Rudra:
dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth.
Above this is the subtle veil; therein they know there are three powers.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are declared to be the powers.
Their retinues, indeed, are many tens of millions in number;
all these mantras are omnipresent, omniscient, and granters of all desires.
Resembling pure crystal, three-eyed, and holding tridents in their hands,
they are endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
Fully endowed with all sovereign powers, they have beautiful crescent moons as their crests; they possess the radiance of pure pearls and moonbeams, appearing like hundred-petaled lotuses.
Accompanied by the lords, they all remain in those worlds, which are filled with various gateways and colorful ramparts blazing with diverse jewels.
Those who have conquered their senses and practice the divine Pāśupata vow are worshipped in all rites in order to propitiate that God.
Those who are devoted to the ash and engaged in recitation and meditation go to the state of Īśvara;
there, indeed, is the Lord, the Blessed One, the God of gods, the Stainless One.
Impelled by the ordinance of Śiva’s will, he exercises his authority;
fifteen worlds are to be purified in succession within the sphere of Īśvara.
O fair-faced one, one should know that at the time of initiation, above the palate is the pure enclosure;
and within that, two powers are traditionally taught.

Knowledge and action are renowned as the two sciences (vidyās), and beyond these, there is that which is designated as existence and non-existence; these are remembered as the two powers within that [reality].
Tejeśa and Dhruveśa are the supreme state of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas);
I shall now describe them according to their measure, situated above the veil of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇāvaraṇa).
Brahmā, Rudra, Pratoda, and Ananta as the fourth;
they know that the three Rudras are located there in the uppermost Pure Enclosure (Suśuddhāvaraṇa).
The one-eyed, tawny-colored Haṃsa has thus been described in brief;
above the enclosure of Śiva, there is one known as Dhruva.
Situated above the enclosure of liberation of Rudrarāja,
I shall now describe the eleven Rudras in brief.
Brahmādaṇḍin, Diṇḍimuṇḍa, and likewise Saurabha;
Janmamṛtyuhara and Praṇīta, who bestows both happiness and suffering.
It is declared that [the winds] are expanded and situated above the palate;
furthermore, one should know that above that lies the auspicious state of Nirañjana, known as Dhruva.
The triad of the Lord’s powers has been described in succession at the summit;
they are proclaimed as being contained within that which is designated as the power of will (icchā-śakti).
And I shall now briefly describe the awakened enclosure above:
Prīta, Pramudita, Pramoda, and Pralambaka.
Viṣṇu, Madana, Gahana, and likewise Prathita—
these are declared to be the eight Rudras, who should be known [as located] in order from the eastern direction onwards.
And I shall now briefly describe the obscuration of the commitments (samayāvaraṇa) above:
Prabhava, Samaya, Kṣudra, Vimala, and likewise Śiva.
Then Ghanas is proclaimed, and after that Nirañjana;
Rudra and Oṃkāra—know these five to be above the palate.
The fifty-nine worlds, beginning with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) and ending with Rudra and the syllable Om (oṃkāra), one should purify in their proper sequence at the time of initiation.
Each one has a retinue of many thousands of millions;
they are all three-eyed, granters of boons, and possess bodies of pure power.
Resembling pure crystal, with ten arms and the moon as their crest-jewel,
they all hold tridents in their hands and are adorned with crowns of matted hair.
All were endowed with every excellence, omniscient, and lords of all;
they were perfected in all the primary marks and adorned with every ornament.
Crowded with Rudra-maidens of divine and captivating forms,
they sport in excellent cities, impelled by the ordinances of Śiva’s will.
Likewise, above Īśvara and below Sadāśiva is the enclosure of Suśiva;
within that, Sadāśiva is to be known.
The god has fifteen eyes, with the crescent moon as his crest;
he is endowed with five faces and ten arms, and possesses great strength.
Resembling pure crystal, shimmering indeed with radiant splendor,
he is seated upon a lion throne, established on a white lotus seat.
Accompanied by the five limbs of Brahmā, endowed with Sakalā and the others,
joined by the ten Śivas, and attended by the eighteen Rudras.
He is the whole, the partless, the void, the one enriched with parts, the one who adorns the sky;
he is the destroyer, abiding at the end of destruction, and is remembered as the eighth, produced from the throat and the lips.
The God of gods, Sadāśiva, is to be known in the middle of the eyebrows;
the Lord is surrounded by Sakala and the others, as well as Oṃkāreśa and the rest, in due order.
Oṃkāreśa, Śiva, Dīpta, Kāraṇeśa, Daśeśaka, Suśiva, Kāleśa, Sūkṣmarūpa, and Sutejas.
And Śarva is declared as the tenth; they are situated up to the zenith.
There are eighteen Rudras outside of them; indeed, hear their names.
Then Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Svayambhū, Agnivīrarāja,
Raurava, Mukuṭa, Visara, Candra, and Bimba sang forth.
Lalita, Siddharudra, Santāna, and Śarva,
as well as Para, Kiraṇa, and Pārameśvara.
He who is called Sādākhya is known as Sakala, whose body consists of mantra;
he is the presiding cause of all, the agent of both emission and reabsorption.
And he is the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon practitioners who perform the rites;
seven crores of mantras are established upon his seat.
The seat is enriched with a hundred thousand petals and possesses the radiance of ten million moons;
it is endowed with five faces, each with three eyes, beginning with the Lord [Śiva] and starting from the left.
Surrounded by Tārā and other distinct Śaktis in the eastern direction,
Jñānaśakti stands on the left and Kriyāśakti on the right.
O Goddess, the supreme power of will (icchā-śakti) is that by which everything is presided over:
[namely] creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace. (SvaT 10.1204)
That [power] by which the Lord of Gods always performs everything on every path is seated upon his lap and is eternally inherent within his own self.
And that very will of Śiva, the God of gods, the Supreme Self,
is he himself in another form, possessing the great body of the five mantras.
The glorious Sadāśiva, the God of gods, assumes forms at will;
those who are called his powers (śaktis) are likewise indeed the leaders of the mantras.
O Goddess, each one is surrounded by billions of *arbuda* lotuses,
as well as by *kharva*, *nikharva*, and other corresponding lotuses of great power.
[They are] endowed with the forms of knowledge, possessing their own essential natures, possessed of immeasurable qualities,
complete with all the [major and minor] marks, and adorned with all ornaments.
Rich with laughter, dance, and graceful charms, with the movements of eyebrows agitated by intoxication,
they resemble hundreds of millions of moons and seem to pour forth nectar.
Together with them, the Rudras always sport at will by the power of the Lord,
in excellent cities that are auspicious on all sides and possess a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Freed from illusory phenomena, stainless and free from the fever of affliction,
they exercise their authority with the unfailing power of omniscience.
Upon the exhaustion of their [karmic] authority, they become peaceful, all-pervading, and auspicious;
impelled by the Supreme, they never again come into existence.
O fair-faced one, the enclosure of Suśiva is known to contain the essence of the mantra;
above that is the enclosure of Bindu, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
There, a lotus greatly radiant and endowed with ten koṭis [of petals] is present;
situated upon that lotus is the deity Śāntyatīta, possessed of great splendor.
Five-faced, large-eyed, ten-armed, and three-eyed,
he possesses the brilliance of a mass of a thousand lightning flashes and is adorned with shimmering rubies.
O lady of excellent vows, Nivṛtti, PratiṣṬhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti are known as the retinue of that Śāntyatīta.
In the left direction of that [deity], Śāntyatītā is situated;
all of them are said to have five faces, ten arms, and the crescent moon as their crest-ornament.
The reality of the bindu (bindutattva) has been fully described as being surrounded by hundreds of millions of cities;
above that is the half-moon (ardhacandra), and above that is the obstructress (nirodhikā).
These two, however, are great stations endowed with five sets of five kalās:
Jyotsnā, Jyotsnāvatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, Vimalā, and Śivā.
These indeed reside in the Half-moon; listen, O Dear One, regarding their presence in the Nirodhinī:
Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā.
The bindu is remembered as half a mātrā, and its own form consists of four kalās;
half of that is the ardhacandra, and its eighth part is the nirodhikā.
O fair-faced one, she brings about the cessation of the gods, beginning with Brahmā; she is renowned as Nirodhinī (the Obstructress), and having pierced through her, O fair-faced one— SvaT_10.1223.
By means of the supreme state called Sādākhya, his body consists of the five mantras;
above that, however, Nāda is remembered, possessing the radiance of pollen on a lotus filament.
It is pervaded by great beings whose radiance is like that of ten million times ten thousand suns;
I shall indeed describe their leaders, five in number, within this world.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā,
as well as Ūrdhvagā— this is declared to be the fifth Kalā.
Upon that [lotus] is a very extensive lotus, whereon stands the Lord, the Master of the Upper Realm;
he resembles ten million moons, has five faces, and three eyes.
The god has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, is peaceful, ten-armed, and possesses a massive body;
he is surrounded by Indhikā and others, holds a trident in his hand, and wears matted locks.
But his upward-moving *kalā* always goes to the lap [of Śiva];
from there, the world of Suṣumṇā exists, and Suṣumṇā is established therein.
The Lord of Suṣumṇā resides there, possessing the luster of ten million times ten thousand moons;
he has ten arms, three eyes, and is seated upon a white lotus.
The glorious one who has the moon as his crest, five-faced and of great body,
has the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* situated on the left and right respectively.
But Suṣumṇā, O lady of excellent hips, is grey like a particle of frost;
the goddess holds a white lotus in her hand and is adorned with a garland of lotuses.
The goddess, who has five faces, is richly adorned, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident; she should be meditated upon by practitioners and others as seated upon his lap.
Indeed, by her, the entire path—whether moving downward or upward—is bound;
for the resonance (nāda), which is the support of the channels, truly pierces through this entire world.
Having emerged from below by means of the downward power (adhaḥśakti) as far as the head of Brahmā above,
it dissolves into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) through the channel as the unmanifest, imperishable sound.
Residing within all beings, it vibrates through the power of Śiva;
knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one should purify that [path] in the sacrifice of Śiva.
Beyond that, one should know the Brahmabila, which is filled with billions of Rudras;
there, the supreme Brahmā is to be known, possessing the splendor of a hundred moons.
The Blessed One has ten arms and three eyes, five faces, and the moon as his crest-jewel;
he holds a trident in his hand and is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
But Brahmāṇī is the supreme Śakti who stands upon the path to liberation;
she remains stationed having blocked the gateway to the path of liberation.
She is the bestower of the path to liberation and is seated upon the lap of Brahmā;
having pierced her here, O fair-limbed one, you must proceed upward, my dear.
Above this, the power (śakti) remains in the form of a sleeping serpent;
she is the support of all worlds. O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe her to you.
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Anyā, Amṛtā, and Amitā—these should be known as pervasive in the center; the remaining [goddesses] follow in order starting from the east.
Having five faces and three eyes, they are highly radiant and possess great strength;
this is declared to be the Śakti-tattva. Listen now, O beloved, to the Śiva-tattva.
Surrounded on all sides by many excellent cities,
it was constructed with golden walls and adorned with jewels and rubies.
I shall now describe the worlds situated right there, which are endowed with all enjoyments in their entirety and from which all qualities of desire arise.
Pervasive and of the nature of space, infinite, without master, and without support,
the pentad of causes is established within the principle of Śiva.
Therein is a lotus, vast and extensive, arising from the infinite and the limitless;
and situated in the center of that lotus is this deity, the Unconditioned.
He bears five faces, is peaceful, omniscient, and the Supreme Lord;
he has ten arms, is greatly radiant, and is the agent of creation and destruction.
He is the benefactor of all, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him,
the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and possesses a radiance equal to ten million billion suns.
The god is adorned all over with a shimmering crest-jewel,
wears divine garments, and is anointed with divine perfumes.
With his chest raised in the lotus posture, wearing the moon as his crest-ornament,
seated upon a jeweled couch, and fanned by the waving of chowries.
Adorned on all sides by hosts of millions and billions of Rudras,
she is all-pervading, of the nature of space, infinite, and without a protector or support.
They have five faces, great heroism, ten arms, and the moon as their crest;
they possess three eyes, hold tridents in their hands, and are endowed with the causal principles.
These [energies] are established starting from the east and ending with the north;
however, the Lord, the imperishable one, remains situated in the center, unsupported.
The goddess Anāśritakalā is seated upon his lap;
thus indeed has the Śiva-tattva been described to you, O beautiful one.
Having purified that, what is above it is known as the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti);
she is to be understood by the name Samanā, and beyond the mind (manas), nothing further arises.
But for all the causal principles situated in their successive order, from Earth up to Śiva, she stands established as their active agent.
She, presided over by Śiva, sustains many eggs;
mounted upon them, Śiva, the supreme cause, acts.
The Great Lord, the cause of all causes, is the agent who brings about creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.
That power which is called *samanā* is known as its instrument;
by means of it, the Lord of the Gods presides over the five lower causes.
This dependent cause belongs to the God who is himself independent;
indeed, he further impels the Lord of the World, who is without a protector.
The infinite Ananta, who is himself without a protector,
should awaken the Lord, the Great God, who is all-pervading, whose form is space, and who pervades the void.
The pervasive one is his instrument, and the Lord is indeed the agent;
Māyā, which exists in the form of action, stands below him as the coiled power (śaktikuṇḍalī).
O virtuous lady, the emergence of the universe—from the effects consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, up to Sadāśiva and beginning with the earthly element—arises from that [source]. (SvaT 10.1264)
All that should be known as *prākṛta* (evolvent), joined with destruction and origination;
it is that power (*śakti*) which was previously described as *samanā* at the summit of the path.

Having meditated upon her, who is radiant with infinite light and possesses the splendor of a thousand shimmering suns, the knower of the ritual procedure should invoke her and cause her to be established.
Then, having performed the ritual service (upacāra), as well as the invocation of Vāgīśī,
her installation, her worship, and likewise the sacrifice of the victim (paśu).
Likewise, [he teaches] the authority regarding the conception and birth [of the embryo],
as well as yoga, enjoyment, dissolution, and immediately thereafter, expiation.

O fair-faced one, having performed the fire-oblation for the lords of the worlds and for those dwelling in the worlds, as well as the oblation for the worlds themselves according to the appropriate method; SvaT 10.1269.
Then one should purify the three principles (tritattva) and the constituent parts in their proper order;
having performed the separation and the severing of the bonds, one should indeed cast down the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, having performed the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta*), the Guru should consecrate the scissors with mantras;
having cut off the topknot and offered it, he should bathe the child.
The preceptor, having become purified and performed the rites of sakalīkaraṇa and so forth,
having placed his topknot at the tip of the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and offered oblations, should immediately thereafter bathe.
O fair-faced one, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor,
after performing the rite for the disciple as well, should worship the Śiva-kumbha.
One should worship Bhairavāgni, who resides in the central region as Bhairava;
having completed the full oblation according to the rule while recollecting the Vāma mantra.
One should recite that [mantra] with effort according to the previously stated characteristics; O fair-faced one, one should contemplate it while casting down the path of what is to be abandoned.
As long as that state is with-mind (samanā), it is known as power (śakti); above that is the state beyond-mind (unmanā).
Herein there is no time, no digits, no movement, no ontological principle (tattva), and no deities.
Perfect nirvāṇa, the supreme purity, is said to be the mouth of the Guru;
O lady of excellent hips, that which transcends it is the supreme, stainless reality.
Through the application of the Guru’s oral instruction, one should be joined to that eternal,
unshakable state, which transcends all causes, is free from passion, stainless, pure, and auspicious.
O sinless one, this path has indeed been described by me in brief as being within the omniscient, supreme reality, which transcends space and is beyond the senses.
Having understood this, O Great Goddess, one attains the supreme state—
within the body, within the deity, within the disciple, and indeed within the flask, in the midst of the fire.
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one is liberated and liberates others as well.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
The eleventh chapter begins.
[Verse 129 is a two-line verse.]
158. This is a six-pāda verse.
Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace this path has been understood by me."
O Lord, the creation of the world has been indicated by you, but not fully described.
"O Mahādeva, please graciously explain the creation of the time-periods (adhvan).
Śrī Bhairava said:
"That subtle, supreme deity, the all-pervading cause, is Śiva."
O lady of excellent vows, he has been described here as the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa);
without desire, he brings forth the entire world, both mobile and immobile.
O beautiful lady, having effortlessly agitated the sky with his own splendor,
that which was thus agitated through its inherent nature is declared to be the material cause.
Therefore, that which has arisen from the void is the void; from the void arises the emergence of touch, and from that the nāda has arisen, as was indeed previously told to you.
O Goddess of the gods, that manifest [sound] is eightfold according to its various distinctions:
resonance (ghoṣa), roar (rāva), tone (svana), sound (śabda), that which is called the burst (sphoṭa), and indeed vibration (dhvani).
The sounds *jhāṅkāra* and *dhvaṅkṛta* are proclaimed as [the first] eight;
the ninth, however, is the Great Sound (*mahāśabda*), which is remembered as pervading them all.
Because he always resounds while abiding within all beings,
the god Sadāśiva is indeed manifest as the very nature of vision and action.
From the *nāda* the *bindu* is produced, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it should be known as tenfold, bestowing the fruits of the ten principles (*tattvas*).
Sadāśiva is to be known as arising from the Bindu, endowed with ten forms according to the ten phonemes and joined with the ten deities; he is accompanied by his eightfold division of limbs.
He is endowed with the five Brahmakalās and the Śaktis who are the limbs of knowledge,
and he is fully possessed of the five great knowledges and the [five] forms.
That very same immutable Śiva, the Supreme Self, exists in two states; he should be known as both that which consists of utterance and that which is devoid of utterance.
And he himself is again twofold by way of the nature of mudrā and mantra; [he is also twofold] by way of the nature of action and knowledge, and by way of the nature of will and form.
In the form of the comprehension of sound, by way of the essential nature of the reality of things,
it is gross, subtle, supreme, and even beyond the supreme— the stainless one.
O Goddess of gods, in the Śiva-āgama, Śiva is to be known as having the nature of space, as well as being Samana and Unmanā, and as transcending Unmanā.
The state of Unmanā and Samanā is presided over by Śiva;
below that, he exists again in the form of the five causes.
O Goddess, having presided over the pentad of causes below,
he is the pervasive one situated at the head of power, beyond the door of the cavity and unconditioned.
And Ananta is the Lord of Suṣumṇā, while Anātha and likewise Ūrdhvaga,
O Great Goddess, are proclaimed as Bindvīśa, whose form is space.
Brahmā himself remains established, presiding over that which is without support;
likewise, Viṣṇu is called "the protectorless," and Rudra is indeed "the infinite."
Vyomarūpīśvara is proclaimed, as well as the pervasive Sadāśiva;
furthermore, O Goddess, the all-pervading Hāṭaka is the Supreme Lord.
O Goddess of gods, he is endowed with hosts of sciences and mantras, the lord of the seven netherworlds; he is Ananta himself, Rudra, whose form is the fire of time.
O Great Goddess, the Lord Hūhuka stands as one who is without protector, abiding in the formless within the path, the sustainer, and indeed remains without support.
Relying upon his own power, he is the one who has sung of you as the "unsupported" (anāśrita);
O fair-faced one, the entire universe, up to the state of Unmanī, is supported by him.
Established upon the summit of the water is Hūhuka, the support of Śakti;
below that is the water element (aptattva), and immediately after that is the fire element (āgneya).
The subtle elements of air and space, the sense organs,
the objects of the senses, the mind, and the ego-principle follow in this sequence.
O Goddess of gods, [the principles are] the Buddhist, the secondary, the natural, and likewise the personal; as well as necessity, time, passion, knowledge, and also limited agency.
The principle of Māyā, as well as Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva;
then Bindu, Ardhendu, Nirodhī, Nāda, and beyond that, the Nāḍī.
Below that, O Goddess, is the Brahmabila; beyond that is the Śaktitattva;
and beyond that is Vyāpinī, conjoined with the five causes.
O Dear One, the Samanā and Unmanā [energies] are joined with the Prakriyāṇḍas;
thus indeed the Prakriyāṇḍa is situated both below and above.
O Goddess, in this manner, such [atomic particles] are established everywhere— below, below, above, and above—
in numbers as infinite as those of the atoms of the self.
In this way, indeed, there are countless and manifold cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*);
O beloved, by describing just one here, the entire temporal path (*adhvan*) has been described.

For just as it is with one, so it is with all; the egg of manifestation (prakriyāṇḍa) exists, O beloved, in its own essential nature within all the eggs of manifestation, O lady of virtuous vows. (SvaT 11.32)
Śiva, however, is all-pervasive, subtle, and situated both outside and within;
he is free from all excellence and devoid of all causes.
Free from creation and destruction, his sphere of experience transcends the phenomenal world;
stainless, pure, and peaceful, he is established as neither below nor above.
Just as space has no top, no middle, and no bottom anywhere,
so too is the Lord Śiva, the supreme cause, omnipresent.
O Goddess, pervading the entire universe, you abide like space within spaces;
knowing this, O lady of excellent limbs, one shall not undergo birth again.
Furthermore, I shall briefly explain the pervasion of the causes:
Brahmā is established as the presiding deity within the principle of earth.
Viṣṇu is established in the principle of water, Rudra is situated in fire,
Īśvara is in the principle of wind, and Sadāśiva is in space.
O lady of virtuous vows, Āditya is remembered as Brahmā, and Soma as Viṣṇu;
Rudra is the lord of the planets, and likewise the sovereign of the constellations.
O Goddess of gods, the sacrificer is himself the god Sadāśiva;
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā, and Vāma is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu.
Aghora is said to be Rudra, and likewise Puruṣa is Īśvara;
but Īśāna, O lady of beautiful hips, is the god Sadāśiva himself.
Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda;
Aghora is the Sāmaveda, and Puruṣa is called the Atharvaveda.
And Īśāna, the best of the gods, is remembered as the essence of all knowledge;
O Goddess, worldly discernment has emerged from Sadyojāta.
O fair-faced one, the Vedic [knowledge] emerged from Vāmadeva, the spiritual (ādhyātmika) from Aghora, and that which is called Atimārga from Puruṣa.
But the great knowledge known as Mantra has emerged from Īśāna; listen again, O lady of excellent vows, to its division according to the principles (tattva). SvaT 11.45.
O Goddess of gods, Brahmā is established pervading the twenty-four principles up to Pradhāna; Janārdana, however, pervades the principle of Puruṣa.
Then Rudra stands pervading everything up to Niyati and Māyā;
likewise, the principle of Vidyā is pervaded by Īśvara.
Above [all], the Lord Sadāśiva remains pervading everything;
O lady of excellent vows, I shall explain this again according to the division of the three principles (tattvas).
Brahmā is established in the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) and up to the end of Māyā;
likewise, Viṣṇu [is established] in the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) as far as the domain of the Unnameable (sādākhya).
Likewise, O fair-faced one, Rudra is to be known within the Śiva-tattva;
he stands pervading the entire path above the Sādākhya level.
He whose self is presided over by Raudrī is indeed proclaimed as Rudra;
Viṣṇu is pervaded by Vāmā, and the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) by Jyeṣṭhā.
Brahmā is known as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), Janārdana as the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the supreme Rudra as the power of will (icchā-śakti); he is celebrated as Śiva.
Viṣṇu, the god Sadāśiva, Brahmā, and likewise Īśvara;
O Goddess, the Lord Īśvara was born from Śiva as Sadāśiva.
From that [Māyā] arises Vidyā, and from Vidyā, in turn, arises Īśvara;
by his own will, the Supreme Lord [creates him] with the tip of the hand of the power of knowledge.
O observer of good vows, he should emanate seventy million mantras, consisting of knowledge and action,
beginning with the earth element and ending with that which is called Sādākhya.
Abiding in the world, they bestow grace upon embodied beings;
pervaded by the power of Śiva, they possess three eyes and the moon as their crest-ornament.
This one Śiva, the supreme cause, the wielder of the trident, endowed with Māyā, remains pervading the universe in manifold ways through the forms of Rudra.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, having observed with the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti),
he is entered by the power of will (icchā-śakti) and, O lady of excellent vows, by the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, eternal, all-pervasive, and imperishable;
having placed his own group of selves within it, the Lord simultaneously agitates them.
Furthermore, when a badarī fruit is struck by a gentle blow,
its seeds emerge, briefly, in all directions— sideways, upward, and downward.
But those here who are the vessels for liberation and who have been meditated upon by Śiva—
all of them go upwards to Śiva, who is supremely stainless.
Those who are vessels for knowledge indeed become the form of mantras as animals;
however, those who possess impurity, karma, and kalās are vessels for saṃsāra.
They go downward here upon this terrible and most cruel path;
from that, Kalā is produced, as well as Vidyā and Rāga.
Time, the principle of necessity (niyatitattva), the principle of the person (puṃstattva), and likewise primordial nature (prakṛti);
furthermore, goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas) are the three qualities of primordial nature.
Sattva is that which produces illumination; rajas is that which produces activity;
tamas is declared to be that which causes obstruction—these three qualities (guṇas) are to be known.
Sattva is proclaimed as Brahmā, rajas as Viṣṇu, and tamas as Rudra.
In the state of Brahmā he creates the worlds; in the state of Viṣṇu, he is the cause of their maintenance.
In his state as Rudra, he withdraws this entire world of moving and non-moving beings, as well as the three states belonging to it: waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

Intellect (dhiṣaṇā) is born from the qualities (guṇas) and is endowed with various states of being; Brahmā is established there in the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) by virtue of his sovereignty.
The Buddhists call him alone the Omniscient One, the supreme state;
and among the qualities of the Arhats, he is the foremost for the proponents of the Vedas.
O Mistress of the Gods, the *pauruṣa* [nature] of the Sāṃkhyas is devoid of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
and in the Yoga scripture, the supreme state is the twenty-sixth principle.
In the Pāśupata vow, the supreme state of Īśvara is proclaimed;
in the Mausula and Kārūka [traditions], the principle of Māyā is celebrated.
Kṣemeśa is the lord of the Brahmans; that is their supreme state. Tejeśa is the lord of the Vaimalas, and his is the eternal place in Pramāṇa.
One whose self is purified by initiation and knowledge, having maintained the practice until the end of the body and having undertaken the skull-vow (kapālavrata), goes to his own respective state.
Those who are devoted to the practice of recitation and the application of sacred ash attain the state of Īśvara;
indeed, the supreme state of the Śaivas transcends all paths.
O Dear One, from the principle of intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra) is born again in three ways;
it is proclaimed as being sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa.
The Bhūtādi is threefold, existing as the Vaikṛta and the Taijasa;
from that Bhūtādi, the subtle elements (tanmātras) arise, and from those, it produced the gross elements.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these five are known as the subtle elements (tanmātras) in their respective order.
From sound, space (ākāśa) was produced; likewise, from touch, wind (vāyu);
from form, fire (tejas) was produced; and from taste, water (āpas) was born.
From fragrance, however, the earth was born; this has been told to you in brief.
Furthermore, from that Vaikārika [ego], the organs of action were born.
The organ of speech, the hands, the feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth—these five organs of action arise from the Taijasa (fiery) ego.
Furthermore, the five organs of cognition likewise arise from it.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these are the organs;
the mind is said to be of both natures, pervading all the senses.
O beautiful one, those which assist the self have been explained according to their true nature:
the self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the outer self (bāhyātman).
I shall explain these briefly: the selfless, the supreme self, and the self;
likewise, the ignorant, the wise, and the one who is becoming wise.
I shall tell you again of the awakened and the well-awakened,
who, relying on the equilibrium of the primary matter (pradhāna), is free from pleasure and pain.
O Goddess, when one abides in that, then he is called the Self;
yet, due to the conjunction with the *puryaṣṭaka*, he wanders through all wombs.
That inner self is to be known as bound by good and evil deeds,
joined with the organs of intellect and action, and enveloped by the great elements.
But at that time, O Goddess, the external self always experiences sense objects;
it is devoid of the existence of the elements and abandoned by even a fraction of the qualities of reality.
When the self is conjoined with the single nature of impurity and obscured by the nature of illusion, it should then be known as "selfless"; thereafter, the supreme self is described.
O Dear One, when one is liberated from impurity, karma, kalā, and the rest, having transcended all paths and being freed from the delusion of māyā; SvaT 11.89.
O Goddess, when it attains stainlessness— that supreme, imperishable state— then the Lord is called the imperishable Supreme Self.
Furthermore, O Goddess, I shall explain briefly for the unawakened:
[the process] within the range from the dissolution of the self consisting of reality down to the earth and the kalās.
Having indeed withdrawn [the universe] during the night of equality with Māyā, the Supreme Lord remains without activity until its emergence once again.
For there is an absence of pleasure, pain, and so forth for the group of selves due to their karma;
the self is deluded by impurity and sleep, with its consciousness, vision, and action obstructed.
O fair-faced one, it does not perceive sounds and the like, nor does it perceive itself;
O beloved, it does not perceive its cause, nor its own place.
Since his faculty of sight and action has been lost, he remains there unaware of all this,
as long as the illusion lasts until the break of day.
The ignorant one has thus been described; now, learn from me about the wise one as well:
when karma has reached full maturity and is drawn forth by the will of the Lord.
Just as the sun favors the visual light of the eyes,
so too does the Lord favor the instruments of the selves.
When consciousness is awakened by *kalā* and its sphere of experience is revealed by *vidyā*,
*rāga*— characterized by the bliss of sense objects— functions as its coloring agent.
Time indeed impels this [individual soul], from the momentary *tuṭi* up to the final dissolution;
and Necessity eternally and invariably joins him with the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Having attained that state of being a person within the reality called Puruṣa, it is neither less nor more than a thousandth part of an atom.
The city is said to be the primary [principle], crowded with manifold manifestations;
because he nourishes that city, he is indeed remembered as Puruṣa.
For Śrīkaṇṭhanātha, by means of destiny and karma, might improperly ensnare the bound soul (paśu) with the net of primary fetters (pradhānapāśa).
The intellect (buddhi), having awakened through the bondage of the three qualities (guṇas) by means of the *vaikārika* [sattva],
is firmly bound by the bondage of the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the sense organs, and enveloped by the gross elements (bhūta).
Bound in this way, he indeed wanders within the realm of the earth and other spheres beginning with Māyā;
therefore, he is called a "saṃsārī" (one who transmigrates) because he wanders again and again.
Since objects such as sound and so forth exist, there is therefore a subject;
he says that objects are "beyond" [the subject], having spread out through various distinctions.
Pervaded by that state, one experiences various ripenings of karma;
because one experiences in this way, therefore one is called the "experiencer" (bhoktṛ).
In that field, O lady of excellent limbs, the knower of it is like a farmer who,
having perceived a great desire, plows with the plowshares of greed.
With a state of delusion, one should always scatter the seeds consisting of dharma and adharma throughout the mind, speech, and body.
Therefore, indeed, from that arises the sprout which brings about the emergence of the fruits of pleasure and pain;
it grows through desire and anger, being thoroughly watered by the water of passion.
In whatever place, at whatever time, and at whatever age a wholesome or unwholesome action was sown, one reaps its fruit at that very time.
The wise one experiences various forms [of experience] through the power of past karma;
because he understands this, he is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
Because he perceives objects, he is proclaimed as "Budha" (the Awakened);
yet when that same person contemplates them in an undesirable form, [he is called otherwise].
But when he is awakening at that time, I shall now tell you:
when he feels revulsion for enjoyments, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious.
Relying on supreme detachment, one should consider these very things to be artificial;
for one understands that everything from the realm of Māyā down to the earth is but a magical illusion.
Sons, friends, wives, well-wishers, kinsmen, and relatives—
whatever wealth has been acquired by me, whether by auspicious or inauspicious means.
But all these others shall enjoy it, free from fear and free from distress;
and I alone shall go to the abode of Yama.
Therefore, these [senses] are indeed not auspicious; they are enemies who bring about misfortune.
This very body, moreover, is constantly loathed by its own master.
Born from semen and blood, corrupted by the serpents of sense-objects,
crowded with various diseases, and agitated by the fear of old age and death.
Thus, being covered in impurity, how could I find delight here?
With a mind constantly agitated, one should indeed reflect upon this again and again.
"O Goddess of gods, how may liberation from this difficult-to-transcend saṃsāra be attained? Thus awakened, one should be absorbed in That and have That as one's supreme goal. (SvaT 11.120)
Then, being liberated from all undertakings, one is said to be "freed"; such a person is declared to be "awakened. Now hear from me concerning the "perfectly awakened."
O you of excellent vows, when one has attained the supreme station—which transcends the paths and is free from all affliction—through initiation, knowledge, yoga, and conduct; SvaT 11.122.
Stainless, immaculate, peaceful, its sphere of activity transcending conceptual proliferation,
unshakable, beyond causes, omniscient, and facing in all directions.
Indeed, he is perfectly satisfied, the primordial Buddha, autonomous, eternal,
possessing unimpaired power and majesty, supremely awakened, and everlasting.
One who is joined to that, whose self is absorbed in it, and who is indeed endowed with its qualities,
is said to be "thoroughly awakened," according to the word of Bhairava.
And without initiation, there is no eligibility for yoga in the Śaiva tradition.
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the various distinctions of internal states (bhāva).
O Dear One, there are thirteen instruments (the ten organs and the three internal faculties) and the object of action is tenfold;
furthermore, there are eleven defects of the senses, and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is indeed threefold.
Intellect is indeed eightfold, while error is fivefold;
I shall state their respective names according to their classification in due order.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well.
Smell, taste, and the subtle element of form, as well as touch and sound— these five are indeed declared to be the subtle elements (tanmātras).
This has been proclaimed as your tenfold function according to the number of names;
they know [the organs] to be speech, hands, feet, the anus, and likewise the generative organ.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose— O Goddess, these are proclaimed as the external instruments, established in a tenfold manner.
The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is traditionally held to be threefold, consisting of mind (manas), ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and intellect (buddhi).
Deafness, lameness, crippledness, as well as the inability to discharge [semen], [are its functions]. (SvaT 11.133)
One should recognize a loss of joy as well as deafness,
the withering of the limbs, and likewise blindness.
Lack of relish, lack of fragrance, and instability of the mind—
these are declared to be the eleven impairments of the faculties (indriyavadha) in their respective order.
"O lady of excellent complexion, I have declared to you that the ego (ahaṅkāra) is threefold: the Taijasa, the one called Vaikṛta, and the Bhūtādi as the third."
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty as the fourth;
likewise, adharma, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty.
These eight qualities of the intellect (buddhi), beginning with dharma, have been fully described:
tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and another, viparyaya.
Andhatāmisra—thus are the five misconceptions described;
these fifty varieties of states have been explained in their proper order.
Furthermore, regarding those eight divisions of the intellect that are established as dharma and so forth—
I shall explain to you how their subdivisions are differentiated.
She binds the person in seven ways on the path of saṃsāra;
yet, through the state of knowledge, she liberates those men who delight in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
Knowledge is declared to be of the nature of sattva; the other three are remembered as being rājasa, and the four beginning with adharma are indeed tāmasa, O fair-faced one.
Dharma is said to be tenfold, and knowledge is traditionally remembered as eightfold;
likewise, dispassion is ninefold, and they know sovereignty to be eightfold.
These very same qualities, when inverted, are proclaimed as non-dharma and so forth:
namely, freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile—
thus, O fair-faced one, has the tenfold Dharma been described.
Tāra, Sutāra, Taraṇa, Tāraka, and Pramodaka;
likewise Pramudita, Ramyaka, and Sadāpramudita.
O Supreme Goddess, this knowledge has been fully explained in brief:
Ambhā, Salilā, Odhā, and another known as Vṛṣṭi.
Sutārā, Supārā, Sunetrā, and Parā are remembered;
the eighth is Kumārī, and likewise Uttamāmbhasikā.
I have indeed described to you the ninefold dispassion,
as well as the powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), and extension (prāpti).

Likewise, there is irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and supreme mastery (vaśitva); the eighth is proclaimed as the power of determining things according to one's desire (yatrakāmāvasāyitva).
O fair-faced one, the eightfold sovereignty has indeed been described;
likewise, anger, lack of service to the guru, and impurity follow thereafter.
Lack of contentment, crookedness, violence, and untruthfulness,
as well as theft, unchastity, and likewise deceitful conduct.
Thus, this compendium of the Dharma has been explained in ten ways:
Atāra, Asutāra, and also Atāraṇa.
And the fourth, O Goddess of Gods, is proclaimed as Atāraka;
likewise Apramoda, Apramudita, and also Aramyaka.
That ignorance is likewise eightfold: Asadā, Apramuditā, Anambhā, Asalilā, Anogha, and Vṛṣṭi, as well as Ajñānā.
Beyond this, one should know the Asutāra, the Asupāra, the Asunetra,
the Akumārī, and likewise the Uttamāmbhasikā.
O Maheśvarī, [the powers] are indeed aṇimā, laghimā, and mahimā;
as well as aprāpti, aprākāmya, and likewise anīśitva.
Lack of mastery, as well as the inability to resolve things according to one's will, and lack of sovereignty— O Goddess of the Gods, these are proclaimed to be eightfold.
And by means of these, such as lack of sovereignty, the Piśācas and others are presided over.
I shall now describe to you how these eight are established within them in sequence:
indeed, lack of sovereignty resides in the Piśāca [state], and lack of dispassion in the Rākṣasa.
That ignorance exists in the Yakṣa [world], and indeed unrighteousness in the Gāndharva;
likewise, righteousness exists in the Aindra [world], while knowledge is established in the Saumya.
In the realm of Prajāpati, however, there is detachment, while sovereignty is established in Brahman;
this [sovereignty] consists of sixty-four qualities and is situated in the station of Brahmā.
That [merit] established in the Prājāpatya rite is fifty-sixfold;
it is proclaimed to be forty-eightfold in the Saumya rite.
O Goddess, the sovereignty of Mahendra is said to possess forty qualities,
while the sovereignty of the Gandharvas is said to possess thirty-two qualities.
The Yakṣa [mantra] is known to possess twenty-four qualities; the Rākṣasa is said to have sixteen;
and the Paiśāca is proclaimed to be eightfold in its sovereign power.
O observer of good vows, that sovereignty remains thus established among the divine classes;
others likewise abide among the divine classes in seven distinct forms.
These very [qualities], becoming thoroughly intermingled among human beings,
exist in various states down to the level of stationary objects, according to their primary or subordinate status.
I shall indeed explain the pervasion of the three qualities as it truly exists:
the gods, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Indra, are presided over by *sattva*.
Gandharvas, yakṣas, and humans are of the rājasa nature, while daityas,
yātudhānas, and piśācas are proclaimed to be tāmasa.
The sages of firm vows are to be known as those in whom rajas and sattva predominate;
they are established upon the earth, mutually overcoming one another.
Those who are completely pervaded by darkness— namely, immobile beings, reptiles,
and those devoid of feet— are proclaimed to be tāmasa.
O lady of excellent vows, those beginning with reptiles and ending with stationary beings are to be known;
within these, there are indeed infinite other wombs as well.
Likewise, among human beings, those infinite varieties cannot indeed be fully described due to the infinite establishment of distinctions arising from the endless differentiation of karma.
But in the world of humans, virtues such as dharma and the like are firmly established; O lady of excellent vows, those various forms of knowledge are bound to dharma and the other virtues.
I shall now explain to you those [treatises] which exist among unrighteous doctrines and other such works,
as well as that treatise on logic in the world which mocks the concepts of permanence and impermanence.
For those who are uncertain engage in disputes through formal debate, wrangling, and cavil; their statements, though grounded in logical reasons, are devoid of reality, O lady of excellent vows.
But for those devoid of the yoga of knowledge and lacking a deity,
no certainty whatsoever arises regarding dharma, artha, kāma, or mokṣa.
Bound by ignorance and motivated by unrighteousness,
those men who take delight therein go to hell.
O beautiful lady, due to a lack of dispassion and a lack of mastery, those four always experience suffering in hell; they are ever-givers of pain in the underworld.
Because they cause delusion for all living beings, they are remembered as being of the nature of darkness (tāmasa);
for worldly knowledge, O Goddess of Gods, is bound by dharma alone.
O lady of excellent vows, the Pāñcarātra, the Vaidika, the Buddhist, and the Ārhata systems are all bound to the knowledge of Dharma through dispassion alone.
O Pārvatī, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya is indeed connected with knowledge and dispassion;
but knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established upon the knowledge of Yoga.
The transcendence of the states of cognition is proclaimed as the *atimārga* (the path beyond);
that knowledge which transcends the world is traditionally known as the *atimārga*.
The worlds are said to be the sacrificial animals on the path of creation and destruction;
those who are established on the transcendent path (atimārga) should be known as having passed beyond them.
Those who observe the skull-vow (kapālavratinaḥ) and likewise those who are Pāśupatas—
for them, no creation exists, as they remain fixed in the eternal Lord.
Because they will go to liberation, which is the cause of no further rebirth;
whereas for worldly beings there is only repeated creation and repeated dissolution.
Mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra, they wander like a water-wheel,
O Dear One, on that eight-spoked wheel joined with the spokes of dharma and the other [qualities].
O Goddess, presided over by Īśvara and eternally struck by the staff [of time],
pierced by impurity, karma, and kalā, it revolves with the force of time.
O Beloved, those who take delight in worldly and such other forms of knowledge,
those who are devoted to the treatises on logic, and others who are performers of evil deeds— [they do not see me].
Deluded by this wheel, they all do not see its end;
those who are to be accomplished among the worldly and other [levels] fall within the range of the limit of the supreme path.
One may effortlessly accomplish all things within the highly exalted knowledge of Śiva;
for that [knowledge] is indeed accomplished by no others, since it is exceedingly pure.
O Goddess, because one is joined to non-existence in the supreme state—
non-existence which transcends conceptualization and whose sphere transcends all manifold elaboration.
It is free from mind, intellect, and the like; devoid of causal discourse; transcending direct perception and other means of valid cognition; the sovereign and the imperishable.
Beyond all logic and scripture, devoid of fetters and mantras,
omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, stainless, and undisturbed.
For it is the one whose nature consists of all powers, independent, without protector, and without beginning;
it is liberated from all excellence and devoid of beginningless existence.
The supreme Śaiva knowledge is traditionally held to transcend the state of all-knowingness;
thus, O fair-faced one, have the principles (tattvas) and the forms of knowledge been created.
By means of these principles, the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has been emitted;
likewise, the various worlds by the hundreds and thousands.
Various scriptures established within the interior of reality, as well as specialized knowledge, sorcery, craftsmanship, and the characteristics of the multitude of supernatural attainments.
Everything is to be understood within the principles (tattvas), and it is seen within all the principles;
for it is through these principles that the ritual procedure and the initiation of Śiva are obtained.
There is no liberation equal to initiation; there is no knowledge higher than Mātṛkā;
there is no wisdom superior to the Prakriyā; and there is no yoga that is without a sign.
All that has been told, O Goddess, in the great ocean of Śiva-knowledge;
thus has emanation been fully described, and now maintenance and withdrawal are being spoken of.
An eighth part of a human blink is known as a *kṣaṇa*;
two *kṣaṇas* should be understood as a *tuṭi*, and two of those are known as a *lava*.
Two lava-s are to be known as one nimeṣa according to the sequence of calculation;
fifteen nimeṣas are proclaimed to be one kāṣṭhā.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are to be known as one *kalā*, and thirty of those constitute a *muhūrta*.
Furthermore, thirty *muhūrtas* make up a human day and night (*ahorātra*).
O beloved lotus-eyed one, three hundred and sixty days and nights are to be known as one human year.
A full hundred years is to be known as the human lifespan;
fifteen days and nights, however, are proclaimed to be one fortnight.
Two fortnights constitute a month, and twice that is a season (ṛtu).
Two seasons make a period (kāla), and three of each of these make a solstice (ayana).
O lady of excellent hips, by those two together a year is proclaimed;
the southern course is night, and the northern course is day.
That is a day and night for the ancestors; by this reckoning, a year is as before.
Likewise, that is a day and night for the gods; there too, a year and so forth are as before.
O Goddess, a cycle of four ages (caturyuga) is to be known as consisting of twelve thousand years;
it is composed of four thousand years for each [age] in due order.
O Goddess, Tretā is to be known as lasting for three [thousand years], and Dvāpara is remembered as lasting for two;
O Beloved, Kali is to be understood as lasting for one thousand years.
I shall now describe the measure of the two twilights in each age:
in the Kṛta age, four hundred [years] are proclaimed as its beginning and its end.

Three hundred years are to be known [as the duration] in the Tretā age, two hundred in the Dvāpara, and one hundred in the Kali age; this is remembered as the measure of the transitional periods (saṃdhyā).
But according to worldly calculation, I shall tell you again:
thirty-four million and twenty thousand.
But according to worldly calculation, O Goddess, this is the number for a cycle of four ages; furthermore, I shall tell you the duration of each individual age.
Ten million seven hundred twenty-eight thousand;
this is the measure of the Kṛta age. Now I shall tell you about the Tretā age.
The measure of the Tretā Yuga is twelve hundred thousand and ninety-six thousand; now learn from me the measure of the Dvāpara Yuga.
O you of virtuous vows, the measure of the Dvāpara age is eight hundred thousand and sixty-four thousand years; now I shall tell you the measure of the Kali age.
Forty-four hundred thousand years— this, O virtuous lady, is said to be the measure of the Kali age in brief.
O Goddess, this measurement is in human years for each age;
seventy-one cycles of the four ages constitute one Manvantara.
The measurement [of time] by means of the ages (yugas), excluding the period of twilight (saṃdhyāmāna), is proclaimed as the standard measure of the ages.
This measurement by divine reckoning is recorded as the standard for a manvantara.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall tell you again according to the worldly conventions: there are sixty-seven hundred thousand and thirty million [years].
O beloved Goddess of the gods, the measure of a Manvantara should be known as twenty thousand [years];
O Queen of the gods, a Kalpa consists of fourteen Manvantaras.
When one Manvantara has passed and another has arrived again,
there is always a transitional period (sandhyā) in between lasting five thousand years.
A thousand [cycles] of all [the ages] at the beginning and likewise again at the end constitute a *kalpa*,
which is declared to be a day of Brahmā, consisting of a thousand sets of four ages (*caturyuga*).
Furthermore, I shall tell you again according to the divine reckoning of years:
it is one koṭi and twenty lakṣas of years.
By divine measure alone, a single day of Brahmā occurs;
the period of the twilight (saṃdhyā) is proclaimed to consist of ninety-six thousand [such days].
But according to worldly calculation, I shall now tell you:
four times ten million and three hundred million years.
O Goddess of the gods, two crores are remembered as the day of Brahmā;
the twilight is proclaimed to be three crores and five hundred thousand.
Likewise, there are forty and sixty thousand;
such indeed is the final junction, and the morning junction is equal to that as well.
O Dear One, this stability of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) together with the hells,
as well as of the seven worlds, has thus been proclaimed.
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I describe to you the withdrawal:
at the end of Brahmā’s own day, that indeed is called the dissolution of the kalpa.
In a single day of Brahmā, fourteen Indras,
having ruled in succession according to the arrangement of the Manvantaras, pass away.
Then, O Goddess, when the Grandfather is asleep, he withdraws the entire universe, whose range extends to the end of the seven worlds; thereafter, the Fire of Time gazes upward.
One should indeed cast forth a great flame from his right face;
from that face, a great flame extends for a hundred thousand yojanas.
Blazing upward with intense speed and difficult to endure,
it ascends through those worlds where beings reside and those who dwell in the nether regions.
When pleasure, pain, and their combination have been exhausted and delusion has largely subsided,
they all become mere existence in the realm of Brahmā.
Those fools remain [in that state] as long as Brahmā does not awaken, until there is again the rising of the fruits of their actions, such as pleasure and pain.
Those who are the lords of the world of Rudra and the lords of the netherworlds,
as well as the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Hāṭakas, and others, remain there, exceedingly pure.
They remain inactive as long as the creation does not arise again;
while the worlds have become empty, an irresistible flame burns.
O Goddess, she would burn the hells and the netherworlds on all sides;
she burns even the three worlds, as far as the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar.
And by smoke, O fair-faced one, the three worlds—
known as Mahājana, Tapaḥ, and Satyaloka— are destroyed, O lady of virtuous vows.
Those whose minds are deluded remain as if dead due to sleep;
thus, having burned the entire world, the flame shall enter the mouth again.
Then, O beloved, great winds arise, born from the breath of Brahmā;
they destroy that ash produced by the burning of the world.
The water born from the perspiration of Brahmā shall again inundate that world;
by that very water, O Goddess, the world shall become a single ocean.
At the end of the night, once again standing at the emergence of the fruits of pleasure and pain for all the world through karma, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, [arises].
Having perceived that [the world] has become empty, the Blessed Lord, by his own will,
effects a sixfold creation according to its previous established order.
First, he creates a dark (tāmasī) creation consisting of hells of various forms dominated by darkness, as well as animals down to the level of stationary beings.
Through the penetration of *tamas* and *rajas*, he would create human beings again;
through the penetration of *rajas* and *sattva*, he would create the Lord of the best of sages.
Having cast off sleep and awakened, the Lord of the World, established in the principle of *sattva*,
creates the gods and their worlds according to the same prior arrangement.
Then Rudra, Indra, the Sun, the Moon, the constellations, and the lords of the planets exercise their respective jurisdictions within their own spheres of activity.
In this manner, he creates day after day and withdraws [the world] at the end of the day;
and the measure of the night is said to be equal to that of the day.
By this day and night, a year is indeed reckoned as before;
when a hundred such years are completed, that is called a Mahākalpa.
O Goddess, listen to my divine years within a hundred Brahma-years:
ninety-one crores and twenty lakhs.
Likewise, there are seven *kharvas* and eight *nikharvas*;
this should be known as one hundred years of Brahmā by one who understands time.
The measurement according to the divine standard has thus been proclaimed;
now, moreover, learn from me the measurement according to the worldly standard.
O Dear One, there are thirty-two crores of years, as well as eight kharvas;
O Goddess of the Gods, there are two kharvas and exactly five nikharvas.
Three *śaṅkus*, one *padma*, and three *sāgaras*— and furthermore,
O Beloved, one *arbuda* and ten million (*koṭi*) years.
Likewise, there are eighty *kharvas*, five *nikharvas*, four *śaṅkus*, and thirty *sāgaras*. O Goddess, this has been fully explained; it should be known by those seeking liberation.
By this worldly measure, it is recorded that one hundred years of Brahmā consist of one *pūrva* multiplied by ten,
and that [unit] multiplied by ten is a *śata*.
A hundred multiplied by ten is proclaimed as a thousand;
a thousand multiplied by ten is indeed proclaimed as ten thousand (ayuta).
Ten tens of thousands (ayuta) make a hundred thousand (lakṣa); ten hundred thousands make a million (niyuta);
ten millions make a ten-million (koṭi); and ten ten-millions likewise make a hundred-million (arbuda).
Ten *arbudas* make a *vṛnda*; ten times that [make] a *kharva*;
ten times those [make] a *nikharva*; and ten of those [make] a *śaṅku*.
Ten *śaṅkus* make one *padma*; ten *padmas* make one *sāgara*;
ten *sāgaras* make one *madhya*; and ten of those are said to make the final [unit].
Having multiplied the last [number] by ten, it is proclaimed as a *parārdha*;
thus, these are the eighteen places of calculation.
At the end of a great kalpa, Brahmā goes to supreme dissolution;
that is declared to be a day for Viṣṇu, and his night is indeed equal to it.
By this measure, his year is prescribed;
and when a hundred years are completed, he too goes to the supreme dissolution.
That which is called the lifespan of Viṣṇu becomes a single day for Rudra;
day by day, he creates two other lords of creatures, Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
The power of Brahmā and the power of Viṣṇu have attained the state of authority;
whatever self they preside over, that [self] acquires their respective designation.
Then, by the will of the Supreme Self,
he exercises authority over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), and likewise Īśvara.
O Goddess of the gods, there are the lords of the worlds, as well as the lords of the realms,
the planets and other [deities], the Mothers, the Rudras, the yogas, the lunar mansions, and the zodiac signs.
Endowed with power and presided over by him, they all become possessed of his prowess and heroism, yet remain established in their own respective positions.
Śiva’s great power is one, and Śiva himself is indeed one and without beginning;
yet that power, O Goddess, is divided into infinite varieties.
In this very manner, Rudra indeed performs creation day after day, and at the end of the day he performs dissolution; his night is indeed equal to that.
By this measure of day and night, his year is constituted;
and when a hundred years are completed, there occurs the destruction of a hundred Rudras at the end of a day and night.
He too goes to the supreme state, having gone to which he becomes partless;
and in that state, yet another becomes a lord equal to him.
O Goddess of the gods, through union with the power of Rudra, he becomes the leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
and the hundred Rudras [arise] at the end of a hundred of his own years.
They proceed to the supreme reality, and from that, the cosmic egg perishes—
the support of the qualities of all beings, the abode of the abode of all principles.
Adorned with mountains, forests, gardens, continents, and oceans;
filled with rows of celestial palaces and embellished by the planets and constellations.
By the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and uragas;
by the ṛṣis, humans, and others who dwell in the seven worlds.
The ornamented world-sphere, together with the hells and the netherworlds (pātālas),
which is the support for all worlds without exception, dissolves into the waters.
Then Kālāgnirudra shall go to dissolution within the principle of Time (kālatattva);
[this applies] starting from the water-principle up to the range ending with Māyā.
Time itself shall withdraw all that, both moving and unmoving;
beyond that, it extends through the pure path as far as the range of the end of power.
Aghora, the destroyer of the terrible, shall withdraw all that which is terrible;
thus Rudra, the Great Lord in the form of Time, is established within these three.
Then, at the end of a hundred [aeons], he withdraws the water;
likewise, at the end of a hundred [aeons], the lords of the coverings beginning with the elements [withdraw theirs].
And they withdraw and create one another, O Queen of the Gods; thus,
when a hundred years have passed for the Lords of Beings.
O Śāṅkarī, O Mistress of the Gods, when those [elements] have gone, the beings then dissolve into the place that is partless;
they create and destroy one another.
Water dissolves into fire, and that fire, in turn, dissolves into wind.
Likewise, the wind, having reached space, dissolves into that very same [space];
and the subtle elements dissolve into their respective sources in the reverse order of their emergence.
The subtle elements, together with the sense organs, dissolve into the ego-sense in due order;
that [ego-sense] dissolves into the intellect, and that [intellect] dissolves into the profound state of equilibrium of the guṇas.
In that state, where the equilibrium of the qualities is indefinable, inconceivable, and beyond comparison,
the entire universe remains as if fast asleep.
The world remains dissolved according to the measure of an atom;
