this is remembered here as the day of the twenty-sixth Rudra.
The progeny, the lords of progeny, and the ancestors together with human beings—
those who have attained perfection through the knowledge of Sāṅkhya, and those who discourse on Brahman according to the Veda.
O Dear One, the *chandas*, the *sāmans*, the syllable *oṃ*, the intellect, and their respective deities—
all these abide during the day within the wise Supreme Lord.
At the end of the day they dissolve, and at the end of the night the origin of the universe occurs;
thirty-six thousand such dissolutions and origins of Brahmās take place.
And a day is said to belong to the Unmanifest (Avyakta) for those Rudras who dwell therein;
at the end of that day, which is the conclusion of the day of Pradhāna, he withdraws everything.
And at the end of the night, Śrīkaṇṭha, the leader of the universe, emits [the world] once again;
by this same principle, the duration of its measure shall also come to pass.
Since thousands of millions of dissolutions have passed away,
from that [arise] Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and likewise Kalā.
At the end of the day of Gahaneśa, all things from the level of *kalā* down to the earth gradually dissolve into one another according to their own measure.
Adorned with the arrangement and design of various worlds,
it is filled with the Rudras and individual souls (kṣetrajñas) as far as the support of the qualities (saguṇādhāra).
At the end of the night, by the impulsion of Gahaneśa, he is born again from the cause that is Mūlaprakṛti.
O Supreme Goddess, this is declared to be a single day-and-night of Prakṛti; O Supreme Goddess, that very period is also called the dissolution of all beings.
By means of ten times the supreme half of Pradhāna,
Māyā withdraws everything and again creates the world.
And having multiplied a parārdha of the time of Māyā by a hundred,
the Lord creates the world and again withdraws it.
Then the god Sadāśiva should withdraw [the universe] according to his own measure,
and he creates it once again at the dawn of his own day.
The great dissolution (mahāpralaya) is said to occur within two days of the state called Sādākhya;
therein, the one whose great body consists of the five mantras undergoes dissolution into the principle of Bindu.
Having pierced the *bindu*, the half-moon, and the *nirodhikā*,
one attains dissolution into the principle of *nāda*, having grasped all that is moving and unmoving.
O Dear One, the Nāda, having pierced the aperture of Brahmā by way of the Suṣumṇā path,
dissolves into the Śakti-tattva at the end of the day of the Śakti-tattva.
O fair-complexioned one, that time should be known as a *parārdha*; for one established in the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), it is the dawn of the pervasive Lord (*vyāpīśa*).
And then, he who is all-pervasive, having the nature of space, would again emanate within that which has the nature of space;
he too dissolves into Ananteśa, he into Anātha, and he into Anāśrita.
This is proclaimed to be the day of the unconditioned God (Anāśrita), multiplied ten million times by the number of parārdhas in the power of time.
By this measure, multiplied by a parārdha,
he too goes to the supreme state, the cause which is not dependent on itself.
That time is known as the state of equilibrium (sāmya), which removes the fear of birth and death;
beyond that, however, there is immeasurable time, which constitutes the ultimate limit.
O Goddess, he is eternal, eternally arisen, and being beyond all parts, he is not divided;
yet he, as the All-pervasive One, should conceive of everything from the beginning up to the earth.
By means of the divisions beginning with the *tuṭi* and the *kalās*, [one perceives] the path of the Goddess, consisting of the moving and the unmoving;
however, that which is above the *unmanā* state, there time does not exist.
No one is healthy, nor is anyone made healthy; he is partless, devoid of time, beyond the state of Śāṅkara and beyond the transmental (unmanā). He is eternal, all-pervasive, and immutable.
Its form at the beginning is just like its form at the end of the eon;
it is formless, liberated from form, beginningless, and devoid of becoming.
The omniscient one and the creator of all, though devoid of qualities such as generosity,
abides in the form of Unmanā at the crown of the head in another aspect.
The God of gods, the Lord of the world, the Supreme Self, the imperishable Śiva,
creates the universe without desire through the sequential application of his powers.
The Goddess said: "There is no action for one who is devoid of desire; and how could one who is inactive create?
Please explain this excellent and secret question out of your grace."
Bhairava said:
Just as fire is produced from a sun-gem when it is heated by the rays of the sun, so too [fire arises] from that sun; therefore, there is no desire for the sun itself in that regard.
Just as a gem has no agency of its own, such is the activity of the Lord;
Śiva is to be known as being like the sun, while Śakti stands like the gem.
Just as time is the regulator of the sprout from a tree that has reached its seasonal period,
so too, through union with Śiva, is the persistence of the world established by Śakti.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Svacchandatantra*.
You have described the emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal of the principles (*tattvas*), as well as the cause of the world's origin; through your grace, this has been heard by me. (SvaT 12.1)
"Explain the knowledge of reality so that accomplishment may arise within those [levels];
I shall describe them in brief, from Earth up to Śiva."
Listen to how the earth exists within the body in its solid form:
it is present in the flesh, in the bones, as well as in the sinews, the hair, and the nails.
The earth element, intensified by its five qualities, is to be known in the marrow and intestines,
as well as in phlegm, blood, raw flesh, urine, lymph, sweat, and fat.
The four qualities of water reside in semen and in cohesion;
fire resides in digestion, burning, and heat.
O Goddess, fire thus abides in manifestation with three characteristics;
wind is characterized by inhalation, exhalation, touch, and its pervasive expansion.
During the discharge of urine and feces, and during the intake of food and drink,
the wind situated in the body by means of these [functions] should be known as having two characteristics.
I shall describe space as it exists, characterized by a single mark;
it should be understood as being hollow in nature and possessing nine types of apertures as its defining characteristic.
O virtuous lady, this quality consisting of sound has been described to you;
the organ of speech utters speech, and that speech is of four kinds.
It consists of the refined (saṃskṛtā), the vernacular (prākṛtī), the corrupted (apabhraṣṭā), and the nasalized (anunāsikā);
it involves cutting, splitting, giving, piercing, and the application of crafts.
Seizing and victory, as well as everything else, reside in the faculty of the hand;
likewise, the even, the low, and the high, as well as clods of earth, thorns, and sand.
Mud, water-fortresses, roads, watchtowers,
and mountains are traversed by the organ of the feet during travel to and from other regions.
The anus is always active in excretion and in the urging toward defecation;
the generative organ produces pleasure and impels one toward those who are approachable or unapproachable.

These [organs] operate within actions; therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, they are the organs of action (karmendriyas). The organs of perception (buddhīndriyas), however, operate through their connection with the intellect (buddhi).
O Dear One, the seven notes are proclaimed to be Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣadha.
Gāndhāra, Madhyama, and Ṣaḍja—these are the three *grāmas*, O Pārvatī;
there are seven notes, three *grāmas*, and twenty-one *mūrcchanās*.
These forty-nine constitute this divine mandala;
for these are known as subtle sounds, abiding as the resonance of all that is moving and unmoving.
I shall now describe the gross [sounds] as they truly are; learn them from me:
those arising from kettledrums, drums, and conchs, and those produced by clay drums and small drums.
There was the sound of flutes and gomukhas, the deep resonance of drums,
various stringed instruments, and those played with the hands.
Arising from conjunction and disjunction, produced from wood, stone, and water,
it consists of the corrupt form, the nasalized sound, the refined Sanskrit, and the Prakrit utterance.
Indeed, through the engagement of the faculty of hearing, it perceives those things established in the seven notes— whether manifest or unmanifest, and whether already spoken or yet to be spoken.
For sound is indeed its object, by which the person (pudgala) perceives what is soft,
hard, rough, and likewise cool.
Hot, slimy clods of earth, mud, and likewise sand;
the blows of arrows, spears, and swords, as well as beating and cutting.
One indeed discerns these: the sense of touch and the tactile faculty;
for this is its object, by which the person (pudgala) perceives.
Listen as I describe the functions of the faculty of sight:
white, red, yellow, black, green, and smoky-grey.
Whether tawny, reddish-brown, or dark brown— especially those of various other kinds—
including men, women, domestic animals, wild beasts, luminous bodies, and all things stationary or moving.
The eye always perceives forms that are devoid of external shape;
for this object known as "form" is that by which the self is awakened.
The tongue perceives the taste—whether sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, or astringent—as well as that which is mixed with these or is simply pleasant. (SvaT 12.28)
For this is its object, taste, by which a person perceives [it]:
as fragrant, divine scent, foul odor, and in many other ways.
Both [nostrils] smell at the tip of the nose; the object known as odor is that by which the field-knower (kṣetrajña), deluded by egoism (ahaṅkāra), perceives.
It rushes through the ten sense-faculties in both conceptualization and discursive thought,
its doubt unimpeded and invincible for all embodied beings.
And this mind has indeed been described as that which binds one to dharma and adharma;
now I shall explain the intrinsic nature of the dharmas of the subtle elements (tanmātras) according to their true meaning.
He smells the fragrance, which is the subtle element of smell, with the tip of his nose;
he perceives the taste, which is the subtle element of taste, as it abides upon the tongue.
The eye perceives color-form, having approached the subtle element of form;
the skin perceives touch, having approached the subtle element of touch.
And one perceives sound as the subtle element of sound by means of the sense of hearing;
this is the subtle property of the elements according to the sequence of their primordial nature.
And from that, the *vaikārika* [ego] arises by which the person (*pudgala*) perceives:
"I am wise, I am an enjoyer, and I am born into a great family. (SvaT 12.36)
"I am the giver and the enjoyer; I am radiant and powerful.
I am the warrior in battle, and my enemies have been conquered by me. (SvaT 12.37)
"I am indeed one of virtuous character, endowed with qualities, and a supreme bringer of welfare;
yet I am also a sinner, ill-behaved, foolish, and ugly in form."

"Nothing has been given, nothing has been enjoyed by me; there is no one as miserable as I"—thus [is the state] of those whose minds are possessed by the ego and who remain under the sway of the sense of "mine."
Ego-attachment binds one to cyclic existence with firm fetters;
this threefold nature of ego-attachment has thus been proclaimed.
Therefore, O lady of virtuous vows, I shall describe to you the attributes of the intellect (buddhi), beginning with dharma:
namely, the fourfold set consisting of dharma, knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya).
Furthermore, unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of mastery—these seven bind; yet that [power] may delude through the state of knowledge.
Intellect performs both determination and [perception] with respect to various objects;
now listen, O beloved, to the characteristics of the eight [qualities], beginning with dharma.
Fasting, recitation, silence, freedom from anger, non-stealing, straightforwardness,
truthfulness, purity, generosity, compassion, and forbearance should always be maintained.
The study of knowledge, modesty, restraint of the senses,
the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility, pilgrimage to sacred fords, and the libations offered to the ancestors.
Granting fearlessness to all sentient beings and protecting their lives—
this is indeed the first quality of wisdom, and it is designated as "Dharma."
For those bound by the karma of their actions who follow the cycle of existence,
there is repeated birth as a mortal, repeated birth in heaven, and again and again, birth as an animal.
The nature of phenomena has been fully explained; now hear from me the nature of gnosis:
it is the aggregate of twenty-four, conjoined with the organs of action.
That [ego-sense] is to be known as belonging to primordial nature (prākṛta), which sets both dharma and adharma in motion;
yet I am its non-agent and devoid of qualities, and thus I have no bondage belonging to primordial nature.
I consider that one is liberated from the very latent impressions (vāsanā) which are produced by nature;
thus I have proclaimed the knowledge of Sāṅkhya, by means of which one is released from nature.
If the Lord were to bind again that one who has been liberated from the bondage of primordial nature (prakṛti),
then once bound, he would transmigrate further as long as he does not find the Divine.
Out of dispassion, one should renounce the Lord, the creator of the world who binds all living beings, as well as sons and beloved, highly esteemed wives.
Elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, friends, enjoyments, and wealth;
likewise, fasting, recitation, visiting sacred fords, the five-fire penance, and lying upon the water.
Having meditated upon these terrible [deities], one abandons the body in an instant by means of mountains,
trees, water, fire, blows, hanging, or starvation.
Relying upon detachment, one may even perform daring deeds;
yet, having attained a state of sovereignty, one does not find satisfaction through material objects.
One should not seek to accomplish the goal of worldly power through wives, wealth, shares, attendants, or vehicles; rather, one should accomplish it through asceticism, vows, and mantras.
War, gambling, as well as deceit, theft, falsehood, and violence— these and other improper acts, including the betrayal of trust through guile, [are to be avoided].
Having attained a state of sovereignty, he nevertheless constantly commits many acts,
being devoted to the injury of living beings and possessing theft, falsehood, and deceit.
The beggar would be the giver of suffering, and unrighteous conduct would prevail;
there would be neither dharma nor adharma, and who could have gone to heaven or attained liberation?
Having fallen into a state of ignorance, he declares everything to be false;
he is constantly miserable, a servant to others, and carries even a burden or a vehicle.
Living in constant hardship, he does not grow weary of his lack of dispassion;
having ruled a kingdom, a provincial governor becomes a village lord after his term as governor.
Fallen from his kingdom, he subsists on half of that [income] as one who is no longer a ruler;
yet he neither grieves nor is distressed, but sports just as he did in his former reign.
This nature of lack of sovereignty has thus been described to you;
now I shall speak of the unmanifest, which consists of the three qualities and is the instigator of saṃsāra.
And because the origin of the world is from Prakṛti, she is so called; I shall now proclaim her nature, which is designated by the names rajas, sattva, and tamas.
The nature of luminosity is *sattva*, and the quality (*dharma*) rests upon *sattva*;
it is always shared and eternally beneficial to sentient beings.
Endowed with patience and compassion, having reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment,
he possesses joy, generosity, fortitude, intelligence, austerity, purity, and likewise self-control.
Truthful speech, equanimity of vision, and the awakening of divine intelligence—
these qualities always abide in that Supreme Person.
He is to be known as one of the *sāttvika* type; now hear from me the characteristics of those characterized by *rajas*:
he is cruel, excessively greedy, full of hatred, and likewise prone to anger.
One possessed by desire wanders constantly, overcome by joy yet afflicted by suffering;
one who is proud is joined with hypocrisy and remains established in egoism.
Constantly delighting in battle and being a hero are the characteristics of the quality of passion (rajas); likewise are being overcome by desire and anger, and being possessed by greed.
Envy, hypocrisy, despondency, intoxication, and madness; sleep, laziness, lethargy, impurity, and ignorance—these likewise [are the afflictions].
A disposition toward unrighteousness, atheism, and a deceitful mind—
these are the signs of darkness seen in such a person.
That person should be known as tamasic, possessing a turbid disposition;
this unmanifest [principle] consists of the three qualities (guṇas), and it is declared to be composed of the three qualities.
Having correctly understood this, one is indeed liberated from the primal qualities (guṇas).
I am not subject to the properties of the qualities, nor am I the agent of the intellect or the ego-maker.
Devoid of the organs of action and devoid of the elements and subtle essences,
I am known as the Puruṣa— non-agent, free from qualities, and pure consciousness alone.
Whatever action has been performed—whether mental, vocal, or physical—I consider it to be done by nature through its instigation; thus, the person (puruṣa) is traditionally held to be a non-doer.
Having thus renounced actions, a man who understands that "I am not the doer, nor is there bondage for me" continues to act constantly [without attachment]. SvaT 12.77.
He would be liberated from primordial nature only as long as the Lord does not create;
yet, deluded by the knowledge of Sāṅkhya, he imagines that liberation has been attained.
For there would be no liberation for him; he would remain for some time in a disembodied state, liberated from primordial nature (prakṛti) and devoid of creation and dissolution.
As long as that Lord, the Supreme Lord, performs creation,
so long is he again cast into the cycle of existence by the bondage of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Cast back again into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, he wanders there,
bound by dharma and adharma, deluded by the knowledge of Sāṅkhya.
"I am the doer and the enjoyer; I am the Lord and I am powerful"—thus utterly deluded by the sense of "mine-ness," one wanders like a waterwheel. (SvaT 12.82)
The knowledge of Sāṅkhya has been proclaimed by me; now hear of the presiding deity of meditation:
one should contemplate the earth in its solid form, girdled by the four oceans.
It is filled with mountains and forests, teeming with beasts and birds;
it is well-established, possesses a yellowish luster, and is endowed with the seed-syllable ŪM.
Having meditated, one attains that accomplishment and wards off poisonous beings;
one becomes unshakable by all spirits, just like the earth itself.
With all his limbs filled with water, he should fill them by means of the meditation on the ocean;
practicing in this way, he shall destroy poisonous beings.
Freed from the burning heat of craving and devoid of calamities,
the perfected one, endowed with his former seed-syllable, shall fill the world.
One who has been impregnated by his own seed may perform thousands of ritual acts;
the wind, whose nature is black dust, should be meditated upon as conjoined with the seed-syllable.
The perfected one, a performer of wonders, indeed fills the bodies of the world;
for his own body is of the nature of void, and the world is likewise of the nature of void.
One should meditate with the seed-syllable of Prakṛti and have various artistic works executed;
likewise, when Fire is meditated upon in the organ of speech, it bestows the perfection of speech.
Indra, meditated upon in the hand, becomes one who possesses powerful arms and is invincible;
Viṣṇu, meditated upon at the feet, bestows the ability to travel great distances.
Mitra, white in color, should be meditated upon at the anus; he is the destroyer of diseases of the anus.
One should meditate with a concentrated mind on Prajāpati, who is dark-complexioned, at the penis.
One becomes a master of the senses and enjoys for a hundred [aeons] according to one's desire;
in the case of the sense of hearing, one should meditate on the various directions joined with the seed-syllable.
One grasps what is said once, and the journey in all directions succeeds;
one should meditate on the wind in the form of black, residing within the skin.
He who is impenetrable by fangs and the like will never experience pain;
one should meditate on Āditya in the eye and likewise on Varuṇa in the tongue.
In the nose, one should contemplate the earth as yellow, and likewise the moon in the mind;
the subtle element of smell as yellow, and the subtle element of taste as white.
The red is the subtle element of form (rūpatanmātra), while the black is designated as the subtle element of touch;
the formless is the subtle element of sound, and it should be meditated upon in the form of a drop (bindu).
One knows the desired success regarding sense objects as well as whatever has been contemplated;
likewise, Rudra in his Vaikārika form should be meditated upon by one who desires success.
Through meditation, one attains perfection that is free from the bondage of ego;
one should meditate with a disciplined mind upon Brahmā as established within the intellect.
By recollecting with the primordial seed-syllable, a flood of knowledge arises;
and divine wisdom is born, which brings about the destruction of doubt.
The past, the present, and the future become directly perceived;
the nature [of reality] is dark-colored, yet it shines forth as red and white.
If one desires one's own accomplishment, one should meditate upon her red heart, which has many feet, arms, and faces, by means of the seed-syllable of reality (tattvabīja).
One becomes accomplished, independent, and endowed with divine vision;
through the practice of yoga for six months, divine vision arises.
Whatever exists in the three worlds becomes directly manifest to him.
This ordinary yoga, which brings about liberation, has been described to you as supreme.
Beyond this, however, the Puruṣa is situated in the midst of the lotus;
having the nature of consciousness, he remains pervading all bodies.
That is renowned as the *jīva* (life-principle), by which that city lives;
when it has departed, the body becomes lifeless and perishes.
It is indeed this [self] that is bound and liberated, and it experiences pleasure and pain;
yet its form, color, or measure is never seen anywhere.
It cannot even be described; it is subtle and possesses infinite forms, being [smaller] than a hundredth part of a hundredth division of the tip of a hair.
His individual soul (jīva) becomes exceedingly subtle, and it is capable of attaining infinity;
it is like the sun in color, radiant as gold, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.
Yogins perceive him with their divine eye as if he were a star;
for he possesses form, bound by time, and endowed with passion, ignorance, and the kalās.
The deity residing in the vital breath (jīva) is to be known by her dark complexion;
she has a white body on the right side and a black form on the left.
The faces, which have those same colors, and especially the mandalas,
bind one through the bondage of karma and bestow pleasure and pain.
And one should understand destiny as being irresistible even by gods and asuras;
it is accompanied by former seeds and meditative absorption, and endowed with two forms.
Through meditation one attains accomplishment and is liberated from the constraints of destiny;
[he is] three-eyed, four-faced, black in color, and four-armed.
One who knows the nature of one's own seed-syllable and meditative absorption is not overcome by time, even when facing the invincible, infinite Lord of Time who is withdrawing [the world].
They revolve like a wheel, devoid of meditation on time;
thus one should always meditate upon time, and the accomplishment of the object of meditation arises.

One should meditate upon Rāga as being red in color, Vidyā as dark-complexioned with beautiful eyes, and Kalā as white in color; indeed, one should meditate upon her as the one who awakens consciousness from another.
She is black in color with red eyes, long teeth, and beautiful eyes;
her hair is brown and stands upright, and she has a stout body and a large belly.
That which repeatedly causes beings, beginning with Brahmā, to fall—
because it stands as an adversary without enmity— is Māyā, a knot difficult to pass beyond.
Those who know the Sāṅkhya, the Vedas, and the Purāṇas, as well as those who are learned in other scriptures and others who propound liberation, are not able to transgress it.
Deluded by illusion, they suffer, desiring liberation where there is no liberation,
through the yoga of meditating on their own seeds according to the nature of their previous meditation.
Having severed that [bond] with the sword of initiation (dīkṣā), they enter the imperishable Śiva.
That Vidyā is known to consist of four phonemes (varṇa) and to pervade all phonemes.
White, red, yellow, and black, she should be meditated upon as being hollow in nature,
mounted upon space and wind, and endowed with beauty and youth.
She should be meditated upon by means of her own seed-syllable, and her very accomplishment arises;
indeed, divine and unfailing accomplishment arises, and one becomes a perfected master of vidyā.
Then, able to assume any form at will, he goes to all the worlds of the Vedas;
[he beholds] Nāreśa, who has the luster of saffron, three eyes, and matted hair.
One should meditate upon the face facing the east; one obtains that meritorious fruit which is the result for one who subsists on air alone, as well as the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
The world comes under one's control, one advances, and attains accomplishment;
this will undoubtedly occur within six months, and likewise for the right [practice].
Resembling a dark blue cloud, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and eyes,
his face is formidable with a frown, and he is adorned with skulls and snakes.
One should meditate upon his right [face], which bears many forms and matted locks,
for the destruction of pleasure and pain, and for the eradication of calamities and fever.
Poisons, planetary afflictions, and all such things are destroyed in an instant through meditation;
the yogi, free from old age and death, blazes like fire.
He indeed moves through all the worlds and, having attained perfection, reaches equanimity;
O Goddess, he is white, three-eyed, and visibly holds a sacred thread and a water-pot.
One should meditate upon the western face, which bestows divine accomplishments,
even after having slain thousands of living beings and hundreds of others' wives.
The pure-souled one, having applied the ointment and attained perfection, becomes Śiva;
his supreme face has three eyes and possesses the luster of a red lotus.
Through his meditative absorption, the entire world comes under his control; of this there is no doubt.
He causes heat, he causes rain, and he likewise creates and even destroys.
He who meditates for one year attains his desired accomplishment;
he should always visualize [the deity] with a white head, holding a trident in hand, and wearing matted hair.
Clad in a tiger skin, holding a rosary and a water-pot,
with a lute and a hand-drum in his hands, and wearing a serpent as his sacred thread.
One should constantly meditate upon Maheśvara as the Linga situated above the moon on the crown of the head;
by this very body, one becomes omniscient and able to assume any form at will.
Through meditation on the sound of a bell, accomplishment will be attained within six months;
indeed, whatever accomplishment he desires shall arise for him in the world of mortals.
But he who performs the meditation on the *liṅga* conjoined with the primordial seed-syllable (*pūrvabīja*) shall,
within one month, perceive the subtle *liṅga* above his body.
Upon seeing that which resembles pure crystal, one is liberated;
moreover, accomplishment arises in the world of humans within six months.
The intellect for perceiving the three worlds arises as direct perception for him;
he may traverse all the worlds and become equal to the Lord.
The moon and the sun shall be its two eyes; wisdom is indeed the wheel of that chariot.
Its horses are the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the mind is the driver, impelled [to action].
The ego (ahaṃkāra) is the warrior; its great bow is the [three] qualities (guṇa);
the senses are its arrows; and Dharma is proclaimed to be the deer.
Thus that yogi sports within the Supreme Self abiding in the heart,
O Supreme Goddess, moving about at will amidst merits and demerits.
"I am not the doer, nor is there bondage for me; everything has the Lord as its cause.
Having realized this knowledge of the Lord, one should renounce all action.
He who resides in the heart as the impeller toward the performance of both dharma and adharma—to him I have gone for refuge; thus, there is no bondage nor any sense of agency for me.
Sadāśiva, endowed with the eightfold division and accompanied by the previously mentioned seed-syllable,
should be meditated upon in the form described above by one who desires the fruit of that accomplishment.
One should indeed meditate upon the pervasive Nāda during the days, nights, and solstices;
through the southern and northern transits, it bestows liberation upon one who knows the equinox.
That sound which resembles the resonance of a bamboo flute is known as Śāntanāda;
he should be understood as Sadāśiva. Now hear the fruit of perfection resulting from meditation upon him.
In one month he becomes radiant; in the second, a master of speech;
in the third, he beholds the Siddhas; and in the fourth, he possesses divine vision.
Success in the world of humans is attained in half a year, without a doubt;
likewise, divine success is attained in one year, while union [with the deity] occurs in the second year.
Having performed the rite of making [the senses] six-faced, one should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva:
[by touching] the two ears with the two thumbs, and the two eyes by means of the index and middle fingers.
With the remaining two [mantras], one whose mind is firmly fixed should worship the nose and the six-faced [deity];
and Sadāśiva is perceived in ten ways in the form of the phonemes.
White, red, yellow, black, greenish-brown,
blue, variegated in color, and beautiful like the luster of crystal.
Having seen all forms, the wise one should abandon them;
he should grasp only the One alone, for all others are merely forms of qualities.
One should thus perceive the *bindu* as resembling the lunar disk, with eyes like a mass of lightning, and having the appearance of shimmering stars.
The Bindu, the Lord, should be meditated upon as conjoined with these digits (kalās): Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
The meditation on the *bindu* has been fully explained; now learn from me the characteristic of the *śakti*:
having gazed at space with eyes closed, [one perceives that which] resembles the rising sun.
And she beholds that great splendor; she is remembered as the sovereign power (śakti).
Yellow, red, black, and crystal-like in appearance, she is enchanting.
The supreme power (pāramā śakti) is to be beheld; having seen it, one attains the state of Śiva. Then, one should contemplate that pervasive power above as having five forms.
Having meditated upon her as endowed with her own causes, one should attain freedom of will;
one should meditate with a disciplined mind on her who is described as Samanā and Unmanā.
Through meditation, one attains perfection as the all-pervading, immeasurable Lord;
and above that is Śiva, the peaceful, whom I have indeed described previously.
Whatever may be seen by the eye, or whatever falls within the range of speech,
whatever the mind reflects upon, and whatever the intellect determines;
Whatever consists of the ego-sense, whatever exists as an object of cognition,
and that which does not exist— all that must be diligently sought right there [within consciousness].
In whatever place he may stay, and in whatever hermitage he may delight,
sitting comfortably with self-restrained mind, one-pointed and concentrated.
Having recollected the Svachanda, one should always meditate upon non-existence;
through the meditation on that reality, one becomes equal to it.
O lady of excellent complexion, those dharmas which were previously taught to him—
by means of the application of those very dharmas, O beloved, he indeed becomes a yogin.
I have explained the meditation on the essential nature and the forms of the principles;
by knowing them thus and meditating upon them, one attains accomplishment and is also liberated.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
The Goddess said: "O Supreme Lord, [tell me] the essence of this tantra, namely the sacrifice."
Tell that in brief, for the benefit of practitioners indeed.
The venerable Bhairava said: [I shall describe] the root seed-syllable, the leader of mantras, the supreme Lord,
seated upon the throne of the *praṇava*, and endowed with limbs and faces.
One should worship the Supreme Lord with the collections of substances mentioned previously;
that itself is the arrangement of the fire-oblation (homa), and that indeed is proclaimed as initiation (dīkṣā).
He who, with a single-pointed and concentrated mind, recites [the mantra] one million times while alone with no companions on the banks of an ocean or a river;
One who has conquered the senses and possesses a single-pointed mind, remaining steadfast in celibacy, should offer one hundred thousand oblations of human flesh mixed with guggulu resin.
O Goddess, one shall accomplish that which is impossible to accomplish; there is no need for deliberation here regarding whatever rites are established in the four seats.
Whether they be inferior, middling, or superior, O fair-faced Goddess of the Gods,
they attain success according to the word of Bhairava.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme *kārikā-kośa*,
knowing which, O Goddess of the gods, practitioners move about here in this world.

Having taken the blood from the heads of heroes fallen by the stroke of a sword held face-to-face, and having written the name of the target (*sādhya*) upon their body with that blood as if with red lac— conjoined with the mantra—
and having heated it thoroughly in a fire of *preta* corpses at night, one recites [the mantra] a hundred times for the sake of that person.

One brings that lord of the asuras, or the preceptor of the lords of the asuras, by means of the speed of the wind. If one has drawn [the figure] with *alaktaka* on the head of a *preta*, and heated it with the fire of a *preta*,
one brings the person to be accomplished from the world of Yama itself by force, as before, without delay.
Taking the dust from the left foot of a dead woman who was hanged, one should,

at midnight, facing [the target], heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood until it is well-heated and recite the mantra joined with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) one hundred times, using blood, lac, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).

Or else, within a hundredth part of a day, he brings Śacī or Ahalyā [under his control]. Having taken up the dust from the foot of a woman who has hanged herself, and having drawn the body of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) with the blood of a corpse and yellow orpiment mixed with lac, [he achieves his goal].

Having prepared a fire of the *preta* class, well-heated and consecrated one hundred times with the mantra joined with the practitioner’s own name, one quickly summons the women of the *yakṣas*, *asuras*, *surās*, and *pannagas*. Having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) with lac and yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on one's own left hand...
This [mantra], interlaced with the name [of the target] and recited a hundred times,
when heated well at night over a smokeless fire of *khadira* wood, brings even the preceptor of the asuras by the force of the wind.
One should write the name of the person to be acted upon on the ground with red *gairika* pigment.

Having stepped upon that which is drawn on the ground with the left hand smeared with fragrant paste and joined with the seed-syllable of reality (tattvabīja), facing the one to be accomplished at the time of midnight,
one brings even a king together with his ministers within a hundredth part of a moment.
One should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) in the center of a human skull using yellow pigment mixed with red;
having written it on the forehead, interlaced with the mantra,
one should take a second human skull and smear it with scented water.
Then, having formed a hollow cavity by joining two skull-halves, one should properly wrap it with a thread made from a corpse.
Having heated it thoroughly with acacia charcoal embers and then smeared it with beeswax,
one should proceed until this wax adhering to the skull-halves has completely melted.
Through the application of one hundred recitations, he draws even the Lord of the Gods in a mere twinkling of an eye.
Having written on a wall with red ochre the name of the target, interspersed with the syllables of the mantra,
and facing the victim at night, he should then recite it while angry, treading upon [the drawing] with his left hand.
Through the application of the syllable *kroṃ* and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), one swiftly summons gods and asuras.
One should offer as oblation human flesh fallen from wounds inflicted by weapons in battle, combined with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Having bound the reversed wheel-mudrā (*viparīta-cakra-mudrā*), one should cast the target (*sādhya*) into its center.
Visualizing [the deity] with his palms pressed together and his face distressed,
one brings even a great man or a lord of the earth within a hundredth part of a day;
grasping a hundred thousand or ten million human heads from which the banners have been struck down by the falling of sharp weapons.
Whoever writes down and worships the abode described as having three forms,
for him Indra, Yama, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Agni, along with the Siddhas and Gandharvas,
bestow a multitude of various excellent accomplishments (*siddhi*) as well as other diverse attainments.
The manifest-unmanifest, as well as the unmanifest-manifest— these are the three forms.
The wise one who properly worships the movements within those abodes attains the threefold accomplishment born from the body of the King of Mountains.
Indeed, for that King of Mountains, whose mind was perfectly resolved,
[he prepared] powdered red sandalwood, as well as mustard seeds and salt.
Having gathered the dust from the feet of the one to be accomplished, one should grind it together while reciting the mantra of Svachchandadeva and rubbing both hands together.
One should offer the powder as an oblation into a funeral pyre or even into the fire of a Caṇḍāla;
facing the target, one should perform this ritual application.
As long as one recites [the mantra] one hundred times, one shall attract the king;
the lord of the earth comes under control, both by his own person and by his wealth.
This application is indeed effective; I tell you, it cannot be otherwise.
Taking that very dust and mixing it with iron filings, [one should proceed].
Having tied it to a rag from a cemetery and recited the mantra seven times,
one should bury it eight finger-breadths deep in the ground at a crossroads, together with the name of the enemy.
If one casts it upon someone by name, that person will be paralyzed in an instant;
having taken that very dust and combined it with the five types of *unmatta* [plants], [one may perform the rite].
Having tied it with a cloth from a corpse, inscribed with the name of the enemy,
and having recited the mantra over it one hundred times, one should quickly bury it in a cremation ground.
The patient may become insane, but once [the poison] has been extracted, he is released from it;
having taken out the cloth, one should purify it with milk.
For this bringing back is indeed already accomplished; there is no doubt.
Then, one should gather flowers from the Raktāśvamāra tree.
One should cause those [mantras] to be recited one hundred and eight times;
then, with a flower over which the mantra has been recited once, one should strike it upon the top of the *liṅga*.
In this manner, one should perform [the rite] day by day for ten days with a well-concentrated mind;
then, having gathered these eleven flowers, [one should proceed].
Then, having gone to a great river, the knower of mantras should cause each [syllable] to flow there one by one in succession, having recited them all at once.
Taking that flower which is their last and which indeed moves against the current,
one should drink it mixed with water, without touching it with the teeth.
Then, having consecrated red *aśvamāraka* flowers one hundred times with mantras,
the wise practitioner should place them on the tip of the index finger and press them down with the thumb.

The knower of mantras, reciting the *Svacchanda* mantra at will, should whirl the flower to the left while uttering the name of the person he wishes to summon; thus he swiftly draws that person toward him.
Having whirled it to the right, he performs the dismissal of that person once again.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
The venerable Bhairava said:
"I shall describe the characteristics of the mudrās as they are established in this tantra."
With the palms of the hands turned upward and joined together, it is proclaimed as the *kapāla* [mudrā].
O Goddess, having turned the left hand sideways, one should press down on the three fingers beginning with the little finger with the thumb,
keeping the forefinger straight.
Having turned the hand away, one should place it upon the region of the shoulder;
this is indeed proclaimed as the Khaṭvāṅga [mudrā]. Now learn from me the Khaḍga mudrā.
O Goddess, one should press down the little finger and the ring finger with the thumb;
with the middle and index fingers pointing upward, this is proclaimed as the Sword Mudrā (khaḍgamudrā).
O fair-faced one, having formed a fist and extended the little finger,
holding it facing oneself— this *sphara* has been described by me to you.
O Goddess of gods, having formed a fist, one should bend the index finger upward;
this is indeed called the goad (aṅkuśa) mudrā. Now learn from me the noose (pāśa) mudrā.
Having made the index finger circular, one should join it at the base of the thumb;
this is indeed called the noose, which binds the nets of the wicked.
O lady of excellent limbs, having formed a fist and extended the index finger— this,
O Bhairavī, is briefly described to you as the *nārāca* [mudrā].
Having formed a fist and extended the index finger and thumb, O Dear One, one should slightly bend the tips; this is proclaimed as the Pināka mudrā.
O fair-faced one, when the hand is extended forward with the fingers joined together,
and that [hand] is turned away, it is proclaimed as the Abhaya (Fearless) mudrā.
Extending the left arm, one should place it upon the knee;
O Goddess, this "bestowed" gesture (prasṛta) should be displayed as the boon-granting mudrā that accomplishes all aims.
Having made the left hand into the shape of a bell and turned it downward, one should rub it with the index finger of the right hand; this is proclaimed as the "Bell" (Ghaṇṭā) mudrā.
With a concentrated mind, one should press the little finger with the thumb;
having extended the other three fingers, it is proclaimed as the trident (triśūla).
The staff indeed, through the clenching of the fist—learn from me the vajra-mudrā:
having placed the left hand below, one should hold it palm-upward with a concentrated mind.
Having turned the right hand downward, one should rub together the thumb and the little finger of both hands and display the Vajra-mudrā.
O lady of excellent vows, O fair-faced one, one should display the ḍamaru joined with the hollow [of the hand] by means of the fist-closure of the right hand. SvaT 14.16.
I shall now describe the mudgara: one should extend both hands forward;
this is indeed called the mudgara. Now learn from me the vallakī as well.
O Goddess, one should extend both hands upward with a concentrated mind;
having bent the two ring fingers, this is proclaimed as the vīṇā mudrā.
One should extend the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger;
one should press the first [finger] with the thumb—this is declared to be the axe (paraśu).
O Great Goddess, one should display these mudrās of Bhairava during invocation,
cessation, and likewise during dismissal.
One should display the skull-cup and the khaṭvāṅga staff even when they are not explicitly mentioned;
for the skull-cup is to be known as white, and the khaṭvāṅga is likewise.
The trident and the iron arrow, the sword with the luster of a blue lotus,
the red *sphara*, and the black *pināka* are thus fully described.
The bell is to be known as having the luster of gold; the goad has the luster of emerald;
the noose resembles crushed collyrium; and the gesture of fearlessness is said to have the appearance of crystal.
O lady of excellent complexion, he should be meditated upon with a serene mind as the Bestower of Boons,
holding a hand-drum resembling gold and a lute of equal radiance.
One should know the staff to be red; one should contemplate the vajra as yellow;
O Goddess, the mallet and likewise the axe are like the color of lapis lazuli.
The seat of the mudrās is fully described as that which gives rise to the fruit of the four aims; O fair-faced one, they are mounted upon the seat of the *praṇava*, beginning with the syllable *oṃ*.
O Great Goddess, those [mantras] which are arranged with their own names and conclude with an obeisance accomplish various fruits.
O Dear One, the characteristic of the mudrās, which is known for making [the practice] free from obstacles,
should be understood with effort and accomplished by one of great soul.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
The venerable Bhairava said:
[Concerning] one who is engaged in recitation, meditation, and so forth, and who observes the conduct and vows...
O fair-faced one, I shall now fully explain the secret kisses for the practitioner.
Bhairava is remembered as the Abode (dhāman), the Guru is remembered as the Bestower of All;
the Sādhaka is to be known as the Mountain, and the Putraka is remembered as Vimala.
The practitioner possesses a beautiful body, while the sisters are proud of their strength;
wine should be known as that which causes exhilaration, and liquor is remembered as that which brings joy.
Fish are to be known as aquatic creatures, and their flesh increases strength;
they say that what is "born" is that which has grown, while what is "dead" is that which is turned away.
They say that blood is nectar; the collection of intestines is the lotus stalk;
semen is declared to be the moon; and the sinew is proclaimed to be the thread.
The cremation ground is to be known as *ḍāmara*, while the *rākṣasa* is terrifying;
the *piśāca* causes the growth of hair, and the menstruating woman is to be known as *ruhā*.
Know that night is indeed concealment and day is illumination;
the eyes are to be known as flickering, and the tongue they know as the grasper.
The hands should be known as the "wealth-givers," while the feet are understood as the "companions.
The male organ generates contentment, and the female organ increases affection.
The weapon (śastra) generates division; the knife (kartarī) accomplishes the task.
The female messenger (dūtī) should be known as the one who brings about union; incense (dhūpa) is said to be that which causes delight.
Fragrance is said to produce contentment; kings are known as its sustainers.
The sacrificial animal is to be understood as the awakener; the sacrificial pap (caru) fulfills all desires.
Food is said to be the means of accomplishment; here, fat and the scum [of boiled rice] are mentioned.
Hearing is the mouth of the quarters, and the skin is remembered as the faculty of sensation.
The nose is said to be "well-established," while the mouth is the "investigator. The movement of the animal (the breath) is to be understood [thus], and the mother is called the nurse.
They know the father to be the creator and the brother to be the protector;
the sister is to be known as the bringer of auspiciousness, and the female friend as the accomplisher of all goals.
They know that which produces qualities to be a friend and that which destroys qualities to be an enemy;
O Goddess, the buttocks are called *chit* and *sphijau*, and the sight is proclaimed as the eye (*cakṣuḥ*). SvaT 15.14.
The ten teeth are to be known as the fragments; the abdomen is remembered as the support.
The heart is called the secret place; indeed, know the hard part to be the bone.
One should know that fat is *vasā*; marrow is remembered as that which produces nourishment (*puṣṭikara*);
know that excrement is *vidūṣikā*, and urine is here called *snāva*.
They know the flower *kāleyaka* to be smoke that bestows stability;
*melaka*, *saṅghāta*, and *putra* are remembered as *uddyotaka*.
The daughter is to be known as the one who gladdens; the agitated is indeed known as the moving.
The defiler is called the paramour; the drunk is indeed the one who salutes.
They say that what has been consumed is "attained" (prāpta), and what has been vomited is "transformed" (vikṛtīkṛta).
One should know that "corrupted" (dūṣita) refers to emaciation (karṣita); the wise understand "consent" (sammata) as the conventional agreement (samaya).
The elder should be known as the protector, while the goat is the youngest;
discipline is the activity of the body, and recitation is traditionally held to be the means of accomplishment.
The *homita* produces accomplishment; *vibhāga* is remembered as that which causes delight. They call *kadamba* a cluster, while *virala* is said to be unjoined.
The disciple is said to be Vimala, and his desire is proclaimed as Ājñā;
that which is the vision of the deity is known by the wise as being struck by the weapon.
A night-stalker is a cat, and clawed animals are tearers.
"Brought" (ānīta) should be understood as "flowing" (sārita), as well as "protected" (rakṣita) and "covered" (pihita).
That which touches the crest-lock (śikhā) should be designated as Śakti;
that which indicates the head should be designated as Bindu.
She who shows her forehead should designate Īśvara;
she who shows her palate is proclaimed by that [act] to be Rudra.
O virtuous one, one should show the tongue; that which does so should be designated as the Vidyā. It should be known that there are seventy million mantras belonging to her.
She who shows the uvula has Ananta shown by her;
she who touches the throat should indicate the principle of Time (kālatattva).
She who shows the heart-lotus should be designated as Puruṣa;
she who shows the navel should be designated as Prakṛti.
O beloved, if the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) were below that, there would be vision;
O Goddess, when it touches the secret [place], egoity (ahaṃkāra) is the presiding deity.
She who displays her hip indicates Vyoman; therein Dhavata is the presiding deity. O Goddess, she who displays her thighs should be designated as Pavana.
She who displays her knees is proclaimed as Tejas;
she who displays her shanks should be designated as Varuṇā.
O Goddess, O beloved, the body consisting of all the Vedas manifests itself for the practitioner who is engaged in worship,
fire-sacrifice, and recitation, and who is absorbed in meditation.
O beloved Mistress of the Gods, for one who is endowed with the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), who knows the divisions of time,
and who is possessed of ritual action, the Yoginīs grant boons.
O Goddess of the Gods, they show the great path endowed with various enjoyments, by going along which one attains the fruit [of the mountain], O Queen of the Mountain King.
O fair-faced one, the Śaktis were commanded by Bhairava [to bestow] various other accomplishments (siddhis), whether inferior, middling, or superior.
And those arising from other tantras will also accomplish [their aims], there is no doubt;
thus, O fair-faced one, has the *melaka* been briefly explained.
Through the yoga of constant practice, she offers her own sacrificial pap (caruka);
by consuming it, O Goddess, one becomes equal to the Lord of Heroes.
Therefore, O woman of excellent complexion, those of purified soul perform fire-offerings and recitation during meditation and worship; consequently, the practitioners of mantra attain success.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Svacchandatantra.
